edus.text: If Britain and France had made peace in 1811, the Napoleonic era would probably have ended very differently: not in a dramatic military collapse of Napoleon, but in a negotiated European order dominated by a still-powerful French Empire.
The most important consequence is that peace in 1811 would have removed the main source of pressure that kept the wider anti-French coalition alive.
Britain was Napoleon’s richest, most persistent enemy.
If London and Paris had settled their conflict, the wars on the Continent would likely have slowed,

and some of the events that actually destroyed Napoleon—especially the invasion of Russia and the great coalition war of 1813–1814—might never have happened, or would have happened in a much weaker form.
The first major effect would have been economic and maritime.
By 1811, both powers were exhausted by long war.
Britain was straining under trade disruption, high debt, and political pressure from merchants;
France was struggling to enforce the Continental System and alienating much of Europe in the process.
A peace settlement would likely have involved Britain recognizing much of Napoleon’s European settlement,
while France would abandon hopes of defeating Britain through commercial blockade.
Britain would remain the dominant naval and colonial power.
It probably would keep most of the overseas gains it had made,
because that was where its bargaining strength lay.
France, in turn, would keep its core continental empire and the political influence it had established over much of western and central Europe.
In other words, the likely compromise is British supremacy at sea and French supremacy on land.
That alone would have transformed European politics.
In the real timeline, Britain subsidized resistance to Napoleon across the Continent and kept pressure on him in Spain and Portugal.
If peace came in 1811, British financial and military support for the Peninsular War would likely end or sharply diminish.
That matters enormously.
The Peninsular War was one of Napoleon’s greatest drains on men, money, and prestige.
Without British armies under Wellington operating in Iberia, French control in Spain would probably remain troubled, but it would be far more sustainable.
Guerrilla resistance would continue,
but Spain would be less likely to become the open wound that it was historically.
Portugal might be forced into accommodation with France or left in a neutralized position under British guarantee.
Either way, Napoleon would no longer be bleeding strength there on the same scale.
The Russian question is crucial.
Napoleon’s invasion of Russia in 1812 came in large part out of the breakdown of his continental system and his rivalry with Tsar Alexander I.
If Britain and France made peace in 1811, one of the central causes of Franco-Russian tension would weaken immediately,
because the continental blockade against British trade would lose much of its purpose.
That does not mean France and Russia would become friends.
Their rivalry over Poland, eastern Europe, and prestige would remain.
But Napoleon would have much less reason to launch the catastrophic invasion of 1812,
and Alexander would have less reason to posture as Europe’s liberator against French domination.
A cold peace or limited confrontation becomes more likely than the vast war that actually wrecked the Grande Armée.
If Napoleon avoids the Russian disaster, his regime becomes much more durable.
In 1811 he was still at the height of his power.
His armies had not yet been broken,
and his legitimacy had recently been strengthened by his marriage into the Austrian imperial family and the birth of an heir.
A peace with Britain at that moment could have frozen Europe in a Napoleonic shape for years, perhaps decades.
The Confederation of the Rhine, the Duchy of Warsaw, the Kingdom of Italy, and satellite monarchies in Spain, Naples, and elsewhere might have persisted, though not all equally securely.
Austria and Prussia, both weakened and cautious after earlier defeats, would probably have accepted the settlement at least for a time.
They might resent it,
but without British money and without a French disaster in Russia, they would be far less likely to risk another major war.
This does not mean Europe would become stable in a modern sense.
Napoleon’s empire had deep structural weaknesses.
It depended heavily on military prestige, family rule, coerced alliances, and constant intervention.
Nationalist resentment in Germany, Spain, and elsewhere would still exist.
French domination of Europe would remain unpopular.
Over time, any serious succession crisis, economic downturn, or major diplomatic quarrel could reopen the conflict.
But the timing would change.
Instead of Napoleon falling in 1814–1815, he might survive much longer and die on the throne,
leaving his son a chance—however uncertain—to inherit a Bonapartist continental bloc.
Britain, meanwhile, would likely emerge richer and more commercially secure in the medium term.
Freed from the immense cost of continental war, it could concentrate on trade, empire, and naval policing.
The end of war would also change domestic politics.
There might be less immediate pressure for military spending, less justification for wartime repression, and perhaps faster reintegration into global commerce.
But Britain would also have to accept a Europe closed off politically by French influence.
It would remain safe from invasion and globally powerful,
yet strategically frustrated by French dominance from the Channel to the Oder.
The biggest long-term implication is that the nineteenth century might lose its familiar post-1815 settlement.
No Congress of Vienna in the same form, no Bourbon restoration in France, no Waterloo as the symbolic end of the revolutionary and Napoleonic age.
The conservative international order associated with Metternich and Castlereagh would be much weaker or delayed.
Liberalism and nationalism might spread in a different pattern,
because Napoleonic institutions would remain embedded across much of Europe under French sponsorship rather than surviving as the mixed legacy of a defeated conqueror.
Germany and Italy might still unify later,
but under very different pressures and perhaps against a longer-lasting French hegemony.
So the clearest answer is this: peace in 1811 would most likely have preserved Napoleon’s empire rather than destroyed it.
Britain would keep the seas and its colonies;
France would keep most of continental Europe.
The Peninsular War would shrink,
the invasion of Russia might never happen,
and the coalition that eventually overthrew Napoleon would probably fail to form.
Europe would become a negotiated bipolar system—British maritime empire and French continental empire—at least for a generation,
with later conflict likely but no longer certain to end in Napoleon’s rapid collapse.

items.question: What If the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant?
human_answers: You are thinking of the Mongol's as a unified force which by this time is not exactly correct. Hulegu and the Ilkhanate were based in Iran (mostly) so the OTL force would not be interested in expanding in Eastern Europe. Batu / Berke and the Golden Horde started their drift towards Islam in this period but their control over the European fringe via their vassals in Kiev and Muscovy wasn't absolute and relied on the tolerance of their Orthodox faith. Any attack on Europe may well become religious in nature (which by itself is an interesting counterfactual) and I suspect any support from the Russian principalities would be lukewarm perhaps even moving towards outright rebellion. It would also be short lived given that the Mongol Civil War is coming. Biggest outcome if the Russian principalities do revolt could be a more Islamised Russia which would be a huge change for world history.

Is there any reason to assume that the forests of western europe were somehow “denser” than those of the eastern? Specifically, those of the Central Russia? BTW, it is not like the Mongols uniformly came from the open steppe: IIRC, Subotai came from Uryankay area which, AFAIK, mostly forests and mountains and he was doing quite well in the Russian forests and pretty much everywhere else. Of course, the Southern direction was much richer than the western one but #1 was the eastern one - China. AFAIK, the South ended up being problematic due to a limited feeding base for the horses but all theories about Mongolian conquest of the west are seemingly ignoring allocation of the resources. The western campaign (including Russia) presumably started with a big force but its second stage, Hungary and Poland, was on a much lesser scale. The map on the OP has “Ulus Jochi” and “Ulus Batu” as separate entities but this was not the case: Batu was a titular head of the Ulus of Jochi. Was there an interest in Mongolia in expanding Ulus Jochi even further at the expense of other endeavors (and other family members)? IMO, this is unlikely because China remained the main theater (BTW, Subotai was sent there after the european campaigns). Were there unlimited human resources? Hardly: part of Hulagu’s force were troops “lended” by Batu. So, with what would Batu conduct his european conquest and why would the Great Khan be interested in its continuation? Formally, the task as formulated by Genghis was fulfilled: the Kipchaks punished and subdued and “the last sea” (Adriatics would do) reached. Was Batu too interested? It does not look like this was a case because he had to create a brand new state from the scratch with the very limited resources (something like 5,000 Mongols).
items.original_question: What if the Mongol Empire had gone to Western Europe instead of the Levant? https://www.reddit.com/r/imaginarymaps/comments/pkb97x/what_if_the_mongols_invaded_europe_the_old_world A sudden interesting thought came to mind. What if, unlike in OTL, the Mongol Empire had not expanded into the Levant and had instead resumed its campaign into Europe? In this TL, during the reign of Möngke Khan, the Mongol Empire invaded Europe again instead of attacking the Abbasid Caliphate. Assume that, starting with the Kingdom of Hungary, they continue pushing westward into the Holy Roman Empire, France, and beyond Western Europe for as long as they keep winning. What I’m curious about is this: 1. What kind of POD would be needed for this to be possible? 2. To what extent would this actually be feasible? - Could the Mongol Empire conquer Western Europe as well, just as it did in Eastern Europe? - Or, unlike in Eastern Europe, would it struggle in Western Europe? 3. If this did happen, what changes would follow? - The Mongol Empire’s advance into Western Europe. - The survival of the Abbasid Caliphate.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise discipline and factional accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames which Mongol forces could plausibly redirect toward Western Europe instead of the Levant, accounting for mid-13th-century fragmentation among the Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, and Great Khanate rather than treating the Mongol Empire as a single unified actor.
criteria.1-2: Treats the Mongols as a fully unified empire and ignores the Levant-to-Europe substitution problem.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Mongol factions but misassigns motives, geography, or command structures in major ways.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some fragmentation, such as Batu/Berke versus Hulagu, but applies it inconsistently.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes Mongol polities and explains which faction could plausibly attack Europe and why.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the scenario in Mongol succession politics, Jochid-Ilkhanid rivalry, and Great Khan priorities while preserving the counterfactual premise.

criteria.name: Logistical and military feasibility in Western Europe
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains the practical constraints on a Mongol westward campaign, including manpower, horse fodder, distance from steppe bases, terrain, fortifications, and competing theaters such as China and Iran.
criteria.1-2: Assumes effortless conquest or impossible failure without discussing logistics or military conditions.
criteria.3-4: Gives generic claims about forests, castles, or cavalry but lacks connection to the actual Mongol operational situation.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several relevant constraints but underdevelops their causal effect on campaign scale and duration.
criteria.7-8: Explains how troop availability, remounts, fodder, fortifications, and distance would shape likely outcomes in Europe.
criteria.9-10: Integrates logistics with Mongol strategic allocation, showing why Western Europe might be raided, coerced, or partially conquered rather than uniformly overrun.

criteria.name: European and Rus' political-religious response
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the treatment of likely reactions by Russian principalities, Hungary, Poland, the Papacy, the Holy Roman Empire, and other European actors, especially whether a westward Mongol push becomes entangled with Orthodox, Catholic, and possibly Islamic alignments.
criteria.1-2: Ignores European and Rus' responses or portrays them as a single unified reaction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions resistance or crusading but with little attention to divisions among European powers or Rus' vassals.
criteria.5-6: Covers some actors, such as the Papacy or Russian princes, but misses key religious or vassalage dynamics.
criteria.7-8: Shows how Mongol demands could provoke Catholic coalitions, Orthodox ambivalence, Rus' rebellion, or opportunistic alliances.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced political-religious map, including Golden Horde Islamization pressures, Orthodox toleration, papal framing, and fragmented European incentives.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain and downstream consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how coherently the answer traces second- and third-order effects of a Mongol turn toward Western Europe, such as altered Crusades, delayed or accelerated Muscovy, changes in Golden Horde authority, papal politics, trade routes, state formation, and possible Islamization of parts of Rus'.
criteria.1-2: Lists isolated outcomes without causal links or long-range implications.
criteria.3-4: Provides a short chain of effects but jumps abruptly or relies on unsupported historical determinism.
criteria.5-6: Develops plausible medium-term effects but gives limited attention to broader Eurasian consequences.
criteria.7-8: Connects campaign choices to regional power shifts, religious developments, and state formation over decades.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent multi-decade chain linking Mongol internal politics, European responses, Rus' trajectories, Crusader states, and Eurasian trade or religious transformations.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly distinguishes plausible, speculative, and unlikely outcomes while avoiding contradictions with known constraints such as the Mongol Civil War, limited Jochid manpower, Hulagu’s Iranian base, and the priority of China.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but contradictory claims and ignores major historical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but still contains major inconsistencies or anachronistic assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible but occasionally overstates certainty or leaves tensions unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, flags uncertain branches, and maintains consistency with key Mongol and European constraints.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly compares plausible branches, explains why some outcomes are more likely than others, and avoids internal or historical contradictions throughout.

items.model_answer:
If the main thrust of Mongol expansion after the conquest of eastern Europe had been directed deep into Western Europe rather than turning toward the Levant and the Islamic world, the most likely result is that parts of Western Europe would have suffered devastating short-term destruction, but long-term Mongol rule there would probably have been shallow and unstable.

In the short run, the Mongols would have been a terrifying opponent. Their cavalry, mobility, intelligence gathering, and ability to exploit political divisions gave them major advantages over fragmented medieval states. Western Europe in the mid-thirteenth century was politically divided, and many rulers were often more concerned with rival Christians than with collective defense. If the Mongols had pressed west after their victories in Poland and Hungary, they might have defeated several field armies and perhaps forced kingdoms such as parts of Germany, Bohemia, northern Italy, or even France into tribute arrangements. Cities that resisted could have faced massacres similar to those seen elsewhere in Eurasia.

But Western Europe was not an easy environment for permanent Mongol domination. Its denser network of stone castles, fortified towns, forests, rivers, and wetter climate reduced some of the advantages of steppe cavalry. The farther west the Mongols moved, the more difficult supply, communication, and horse grazing became. Western Europe also had stronger urban institutions and more entrenched local elites than many steppe-border regions. So while the Mongols could likely win campaigns and terrorize large regions, ruling all of Western Europe directly would have been much harder than conquering open steppe or fragmented agrarian empires already accessible from Central Asia.

A plausible medium-term outcome is not full conquest of all Western Europe, but a pattern of raids, tribute extraction, and the temporary subordination of some kingdoms. The Holy Roman Empire, northern Italy, and perhaps France might have been forced into emergency alliances much earlier than they historically were. The papacy could have tried to frame resistance as a pan-Christian cause, perhaps accelerating ideas of common European defense. In that sense, a major Mongol invasion might paradoxically have pushed Western Europe toward greater political coordination.

The biggest global consequence would likely be in the eastern Mediterranean and the Islamic world. If Mongol attention had shifted west instead of south, the Mamluks in Egypt might have faced less pressure, and key events such as the Mongol-Mamluk struggle in Syria could have unfolded very differently or not at all. Baghdad had already fallen in 1258, but a reduced Mongol push into the Levant might have meant a stronger, more durable Mamluk-led Islamic eastern Mediterranean. That in turn could have affected trade routes, Crusader survival, and Byzantine politics.

For Western Europe itself, one important effect might have been military adaptation. European rulers would probably have learned faster from Mongol tactics, improving cavalry coordination, reconnaissance, communications, and perhaps the use of missile troops. Fortification systems would likely have expanded further. Taxation and state-building might also have accelerated, because resisting the Mongols required money, central authority, and mobilization on a large scale. So even if the Mongols did not remain, the shock of invasion could have strengthened some monarchies and weakened others.

There is also a chance that the demographic and economic damage could have been severe enough to delay parts of Western Europe’s later rise. Repeated sackings of major commercial centers in Italy, France, or the Rhineland might have disrupted trade, banking, and urban growth. If that destruction had been sustained, the later balance of power between Europe and the Islamic world could have shifted. But because Mongol control in the far west would likely have been difficult to maintain, Europe might eventually have recovered much as other invaded regions did.

So the best overall answer is this: a full Mongol turn into Western Europe could have produced a catastrophic generation of warfare, tribute, and political upheaval, but probably not a lasting Mongol Europe. The Mongols were capable of defeating western armies and devastating western kingdoms, yet the geography, fortifications, and logistical constraints of Western Europe make long-term domination less likely. The deeper legacy would probably have been a more militarized, more politically coordinated Western Europe, alongside a different balance of power in the eastern Mediterranean because the Levant would have faced less Mongol pressure.

items.question: What If Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop?
human_answers: I can easily see Quebec not wanting to be part of either France, or USA. So they'll opt for independence. France never really wanted it back, so they won't get into their own American Revolution. Even if they did, it is the cost that will impact the French Revolution. The cost will add to French woes. This notion that France will rise up in revolution because Quebec wants independence is erroneous. France wanted regime/gov't change, which is not at all what Quebec wants (independence). France will add Quebec to the list of grievances. That does NOT make Quebec the birthplace of this alt FR. There were various causes of the ARW. One of them was putting Ohio under Canadian jurisdiction. Plus the French and Indian War was fought over the Ohio Valley, and led to a lot of the grievances leading to ARW. No one considers Ohio the birthplace of the AR. Semantics? maybe, but I don't think so.

It is difficult to ascertain how the French in Canada felt, as they lived in a quasi-medieval subsistence economy. Although not under full-blown feudalism, their society was paternalistic, hierarchical, and agrarian. The Church and the seigneurs (many of the seigneuries were owned by religious orders) were the pillars of authority. This is crucial in explaining the lack of widespread revolutionary fervour. However, in the late eighteenth century, there remained a cultural and sentimental connection to France, particularly to the Ancien Régime and the monarchy. After the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, masses were said for them, and the French press in Quebec noted this. They were mourning the grandson of their last French sovereign, not celebrating the secular republic that executed him. In December 1778, from Boston, French Admiral d’Estaing called on the Canadiens to rise and rejoin their motherland, but this was difficult as Canada was where most British forces were stationed. It is unclear whether they wished to return to France, but the Continental Congress felt uneasy about the French returning to North America. Because the Canadiens were largely illiterate (literacy was still below 40% in 1850), it is difficult to say whether they were politically sophisticated, as the colony had been largely marginal and lacked a large merchant class under French rule. Education was not widespread and was largely controlled by seminaries or convents. It was even less politically sophisticated than the Spanish colonies in the Americas. My guess is that independence would have been the least likely of options, unless the Bishop of Quebec assumed the role of head of government.

Then the place will find a way to get out of American control ASAP. Mismatched expectations and all that because of a fundamental misreading by the Continental Army/Congress of the situation, particularly WRT the Quebec Act. The French never wanted to retain Canada après la Conquête because the sugar colonies in the Caribbean were far more valuable, plus lots of bad blood between the Canadiens and Versailles about which direction their part of New France should go. You'd basically be accelerating the French Revolution's TL but with a Canadien cause - and this time the British would come off as the good guys by allying with the habitants, whether or not it takes it back under its wing or accepts it as an independent country but under the British sphere of influence. And it finds a way to get out of the US ASAP, particularly if the initial military occupation goes as OTL and they basically alienated everyone. More probable than getting annexed by the US. Considering Quebec in this case would be a direct cause for the French Revolution ITTL, that's easy to remark on. While still predominantly Francophone (albeit with Canadian French given the same recognition as, say, Brazilian Portuguese), society and culture would take a more, say, Argentine or Uruguayan-like direction but w/ its own quirks (including probably far more indigenous influence) and probably different relationships among groups that would be relatively more egalitarian and opposed to reinstating the colonial relationship. Considering the British would still be next door viz. Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, as well as the HBC doing its thing, British influence would remain strong and that would include the cultural sphere, too.

It depends on how the Americans treat the Canadiens, and how they handle the Iroquois. If the Americans can't keep the Iroquois mostly neutral, and if they prevent them from trading with the Canadiens, then Quebec will want want to leave in a hurry. If the Americans could be deft in the administration of Quebec, better in battle, luckier with allied victories, and more skillful in peace negotiation I think there is a good chance that the Canadiens would want to be in a confederacy, or a customs union with a mutual defense pact. The centralizing reforms of the Constitution would likely have been opposed by the Canadiens as antifederalism, which brings me to the next point, though it is possible they could remain in the union if it transitions from Articles of Confederation to Constitution. While the Canadiens would most likely have forbade slavery, that doesn't mean they would have been abolitionists in the vein of the northeastern Calvinists and Quakers. While they could have been like the 1840s and 1850s Free Soilers, their antifederalism and relative lack of industrialization might have moved them into common cause with Southern states. The Canadiens also could have been aligned with the "Westerners" in looking for federally funded internal developments to help with their access to Atlantic ports, and their access to settling Upper Canada and Indiana/Illinois Territory. Being so close to Nova Scotia and Newfoundland the Canadiens could also be interested in a strong navy. So perhaps an American Quebec could be allied with someone like Calhoun. As for the issue of Loyalist Migration, their emigration would likely have been reduced if they didn't have British Upper Canada as a destination. Many of the Loyalists would have resigned themselves to life in the new government. There still would have been Loyalist emigration from both America and Lower Canada, and there would still be a movement of Loyalists to Upper Canada and other territories despite them being no longer British Empire owned. So those populations would have thrown a new political impulse into the country later especially after the Constitution is ratified.

I'd assume a French route with independence after the French revolution. Maybe some nobility or rich flee to Quebec during the revolution. I'd think US keeps what it would get otl plus Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward island. Ontario might go to the U.S. While Newfoundland and Labrador goes to Quebec. The American loyalists could be moved into western Canada to try to colonize Western Canada. England might be more harsh in dealing with the Oregon territory. You could see a war over it with Quebec siding with a side. Should U.S. Win they might get British Columbia in the treaty. Quebec might get islands in Nunavut. Russia in this timeline would probably favor selling Alaska to England. With more northern territory. I can see the South looking for more Mexican territory. There's a possibility the slave and free state addition could continue on longer. This causes a delay of the civil war potentially.
items.original_question: What if Americans capture Quebec in 1775. How does Quebec's culture & society develop? So having just watched a new video from Blue, it gave me an idea of dusting off an old topic I used to talk about In 1775, the Continental Army under Generals, Richard Montgomery, Daniel Morgan, James Livingston, and Benedict Arnold (Yes, that Benedict Arnold) marched north into Canada in an attempt to capture Quebec from the British and persuade the French Canadians in joining the revolution. It went well for part of the expedition at first, with Montgomery nearly capturing British Govenor Guy Carleton in Montreal. Meanwhile Arnold's part journeyed through the wilderness to get to Quebec City, which was very difficult. However, by the time the Americans gotten to Quebec, a snowstorm occurred and the battle turned into an utter disaster. Montgomery got killed, Arnold was wounded, smallpox plagued the Americans, the British suffered few causalities, and the Americans managed to alienate the Canadians. Meanwhile, Carleton received reinforcements and made a counter offensive that drove the Americans back to Fort Ticonderoga. For context, what if the Americans captured Quebec? Say Montgomery captured Govenor Guy Carleton and the Americans managed to catch Quebec City by surprise. In my previous thread about the fate of Quebec (Roughly around Lower Canada; Upper Canada is a whole other can of worms), there were four possibilities I gave, but we're going to talk about three: A) French route- The Americans offer Quebec back to France for support in their war, meaning France regains Quebec by the end of the war B) American route- The Americans annex Quebec, making Quebec part of the USA. C) Independent route- The Americans make Quebec into a sister republic, making Quebec independent by the end of the war. (There's no British route since that OTL) Now, I want to focus on one particular aspect of the fate of Quebec: Culture. If Quebec wasn't under the British/TTL Canada, what would culture be like for the French Canadians. Depending on the route we take, how would culture, society, art, cuisine, fashion, etc, develop for the French Canadians? In the French route, how would Quebec be affected by the French Revolution? In the American route, how would Quebec develop under the USA? In the Independent route, how would Quebec develop stuck between the British and Americans while having access to the St Lawrence?

items.model_answer:
If the Americans had captured Quebec in 1775 and held it, Quebec would probably still have remained overwhelmingly French-speaking and Catholic for a long time, but its political identity would have developed very differently. Instead of becoming the core of a British Canadian state, it would have been folded into the revolutionary world of the United States. That would not mean rapid assimilation into Anglo-America, though. In the late eighteenth century the American rebels were not in a strong position to replace Quebec’s population, religion, or legal customs overnight, and they would have had good reasons to conciliate the French Canadian majority.

The first big issue would have been religion and law. One of the main reasons the Continental Congress tried to win over Quebec in the first place was by promising liberties rather than forced cultural change. If the Americans had succeeded, they likely would have had to preserve Catholic worship, tolerate the Church, and probably leave much of French civil law and seigneurial landholding in place, at least temporarily. Otherwise they would have faced constant resistance from a population that was already wary of both British and American Protestants. So in the short run, Quebec might have resembled a more northern version of later Louisiana: politically attached to the United States, but socially and legally distinct.

That said, integration into the United States would still have changed Quebec’s trajectory in major ways. The American Revolution and the political culture that followed were less accepting of corporate privileges, aristocratic hierarchy, and established church influence than either old France or the British imperial settlement in Quebec. Over time, American state-building would likely have weakened the seigneurial system earlier, reduced the political power of the Catholic clergy, and promoted elected institutions more aggressively. Quebec society might therefore have become more republican and locally political earlier than it did under British rule, but not necessarily more culturally English at first.

Language would be the central long-term question. Under British Canada, French survived in large part because Quebec became the demographic and institutional center of French Canada. If Quebec became part of the United States, French would probably remain dominant locally for decades, especially in the countryside and parish life, but it would face stronger pressure from English over the nineteenth century. Migration from New England and New York into the St. Lawrence valley would likely be heavier than in actual history, especially after independence and westward expansion stabilized. American commercial networks, courts, newspapers, and politics would reward English. French would survive, but probably in a more regionally confined and defensive way, rather than as the language of a future province leading a bilingual federation.

This means Quebec’s culture might evolve into something like a large-scale northern analogue of Cajun or Creole Louisiana, though more populous and therefore more resilient. French Canadian identity would still exist, but perhaps less as the basis for a quasi-national project and more as an ethnic, regional, and religious identity inside the United States. Instead of becoming one of the “founding peoples” of Canada, French speakers in Quebec might become one of several major American minority cultures. Their institutions—schools, churches, local courts, presses—could still be substantial, but they would likely have to fight harder to preserve them against pressures for linguistic and civic standardization.

There is also the question of slavery, race, and continental politics. If Quebec joined the United States early, it would almost certainly enter as a free or gradually freeing region, since slavery there was limited and the climate and economy did not favor plantation development. That would place it in the northern political orbit. In the nineteenth century, a French Catholic Quebec inside the United States might become associated with northern anti-slavery politics, immigrant Catholic politics, and resistance to nativist Protestant movements. Its Catholics would likely face the same anti-Catholic suspicion that Irish and other Catholic groups later encountered, but because Quebec’s population was older, rooted, and regionally concentrated, it could respond with stronger local solidarity.

The biggest difference from real history is that there would probably be no Confederation in the form we know it, and no Quebec as the principal French-speaking province within Canada. Without British Quebec anchoring a northern empire, the rest of British North America might fragment, shrink, or reorganize around the Maritimes and the far interior. That matters because real Quebec’s culture was preserved not only by local stubbornness but by its constitutional place in Canada. Inside the United States, Quebec would lack that same kind of guaranteed national bargaining position. It might still keep its language and faith, but with less formal protection and more dependence on local majorities and state rights.

So the most likely outcome is not that Quebec becomes instantly “Americanized,” nor that it remains unchanged. Rather, it becomes a French-speaking, Catholic, increasingly republican society inside the early United States, preserving much of its local culture at first but gradually experiencing stronger assimilationist pressure than it did in Canada. By the late nineteenth or twentieth century, it would probably still be recognizably French in language, memory, and religion, but less institutionally secure, less nationally central, and more like a powerful regional minority culture than a coequal national one.

nodes.text: If the Americans had captured Quebec in 1775 and held it, Quebec would probably still have remained overwhelmingly French-speaking and Catholic for a long time,
but its political identity would have developed very differently.
Instead of becoming the core of a British Canadian state, it would have been folded into the revolutionary world of the United States.
That would not mean rapid assimilation into Anglo-America, though.
In the late eighteenth century the American rebels were not in a strong position to replace Quebec’s population, religion, or legal customs overnight,
and they would have had good reasons to conciliate the French Canadian majority.
The first big issue would have been religion and law.
One of the main reasons the Continental Congress tried to win over Quebec in the first place was by promising liberties rather than forced cultural change.

If the Americans had succeeded, they likely would have had to preserve Catholic worship, tolerate the Church, and probably leave much of French civil law and seigneurial landholding in place, at least temporarily.
Otherwise they would have faced constant resistance from a population that was already wary of both British and American Protestants.
So in the short run, Quebec might have resembled a more northern version of later Louisiana:
politically attached to the United States, but socially and legally distinct.
That said, integration into the United States would still have changed Quebec’s trajectory in major ways.

The American Revolution and the political culture that followed were less accepting of corporate privileges, aristocratic hierarchy, and established church influence than either old France or the British imperial settlement in Quebec.
Over time, American state-building would likely have weakened the seigneurial system earlier, reduced the political power of the Catholic clergy, and promoted elected institutions more aggressively.
Quebec society might therefore have become more republican and locally political earlier than it did under British rule,
but not necessarily more culturally English at first.
Language would be the central long-term question.
Under British Canada, French survived in large part because Quebec became the demographic and institutional center of French Canada.
If Quebec became part of the United States, French would probably remain dominant locally for decades,
but it would face stronger pressure from English over the nineteenth century.
Migration from New England and New York into the St. Lawrence valley would likely be heavier than in actual history.
American commercial networks, courts, newspapers, and politics would reward English.
French would survive,
but probably in a more regionally confined and defensive way.
This means Quebec’s culture might evolve into something like a large-scale northern analogue of Cajun or Creole Louisiana.
French Canadian identity would still exist,
but perhaps less as the basis for a quasi-national project and more as an ethnic, regional, and religious identity inside the United States.
Instead of becoming one of the “founding peoples” of Canada, French speakers in Quebec might become one of several major American minority cultures.
Their institutions could still be substantial,
but they would likely have to fight harder to preserve them.
There is also the question of slavery, race, and continental politics.
If Quebec joined the United States early, it would almost certainly enter as a free or gradually freeing region.
That would place it in the northern political orbit.

In the nineteenth century, a French Catholic Quebec inside the United States might become associated with northern anti-slavery politics, immigrant Catholic politics, and resistance to nativist Protestant movements.
Its Catholics would likely face the same anti-Catholic suspicion that Irish and other Catholic groups later encountered,
but because Quebec’s population was older, rooted, and regionally concentrated, it could respond with stronger local solidarity.
The biggest difference from real history is that there would probably be no Confederation in the form we know it, and no Quebec as the principal French-speaking province within Canada.
Without British Quebec anchoring a northern empire, the rest of British North America might fragment, shrink, or reorganize.
That matters because real Quebec’s culture was preserved not only by local stubbornness but by its constitutional place in Canada.
Inside the United States, Quebec would lack that same kind of guaranteed national bargaining position.
It might still keep its language and faith,
but with less formal protection and more dependence on local majorities and state rights.
So the most likely outcome is not that Quebec becomes instantly “Americanized,” nor that it remains unchanged.
Rather, it becomes a French-speaking, Catholic, increasingly republican society inside the early United States,
preserving much of its local culture at first but gradually experiencing stronger assimilationist pressure than it did in Canada.
By the late nineteenth or twentieth century, it would probably still be recognizably French in language, memory, and religion,
but less institutionally secure, less nationally central, and more like a powerful regional minority culture than a coequal national one.

items.question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed?
human_answers: With this POD, Spain and, especially, France may have a very different trajectory from 1776. Both have been looking for a way to get back at Britain for the disastrous 7YW. ARW provided that way, OTL. That involvement did 2 things (more than that, but)...it waylaid the slow progress Spain was making up the Pacific Coast, and most importantly, helped set the stage for the French Revolution. There will be another war. Maybe the WoBavarian Succession spins out of control. Maybe Britain decides to assist Portugal in its struggles against Spain in mid-late 1770s, and this spins out of control. Maybe one or the other leaves the path to the French Revolution still on track. Or, maybe the wars are delayed, and FR as we know it is butterflied. That is beyond BIG. And, this all assumes that the colonies remain at peace, not rising up for round 2, or 3. During the Nootka Crisis, Spain looked to France for assistance, which it didn't get because of the FR. Plus, throughout the 18th century, France didn't go to Spain's aid, but, rather, expected it to be the other way around. I wouldn't count on France backing Spain in the Nootka Crisis, even if there was no FR. If left by its lonesome, Spain likely backs down as OTL. Or maybe Spain has used the decade or 2 of peace to continue settling the Pacific north coast.

I guess if England would have kept the economically important and more or less developed 13C it would have a smaller interest in Notka/Oregon/access to the pacific. If the ARW ends in 1775/1776 then yes, Spain would have had more time and resources to actually colonize Notka. To be honest, I never understood why so many people believe that with a failed ARW, the French R. simply never happens. France was still economically and politically and socially in a bad situation. So yeah, I think the FR still would have happened. Maybe sooner or later (most likely a bit later) and maybe less bloody, but IMO it still would have happened nonetheless. And yeah, France and Spain still would have tried to get revenge on England. How realistic is that if the ARW ends in 1775/1776? I mean the whole American mythos of Americans rising up against the british crown is not that true. A lot of American colonists were loyal to the crown. Its not that every peasant in the 13C rose up against George III and with that rebellion or uprising put down quickly, I think the motivation for another rebellion would be low. How realistic is a peaceful solution to the pacific question? So England keeps the 13C and let's say that that James Cook dies earlier so there is no English expedition at the pacific coast and England has less information and is less interested in these regions. And if Spain has more time, money to colonize Notka could England have decided to just let Spain have it?
items.original_question: Administration of British colonies in North America if the USA would have never existed? I have seen several maps of North America in alternate history scenarios where the 13 colonies lost in 1775/1776. IF England would have won, how would they have administered their colonies in North America afterwards in the late 18th, the 19th, and the 20th century? Would they have administered their colonies separately (Pensilvania, Massachusetts, Newfoundland, Quebec, "Canada?", Florida, Louisiana, Oregon etc.) or would they have united them sooner or later in a big north american british dominion? Also, would they have eventually taken oregon/nootka? what about louisiana and alaska from france and russia respectively? PS: Yes I know there are a lot of "What if the US lost the war of 1776..." threads here but this is mostly about the administration of these colonies

items.model_answer:
If the United States had never come into existence, the British colonies in North America would probably have remained under British imperial administration at first, but they would not likely have stayed forever as tightly controlled colonies. The most plausible long-term outcome is that they would have evolved into something like Canada, Australia, or New Zealand: self-governing British dominions within the Empire, and eventually independent states or a federated North American dominion.

In the short term, administration would have continued through the British system already in place before independence. London governed through the Crown, the Board of Trade, colonial governors, and local assemblies. Each colony had its own charter, governor or lieutenant governor, courts, and elected assembly, but ultimate authority rested with Parliament and the Crown. Britain had already been trying after the Seven Years’ War to tighten imperial control, raise revenue, station troops, and regulate westward expansion. If no American break had occurred, this central oversight likely would have continued for some time, though Britain would probably have had to compromise more with colonial elites to keep the colonies stable.

Over time, the colonies would likely have gained more internal self-government. The British Empire in the nineteenth century increasingly shifted toward granting settler colonies control over domestic affairs while Britain retained authority over foreign policy, defense, and constitutional matters. In that scenario, the mainland colonies might have followed a path similar to British North America after 1776: provincial governments first, then perhaps regional unions, and eventually a larger federation. A single “British North America” stretching far beyond historical Canada is conceivable, though not guaranteed; regional divisions between New England, the Middle Colonies, the South, and the frontier might also have produced multiple dominions rather than one.

Slavery would have made administration especially complicated. Since Britain abolished slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s, a British North America that still included the southern mainland colonies would almost certainly have faced imperial emancipation. That could have caused major political conflict, perhaps even rebellion by slaveholding colonies, and might have led to some kind of restructuring or separation within British North America. So even if the USA never existed, the mainland colonies might not have remained one unified political unit.

Westward expansion would also have been different. Britain had tried to limit settlement beyond the Appalachians in 1763, partly to reduce conflict with Indigenous nations. Without an independent United States pushing aggressively westward as it did historically, expansion may have been slower, more negotiated, and more directly shaped by imperial strategy. But it would still probably have happened eventually, especially given settler population growth and imperial rivalry with Spain, France, and later Russia in North America.

By the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, the most likely administrative form would have been a dominion or a set of dominions under the British Crown, with responsible parliamentary government modeled on Westminster. In the very long run, these entities would probably have become fully sovereign, as Canada did, while perhaps retaining the monarch as head of state for some time.

So the simplest answer is: if the USA had never existed, Britain would probably not have ruled the North American colonies forever as old-style colonies. They would most likely have moved from crown-and-parliament administration, to self-governing dominions within the British Empire, and eventually to independence, either as one large federated British North American state or as several successor states.

edus.text: If the United States had never come into existence, the British colonies in North America would probably have remained under British imperial administration at first,
but they would not likely have stayed forever as tightly controlled colonies.
The most plausible long-term outcome is that they would have evolved into something like Canada, Australia, or New Zealand:
self-governing British dominions within the Empire,
and eventually independent states or a federated North American dominion.
In the short term, administration would have continued through the British system already in place before independence.
London governed through the Crown, the Board of Trade, colonial governors, and local assemblies.
Each colony had its own charter, governor or lieutenant governor, courts, and elected assembly,
but ultimate authority rested with Parliament and the Crown.
Britain had already been trying after the Seven Years’ War to tighten imperial control, raise revenue, station troops, and regulate westward expansion.
If no American break had occurred, this central oversight likely would have continued for some time,
though Britain would probably have had to compromise more with colonial elites to keep the colonies stable.
Over time, the colonies would likely have gained more internal self-government.

The British Empire in the nineteenth century increasingly shifted toward granting settler colonies control over domestic affairs while Britain retained authority over foreign policy, defense, and constitutional matters.
In that scenario, the mainland colonies might have followed a path similar to British North America after 1776:
provincial governments first,
then perhaps regional unions,
and eventually a larger federation.
A single “British North America” stretching far beyond historical Canada is conceivable, though not guaranteed;
regional divisions between New England, the Middle Colonies, the South, and the frontier might also have produced multiple dominions rather than one.
Slavery would have made administration especially complicated.
Since Britain abolished slavery in most of its empire in the 1830s, a British North America that still included the southern mainland colonies would almost certainly have faced imperial emancipation.
That could have caused major political conflict, perhaps even rebellion by slaveholding colonies,
and might have led to some kind of restructuring or separation within British North America.
So even if the USA never existed, the mainland colonies might not have remained one unified political unit.
Westward expansion would also have been different.
Britain had tried to limit settlement beyond the Appalachians in 1763, partly to reduce conflict with Indigenous nations.
Without an independent United States pushing aggressively westward as it did historically, expansion may have been slower, more negotiated, and more directly shaped by imperial strategy.
But it would still probably have happened eventually,
especially given settler population growth and imperial rivalry with Spain, France, and later Russia in North America.

By the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, the most likely administrative form would have been a dominion or a set of dominions under the British Crown, with responsible parliamentary government modeled on Westminster.
In the very long run, these entities would probably have become fully sovereign, as Canada did,
while perhaps retaining the monarch as head of state for some time.
So the simplest answer is: if the USA had never existed, Britain would probably not have ruled the North American colonies forever as old-style colonies.
They would most likely have moved from crown-and-parliament administration, to self-governing dominions within the British Empire, and eventually to independence,
either as one large federated British North American state or as several successor states.

items.question: What If the Southern Ming had survived?
human_answers: I foresee a successful Chinese expedition to retake the North within a decade or two. Sichuan was perhaps ironically where the most effective anti-Qing forces were based in OTL. Remnants of Zhang Xianzhong and Li Zicheng’s forces continued fighting there for decades until well into Kangxi’s reign IOTL. The site saw repeated struggles between different forces for many decades. It’s actually the reason for the significant decline in the population of Sichuan IOTL, not Zhang Xianzhong’s Sichuan massacre. Population wise, the Qing Dynasty would have difficulty regrowing the population of the north due to lack of food. The North has always been a basket case since the end of the Northern Song Dynasty. During the Ming Dynasty, Southern China had at least two times the population of the North. And that is before the collapse of the Ming Dynasty Which saw massive fighting. You see plenty of areas throughout Northern China eating rice as staples today, but the truth was that this is evidence for how much northerners have come to rely on Southern grain. Rice does not grow in the North, and has to be imported from the South. Before the Sui-Tang Dynasties when the Grand Canal was not built, Northern diet was based on wheat. Still is to a lesser extent today. After this period, they became increasingly reliant on Southern crops until from the Ming Dynasty onwards, they became entirely reliant on it. Northern Qing can’t just regrow when they don’t even have the rice to feed the people. As time goes on, even by the 17th century, warfare is gonna increasingly dependant upon firearms, meaning population,technology and economy is gonna become decisive in eventual Southern victory. Individual prowess of the troops that the Manchus relied heavily on will become less relevant,especially as the Qing simply does not have Manchu population to supply large armies to both stamp out rebellions or to fight the Southern dynasty. The Manchus iotl exploited a critical window before that was gonna be a problem to conquer the South.

This is what I have in mind: 1. In OTL, as I understand it, by this point the Ming dynasty’s North China had been devastated, the population had grown unevenly, and the state had come to depend heavily on Jiangnan’s grain resources. In that situation, if the Qing were to occupy only North China while the Ming retained control of Jiangnan, the Qing would likely suffer from serious food shortages. Under such conditions, I think it is highly likely that the Qing would resort to massacres in North China similar to the Yangzhou massacre seen in OTL. However, in the end, the Qing might later face the problem of overpopulation once again. Personally, when it comes to the Malthusian trap, I think the Northern Qing would suffer from it more severely than the Southern Ming. What do you think? 2. In OTL, the Dzungars were destroyed by Qing expeditions. However, in this timeline, the Dzungars would likely expand their power significantly across Mongolia and Tibet. Unlike in OTL, the Qing would probably remain largely on the defensive. As a result, the Dzungars would not be destroyed and would likely enjoy a substantial imperial existence until they were eventually conquered by the Russian Empire. Russia, too, would likely push into Manchuria more frequently and more deeply than it did in OTL. The Qing would have a much harder time containing them and would probably have to request military assistance from Joseon more often than in OTL . It is even possible that, unlike the Treaty of Nerchinsk, Russia might succeed in extracting territorial gains much deeper inside the region. And here is the next question. In your view, assuming that the Southern Ming and the Northern Qing both survived until the mid-18th century, which state do you think would collapse first? And in what ways do you think each polity would face its respective crises? First of all, in OTL, the course of the Yellow River changed in the 1850s. This could also have significant effects on China.

Why do you say they will sinicise faster? By contrast, I think they’d sinicise even slower, as they can’t hope to match the southern Ming in chineseness and so would have to rely on other pillars of legitimacy to prop up their rule, perhaps leaning further into Tibetan Buddhism. Edit- looking more into how Tibetan Buddhism had spread so deeply into Mongol society in the late 16th century, people seem to say that the Qing need to appeal to Taoist and Confucian ideologies meant they could not be called a primarily Buddhist state. Ittl, I think the Qing would lean much more heavily into buddhist kingship, and this might also make their policy towards Han people less racist- there would be a way for Han people to politically abandon the Confucian-Taoist kingship embodied by the Ming, by adopting Tibetan Buddhism, which would make them part of the ruling group without becoming Manchu. Why do you say it didn’t happen in India? As an aside, there was a mid 17th century equivalent to the treaty of Westphalia in Central Asia, the Great Code of 1640, by which various Oirat and Mongol clans agreed to act as a collective body to uphold general peace and a universal legal code, while upholding the sovereignty of the individual tribes. Otl, it became irrelevant once the Qing got rid of any form of Mongol sovereignty by defeating the Dzunghars and winning the Khalkha Mongols to their cause, but in a world where the Qing aren’t so powerful, the “Holy Mongol Empire” likely maintains its constitutional structure for longer. Instead of a Dzunghar khanate, we’d therefore talk Ming China allying with the Western Yuan Dynasty to hold back the Qing, and perhaps the federal Yuan would be more successful than the Dzunghar were otl in their wars against the Kazakhs/the Khanates of Bukhara. Or perhaps, the Qing end up functioning as the Austria analogue- personally controlling by far the most land and people, but still unable to strip away the autonomy of the various Mongol and oirat ulus’, who regularly meet and would all revolt against imperial overreach.
items.original_question: If the Southern Ming had survived? Thread 'Perpetual Brightness: Surviving Southern Ming' Apr 12, 2006 Once, the Confucian school outside Quanzhou had bustled with students and scholars. Some of China’s greatest administrators had come from there, and in its day the school had been a center of learning. But since the famines, and the Manchu invasion, the school had grown quiet. The buildings were dilapidated, with peeling paint and rotten timber. There was only one man there, in the dark of night, standing by a fire. The man watched as the flames cast a red glow over the temple, as it consumed the robes of a scholar. An Empire was collapsing outside its walls, but inside the silence was... Faeelin Replies: 168 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: Before 1900 In OTL, after an empire collapsed in China, there were many cases where it was not completely destroyed and replaced by another empire, but instead split into northern and southern regimes. Even before the Qing dynasty, the Jurchen states themselves formed a northern empire, while the Southern Song continued to exist in the south. In the 17th century, the Ming dynasty, like the Song before it, also established the Southern Ming. However, it ultimately fell after only twenty years. Was there no way for the Southern Ming to survive? The problems of the Southern Ming, as I see them, are as follows. 1. In the case of the Southern Song, all other imperial claimants were captured by the Jurchens, and as a result, a person low in the line of succession became the only remaining claimant. This, paradoxically, allowed him to secure a certain degree of legitimacy and take power. By contrast, the Southern Ming began in a situation where the legitimate imperial princes had largely been captured from the outset, while there were still too many lower-ranking imperial relatives remaining. This excess of potential claimants triggered disputes over the imperial succession. 2. In the case of the Jin dynasty, it had not yet fully subdued the Western Xia or the Mongols. In particular, the Mongols were later unified by Genghis Khan, who went on to establish the most powerful nomadic empire in history. At the time, the Goryeo dynasty was nominally a tributary state of the Jin, but it had not been decisively subdued through war. The Jin lacked the capacity to invade Goryeo and had no choice but to settle for maintaining relatively moderate relations. In other words, the Jin dynasty could not devote all of its national strength to the conquest of the Southern Song. By contrast, the Qing dynasty had already conquered the Chahar Mongols and had invaded the capital of the Joseon dynasty, forcing it into clear submission. Although the Dzungars and Russia would later enter the Chinese arena, this occurred only after the game had effectively already been decided. 3. The Southern Song was able to survive thanks to outstanding generals such as Yue Fei and Han Shizhong, who successfully defeated the Jurchen armies. By contrast, on the eve of the Ming dynasty’s collapse, Wu Sangui’s forces—virtually the only remaining elite army—defected outright to the Qing side. As a result, the Southern Ming was forced to struggle on with inadequate military strength, trapped in a situation where incompetent warlords fought among themselves in constant internal conflict. Taking these factors into account, I think that for the Southern Ming to have survived for a long time, things would have had to be different from the very beginning. “Before the fall of Beijing, the Chongzhen Emperor decides to transfer the capital to Nanjing. Abandoning Beijing, he withdraws south, and Wu Sangui’s army joins the emperor’s entourage and moves to Nanjing as well.” In effect, this would mean that the Chongzhen Emperor is “ceding North China to the Jurchens,” but even so, the southern regions would be far more securely preserved. However, he did not do so. The reasons lie here. In short, he was an “indecisive and irresolute emperor,” and as a result, instead of taking responsibility for such a momentous decision, he merely kept postponing it. What I am curious about is this: 1. If the Chongzhen Emperor were to decide on relocating the capital, what kind of POD (point of divergence) would need to occur? 2. If the Southern Ming had survived at least until the 19th century, how would East Asian history from the 17th to the 19th centuries have changed? Assuming the Southern Ming succeeded in repelling the initial Qing offensives, who would be in the more advantageous position thereafter? If the Southern Ming were to endure, how would Western powers in the 19th century approach China?

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Southern Ming had survived?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Initial Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer anchors its reasoning in a plausible survival scenario for the Southern Ming and correctly handles the 1640s balance among Southern Ming, Qing, Ming loyalists, rebels, Jiangnan, Sichuan, Manchuria, Mongolia, and frontier actors.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or distorts the premise; treats the Ming as simply restored everywhere or the Qing as absent without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges a surviving Southern Ming but gives vague or historically weak starting conditions with major omissions.
criteria.5-6: Establishes a plausible north-south division but only partially accounts for regional military, fiscal, and demographic realities.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in credible 1640s conditions, including Jiangnan resources, Qing northern control, loyalist forces, and rebel remnants.
criteria.9-10: Defines a highly plausible survival path and carefully preserves the altered-but-recognizable constraints facing Southern Ming, Qing, rebels, Mongols, Joseon, Russia, and inland provinces.

criteria.name: Causal Mechanism Depth: Demography, Food, Fiscal Capacity, and Military Change
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the material mechanisms that would shape Southern Ming survival, especially southern grain, northern devastation, Grand Canal dependence, taxation, manpower, firearms, logistics, and Qing limitations.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported claims of inevitable victory or collapse with little mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions factors such as population or food but does not connect them convincingly to state capacity or military outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Explains some key mechanisms, such as Jiangnan wealth or northern shortages, but leaves major causal links underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Shows how grain flows, taxation, manpower, firearms, logistics, and Manchu demographic limits would affect the Ming-Qing struggle over decades.
criteria.9-10: Integrates economic, demographic, ecological, fiscal, and military mechanisms into a coherent explanation of why either Southern Ming recovery, Qing entrenchment, or durable partition is plausible.

criteria.name: Long-Range Geopolitical and Cultural Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects beyond the immediate Ming-Qing conflict, including Mongolia, Tibet, Dzungars/Oirats, Russia, Joseon, Manchuria, legitimacy strategies, Sinicization, Buddhist kingship, and possible treaty/frontier changes.
criteria.1-2: Discusses only a short civil-war outcome and ignores wider Eurasian and cultural consequences.
criteria.3-4: Adds a few external actors but treats them as disconnected side notes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several downstream effects, such as Dzungar survival or Russian pressure, but with limited causal integration.
criteria.7-8: Connects Southern Ming survival to Qing frontier weakness, Mongol/Oirat politics, Tibetan Buddhism, Joseon, Russia, and altered legitimacy strategies.
criteria.9-10: Provides a broad, well-linked long-range map of East and Inner Asian consequences, including frontier diplomacy, religious-political identity, Mongol autonomy, Russian expansion, and altered Qing or Ming state formation.

criteria.name: Temporal Chain Coherence and Path Dependence
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer builds a plausible sequence from the 1640s through later crises instead of jumping to conclusions, while accounting for feedback loops, windows of opportunity, and changing constraints over time.
criteria.1-2: Presents an arbitrary endpoint with no chronological chain.
criteria.3-4: Uses a loose timeline but with large unexplained leaps or reversed causality.
criteria.5-6: Gives a broadly sequential account but misses important feedbacks between war, taxation, famine, legitimacy, and frontier pressure.
criteria.7-8: Develops a credible multi-decade chain showing how early survival changes later military, fiscal, demographic, and diplomatic options.
criteria.9-10: Constructs a rigorous long-range trajectory with path-dependent turning points, plausible contingency, and changing incentives for Ming, Qing, rebels, and frontier states.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Plausibility, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids deterministic overreach, acknowledges competing plausible outcomes, and remains internally consistent about Southern Ming strength, Qing weakness, Sinicization, legitimacy, and external pressures.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute claims, contradicts itself, or asserts implausible outcomes without caveats.
criteria.3-4: Shows some uncertainty but still contains major contradictions or one-sided determinism.
criteria.5-6: Offers plausible outcomes with limited caveats, though some tensions or unsupported assumptions remain.
criteria.7-8: Balances several plausible trajectories, flags uncertainties, and maintains consistency across military, cultural, and geopolitical claims.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; tests counterarguments; and avoids contradictions while preserving a nuanced open-ended forecast.

items.model_answer:
If the Southern Ming had survived, the most plausible result is not a simple “China stays the same but without the Qing,” but a very different early modern East Asia in which China remained a Han-ruled, maritime-facing, fiscally strained empire that probably survived only by reforming more than the late Ming ever had.

The first question is what “survived” means. If the Southern Ming merely held on in the far south for a while, then it would likely have become a reduced regional state, perhaps centered on the lower Yangzi, Fujian, Guangdong, or the southwest, coexisting uneasily with a Qing north. But if we mean that it successfully resisted the Manchus and reestablished control over most of China, then the long-term consequences would have been much larger.

In that stronger scenario, the biggest immediate difference is political legitimacy. The Qing solved the dynastic crisis by conquering China and then building a durable imperial order that combined Manchu military power with Confucian statecraft. A surviving Southern Ming would instead have had to restore legitimacy after catastrophic collapse. That would likely require punishing factionalism, rebuilding central authority, and finding a way to reconcile scholar-official elites, regional commanders, and powerful merchants. In other words, the dynasty would survive only if it became less like the late Ming in its final decades. A restored Southern Ming probably would have been more militarized, more dependent on regional armies and naval forces, and more willing to tolerate practical reforms in taxation, defense, and trade.

That matters because the late Ming state had serious structural weaknesses: fiscal shortfalls, elite tax evasion, military decay, and intense court factionalism. The Qing inherited these problems but also benefited from conquest institutions and a relatively disciplined ruling coalition. The Southern Ming did not have that advantage. So survival would probably mean a more reformist and less ideologically rigid regime than the pre-1644 Ming. It might have strengthened coastal defense, integrated maritime commerce into state revenue, and worked more closely with powerful southeast commercial networks.

This leads to one of the clearest counterfactual effects: maritime policy. The Qing, especially in the early decades, imposed severe coastal evacuations and restrictions because of anti-Qing resistance such as Zheng Chenggong’s movement on Taiwan. A surviving Southern Ming would have had every reason to do the opposite. It would probably have leaned heavily on naval power, overseas Chinese merchant networks, and customs revenue. That could have produced a more outward-looking state, especially in Fujian and Guangdong, and perhaps a stronger official engagement with trade in Southeast Asia, Japan, and European merchants. China might not have become “modern” early in any simple sense, but its political economy could have been more commercially integrated and sea-oriented than under the early Qing.

Taiwan would also likely have developed differently. Under a surviving Southern Ming, the Zheng regime might have remained not as an anti-dynastic refuge but as a strategic maritime base within a broader Ming restoration. Taiwan might have been incorporated earlier and more deliberately into a Chinese imperial system, perhaps as a naval frontier rather than as a marginal prefecture. That could have shifted the island’s demographic and political development significantly.

Another major difference concerns Inner Asia. The Qing was not just a Chinese dynasty; it was also an Inner Asian empire. It conquered and governed Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang in ways that profoundly shaped the borders of modern China. A surviving Southern Ming would have had a much harder time doing this. The Ming lacked the Qing’s Manchu-Mongol political networks, banner institutions, and steppe legitimacy. So even if the Southern Ming recovered China proper, it is far from certain that it would have incorporated Xinjiang, Tibet, and Mongolia to the same degree. The map of modern China might therefore be much smaller or at least much looser in those frontier zones. This is probably the single biggest long-term geopolitical difference.

Relations with Europe would also change, but not necessarily in the simplistic direction of “better modernization.” The Southern Ming already existed in a world where Jesuits, silver trade, firearms, and maritime commerce were important. A surviving regime may have been more open to using European artillery specialists, merchants, and diplomatic intermediaries. It may also have been less inclined than the Qing to tightly regulate foreign contact in the early period. But openness to trade is not the same as industrialization or military revolution. The court would still be a Confucian agrarian empire with strong reasons to fear disorder and foreign influence. So one should expect selective engagement, not a sudden transformation into a naval-capitalist power.

Still, in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the absence of the Qing could matter a great deal. The Qing’s high-Qing prosperity and territorial expansion gave China great scale and prestige, but later the dynasty also became identified with ethnic tensions, frontier overstretch, and the challenge of ruling a huge multiethnic empire under mounting Western pressure. A Southern Ming China, if more compact and more maritime, might have faced a different set of nineteenth-century crises. It might have been more vulnerable at sea but less burdened by Inner Asian commitments. It might have had stronger merchant institutions and coastal militaries, which could have helped in confronting Western powers. On the other hand, if it remained fiscally weak and regionally fragmented, it might have succumbed even earlier to internal rebellion or foreign pressure.

Culturally, the consequences would be significant but subtler than people often assume. Many features commonly associated with “traditional China” in the West were shaped by the Qing, including hairstyle regulations like the queue, banner institutions, and certain forms of ethnic hierarchy. Without Qing rule, those features disappear or look very different. Elite culture might show more continuity with late Ming tastes: stronger urban commercial culture, literati individualism, and perhaps more visible links between high culture and merchant wealth. But Confucian orthodoxy, civil examinations, and gentry dominance would likely remain central unless the regime undertook unusually deep reforms.

So the most likely answer is this: if the Southern Ming had truly survived and restored itself, China would probably have remained a major unified empire, but one that was more Han-identified, more coastal and commercial, less successful in Inner Asian expansion, and forced into earlier military-fiscal reform. East Asia would be reshaped accordingly: Taiwan’s role would change, maritime trade might become more central, and the territorial foundations of modern China could be very different. The best-case version is a more adaptive, sea-oriented Ming revival. The worst-case version is a brittle, faction-ridden remnant state that survives temporarily but fails to match the Qing’s territorial and institutional achievements.

The Southern Ming did not have that advantage.

It conquered and governed Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang in ways that profoundly shaped the borders of modern China.
A surviving Southern Ming would have had a much harder time doing this.
The Ming lacked the Qing’s Manchu-Mongol political networks, banner institutions, and steppe legitimacy.

The Southern Ming already existed in a world where Jesuits, silver trade, firearms, and maritime commerce were important.

It may also have been less inclined than the Qing to tightly regulate foreign contact in the early period.

The court would still be a Confucian agrarian empire with strong reasons to fear disorder and foreign influence.
So one should expect selective engagement, not a sudden transformation into a naval-capitalist power.

but later the dynasty also became identified with ethnic tensions, frontier overstretch, and the challenge of ruling a huge multiethnic empire under mounting Western pressure.

It might have been more vulnerable at sea but less burdened by Inner Asian commitments.
It might have had stronger merchant institutions and coastal militaries, which could have helped in confronting Western powers.
On the other hand, if it remained fiscally weak and regionally fragmented,
it might have succumbed even earlier to internal rebellion or foreign pressure.
Culturally, the consequences would be significant but subtler than people often assume.

Without Qing rule, those features disappear or look very different.

The best-case version is a more adaptive, sea-oriented Ming revival.
The worst-case version is a brittle, faction-ridden remnant state that survives temporarily but fails to match the Qing’s territorial and institutional achievements.
