items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

criteria.5-6: Includes Austria, Spain, or the HRE but with shallow or one-sided analysis.
criteria.7-8: Considers Austria’s military limitations, possible Spanish expectations, divided German responses, and the diplomatic shock of partitioning Habsburg territory.
criteria.9-10: Shows nuanced interaction among Austrian vulnerability, Eugene’s aging military leadership, Spain’s uncertain alliance value, HRE mobilization limits, German state divisions, and possible Ottoman pressure on Austria’s eastern flank.

criteria.name: Military, Financial, and Logistical Causal Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer grounds its scenario in concrete 18th-century power mechanisms: armies, fortresses, finance, naval capacity, logistics, and alliance credibility.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported assertions about who wins without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions armies or money in generic terms without connecting them to outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some relevant factors such as British finance, French land power, Dutch forts, or Austrian weakness.
criteria.7-8: Connects military and financial capacities to likely bargaining, deterrence, campaign outcomes, and defensive lines in the Low Countries.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent mechanism-based assessment using naval supremacy, credit systems, fortress networks, supply lines, French land access, Dutch barrier defenses, and Austria’s multi-front constraints.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer develops plausible downstream consequences over decades while acknowledging uncertainty and avoiding internal contradictions or anachronism.
criteria.1-2: Gives an implausible or contradictory chain of events with little historical grounding.
criteria.3-4: Offers some consequences but they are abrupt, deterministic, or poorly linked to the premise.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short-term outcome and some longer-term effects, but with gaps or overconfidence.
criteria.7-8: Traces coherent effects on the balance of power, Anglo-French relations, Dutch security, Austrian strategy, and later European conflicts while noting uncertainties.
criteria.9-10: Builds a disciplined long-range causal chain showing how the partition could reshape Franco-Dutch borders, Habsburg priorities, British continental alliances, HRE politics, and future wars, with careful caveats and no major contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century, the consequences would likely have been significant for the balance of power in western Europe, for the later history of Belgium, and for the rivalry among Austria, France, Prussia, and the Dutch Republic.

The Austrian Netherlands roughly corresponded to most of present-day Belgium and Luxembourg. In the 18th century, it was a strategic buffer zone between France and the Dutch Republic and also an important outpost of Habsburg influence far from Vienna. A partition would most plausibly have happened during one of the major continental settlements, especially after the War of the Austrian Succession or during the diplomatic reshuffling associated with the French Revolutionary era. The exact outcome would depend on who divided it, but the most likely beneficiaries would have been France, the Dutch Republic, and perhaps Prussia or a German prince backed by Austria.

If France had annexed the western and more economically valuable provinces earlier in the century, it would have pushed its frontier northeastward and strengthened its position along the Scheldt and Meuse. That would have alarmed both Britain and the Dutch Republic, because one of their long-term strategic goals was to prevent France from controlling the Low Countries. A French gain there would probably have triggered stronger coalition politics against France and could even have accelerated British military involvement on the continent.

If the Dutch Republic had taken some northern portions or fortified lines, the main effect would have been defensive rather than expansionist. The Dutch wanted security more than territory. A partition favoring them might have created a broader Dutch barrier against France, but it would also have increased the Republic’s administrative and military burdens at a time when Dutch power was already in relative decline. So even if the Dutch gained territory, it might not have translated into long-term strength.

For Austria, losing the Austrian Netherlands in a partition would probably have been accepted only in exchange for compensation elsewhere, most likely in Germany or Italy. Vienna often regarded the territory as difficult to defend and geographically detached from its core lands. In that sense, partition might actually have fit Austrian strategic logic if it were compensated adequately. Austria might then have focused even more heavily on central and eastern Europe, reducing its involvement in the far west.

The most important long-term effect is that a partition would likely have prevented the later emergence of Belgium in the form it took in 1830. Belgian identity in the modern political sense was already complex and regionally divided; if the territory had been split among neighboring powers before the revolutionary era, there may never have been a single Belgian state created after the Napoleonic period. Instead, the region could have resembled Poland’s fate in another form: its provinces absorbed into larger states, with local identities surviving but without sovereign unity.

Economically, partition would have disrupted one of Europe’s most urbanized and commercially active regions. Different provinces had different legal traditions, fiscal systems, and trading links. Incorporation into France might have modernized administration in some areas, while attachment to the Dutch or German states might have preserved more local autonomy. The Scheldt question would have become even more politically sensitive, especially for Antwerp. If France controlled Antwerp, it could have developed into an even earlier strategic port against Britain. If the Dutch kept influence over access to the Scheldt, Antwerp’s revival might have remained blocked longer.

There would also have been cultural and political consequences. The Austrian Netherlands contained Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, along with strong provincial identities such as Brabant and Flanders. Partition could have hardened linguistic and political frontiers earlier than actually happened. Some Flemish areas might have been drawn more closely into a Dutch orbit, while Walloon areas might have been drawn more tightly into France. That, in turn, could have reduced the later tension inside a unified Belgian state simply because such a state might never have existed.

In a broad historical sense, an 18th-century partition of the Austrian Netherlands would probably have made western Europe less buffered and more polarized. The territory’s historical role was to sit between major powers. Once divided, that mediating space would disappear. France might become stronger and more threatening, Austria less western, and the Dutch more exposed or overextended. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 would then have had a very different problem to solve, and the Kingdom of the Netherlands or Belgium as later created might not have emerged at all.

So the short answer is that partition would likely have reshaped the western European state system: strengthening some neighbors in the short term, weakening Austria’s role in the Low Countries, and making the eventual creation of Belgium much less likely.

edus.text: If the Austrian Netherlands had been partitioned in the 18th century, the consequences would likely have been significant for the balance of power in western Europe, for the later history of Belgium, and for the rivalry among Austria, France, Prussia, and the Dutch Republic.
The Austrian Netherlands roughly corresponded to most of present-day Belgium and Luxembourg.
In the 18th century, it was a strategic buffer zone between France and the Dutch Republic and also an important outpost of Habsburg influence far from Vienna.

A partition would most plausibly have happened during one of the major continental settlements, especially after the War of the Austrian Succession or during the diplomatic reshuffling associated with the French Revolutionary era.
The exact outcome would depend on who divided it,
but the most likely beneficiaries would have been France, the Dutch Republic, and perhaps Prussia or a German prince backed by Austria.

If France had annexed the western and more economically valuable provinces earlier in the century, it would have pushed its frontier northeastward and strengthened its position along the Scheldt and Meuse.
That would have alarmed both Britain and the Dutch Republic,
because one of their long-term strategic goals was to prevent France from controlling the Low Countries.
A French gain there would probably have triggered stronger coalition politics against France
and could even have accelerated British military involvement on the continent.
If the Dutch Republic had taken some northern portions or fortified lines, the main effect would have been defensive rather than expansionist.
The Dutch wanted security more than territory.
A partition favoring them might have created a broader Dutch barrier against France,
but it would also have increased the Republic’s administrative and military burdens at a time when Dutch power was already in relative decline.
So even if the Dutch gained territory, it might not have translated into long-term strength.
For Austria, losing the Austrian Netherlands in a partition would probably have been accepted only in exchange for compensation elsewhere, most likely in Germany or Italy.
Vienna often regarded the territory as difficult to defend and geographically detached from its core lands.
In that sense, partition might actually have fit Austrian strategic logic if it were compensated adequately.
Austria might then have focused even more heavily on central and eastern Europe, reducing its involvement in the far west.
The most important long-term effect is that a partition would likely have prevented the later emergence of Belgium in the form it took in 1830.
Belgian identity in the modern political sense was already complex and regionally divided;
if the territory had been split among neighboring powers before the revolutionary era, there may never have been a single Belgian state created after the Napoleonic period.
Instead, the region could have resembled Poland’s fate in another form:
its provinces absorbed into larger states, with local identities surviving but without sovereign unity.
Economically, partition would have disrupted one of Europe’s most urbanized and commercially active regions.
Different provinces had different legal traditions, fiscal systems, and trading links.
Incorporation into France might have modernized administration in some areas,
while attachment to the Dutch or German states might have preserved more local autonomy.
The Scheldt question would have become even more politically sensitive, especially for Antwerp.
If France controlled Antwerp, it could have developed into an even earlier strategic port against Britain.
If the Dutch kept influence over access to the Scheldt, Antwerp’s revival might have remained blocked longer.
There would also have been cultural and political consequences.
The Austrian Netherlands contained Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, along with strong provincial identities such as Brabant and Flanders.
Partition could have hardened linguistic and political frontiers earlier than actually happened.
Some Flemish areas might have been drawn more closely into a Dutch orbit,
while Walloon areas might have been drawn more tightly into France.
That, in turn, could have reduced the later tension inside a unified Belgian state
simply because such a state might never have existed.
In a broad historical sense, an 18th-century partition of the Austrian Netherlands would probably have made western Europe less buffered and more polarized.
The territory’s historical role was to sit between major powers.
Once divided, that mediating space would disappear.
France might become stronger and more threatening, Austria less western, and the Dutch more exposed or overextended.
The Congress of Vienna in 1815 would then have had a very different problem to solve,
and the Kingdom of the Netherlands or Belgium as later created might not have emerged at all.
So the short answer is that partition would likely have reshaped the western European state system:
strengthening some neighbors in the short term,
weakening Austria’s role in the Low Countries,
and making the eventual creation of Belgium much less likely.

items.question: My Alternative History Scenario: What If Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799?
human_answers: It's very obscure and I couldn't track down the reference this morning, which I think came from some book on the First Serbian Uprising. The Turkish fortress on the island blocked easy communication between the Serbs and the Russian forces in Wallachia. Well, Russia sent an auxiliary force into Poland to aid Napoleon, as promised, and was rewarded with Tarnopol in the peace treaty. So it looks like a victory. But in reality as you say Russia did very little but go through the motions and Napoleon gave them the merest scrap of a reward. Despite the common view, I don't think Alexander ingratiated himself to Vienna by doing this and I don't think Austria would have been more active in 1812 had things been different in 1809. Fair enough. Austria was at least thought to be supplying weapons to the Sultan in 1829, though I don't know if that was confirmed to actually be true.

Why would Hapsburgs or Hohenzollerns circa 1803 care about the US? None of them had colonies in the Western hemisphere (or anywhere else) and, IIRC, at that time the former colonies were not ideologically, not to mention economically or militarily, of a any serious importance for the continental Europe. Which, putting aside Spain, leaves “certain trade arrangements” and the obvious question is what these arrangements would be? Would they hurt or benefit France? In OTL to a great degree the French bellicosity was supported by the strategic factor called “Bonaparte” who, besides military glory, provided looting (both on state and individual levels) on the “industrial” scale. It seems that ITTL French government behaves “Napoleonic” without Napoleon, which brings some obvious questions without clear answers to which episode with tearing the document looks as an act of imbecility. AFAIK, none of the OTL generals of that period were that good in both areas and without Bonaparte the war of 2nd coalition most probably would end due to the exhaustion of both sides without too much to show for it (in OTL in 1799 the French were kicked out of Italy and exercises on the Danube led to nowhere for either side so the only area of clear success was Switzerland). Which means that enthusiasm in France is unlikely and, in OTL the Directory was in almost permanent fiscal crisis. So, it would be quite interesting to find out in more details how the things were proceeding (including financial aspect) without Nappy? Were ITTL any indications of the Russian desire to conquer Hungary? Anyway, this was clearly not an consideration during the 2nd Coalition when Austria asked for the Russian help (at least in OTL). BTW, without Nappy, is Paul still on the throne? If yes, and if the 2nd Coalition ended along the OTL lines, the issue would be not Francis’ reluctance but Paul’s refusal to deal with a former ally who screwed him up. Alexander hated Napoleon on a personal level, which mostly defined his actions in the 3rd and 4th coalitions, but, while being pro-British, was not actively anti-French in general. Anyway, it does not look like he would be doing Francis’ bidding. Why not Greenland? The XVII - XVIII centuries coalition wars against the Ottomans demonstrated to the Russians that the Austrians are, at best, useless as the allies and impotent as the enemies. If Austria is at war with France, whoever is the Russian emperor, can start war with the OE without paying any attention to Vienna’s position. Besides, how would Russia simultaneously fight the French and the OE? Obviously, expecting that after the French war the Hapsburg emperor is going to honor his generous promise to grant Russia the Ottoman territories (how about the Ottoman consent?) assumes a rather unrealistic level of a naivety on the Russian side. Which is of no importance to Vienna and Berlin by the obvious reason: none of them has colonies in the Americas. Then, the US in the early 1800s as a serious military threat? In 1812 it had less than 10,000 troops when war started and its navy had 12 frigates. Yes, and the question is how an obvious idiot managed to become the head of the French government and how his actions got approval of the parliament?
items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

rubrics.question_focus: My Alternative History Scenario: What If Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799?

criteria.name: Point-of-divergence fidelity and immediate 1799 feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer treats the counterfactual premise precisely: Napoleon is unable to return from Egypt to France in 1799, and the immediate consequences follow from realistic naval, military, political, and communications conditions of that year.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or changes the premise, e.g. lets Napoleon return anyway or makes unrelated changes without justification.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges Napoleon’s absence but gives vague or implausible immediate effects with little attention to Egypt, Britain, or France in 1799.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short-term setup, including Napoleon’s isolation/capture/death and some effects on Egypt and France, but misses key constraints.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains how Napoleon fails to reach France and traces credible immediate effects on Egypt, the British, the Directory, and French morale.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the divergence in 1799 conditions and integrates naval interception, Egyptian campaign collapse, information delays, French politics, and coalition timing.

criteria.name: French domestic political trajectory without Brumaire
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer reasons through the fate of the Directory, possible alternative coups, republican institutions, generals, finances, public opinion, and the absence of Napoleon’s personal authority.
criteria.1-2: Assumes France simply follows the same Napoleonic path without Napoleon or gives no domestic political explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions instability in France but does not identify actors, institutions, fiscal crisis, or plausible alternatives to Napoleon.
criteria.5-6: Discusses the Directory, coup risk, and military politics, but relies on broad claims or underdeveloped mechanisms.
criteria.7-8: Explains credible alternatives such as Sieyès using another general, a continued Directory, Jacobin/royalist pressure, or military stalemate.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes factional politics, army patronage, fiscal exhaustion, legitimacy, and why any successor regime would or would not reproduce Bonapartist outcomes.

criteria.name: Second Coalition and military-diplomatic causality
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly models the 1799-1802 war without Napoleon’s return, especially Italy, Switzerland, the Danube, Austria, Britain, Russia, and the likelihood of peace or continued war.
criteria.1-2: Presents arbitrary victories or defeats with no relation to actual 1799 military and diplomatic conditions.
criteria.3-4: Names some coalition powers but gives simplistic outcomes, such as automatic French collapse or automatic French dominance.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that France was under pressure in Italy and Europe, but gives only partial causal links to coalition behavior.
criteria.7-8: Connects Napoleon’s absence to campaigns, coalition coordination problems, Austrian and Russian aims, British strategy, and peace prospects.
criteria.9-10: Balances French resilience with coalition limitations and gives a nuanced account of likely military stalemate, altered treaties, and divergent Austrian/Russian/British incentives.

criteria.name: Long-range European and global downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage and coherence of major downstream consequences after the immediate crisis, including whether the Napoleonic Wars, Holy Roman Empire, German and Italian reorganization, Spanish crisis, Louisiana, Britain, Russia, Austria, and Ottoman affairs change plausibly.
criteria.1-2: Provides little beyond 1799 or jumps to distant outcomes without causal bridges.
criteria.3-4: Lists some later differences but treats them as disconnected speculation.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major effects, such as no Empire or altered coalitions, but omits important knock-on consequences.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent medium- and long-term chain affecting France, Germany, Italy, Britain, Russia, Austria, Spain, and colonial affairs.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning across European institutions, nationalism, war finance, imperial reform, colonial policy, and Ottoman/Russian dynamics while preserving causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, plausibility, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradictions with the premise and known constraints; and does not overstate obscure or unsupported claims.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, anachronisms, or confident claims that violate the premise or basic historical facts.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but also unsupported leaps, internal inconsistencies, or overconfident deterministic conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with some uncertainty noted, but includes gaps or weakly justified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals uncertainty, explains assumptions, avoids deterministic overreach, and maintains internal consistency across the timeline.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates high-probability consequences from speculative branches, flags evidentiary limits, and rigorously checks all claims against the 1799 counterfactual logic.

items.model_answer:
If Napoleon could not return to France in 1799, the most likely outcome is that there would be no Coup of 18 Brumaire, no Consulate under Napoleon, and probably no Napoleonic Empire in the form we know. France would still likely move away from unstable revolutionary republicanism, but through a different strongman or military-political coalition. The broader result would be a weaker, less centralized France, a different balance of power in Europe, and a much less sweeping spread of Napoleonic legal and political reforms.

In the short term, the key issue is the condition of France in 1799. The Directory was unpopular, corrupt, and militarily strained. It was vulnerable to collapse even without Napoleon. His importance was that he provided a uniquely prestigious, politically useful, and publicly admired figure around whom plotters such as Sieyès could build a new regime. If Napoleon was stuck in Egypt, captured at sea, killed, or simply delayed too long, Sieyès would still probably seek a coup, but he would need another general. Jean Moreau would be an obvious candidate, and Jourdan or Bernadotte might also matter, though each had different political instincts and less personal magnetism. A coup could still happen, but it would probably be messier and less decisive.

That matters because Napoleon was not just a general available for use; he was unusually good at dominating allies, outmaneuvering rivals, and converting a provisional seizure of power into a durable personal regime. Without him, a post-Directory government might be more collective and more fragile. A revised constitution could emerge, perhaps creating a stronger executive and limiting democratic participation, but it might not so quickly become a personal dictatorship. France would likely still centralize state power, because the revolutionary decade had already pushed politics in that direction, yet the specific Napoleonic blend of authoritarianism, plebiscitary legitimacy, administrative efficiency, and military glory would be hard to replicate.

Militarily, the consequences could be enormous. In actual history Napoleon’s campaigns of 1800, especially Marengo, stabilized the new regime and restored French dominance over Austria. Without him, France would still have strong armies and capable generals, but victory would be less assured and less theatrically tied to one man. Moreau was a competent commander and might still win important battles, but he was not likely to found an empire from them. This means France might negotiate from a less dominant position. The War of the Second Coalition could end in compromise rather than in the unmistakable reassertion of French supremacy associated with Napoleon’s rise.

If France remains under a more collective authoritarian republic, peace with Britain might also look different. Napoleon’s personal ambition and strategic vision helped drive the renewed cycle of continental war after the brief Peace of Amiens. Another regime might be more cautious, more interested in consolidating the gains of the Revolution inside France and its satellite republics than in seeking continental hegemony. There would still be deep Anglo-French rivalry, so conflict would not disappear, but the scale and intensity of the Napoleonic Wars might never develop in the same way.

The internal development of France would also diverge. Some changes often associated with Napoleon were already broadly desired: administrative rationalization, reconciliation with parts of the old elite, financial stabilization, and an end to revolutionary chaos. So a non-Napoleonic government might still create a stronger bureaucracy, a national bank, and a more orderly tax system. But the Civil Code, the Concordat with the Church, the lycée system, and the prefectural structure might emerge more slowly, in altered form, or under different names. The legal unification of France and its export across Europe would be much less dramatic. The same is true of careers open to talent: some meritocratic features of the Revolution would survive, but they might be less consistently institutionalized.

For Europe as a whole, the biggest difference is that there may be no vast Napoleonic imperial expansion. Without Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, the Continental System, the Peninsular War, and the invasion of Russia, the old monarchies would face less existential shock. The Holy Roman Empire might survive longer, perhaps in weakened reforming form rather than being swept away in 1806. German and Italian nationalism would probably develop more slowly, because Napoleon both destroyed old structures and unintentionally stimulated national reaction against French domination. Prussia might reform less quickly without the humiliations of 1806. Russia would remain important, but without the patriotic myth of 1812 as we know it. Britain would still expand commercially and overseas, but in a Europe not dominated by one continental super-rival.

This also affects colonial history. Napoleon’s role in the Haitian Revolution and the sale of Louisiana were highly consequential. If he never returns to power, France might not mount the same large expedition to Saint-Domingue, or at least not under the same assumptions. Haitian independence might come earlier, or through a different diplomatic path. Louisiana might remain French somewhat longer, or be sold later under different conditions. That in turn could affect U.S. westward expansion, though the United States would still likely grow. A weaker or more cautious French regime might focus less on grand imperial restoration and more on European survival.

One should be careful, though, not to imagine that Napoleon alone created modern Europe. Many of the forces that empowered him were already present: state centralization, mass conscription, revolutionary ideology, and the collapse of old-regime legitimacy in France. If he does not return in 1799, France does not simply become peaceful and stable. It still faces factionalism, war, and pressure for a stronger executive. So the most plausible alternative is not “no authoritarian turn,” but “a different authoritarian turn.” France likely ends the Directory anyway, but under a less brilliant and less domineering ruler.

So the best concise answer is this: if Napoleon could not make it back to France in 1799, the Directory would probably still fall, but Napoleon’s specific seizure of power would not happen. France might be taken over by another general-backed regime, perhaps with Sieyès playing a larger role, yet it would likely be less stable, less militarily spectacular, and less personally dictatorial. Europe would probably avoid the full Napoleonic cycle of empire and total continental war. Revolutionary France would still matter greatly, but the map, laws, and political development of nineteenth-century Europe would be transformed more gradually and less violently.

edus.text: If Napoleon could not return to France in 1799, the most likely outcome is that there would be no Coup of 18 Brumaire, no Consulate under Napoleon, and probably no Napoleonic Empire in the form we know.
France would still likely move away from unstable revolutionary republicanism,
but through a different strongman or military-political coalition.
The broader result would be a weaker, less centralized France, a different balance of power in Europe, and a much less sweeping spread of Napoleonic legal and political reforms.
In the short term, the key issue is the condition of France in 1799.
The Directory was unpopular, corrupt, and militarily strained.
It was vulnerable to collapse even without Napoleon.
His importance was that he provided a uniquely prestigious, politically useful, and publicly admired figure around whom plotters such as Sieyès could build a new regime.
If Napoleon was stuck in Egypt, captured at sea, killed, or simply delayed too long,
Sieyès would still probably seek a coup,
but he would need another general.
Jean Moreau would be an obvious candidate,
and Jourdan or Bernadotte might also matter,
though each had different political instincts and less personal magnetism.
A coup could still happen,
but it would probably be messier and less decisive.
That matters because Napoleon was not just a general available for use;
he was unusually good at dominating allies, outmaneuvering rivals, and converting a provisional seizure of power into a durable personal regime.
Without him, a post-Directory government might be more collective and more fragile.
A revised constitution could emerge, perhaps creating a stronger executive and limiting democratic participation,
but it might not so quickly become a personal dictatorship.
France would likely still centralize state power,
because the revolutionary decade had already pushed politics in that direction,
yet the specific Napoleonic blend of authoritarianism, plebiscitary legitimacy, administrative efficiency, and military glory would be hard to replicate.
Militarily, the consequences could be enormous.
In actual history Napoleon’s campaigns of 1800, especially Marengo, stabilized the new regime and restored French dominance over Austria.
Without him, France would still have strong armies and capable generals,
but victory would be less assured and less theatrically tied to one man.
Moreau was a competent commander and might still win important battles,
but he was not likely to found an empire from them.
This means France might negotiate from a less dominant position.
The War of the Second Coalition could end in compromise rather than in the unmistakable reassertion of French supremacy associated with Napoleon’s rise.
If France remains under a more collective authoritarian republic, peace with Britain might also look different.
Napoleon’s personal ambition and strategic vision helped drive the renewed cycle of continental war after the brief Peace of Amiens.
Another regime might be more cautious, more interested in consolidating the gains of the Revolution inside France and its satellite republics than in seeking continental hegemony.
There would still be deep Anglo-French rivalry,
so conflict would not disappear,
but the scale and intensity of the Napoleonic Wars might never develop in the same way.
The internal development of France would also diverge.

Some changes often associated with Napoleon were already broadly desired: administrative rationalization, reconciliation with parts of the old elite, financial stabilization, and an end to revolutionary chaos.
So a non-Napoleonic government might still create a stronger bureaucracy, a national bank, and a more orderly tax system.
But the Civil Code, the Concordat with the Church, the lycée system, and the prefectural structure might emerge more slowly, in altered form, or under different names.
The legal unification of France and its export across Europe would be much less dramatic.
Some meritocratic features of the Revolution would survive,
but they might be less consistently institutionalized.
For Europe as a whole, the biggest difference is that there may be no vast Napoleonic imperial expansion.
Without Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, the Continental System, the Peninsular War, and the invasion of Russia, the old monarchies would face less existential shock.
The Holy Roman Empire might survive longer, perhaps in weakened reforming form rather than being swept away in 1806.
German and Italian nationalism would probably develop more slowly, because Napoleon both destroyed old structures and unintentionally stimulated national reaction against French domination.
Prussia might reform less quickly without the humiliations of 1806.
Russia would remain important, but without the patriotic myth of 1812 as we know it.
Britain would still expand commercially and overseas, but in a Europe not dominated by one continental super-rival.
This also affects colonial history.
Napoleon’s role in the Haitian Revolution and the sale of Louisiana were highly consequential.
If he never returns to power, France might not mount the same large expedition to Saint-Domingue, or at least not under the same assumptions.
Haitian independence might come earlier, or through a different diplomatic path.
Louisiana might remain French somewhat longer, or be sold later under different conditions.
That in turn could affect U.S. westward expansion,
though the United States would still likely grow.
A weaker or more cautious French regime might focus less on grand imperial restoration and more on European survival.
One should be careful not to imagine that Napoleon alone created modern Europe.
Many of the forces that empowered him were already present: state centralization, mass conscription, revolutionary ideology, and the collapse of old-regime legitimacy in France.
If he does not return in 1799, France does not simply become peaceful and stable.
It still faces factionalism, war, and pressure for a stronger executive.
So the most plausible alternative is not “no authoritarian turn,” but “a different authoritarian turn.”
France likely ends the Directory anyway,
but under a less brilliant and less domineering ruler.
So the best concise answer is this:
if Napoleon could not make it back to France in 1799, the Directory would probably still fall, but Napoleon’s specific seizure of power would not happen.
France might be taken over by another general-backed regime, perhaps with Sieyès playing a larger role,
yet it would likely be less stable, less militarily spectacular, and less personally dictatorial.
Europe would probably avoid the full Napoleonic cycle of empire and total continental war.
Revolutionary France would still matter greatly,
but the map, laws, and political development of nineteenth-century Europe would be transformed more gradually and less violently.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Integration and Point of Divergence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly uses the specific premise that a successful Greek 'Great Plan' and the Greek War of Independence trigger an early Ottoman collapse, rather than drifting into generic Ottoman decline or ordinary Greek independence.
criteria.1-2: Barely addresses the premise; treats history as mostly unchanged or gives generic remarks about Greece or the Ottomans.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Greek success or Ottoman weakness but leaves the timing, scale, and causal trigger vague.
criteria.5-6: Uses the premise consistently, with a plausible early-19th-century divergence, but underdevelops why Greek success causes wider collapse.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains how a larger Greek victory destabilizes Ottoman authority across multiple provinces and alters European calculations.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the divergence in the 1820s-1830s and rigorously traces how Greek military, ideological, fiscal, and legitimacy shocks accelerate systemic Ottoman breakdown.

criteria.name: Great Power Diplomacy and Intervention Logic
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of Britain, France, Russia, Austria, and other European actors, including their anti-revolutionary instincts, strategic rivalry, religious politics, and likely management of collapse.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the Great Powers or portrays them with anachronistic, simplistic motives.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some powers but reduces their behavior to religion or pro-Greek sympathy without strategic nuance.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes competing motives such as balance of power, fear of revolution, and Russian access to the Straits, but gives a thin causal account.
criteria.7-8: Explains why powers might hesitate, intervene selectively, partition influence, or back particular claimants while balancing one another.
criteria.9-10: Offers a sophisticated, period-appropriate diplomatic chain involving Britain, France, Russia, Austria, and possibly Muhammad Ali, with credible tradeoffs over Greece, the Straits, Egypt, the Balkans, and the Adriatic.

criteria.name: Regional Partition, State Formation, and Local Actors
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of likely outcomes for Greek expansion, Balkan Christian polities, Anatolia, Egypt, Albania, the Danubian principalities, the Straits, and Muslim and Christian populations after Ottoman collapse.
criteria.1-2: Gives only a broad claim that the Ottoman Empire collapses, with no regional breakdown.
criteria.3-4: Discusses Greece or the Balkans alone and neglects most other Ottoman territories and local power centers.
criteria.5-6: Covers several regions but relies on static borders or implausibly neat partitions.
criteria.7-8: Identifies multiple successor arrangements, including Greek territorial gains, Balkan autonomy, Egyptian ambitions, and contested control of the Straits or Anatolia.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced, messy map of successor states, protectorates, spheres of influence, refugee flows, sectarian conflict, and elite bargains shaped by both local actors and Great Power sponsorship.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain and Downstream Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer projects consequences beyond the immediate war, including effects on nationalism, imperial competition, trade routes, Egypt and India strategy, Russia's southern policy, Austria's Balkan position, and later European crises.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the immediate collapse with little or no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Lists later effects but with weak links to the initial counterfactual.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible medium-term sequence but omits major geopolitical or economic knock-on effects.
criteria.7-8: Traces coherent consequences over decades for European balance of power, Eastern Mediterranean strategy, Balkan nationalism, and colonial logistics.
criteria.9-10: Builds a robust long-range chain showing how early Ottoman collapse reshapes 19th-century diplomacy, the Crimean War question, Suez/Egypt strategy, nationalist movements, imperial rivalries, and alliance structures.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes while avoiding internal contradictions, anachronisms, and overdetermined claims.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but implausible claims, contains major contradictions, or uses clearly anachronistic assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but frequently overstates certainty or contradicts known early-19th-century constraints.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible and internally consistent, though some claims are underqualified or insufficiently justified.
criteria.7-8: Carefully signals uncertainty, offers alternatives where evidence is ambiguous, and keeps mechanisms consistent with the 1820s-1830s context.
criteria.9-10: Maintains strong causal discipline throughout, explicitly weighs rival pathways, avoids hindsight determinism, and keeps all speculative claims compatible with the counterfactual premise and period constraints.

items.model_answer:
If the Greek “Great Plan” had succeeded early—meaning the Greek War of Independence not only created an independent Greece but also triggered a much broader and premature collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s or 1830s—the political map of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean would likely have changed dramatically, and much earlier than it did in real history.

The most immediate result would probably have been the creation of a much larger Greek state, likely centered not just on the Peloponnese and central Greece but also claiming Constantinople, western Anatolia’s Greek-populated coast, many Aegean islands, and perhaps parts of Thrace. Whether Greece could actually have controlled all of this territory is another matter, but the “Great Idea” would have become the founding principle of the new order rather than a later irredentist dream. Constantinople might have become either a Greek capital, an international city, or the main object of rivalry among the great powers.

An early Ottoman collapse would also have opened space for other Balkan national movements much sooner. Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and possibly Albania would likely have sought independent or semi-independent states decades earlier. But this would not necessarily have meant a peaceful liberation. The Ottoman Empire had held together a vast multiethnic region, and its sudden disappearance would have produced a scramble over borders, populations, ports, and holy cities. In that sense, the Balkans might have entered their age of nationalist conflict much earlier, perhaps in the mid-19th rather than the early 20th century.

The great powers would have been decisive. Russia would likely have tried to present itself as protector of Orthodox Christians and push toward the Straits. Britain would have feared Russian access to the Mediterranean and probably opposed any settlement that made Greece too large or too dependent on Russia. France might have supported intervention for prestige and influence. Austria, deeply worried about nationalism and instability in the Balkans, would probably have resisted revolutionary fragmentation. So a successful Greek-led collapse of the Ottoman Empire could easily have triggered not just local wars but a major European diplomatic crisis, possibly even a continent-wide war well before the Crimean War.

There would also have been major consequences for Muslim populations. If Ottoman authority had broken suddenly in Europe and the Aegean, many Muslim communities would likely have fled, been expelled, or faced reprisals, just as Christians in contested areas might have suffered in return during the struggle. The region’s demographic reshaping—population flight, ethnic cleansing, refugee movements—could have begun a century earlier. The pattern seen later in the Balkans and after the Greco-Turkish War might have been compressed into an earlier and more chaotic phase.

In the Arab provinces, the effects are less certain. A Greek success in the Balkans would not automatically destroy Ottoman power in Syria, Iraq, or Arabia, but it could have accelerated the rise of semi-independent rulers such as Muhammad Ali in Egypt. In fact, Egypt might have emerged as the real successor power in much of the former Ottoman Middle East. Instead of a long Ottoman 19th century followed by gradual European penetration, the eastern Mediterranean might have been divided earlier between local successor states and direct great-power influence.

Economically and culturally, an enlarged Greek state controlling major ports and trade routes could have become a powerful maritime kingdom, especially if it incorporated Constantinople and the Aegean coast. Greek merchant networks were already strong; with state backing, they might have dominated eastern Mediterranean commerce. On the other hand, trying to rule over huge mixed populations with limited institutions might have overstretched the new state from the start.

The biggest long-term question is whether this would have prevented later disasters or merely moved them earlier. It might have prevented the exact sequence of the late Ottoman decline, the Balkan Wars, and the First World War’s Near Eastern front. But it probably would not have removed the underlying tensions of nationalism, imperial rivalry, and ethnic competition. More likely, it would have shifted the “Eastern Question” forward by several decades. Instead of asking how to manage a weakening Ottoman Empire in the late 19th century, Europe would have faced the same question in the 1820s or 1830s, under even less stable conditions.

So the most plausible answer is that an early success of the Greek Great Plan would have produced a larger and more ambitious Greece and a much earlier end to Ottoman dominance in Europe, but at the cost of intense great-power competition, unstable successor states, and earlier nationalist wars across the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean. It would have been a revolutionary transformation, but probably not a peaceful one.

edus.text: If the Greek “Great Plan” had succeeded early—meaning the Greek War of Independence not only created an independent Greece but also triggered a much broader and premature collapse of the Ottoman Empire in the 1820s or 1830s—
the political map of southeastern Europe and the eastern Mediterranean would likely have changed dramatically, and much earlier than it did in real history.
The most immediate result would probably have been the creation of a much larger Greek state,
likely centered not just on the Peloponnese and central Greece but also claiming Constantinople, western Anatolia’s Greek-populated coast, many Aegean islands, and perhaps parts of Thrace.
Whether Greece could actually have controlled all of this territory is another matter,
but the “Great Idea” would have become the founding principle of the new order rather than a later irredentist dream.
Constantinople might have become either a Greek capital, an international city, or the main object of rivalry among the great powers.
An early Ottoman collapse would also have opened space for other Balkan national movements much sooner.
Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and possibly Albania would likely have sought independent or semi-independent states decades earlier.
But this would not necessarily have meant a peaceful liberation.
The Ottoman Empire had held together a vast multiethnic region,
and its sudden disappearance would have produced a scramble over borders, populations, ports, and holy cities.
In that sense, the Balkans might have entered their age of nationalist conflict much earlier, perhaps in the mid-19th rather than the early 20th century.
The great powers would have been decisive.
Russia would likely have tried to present itself as protector of Orthodox Christians and push toward the Straits.
Britain would have feared Russian access to the Mediterranean and probably opposed any settlement that made Greece too large or too dependent on Russia.
France might have supported intervention for prestige and influence.
Austria, deeply worried about nationalism and instability in the Balkans, would probably have resisted revolutionary fragmentation.

So a successful Greek-led collapse of the Ottoman Empire could easily have triggered not just local wars but a major European diplomatic crisis, possibly even a continent-wide war well before the Crimean War.
There would also have been major consequences for Muslim populations.
If Ottoman authority had broken suddenly in Europe and the Aegean,
many Muslim communities would likely have fled, been expelled, or faced reprisals,
just as Christians in contested areas might have suffered in return during the struggle.
The region’s demographic reshaping—population flight, ethnic cleansing, refugee movements—could have begun a century earlier.
The pattern seen later in the Balkans and after the Greco-Turkish War might have been compressed into an earlier and more chaotic phase.
In the Arab provinces, the effects are less certain.
A Greek success in the Balkans would not automatically destroy Ottoman power in Syria, Iraq, or Arabia,
but it could have accelerated the rise of semi-independent rulers such as Muhammad Ali in Egypt.
In fact, Egypt might have emerged as the real successor power in much of the former Ottoman Middle East.
Instead of a long Ottoman 19th century followed by gradual European penetration,
the eastern Mediterranean might have been divided earlier between local successor states and direct great-power influence.
Economically and culturally, an enlarged Greek state controlling major ports and trade routes could have become a powerful maritime kingdom,
especially if it incorporated Constantinople and the Aegean coast.
Greek merchant networks were already strong;
with state backing, they might have dominated eastern Mediterranean commerce.
On the other hand, trying to rule over huge mixed populations with limited institutions might have overstretched the new state from the start.
The biggest long-term question is whether this would have prevented later disasters or merely moved them earlier.
It might have prevented the exact sequence of the late Ottoman decline, the Balkan Wars, and the First World War’s Near Eastern front.
But it probably would not have removed the underlying tensions of nationalism, imperial rivalry, and ethnic competition.
More likely, it would have shifted the “Eastern Question” forward by several decades.
Instead of asking how to manage a weakening Ottoman Empire in the late 19th century,
Europe would have faced the same question in the 1820s or 1830s, under even less stable conditions.
So the most plausible answer is that an early success of the Greek Great Plan would have produced a larger and more ambitious Greece and a much earlier end to Ottoman dominance in Europe,
but at the cost of intense great-power competition, unstable successor states, and earlier nationalist wars across the Balkans and eastern Mediterranean.
It would have been a revolutionary transformation,
but probably not a peaceful one.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Boundary Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines the timing, scale, causes, and settlement pattern of a massive French migration to the United States, rather than treating the premise as a vague demographic fact.
criteria.1-2: Leaves the premise undefined or assumes a single outcome without specifying when, why, or how the French become a major US community.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one setup factor such as timing or location but does not explain how it shapes the scenario.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several key variables, such as Napoleonic-era versus late-19th-century migration, religious identity, or settlement region, with some causal relevance.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent scenario around timing, migration scale, motives, and settlement geography, while noting that different assumptions produce different outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly frames multiple plausible variants and shows how each would alter US demography, politics, assimilation, and international context.

criteria.name: Settlement Geography and Regional Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer reasons about where French immigrants would settle and how that would affect regional development, especially Louisiana, New Orleans, the South, Texas, Florida, the Midwest, or the Northeast.
criteria.1-2: Ignores geography or treats French immigrants as evenly distributed across the US.
criteria.3-4: Names likely regions of settlement but gives little explanation of their consequences.
criteria.5-6: Connects French settlement to plausible regions such as former Louisiana or New Orleans and describes some local cultural or economic effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains how concentrated versus dispersed settlement would affect assimilation, bilingualism, urban growth, regional identity, and sectional politics.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced regional map of likely settlement and traces long-range consequences for the South, Gulf Coast, frontier expansion, and national integration.

criteria.name: Religious, Racial, and Assimilation Dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses treatment of how a large French Catholic and European-origin population would interact with 19th-century American racial, religious, and ethnic hierarchies.
criteria.1-2: Ignores religion, race, ethnicity, and assimilation or makes anachronistic assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Catholicism or whiteness but gives a shallow or one-sided account of social reactions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes likely anti-Catholic tension alongside the relative advantages French immigrants would have as Europeans in a racialized society.
criteria.7-8: Explains how French language, Catholic institutions, class status, education, and perceived whiteness would affect assimilation and nativist backlash.
criteria.9-10: Carefully balances anti-Catholicism, ethnic prejudice, class differences, racial privilege, and regional variation without implying deterministic acceptance or rejection.

criteria.name: Political and Long-Range Institutional Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer develops downstream effects on US politics, sectional conflict, party coalitions, slavery, the Civil War, federalism, language policy, and possible alternate national boundaries.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful political consequences beyond saying the US would be more French.
criteria.3-4: Mentions politics or the Civil War only speculatively without causal links.
criteria.5-6: Offers plausible effects on voting blocs, Catholic politics, Southern society, or sectional tensions, but with limited depth.

items.model_answer:
If the French became one of the largest communities in the United States, the country would likely still remain recognizably American, but its culture, politics, language, and international orientation would be noticeably different.

The biggest change would be cultural. French language and customs would probably have a much stronger public presence, especially in major cities and in regions where French settlement was dense. Bilingualism in English and French might become common in schools, government services, media, and business, much as Spanish has a major presence today. American food culture would also shift: French culinary traditions, café culture, bread, cheese, wine, and regional cooking styles could become more mainstream parts of everyday life rather than markers of elite taste.

Politically, a very large French-origin population might strengthen support for a more centralized state in some areas, depending on when and how that population arrived. French political traditions have often placed greater trust in public administration, secular education, and national cultural policy than the classic American preference for localism and limited government. That would not automatically make the US “more French,” but it could push debates over welfare, education, religion in public life, and labor protections in a different direction.

Religion and secularism could also develop differently. If many of these French Americans came from historically Catholic backgrounds, Catholic institutions might become even more influential than they already were. But if they carried modern French republican ideas, the US might also adopt a stronger form of secular public culture, with sharper boundaries between religion and state.

Regionally, places with French roots such as Louisiana would likely hold much greater national influence. French-derived legal traditions, architecture, music, and local identities might spread beyond isolated pockets and become part of the national mainstream. The symbolic story Americans tell about themselves might also change: instead of being framed mainly as an Anglo-Protestant society later diversified by immigration, the US might be understood from the beginning as a dual Anglo-French or even broader multilingual republic.

Foreign policy could be affected too. A large French-American community might make the US somewhat more attentive to France, Quebec, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa where French influence was strong. Diplomatic and commercial ties with the Francophone world would probably deepen.

That said, the exact outcome would depend on timing. If the French became one of the largest communities through colonial settlement early in US history, the entire national identity could be fundamentally reshaped. If it happened later through immigration, the French would more likely become a major ethnic bloc within an already English-dominant system. In either case, the most likely result is not that America becomes “French,” but that it becomes more bilingual, more culturally continental, and more shaped by French traditions than in our timeline.
