human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.
items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.

items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505, the most likely result is not a permanently independent Naples, but a stronger short-term Aragonese-Neapolitan bloc in Italy and a very different dynastic future for England. The key consequence is that Catherine would leave the Anglo-Spanish marriage market after Arthur’s death and be redirected into Mediterranean dynastic politics. That would shift her from being the future queen of England to being a queenly figure in the orbit of Naples, Valencia, and the wider Crown of Aragon.

The first and biggest immediate effect would be on English history. Henry VIII would almost certainly never marry Catherine. Without that marriage, there is no Princess Mary in the same form, no “King’s Great Matter” over annulment from Catherine, and therefore no Reformation in England triggered in the same way or at the same moment. England might still eventually break with Rome for other reasons, but the specific chain of events that produced the English Reformation would be broken. Henry would need a different foreign bride, probably from France, Burgundy-Habsburg circles, or a lesser Iberian line. That alone makes this a major European divergence.

For Naples, the marriage would matter because Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was heir to the dispossessed Neapolitan Trastámara line. Catherine herself was the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, whose policies had brought Naples under Spanish-Aragonese control. A marriage between Catherine and Ferdinand would symbolically reconcile two branches of the wider Aragonese world: the ruling Spanish monarchy and the old Neapolitan royal house. It could be used to strengthen legitimacy in southern Italy, especially among elites who still remembered the old Neapolitan dynasty. In that sense, the marriage could have given Naples a more distinct court identity within the Spanish system.

But “independent Naples” is the harder part. In 1505, Naples was strategically too important for Ferdinand the Catholic to let go easily. It was a core Mediterranean possession, essential for projecting power into Italy and checking France. Even if Catherine and Ferdinand were installed in Naples, they would probably rule as dependents or viceroyal royals under Spanish supremacy, not as fully sovereign monarchs. Ferdinand the Catholic was not in the habit of creating genuinely independent cadet kingdoms when direct control served his interests better. So the realistic outcome is a semi-autonomous Naples, perhaps with more local prestige and dynastic coloration, rather than complete independence.

Still, over time, a Catherine-Ferdinand marriage could create conditions for partial separation. If they had sons, those children might become the nucleus of a junior Aragonese-Neapolitan branch. In a succession crisis, especially after the deaths of Isabella of Castile and then Ferdinand the Catholic, Naples could become attached to this cadet line instead of being absorbed so tightly into the emerging Habsburg monarchy under Charles. That would be the best path toward “independent Naples”: not immediate separation in 1505, but gradual dynastic differentiation aided by Italian politics and Habsburg overstretch.

This matters because the Habsburg inheritance was about to transform Europe. Historically, Naples became part of the massive Habsburg system under Charles V. If Catherine were in Naples and her husband’s line were politically useful, some anti-Habsburg forces—French, papal, Venetian, or local baronial—might support a distinct Neapolitan monarchy as a buffer state. Catherine’s royal status as daughter of the Catholic Monarchs would enhance that claim. Naples could then resemble a satellite kingdom with its own court, diplomacy, and succession, though still under strong Spanish influence.

However, several constraints make full success unlikely. France would oppose any settlement that strengthened an Aragonese cadet branch in Italy. Spanish rulers would fear that autonomy in Naples could invite renewed French intervention. Neapolitan barons were often divided and could be unreliable partners in state-building. And Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, though dynastically significant, was not in a strong independent power position. So unless the Spanish monarchy itself fragmented more than it historically did, Naples would probably remain tied to the larger Spanish imperial framework.

The most plausible long-run counterfactual, then, is this: Catherine’s marriage to Ferdinand of Calabria produces a more locally rooted and ceremonially royal Naples, perhaps one with intermittent claims to separate status, but not a cleanly independent kingdom right away. The larger historical transformation happens elsewhere. England loses Catherine, so the Tudor succession and the English Reformation are radically altered. Italy gains a potentially stronger Aragonese-Neapolitan dynastic center, but one that would still struggle to escape Spanish control unless broader Habsburg politics gave it an opening.

So if Catherine marries Ferdinand in 1505, “independent Naples” becomes more thinkable, but only as a contingent later development. The immediate and certain result is not Neapolitan independence; it is the removal of Catherine from English history and the creation of a more dynastically coherent southern Italian branch of the Aragonese world.

edus.text: If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, in 1505, the most likely result is not a permanently independent Naples,
but a stronger short-term Aragonese-Neapolitan bloc in Italy and a very different dynastic future for England.
The key consequence is that Catherine would leave the Anglo-Spanish marriage market after Arthur’s death
and be redirected into Mediterranean dynastic politics.
That would shift her from being the future queen of England
to being a queenly figure in the orbit of Naples, Valencia, and the wider Crown of Aragon.
The first and biggest immediate effect would be on English history.
Henry VIII would almost certainly never marry Catherine.
Without that marriage, there is no Princess Mary in the same form,
no “King’s Great Matter” over annulment from Catherine,
and therefore no Reformation in England triggered in the same way or at the same moment.
England might still eventually break with Rome for other reasons,
but the specific chain of events that produced the English Reformation would be broken.
Henry would need a different foreign bride, probably from France, Burgundy-Habsburg circles, or a lesser Iberian line.
That alone makes this a major European divergence.
For Naples, the marriage would matter
because Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was heir to the dispossessed Neapolitan Trastámara line.
Catherine herself was the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella,
whose policies had brought Naples under Spanish-Aragonese control.
A marriage between Catherine and Ferdinand would symbolically reconcile two branches of the wider Aragonese world:
the ruling Spanish monarchy and the old Neapolitan royal house.
It could be used to strengthen legitimacy in southern Italy,
especially among elites who still remembered the old Neapolitan dynasty.
In that sense, the marriage could have given Naples a more distinct court identity within the Spanish system.
But “independent Naples” is the harder part.
In 1505, Naples was strategically too important for Ferdinand the Catholic to let go easily.
It was a core Mediterranean possession,
essential for projecting power into Italy and checking France.
Even if Catherine and Ferdinand were installed in Naples,
they would probably rule as dependents or viceroyal royals under Spanish supremacy,
not as fully sovereign monarchs.
Ferdinand the Catholic was not in the habit of creating genuinely independent cadet kingdoms
when direct control served his interests better.
So the realistic outcome is a semi-autonomous Naples,
perhaps with more local prestige and dynastic coloration,
rather than complete independence.
Still, over time, a Catherine-Ferdinand marriage could create conditions for partial separation.
If they had sons,
those children might become the nucleus of a junior Aragonese-Neapolitan branch.
In a succession crisis,
especially after the deaths of Isabella of Castile and then Ferdinand the Catholic,
Naples could become attached to this cadet line
instead of being absorbed so tightly into the emerging Habsburg monarchy under Charles.
That would be the best path toward “independent Naples”:
not immediate separation in 1505,
but gradual dynastic differentiation aided by Italian politics and Habsburg overstretch.
This matters
because the Habsburg inheritance was about to transform Europe.
Historically, Naples became part of the massive Habsburg system under Charles V.
If Catherine were in Naples
and her husband’s line were politically useful,
some anti-Habsburg forces might support a distinct Neapolitan monarchy as a buffer state.
Catherine’s royal status as daughter of the Catholic Monarchs would enhance that claim.
Naples could then resemble a satellite kingdom with its own court, diplomacy, and succession,
though still under strong Spanish influence.
However, several constraints make full success unlikely.
France would oppose any settlement that strengthened an Aragonese cadet branch in Italy.
Spanish rulers would fear that autonomy in Naples could invite renewed French intervention.
Neapolitan barons were often divided
and could be unreliable partners in state-building.
And Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, though dynastically significant, was not in a strong independent power position.
So unless the Spanish monarchy itself fragmented more than it historically did,
Naples would probably remain tied to the larger Spanish imperial framework.
The most plausible long-run counterfactual, then, is this:
Catherine’s marriage to Ferdinand of Calabria produces a more locally rooted and ceremonially royal Naples,
perhaps one with intermittent claims to separate status,
but not a cleanly independent kingdom right away.
The larger historical transformation happens elsewhere.
England loses Catherine,
so the Tudor succession and the English Reformation are radically altered.
Italy gains a potentially stronger Aragonese-Neapolitan dynastic center,
but one that would still struggle to escape Spanish control
unless broader Habsburg politics gave it an opening.
So if Catherine marries Ferdinand in 1505,
“independent Naples” becomes more thinkable,
but only as a contingent later development.
The immediate and certain result is not Neapolitan independence;
it is the removal of Catherine from English history
and the creation of a more dynastically coherent southern Italian branch of the Aragonese world.

items.question: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980
human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!

criteria.3-4: Recognizes some major emitters but gives a shallow or partially anachronistic chronology of who drove emissions after 1980.
criteria.5-6: Mostly accurate on broad emissions timing, distinguishing early Western dominance from later Chinese and Indian growth, with minor omissions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly tracks major emitter shifts across the 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, and later, using this chronology to shape the counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates historical emissions sequencing, industrialization timing, and bloc-level comparisons to evaluate whether post-1980 warming could plausibly be curbed.

criteria.name: Decarbonization Mechanism Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the specificity and plausibility of proposed mechanisms for curbing warming after 1980, especially nuclear expansion, coal displacement, renewables cost curves, efficiency, carbon treaties, and fossil-fuel lock-in.
criteria.1-2: Offers vague claims such as 'use clean energy' without explaining feasible mechanisms or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plausible technologies or policies but ignores cost, deployment speed, political resistance, or energy-system inertia.
criteria.5-6: Provides one or two workable mechanisms, such as Western nuclear buildout or coal limits, with some attention to feasibility.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple mechanisms and constraints, including nuclear politics, renewable timing, grid deployment, coal dependence, and international policy leverage.
criteria.9-10: Builds a highly plausible decarbonization pathway with detailed technological, economic, political, and institutional mechanisms appropriate to the 1980 onward timeline.

criteria.name: Developing-World Industrialization and Trade Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the central downstream issue: how China, India, and other developing economies industrialize if the West curbs emissions, and whether trade, technology transfer, delayed growth, or carbon standards change their trajectories.
criteria.1-2: Ignores China, India, and developing-country growth or assumes they simply copy Western decarbonization without constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions China or India but gives little explanation of energy affordability, domestic coal, export markets, or development incentives.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that developing-country industrialization is a major challenge and links it to coal, trade, or technology access.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes how Western decarbonization, carbon tariffs, WTO-era trade, Soviet/Russian alternatives, or technology transfer could alter Chinese and Indian emissions.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of developing-world growth paths, including affordability, domestic resources, export dependence, geopolitical contingencies, and whether global emissions fall despite later industrialization.

criteria.name: Climate Outcome Reasoning and Greenhouse-Gas Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer connects emissions changes to climate outcomes, including cumulative CO2, timing of warming, methane, land use, transport, agriculture, and the distinction between delaying warming and preventing it in the long run.
criteria.1-2: Conflates annual emissions with temperature outcomes or ignores cumulative emissions and climate lag.
criteria.3-4: Makes broad claims about reduced warming but gives little explanation of cumulative carbon, timing, or non-CO2 gases.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that lower emissions reduce warming and includes some discussion of climate lag or non-CO2 sources.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes short-term delay from long-term prevention and covers major sectors such as electricity, transport, industry, agriculture, and methane.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously links sectoral emissions pathways to cumulative forcing and temperature outcomes, explicitly assessing whether warming is merely postponed or durably limited.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the overall counterfactual chain from post-1980 interventions to late-20th and 21st-century outcomes, including internal consistency, handling of contingencies, and calibrated confidence.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, deterministic assertions, or contradictions that break the counterfactual chain.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable scenario but weak causal links, unsupported leaps, or unacknowledged conflicts between assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent chain with some uncertainty acknowledged, though parts remain underdeveloped or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Develops a consistent multi-decade causal pathway, flags key contingencies, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly reasoned long-range scenario with explicit causal dependencies, alternative branches, uncertainty calibration, and careful distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions.

items.model_answer:
If the world had seriously moved to curb global warming after 1980, the most likely result is that climate change would still exist, but it would be much milder, slower, and easier to manage than it is today.

By 1980, scientists already understood the basic greenhouse effect and were becoming increasingly confident that rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels would warm the planet. If governments had acted then with strong policies—such as limiting coal use, improving energy efficiency, investing early in solar, wind, nuclear power, public transit, and protecting forests—global emissions could have peaked much earlier. That would have meant lower atmospheric CO2 concentrations, less total warming, and fewer extreme climate impacts by the 2000s and 2020s.

In practical terms, the world might now have lower average temperatures, slower sea-level rise, less glacier melt, and reduced risks of heat waves, droughts, floods, and intense storms. Some damage would still occur because the climate system responds slowly and because industrial emissions had already built up before 1980. But many of today’s most dangerous trends would likely be less severe. Coral reefs, Arctic sea ice, and vulnerable ecosystems would probably be in better condition. Food and water stress in some regions would also likely be less intense.

Economically, early action would probably have been cheaper overall than delayed action. The transition away from fossil fuels would have been gradual rather than rushed, allowing infrastructure to be replaced over time. Cities, industries, and transport systems could have adapted earlier. While some sectors—especially coal, oil, and gas—would have faced disruption, new industries in clean energy and efficiency would likely have grown sooner. Many economists argue that acting early reduces both future climate damages and the cost of emergency adaptation.

Politically, an early response after 1980 might also have changed international relations. Climate cooperation could have become a major global project before emissions grew rapidly in emerging economies. Rich countries, which were then responsible for most historical emissions, would have had more opportunity to lead and finance cleaner development elsewhere. That might have reduced some of the fairness disputes that later complicated climate negotiations.

However, this outcome would have depended on how strong the response was. Small symbolic steps after 1980 would not have been enough. To truly curb global warming, countries would have needed sustained international cooperation, carbon regulation, technological innovation, and public support over decades. That would have been politically difficult, especially because fossil fuels were deeply tied to economic growth and geopolitical power.

So the best short answer is this: if the world had moved decisively after 1980 to curb global warming, we would probably still face climate change today, but it would likely be significantly less dangerous, less costly, and less destabilizing than the version we are now experiencing.

edus.text: If the world had seriously moved to curb global warming after 1980,
the most likely result is that climate change would still exist,
but it would be much milder, slower, and easier to manage than it is today.
By 1980, scientists already understood the basic greenhouse effect
and were becoming increasingly confident that rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels would warm the planet.
If governments had acted then with strong policies—such as limiting coal use, improving energy efficiency, investing early in solar, wind, nuclear power, public transit, and protecting forests—
global emissions could have peaked much earlier.
That would have meant lower atmospheric CO2 concentrations, less total warming, and fewer extreme climate impacts by the 2000s and 2020s.
In practical terms, the world might now have lower average temperatures, slower sea-level rise, less glacier melt, and reduced risks of heat waves, droughts, floods, and intense storms.
Some damage would still occur
because the climate system responds slowly
and because industrial emissions had already built up before 1980.
But many of today’s most dangerous trends would likely be less severe.
Coral reefs, Arctic sea ice, and vulnerable ecosystems would probably be in better condition.
Food and water stress in some regions would also likely be less intense.
Economically, early action would probably have been cheaper overall than delayed action.
The transition away from fossil fuels would have been gradual rather than rushed,
allowing infrastructure to be replaced over time.
Cities, industries, and transport systems could have adapted earlier.
While some sectors—especially coal, oil, and gas—would have faced disruption,
new industries in clean energy and efficiency would likely have grown sooner.
Many economists argue that acting early reduces both future climate damages and the cost of emergency adaptation.
Politically, an early response after 1980 might also have changed international relations.
Climate cooperation could have become a major global project before emissions grew rapidly in emerging economies.
Rich countries, which were then responsible for most historical emissions, would have had more opportunity to lead and finance cleaner development elsewhere.
That might have reduced some of the fairness disputes that later complicated climate negotiations.
However, this outcome would have depended on how strong the response was.
Small symbolic steps after 1980 would not have been enough.
To truly curb global warming, countries would have needed sustained international cooperation, carbon regulation, technological innovation, and public support over decades.
That would have been politically difficult,
especially because fossil fuels were deeply tied to economic growth and geopolitical power.
So the best short answer is this:
if the world had moved decisively after 1980 to curb global warming,
we would probably still face climate change today,
but it would likely be significantly less dangerous, less costly, and less destabilizing than the version we are now experiencing.

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini

items.model_answer:
If none of the seven Catholic bishops deprived under Elizabeth I in 1558–59 had died when they did, the English Reformation under Elizabeth would probably still have gone forward, but more slowly, more awkwardly, and with greater legal and political strain.

The key issue is that Elizabeth’s religious settlement depended not just on Parliament, but on the church hierarchy. In reality, the Marian bishops overwhelmingly refused to accept the royal supremacy and the new settlement, and their deaths over the next few years helped Elizabethan Protestantism consolidate because vacancies could be filled with loyal Protestant bishops. If those bishops had all remained alive longer, Elizabeth would have faced a much more entrenched Catholic episcopate.

That would matter in several ways. First, the crown would have had fewer bishoprics to refill with reformers. Bishops were essential administrators: they ordained clergy, supervised dioceses, enforced conformity, and gave the settlement institutional depth. Without vacancies, Elizabeth would have had to rely more heavily on deprivation, legal pressure, and extraordinary mechanisms rather than normal succession. The settlement could still be imposed, but it would look less settled and more coercive.

Second, Catholic resistance inside the Church of England would likely have been stronger in the early 1560s. The Marian bishops had prestige, learning, and symbolic authority. If all seven had remained alive, they could have served as focal points for recusant and conservative resistance, even if imprisoned or marginalized. Their continued presence would have made it harder for the regime to claim broad ecclesiastical legitimacy.

Third, international and domestic politics might have become more dangerous. A living body of senior Catholic bishops could have encouraged hopes among English Catholics, as well as among Spain, the papacy, and Mary Queen of Scots, that Elizabeth’s settlement was reversible. That would not necessarily mean immediate rebellion, but it could have stiffened resistance and increased the sense that England’s confessional future was still undecided.

Even so, it is unlikely that simply keeping those seven bishops alive would have reversed Elizabeth’s religious policy. Elizabeth had the crown, Parliament, key lay elites, and growing control over patronage. The Marian episcopate had moral authority but not decisive political power. Unless their survival were paired with some larger change—such as foreign intervention, a stronger Catholic faction at court, or a succession crisis—they probably could not have restored England to Rome.

So the most plausible counterfactual is not “no Elizabethan settlement,” but “a weaker, more contested, and less smoothly institutionalized Elizabethan settlement in its first decade.” Protestantism would still likely win in the long run, but Catholic resistance would have had more senior leadership, and the regime would have had a harder time turning legal change into a functioning national church.

edus.text: If none of the seven Catholic bishops deprived under Elizabeth I in 1558–59 had died when they did, the English Reformation under Elizabeth would probably still have gone forward,
but more slowly, more awkwardly, and with greater legal and political strain.
The key issue is that Elizabeth’s religious settlement depended not just on Parliament, but on the church hierarchy.
In reality, the Marian bishops overwhelmingly refused to accept the royal supremacy and the new settlement,
and their deaths over the next few years helped Elizabethan Protestantism consolidate
because vacancies could be filled with loyal Protestant bishops.
If those bishops had all remained alive longer, Elizabeth would have faced a much more entrenched Catholic episcopate.
That would matter in several ways.
First, the crown would have had fewer bishoprics to refill with reformers.
Bishops were essential administrators: they ordained clergy, supervised dioceses, enforced conformity, and gave the settlement institutional depth.
Without vacancies, Elizabeth would have had to rely more heavily on deprivation, legal pressure, and extraordinary mechanisms rather than normal succession.
The settlement could still be imposed,
but it would look less settled and more coercive.
Second, Catholic resistance inside the Church of England would likely have been stronger in the early 1560s.
The Marian bishops had prestige, learning, and symbolic authority.
If all seven had remained alive, they could have served as focal points for recusant and conservative resistance, even if imprisoned or marginalized.
Their continued presence would have made it harder for the regime to claim broad ecclesiastical legitimacy.
Third, international and domestic politics might have become more dangerous.
A living body of senior Catholic bishops could have encouraged hopes among English Catholics, as well as among Spain, the papacy, and Mary Queen of Scots, that Elizabeth’s settlement was reversible.
That would not necessarily mean immediate rebellion,
but it could have stiffened resistance and increased the sense that England’s confessional future was still undecided.
Even so, it is unlikely that simply keeping those seven bishops alive would have reversed Elizabeth’s religious policy.
Elizabeth had the crown, Parliament, key lay elites, and growing control over patronage.
The Marian episcopate had moral authority but not decisive political power.

Unless their survival were paired with some larger change—such as foreign intervention, a stronger Catholic faction at court, or a succession crisis—they probably could not have restored England to Rome.
So the most plausible counterfactual is not “no Elizabethan settlement,” but “a weaker, more contested, and less smoothly institutionalized Elizabethan settlement in its first decade.”
Protestantism would still likely win in the long run,
but Catholic resistance would have had more senior leadership,
and the regime would have had a harder time turning legal change into a functioning national church.

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." While Rome and Persia lost some cities along the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the Sasanian Empire retains Mesopotamia, and Rome defends the cities on the western coast of the Arabian peninsula, bordering the Red Sea and Judea. The Arabian Empire is then created as a religiously fanatical, militarized, yet mercantile and diplomatic empire. Islam still spreads through Islamic traders, though not as strongly in North Africa or the Mediterranean as a whole thanks to the Roman Tribunal Republic's stability and already existing religions. [By the first millennium CE, Rome's political system works like this:] [Provinces are ruled by Provincial Tribunes, elected by the people of the province from those who have not been in the military for at least four years. Additionally, some large cities, particularly coastal entrepot cities, become provinces in their own right. Each province can pass their own laws and manage their own administration, paying taxes to the Tribunal Treasury in Rome and following senatorial law]. [Each province (plus the city of Rome) elects two senators to represent them in the Tribunal Senate. No senator may have been in the military within the previous four years. The Tribunal Senate has no Consuls, instead having an "Orator," which is basically their Speaker. The longest-serving senator automatically becomes Orator. If the Senate passes a law, it can be vetoed by Provincial Tribunes if at least half of them vote on to veto the Senate law within one year of its passing. Provincial Tribunes may vote to send a law to the Senate for consideration, and if it is sent to the Senate and the Senate approves it, it cannot be vetoed no matter how many tribunes veto it]. [Caesars are appointed by the Senate in a time of dire war with a term of two years, after which point (if the war is still ongoing) the Senate can either replace them or affirm their trust in them. This repeats until the dire war is over]. In 1000 CE, to celebrate one thousand years of popular rule following the Dimidiatio Senatus, celebrations are held across Rome, and the Roman Tribunal Republic changes its formal name to the "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIM), or "Republic between seas," for the grand republic lies between multiple seas: Mare Ponticum (the Black Sea), Mare Mediterraneus (the Mediterranean Sea), Mare Hibericum (Atlantic Ocean west of Iberia and the Canary Islands), Mare Britannicum (the North Sea and Atlantic Ocean around Britain and Ireland), and Mare Rubrum (the Red Sea and Indian Ocean). Thoughts?

rubrics.question_focus: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?

criteria.name: Point-of-Divergence Fidelity and Late Republican Political Mechanics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly handles the premise that Sulla fights Mithridates while Marius, rather than Sulla, marches on Rome, using accurate Roman political institutions, factions, procedures, and actors circa 88-86 BCE.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or misstates the premise; treats Rome as a modern state or invents impossible institutions without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Uses the premise but relies on major anachronisms or simplistic populares-vs-optimates assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Captures basic factional conflict, Senate politics, tribunician power, and Marius's role, with some inaccuracies.
criteria.7-8: Shows strong command of Roman procedures, client networks, magistracies, mobs, legality, and factional constraints.
criteria.9-10: Builds the divergence from precise late-Republican mechanics, including Senate sessions, Italian citizenship, veterans, urban violence, and Marius's age/health.

criteria.name: Military Plausibility: Rome, Sulla, Marius, and Mithridates
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically models military capacity, command legitimacy, army loyalty, logistics, and the interaction between Sulla's eastern campaign and Marian control of Rome.
criteria.1-2: Depicts armies, commanders, or battles in ways incompatible with Roman military reality.
criteria.3-4: Mentions military conflict but ignores logistics, veteran loyalty, or Sulla's historical battlefield advantages.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible broad military sequence but leaves key command or supply mechanisms underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains why soldiers follow particular leaders, how Sulla returns or is contained, and how Rome could be defended.
criteria.9-10: Integrates Mithridatic-war constraints, Italian recruitment, urban warfare, provincial commands, and the likely limits of citizen militias or emergency garrisons.

criteria.name: Institutional Evolution and Anti-Sullan Aftermath
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the plausibility of downstream Roman political development after a Marian or populares victory, including whether reforms, purges, tribunician expansion, or anti-general safeguards emerge coherently.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to a wholly new regime with no causal bridge from Republican norms.
criteria.3-4: Adds institutions such as a tribunal republic or standing city guard without explaining who supports them or why.
criteria.5-6: Connects victory to some reforms but underplays elite resistance, legality, or gradualism.
criteria.7-8: Shows institutional change as contested, incremental, and rooted in Roman precedent and factional bargaining.
criteria.9-10: Convincingly traces how proscriptions, land reform, Italian citizenship, military commands, tribunician powers, and safeguards against marches on Rome evolve from the altered civil war.

criteria.name: Long-Range Mediterranean and Eurasian Consequence Chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer coherently extends the counterfactual across centuries, including Rome's survival, Persia, Christianity, Islam, Germanic/Celtic relations, trade, and invasions such as the Huns.
criteria.1-2: Makes sweeping claims about Christianity, Islam, Persia, or medieval geopolitics with no causal connection.
criteria.3-4: Provides a long timeline but relies mostly on arbitrary butterfly effects or namedrop history.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major downstream effects with partially plausible but uneven causal links.
criteria.7-8: Explains how altered Roman institutions reshape religion, migration, diplomacy, trade, and imperial frontiers over time.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a disciplined centuries-long chain, distinguishing robust consequences from fragile contingencies and addressing major Mediterranean, Near Eastern, and European knock-on effects.

criteria.name: Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids internal contradictions, calibrates confidence, and distinguishes plausible mechanisms from speculative or story-driven elements in this specific Roman counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself repeatedly or presents implausible outcomes as certain without reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent ideas but frequent unsupported leaps, overconfidence, or incompatible assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent, with some uncertainty noted, but contains unresolved tensions or thin mechanisms.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags speculative branches, manages causal dependencies, and avoids most contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Offers a tightly controlled counterfactual model with explicit assumptions, alternative paths, proportional causation, and no major contradictions across the ancient-to-medieval timeline.

items.model_answer:
If Sulla had gone east to fight Mithridates as in real history, but Marius had been the one to march on Rome first, the Roman Republic would probably still have entered a cycle of civil war, but the political meaning of that crisis would have changed in important ways. The likely result is not a stable Marian victory, but a more chaotic and less legitimate seizure of power that weakens Marius’s standing, strengthens Sulla’s eventual claim to be the savior of the state, and may even make Sulla’s later dictatorship harsher and easier to justify in Roman political culture.

The first thing to notice is that Sulla’s original march on Rome in 88 BCE was shocking precisely because it broke a taboo. He claimed he was defending his lawful command against political enemies who had used violence and legislation to strip it from him. If we reverse the action and make Marius the first Roman commander to lead troops on the city, then Marius becomes the obvious author of the taboo-breaking act. That matters because Roman elite politics depended heavily on appearances of legality and ancestral custom. Marius already had enemies among the senatorial class, and although he had prestige as the conqueror of Jugurtha and the Cimbri, he did not have the same constitutional argument Sulla had for defending a duly assigned command. If Marius marches first, many neutrals in the Senate and among the Italian elites are more likely to see him as an aging strongman grasping for one last eastern command and personal revenge.

In the short term, Marius could probably take Rome if he had troops willing to follow him. The city was not designed to resist a determined army, and political violence had already become normal. Once in control, he and his allies would likely purge opponents, force through legislation, and try to secure the Mithridatic command for Marius. But this is where the scenario becomes unstable. Marius in 88 was old, in poor health, and politically dependent on radical allies such as Sulpicius. His coalition was less coherent than it looked. If he seizes Rome, he still has to solve the problem of Sulla and the eastern war. Since Sulla is already on the way east in this scenario, Marius would either need to recall him, replace him, or send another force after him. None of those options are easy. Sulla had loyal veterans and personal authority; simply declaring him an outlaw would not remove him.

That means the eastern war becomes the hinge of the whole counterfactual. Sulla in the east would now be in an even stronger propaganda position than he was historically. He could present himself not as the first violator of the Republic, but as the lawful magistrate and commander whose enemies had seized Rome by force while he was serving the state abroad. Fighting Mithridates successfully would magnify that legitimacy. Every victory in Greece and Asia Minor would increase his prestige, attract support from senators fleeing Marian rule, and reassure allies and provincials that he, not Marius, represented Roman order. In effect, Marius’s march would hand Sulla the moral high ground.

Marius himself might not live long enough to consolidate his revolution. Historically he died in early 86 BCE, shortly after taking power again. That fact is crucial. Even if he marched on Rome first and controlled the city, his death would likely leave his faction fragmented. The Marian movement was never just Marius; it included Cinna, Carbo, and other populares or anti-Sullan figures. But without Marius’s prestige, the regime would become a coalition of convenience rather than a personal domination. Cinna might still emerge as the central figure, but now he would inherit a government founded even more openly on military seizure of the capital. That would make compromise with Sulla harder, not easier.

So the most probable medium-term outcome is a Sullan return from the east under even more favorable conditions than in actual history. Historically, when Sulla came back in 83 BCE, he could already claim military glory and support from many aristocrats. In this alternate version, he returns not as a man who had himself first marched on Rome and thereby tainted his cause, but as the avenger of a Rome violated by Marius. That likely broadens his coalition. More senators, equestrians, and municipal elites in Italy might back him earlier. Pompey, Crassus, and other ambitious men would still have strong incentives to join him, perhaps even more readily. The war in Italy might therefore be shorter, though still brutal.

If Sulla wins under those conditions, the aftermath could be even more severe. Historically, Sulla justified his dictatorship as a restoration of the Republic after revolutionary disorder, but his own earlier actions complicated that claim. In this scenario, he has a cleaner narrative: Marius broke the sacred barrier, Marius and his followers murdered citizens, and Sulla returned from a foreign war to restore law. That could make the proscriptions politically easier to sell and perhaps broader in scope, because resistance to them among the elite would be weaker. Sulla’s constitutional reforms might also face less immediate opposition. Ironically, Marius marching first could produce a stronger, more confident Sullan settlement.

Would this save the Republic in the long run? Probably not. The deeper structural problems remain: armies loyal to generals, competition for extraordinary commands, the political integration of Italy after the Social War, and the inability of republican institutions to manage elite rivalry. In fact, having Marius rather than Sulla initiate the military seizure of Rome does not remove the precedent; it merely changes who bears the blame. Once one Roman commander has marched on the city, others can do so. The taboo is still broken. Caesar’s later path becomes no less imaginable, and perhaps more so, because the lesson would still be that armed force decides constitutional disputes.

There is also a chance of a more dramatic divergence if Marius’s seizure of Rome collapses quickly. If his support is weaker than expected, or if the city resists long enough for anti-Marian forces to rally, he could fail and be politically ruined before Sulla even returns from the east. In that case Sulla might never need a second civil war on the same scale; he could finish Mithridates and come home to dominate politics with less bloodshed. But this seems less likely than a temporary Marian success followed by a stronger Sullan comeback, because Rome’s institutions were already too compromised to contain a determined armed intervention.

So the best overall answer is that if Marius marched on Rome while Sulla fought Mithridates, Marius would probably win the city briefly but lose the larger contest. He would be remembered as the first man to turn a Roman army against Rome, while Sulla would return from the east with enhanced legitimacy, broader support, and an even stronger claim to refound the state by force. The Republic would still be fatally damaged, but the title “heir to Sulla” in political method might belong first to Marius in this scenario, even as Sulla remained the ultimate victor.
