criteria.5-6: Correctly covers the main fixes and gives plausible first-order effects on speed, reliability, altitude use, or pilot comfort.
criteria.7-8: Connects specific modifications to concrete performance changes while noting remaining issues such as controls, roll rate, or dive flaps.
criteria.9-10: Provides a technically grounded, nuanced account of the NACA changes, their limits, likely production incorporation, and interaction with later P-38 variants.

criteria.name: Operational and tactical causal chain in the European air war
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer traces effects from an improved early P-38 to 8th Air Force escort operations, bomber losses, fighter group retention, pilot training, Luftwaffe attrition, and escort doctrine.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to broad war outcomes with little or no operational reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Gives a simple claim such as 'better escorts reduce losses' without explaining timing, units, tactics, or opposition.
criteria.5-6: Explains plausible changes to bomber escort capability and loss rates, with some attention to 1943-44 conditions.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain involving P-38 deployment, high-altitude reliability, training, fighter mix, and Luftwaffe responses.
criteria.9-10: Integrates aircraft performance, 8th AF decisions, escort range, combat tactics, attrition dynamics, and timing into a convincing operational counterfactual.

criteria.name: Industrial, logistical, and procurement constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for wartime production pressures, Lockheed capacity, Allison engine supply, Merlin/P-51 competition, cost of twin-engine fighters, retrofit versus production-line changes, and USAAF procurement behavior.
criteria.1-2: Ignores production and procurement constraints or assumes unlimited rapid adoption.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges constraints vaguely but does not apply them to the P-38, P-51, or USAAF choices.
criteria.5-6: Discusses key constraints such as twin-engine cost, production disruption, or competing fighter programs.
criteria.7-8: Balances improved P-38 attractiveness against realistic factory, engine, logistics, and training limitations.
criteria.9-10: Shows detailed causal reasoning about how procurement, production blocks, spare parts, engines, and opportunity costs would shape the alternate fighter force.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and proportionality
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer plausibly extends the counterfactual beyond immediate performance, including bomber campaign tempo, P-51 demand, Normandy timing, postwar reputation, P-38K or F-82 implications, and possible Korean War service, without exaggeration.
criteria.1-2: Presents implausible sweeping outcomes such as decisively changing the war with no chain of support.
criteria.3-4: Mentions downstream effects but treats them as automatic or disconnected from earlier mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several plausible downstream consequences while keeping war-outcome claims moderate.
criteria.7-8: Explores second- and third-order effects with appropriate caveats about logistics, strategy, and competing bottlenecks.
criteria.9-10: Offers a well-scaled long-range analysis distinguishing likely, possible, and unlikely effects across wartime and postwar trajectories.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer clearly distinguishes evidence, inference, and speculation; handles uncertain items such as Meredith effect, dive flaps, canopy changes, automatic engine controls, and P-38K adoption; and avoids internal contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident unsupported claims, contradicts itself, or ignores uncertainty entirely.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but still relies on inconsistent or overconfident assertions.
criteria.5-6: Generally separates likely from speculative outcomes and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Explicitly calibrates uncertain mechanisms, alternative paths, and dependencies while maintaining a coherent scenario.
criteria.9-10: Consistently manages uncertainty, flags weak evidence, compares plausible alternatives, and preserves internal causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II, the biggest likely effect is that the aircraft would have become a far more consistently successful long-range fighter much earlier, especially in Europe. The P-38 was already fast, heavily armed, and had excellent range, but it suffered from important problems in compressibility dives, high-altitude handling, cockpit heating, engine management complexity, and reliability in cold European conditions. If NACA had solved a substantial share of those issues early, the aircraft’s combat record and strategic role could have changed a lot.

In the short term, the USAAF would probably have had a better escort fighter before the P-51 fully matured into that role. That matters because one of the central air-war problems in 1943 was getting bombers deep into enemy territory with fighter protection. A better early-war P-38 would likely have reduced bomber losses on some long-range missions and improved the performance of escort units over Western Europe. It would not automatically replace the P-51, since the Mustang still had major advantages in simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and high-altitude efficiency, but it could have narrowed the gap enough that the P-38 remained a first-rank escort fighter in Europe rather than becoming more marginal there.

In the Mediterranean and Pacific, the effects might have been even stronger. The P-38 was already highly valuable in those theaters because its range was crucial. A significantly improved version entering service earlier would likely have increased Allied air superiority sooner, improved interception capability over long distances, and made reconnaissance, ground attack, and anti-shipping missions more effective. In the Pacific especially, where distances were enormous and twin-engine range mattered greatly, an earlier-optimized P-38 could have increased pressure on Japanese air and naval operations and perhaps accelerated Allied control of key areas. American aces and long-range units there might have become even more effective.

There could also have been industrial and doctrinal consequences. If the P-38 had performed better earlier, the USAAF might have invested more heavily in refining and producing it rather than shifting emphasis so decisively toward the P-51 for European escort work. Training pipelines would also have adapted: pilots and mechanics might have become more proficient with twin-engine fighter operations sooner, reducing operational losses caused by complexity. The aircraft’s reputation, which was mixed in Europe and much better elsewhere, would likely have improved across the board.

Still, the change should not be exaggerated. Even a much-improved P-38 would not by itself transform the war. Allied victory depended on production scale, pilot training, radar, logistics, intelligence, and overwhelming industrial power. The P-51, P-47, and other aircraft would still matter enormously. Also, “significantly improved” could mean different things: if NACA only fixed aerodynamic issues like compressibility, the impact would be meaningful but limited; if it also solved engine reliability, cockpit environment, and maintenance complexity, then the effect could be substantially larger.

So the most plausible answer is that an early, significantly improved P-38 would have given the Allies a better long-range fighter sooner, especially improving bomber escort in Europe and strengthening already successful operations in the Mediterranean and Pacific. It probably would have raised Allied effectiveness and reduced some losses, but it would not have radically changed the ultimate outcome of the war.

edus.text: If NACA had significantly improved the P-38 early in World War II, the biggest likely effect is that the aircraft would have become a far more consistently successful long-range fighter much earlier, especially in Europe.
The P-38 was already fast, heavily armed, and had excellent range,
but it suffered from important problems in compressibility dives, high-altitude handling, cockpit heating, engine management complexity, and reliability in cold European conditions.
If NACA had solved a substantial share of those issues early, the aircraft’s combat record and strategic role could have changed a lot.
In the short term, the USAAF would probably have had a better escort fighter before the P-51 fully matured into that role.
That matters because one of the central air-war problems in 1943 was getting bombers deep into enemy territory with fighter protection.
A better early-war P-38 would likely have reduced bomber losses on some long-range missions and improved the performance of escort units over Western Europe.
It would not automatically replace the P-51,
since the Mustang still had major advantages in simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and high-altitude efficiency,
but it could have narrowed the gap enough that the P-38 remained a first-rank escort fighter in Europe rather than becoming more marginal there.
In the Mediterranean and Pacific, the effects might have been even stronger.
The P-38 was already highly valuable in those theaters because its range was crucial.

A significantly improved version entering service earlier would likely have increased Allied air superiority sooner, improved interception capability over long distances, and made reconnaissance, ground attack, and anti-shipping missions more effective.

In the Pacific especially, where distances were enormous and twin-engine range mattered greatly, an earlier-optimized P-38 could have increased pressure on Japanese air and naval operations and perhaps accelerated Allied control of key areas.
American aces and long-range units there might have become even more effective.
There could also have been industrial and doctrinal consequences.
If the P-38 had performed better earlier, the USAAF might have invested more heavily in refining and producing it rather than shifting emphasis so decisively toward the P-51 for European escort work.
Training pipelines would also have adapted:
pilots and mechanics might have become more proficient with twin-engine fighter operations sooner, reducing operational losses caused by complexity.
The aircraft’s reputation, which was mixed in Europe and much better elsewhere, would likely have improved across the board.
Still, the change should not be exaggerated.
Even a much-improved P-38 would not by itself transform the war.
Allied victory depended on production scale, pilot training, radar, logistics, intelligence, and overwhelming industrial power.
The P-51, P-47, and other aircraft would still matter enormously.
Also, “significantly improved” could mean different things:
if NACA only fixed aerodynamic issues like compressibility, the impact would be meaningful but limited;
if it also solved engine reliability, cockpit environment, and maintenance complexity, then the effect could be substantially larger.

So the most plausible answer is that an early, significantly improved P-38 would have given the Allies a better long-range fighter sooner, especially improving bomber escort in Europe and strengthening already successful operations in the Mediterranean and Pacific.
It probably would have raised Allied effectiveness and reduced some losses,
but it would not have radically changed the ultimate outcome of the war.

items.question: What If The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons)
human_answers: The problem with keeping "TOS" on the air is its consistently poor ratings. In third season, it never got out of the bottom 50 (&, IIRC, was #52 when cancelled). NBC recognizing the better demos early enough might save it in spite of that, much the same way golf gets broadcast despite poor numbers: it attracts a desirable audience. They had two great opportunities to set up a continuing villain, undermined (I suspect) by inability to cast the same actor each time: "Tribbles" & "Day of the Dove". It would have taken more forethought about what Klingons would be like to achieve it, but I'd have loved "DotD" to end with Kirk saying, "Die well, Kang.", & a surprised Kang to say, "Die well, Kirk."--in essence, to be forced to acknowledge UFP as peers. (I know, I know, they didn't even have the concept for the bat'leth , yet...) Depressingly, the writing would have to get a lot better. Even if you take out "Spock's Brain", you've already been saddled with "Errand of Mercy" (the Organian Treaty) in S.1 & "Omega Glory" in S.2. About half of S.3 is pretty awful. Even Dorothy's "Enterprise Incident" has a major flaw, one that would recur for the rest of the franchise: doesn't Starfleet Intelligence have it's own f*ng operatives? You've also got two big issues: personality conflict between Shat's ego & just about everybody, & Leonard being really sick of playing Spock. That said, I'll be watching to see how you save the show, & what butterflies that has down the road.

NBC CONDUCTS STUDY ON TREK: NIELSEN RATINGS NOT FULLY ACCURATE? NBC is unsure of how to handle Star Trek, the big hit with younger American television viewers but a ratings laggard with the general public. The network conducted a study to determine exactly what it has with the science fiction series and its findings were surprising. They determined that younger Americans often watched Star Trek in groups, and it was one of the most popular shows among the age 20-30 and age 30-40 brackets. They also determined that Captain Kirk, Mr. Spock, and the rest of the characters were extremely popular with young kids, who often wanted to stay up past their bedtimes on Friday night to see where they and the Enterprise would go next. However, NBC found a significant decline in popularity among viewers older than 50. Due to this wide age disparity, NBC is mulling over whether they will place Star Trek on Mondays in The Man From U.N.C.L.E.'s old time slot at 8 PM; U.N.C.L.E. was pulled in January and is unlikely to return to television. The Monday 8 PM time slot is often popular with younger audiences, but comes with great competition as is well known in the industry. NBC contacted Gene Roddenberry, the show's creator, Herb Solow, the showrunner at Paramount, who recently acquired Desilu Studios, and Robert Justman, one of the show's producers, for a planning session to widen the show's popularity for a general audience. Roddenberry objected to NBC's proposal to make Star Trek a show with a more pragmatic, less optimistic future. He also objected to the idea that the show had to appeal to older audiences, arguing that the strength of the show was rooted in the creative storytelling that attracted younger adults and children. Solow and Justman also disagreed to an extent but determined that parts of the show had to be remodeled in order to make it a wider hit. Ideas for the third season were pitched to the network; one was rumored to involve Mr. Spock's brain being removed from his body, while another was rumored to have the Enterprise enter Romulan space unprovoked in order to spy on them, a major diversion from the normal behavior of the Enterprise crew.
items.original_question: What if The Enterprise completes its five year mission (Star Trek survives for 5 seasons) One of the worst decisions ever made by a television network was NBC's cancellation of Star Trek (the Original Series) after its third season in 1969. After two years of middling ratings placed Star Trek in the Friday Night death time slot, at 10:00 PM, so fewer fans would be able to watch the series. In our timeline, NBC killed off Star Trek, but it went to syndication where it became more popular than ever in the 1970s. NBC knew of the depth of Star Trek fandom but had no idea how deep it ran until they no longer made the show. So here we go...the divergence point. NBC REEVALUATING ITS PRIMETIME LINEUP March 1, 1968 NBC, having finished a distant second in the ratings battle with CBS, was forced to reevaluate its primetime lineup to see where they could find potential strength for the fall 1968 television season. Two shows which faced the chopping block this season were The Man From U.N.C.L.E., on Mondays from 8:00 to 9:00 PM, and Star Trek, on Fridays from 8:30 PM to 9:30 PM. The Man From U.N.C.L.E faced a lot of turbulence when showrunners decided to turn the spy show into a comedy. Its ratings, formerly very competitive with CBS, dropped dramatically in the 1967-68 season; NBC is pondering what direction the show can turn to next. Star Trek was rumored to be cancelled because it rated poorly with an audience of older Americans, but its largely young fanbase swarmed NBC with tens of thousands of letters demanding its renewal. NBC is undecided at this point about U.N.C.L.E.'s fate but is bringing Star Trek back for a third season. However, the suits at the Peacock Network are uncertain about which timeslot to place Star Trek in. Could it replace U.N.C.L.E. on Monday or will NBC try to move it later to Friday night, where its chances of survival are slim?

items.model_answer:
If Star Trek: The Original Series had survived long enough for the Enterprise to actually complete its five-year mission on television, the most important change is that Star Trek probably would have become a mainstream success much earlier, and the whole franchise would have developed in a smoother, less improvised way.

In the real timeline, the original series was cancelled after three seasons, and a lot of what made Star Trek into a giant cultural force came later through syndication, fan activism, the animated series, and then the films. If it had run for five full seasons, NBC and the studio would have had much stronger proof that the show could sustain an audience. That likely means Star Trek would not have been remembered first as a “cancelled cult classic,” but as a successful network science-fiction drama that completed its intended arc.

Creatively, two extra seasons would probably have changed the internal identity of Star Trek. The show would have had more time to deepen Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and the broader crew, and to revisit worlds, enemies, and political ideas that in reality were left underdeveloped. The Federation, Starfleet, and the Klingons in particular might have been defined more clearly much earlier. The sense of a genuine long voyage through space would also have landed more fully; as aired, the “five-year mission” is iconic, but it was never actually completed on screen. Finishing it would have given the series a stronger narrative closure.

That said, there is an important complication: by the third season the budget was strained, morale was down, and network support had weakened. So a fourth and fifth season are not automatically better seasons. If the show simply limped on under the same conditions, it could have produced more uneven episodes and damaged its reputation. For this counterfactual to really matter, the show would need either better scheduling, better funding, or at least more stable production. If that happened, the extra years could have been some of the most important in establishing the franchise’s canon and tone.

The later history of Star Trek would likely change a lot. The animated series might never happen, or would happen differently, because there would be less need to “revive” a recently cancelled property. The first wave of fandom might still grow, but it would be less centered on saving a lost show and more around extending a successful one. Star Trek conventions and fan culture would still exist, but perhaps with a slightly less oppositional, grassroots identity. The famous story of fans rescuing Star Trek from cancellation is one of the foundations of modern fandom; if the show lasts five seasons, that myth is weaker.

The movies would also probably be different. In our timeline, Star Trek: Phase II was conceived in the 1970s as a return to television, then became Star Trek: The Motion Picture after Star Wars changed Hollywood’s view of science fiction. If TOS had already completed a respected five-season run, Paramount might have moved earlier either toward a sequel series or toward feature films with more confidence. The franchise might have reached the big screen sooner, or with a different cast balance and tone. It is even possible that some ideas later used in The Next Generation or the films would have been used up in seasons four and five of the original show.

There is also a broader television-history effect. A five-season Star Trek would likely have strengthened the position of serious science fiction on American television in the early 1970s. Networks might have been a little more willing to back ambitious speculative shows, especially ones mixing adventure with social commentary. Star Trek was already influential, but a longer original run would have made that influence more immediate and institutional rather than delayed and retrospective.

At the level of franchise mythology, completing the mission would have changed how people think about the Enterprise crew. Kirk’s era might feel more complete and self-contained, more like a finished chapter than a brilliant fragment that later generations kept expanding. The original cast might become even more dominant in the public imagination, which could have made it slightly harder for later incarnations like The Next Generation to step out from their shadow. In our timeline, TNG benefited from there being a gap and a sense that Star Trek was bigger than one cancelled 1960s show. A fuller, more definitive five-season TOS might have made succession trickier.

So the short answer is: if the Enterprise had completed its five-year mission on TV, Star Trek probably becomes more successful sooner, more narratively complete, and more clearly defined in its original form. But it might also lose some of the underdog, fan-saved quality that became central to its legend. Ironically, part of Star Trek’s power in real history came from the fact that it did not finish cleanly; it had to be rediscovered, defended, and rebuilt. A five-season run would likely make it stronger as a 1960s-70s television success, but possibly a little less mythic as a cultural comeback story.

In the real timeline, the original series was cancelled after three seasons,
and a lot of what made Star Trek into a giant cultural force came later through syndication, fan activism, the animated series, and then the films.
If it had run for five full seasons,
NBC and the studio would have had much stronger proof that the show could sustain an audience.
That likely means Star Trek would not have been remembered first as a “cancelled cult classic,”

Creatively, two extra seasons would probably have changed the internal identity of Star Trek.
The show would have had more time to deepen Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and the broader crew,

The Federation, Starfleet, and the Klingons in particular might have been defined more clearly much earlier.

as aired, the “five-year mission” is iconic,
but it was never actually completed on screen.
Finishing it would have given the series a stronger narrative closure.

by the third season the budget was strained, morale was down, and network support had weakened.
So a fourth and fifth season are not automatically better seasons.
If the show simply limped on under the same conditions,
it could have produced more uneven episodes and damaged its reputation.
For this counterfactual to really matter, the show would need either better scheduling, better funding, or at least more stable production.

Star Trek conventions and fan culture would still exist,
but perhaps with a slightly less oppositional, grassroots identity.

if the show lasts five seasons, that myth is weaker.

then became Star Trek: The Motion Picture after Star Wars changed Hollywood’s view of science fiction.

items.question: What If Complicate the US Civil War
human_answers: No Free State even tried to secede, and 4 Slave States stayed in the Union. The Constitution conceives of no right of secession. The only theoretical way the Union can be dissolved is in a Convention of the States. Kentucky is the only State I can think of that might have decided to join the CSA. If the Union Army had invaded Kentucky at the onset of civil war she might have gone South. Most of the States population lived in or near the Ohio Valley and although Southern in culture they were economically tied more with the States north of the river. Kentucky was not so dependent on Slavery as to be willing to fight for it. Geography forced NC to join the CSA, and Delaware to stay in the USA. No Free State had any realistic chance or convincing reason to leave the Union. The economic, cultural, and political pull of the Union was too strong for the Free States to break away. The Free States held the majority of the population, industry, rail links, shipping, national finance, food production, international commerce, and sources of gold & silver. These factors are the ones that are usually discussed in assessing why the Union won the war and they are also the reasons the Union held together. There must be a compelling reason to break away from the center of national power. Slavery was the economic and emotional issue that could do it. No Free State had so strong a grievance to secede. Virginia was a State that stood on a knifes edge till Fort Sumpter forced the issue. If the Old Dominion stayed with the Union North Carolian might've stayed in to. In that scenario the ACW would last 2 years with half the death toll. However, this is really unlikely because Virginia was simply unwilling to fight against the rest of the South. The positions of the States were pretty fixed and only a much earlier POD would be needed to change the lineup of States.

This the top paragraph of my comment of that video: The 1792 Presidential Succession Act was for if BOTH the President and Vice President died or were unavailable to serve during their terms of office. Under a scenario in which President-Elect Lincoln is assassinated, then on March 4 Hannibal Hamblin takes the oath of office as Vice President then immediately takes the oath of office for President. Cody forgot that John Tyler was the first Vice President to become President, the second was Millard Fillmore in 1850 when Zachary Taylor died. So there were two examples of Vice Presidents becoming President before Lincoln's assassination (whenever it happens). And in case anyone wants to bring up the Electoral College, it was certified on February 13 so if Lincoln is shot February 23 which I assume the POD takes place on then Hamblin becomes President. So Cody's badly researched scenario for outgoing Vice President Breckinridge (who is NOT the President Pro Tempore) becoming President then getting kicked out for Seward is complete garbage.
items.original_question:
AHC: Complicate the US Civil War

Some time ago, somewhere, I stumbled upon some talk about the US Civil War - and of course, the good ol' debate what it was all about appeared - states rights, whatnot; but then, a single person rugged the whole debate with an argument that went something along these lines: The American Civil War was about states' rights, but not their rights to slavery - instead, it was about the states' rights to secede. This I found to be, pretty much, the final word on that whole argument - sure, slavery was the cause of the Civil War - but in the same manner tensions between Great Powers were the cause of WW1. Whereas the World War was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand, essentially making the war about it in the first place - the Civil War wasn't started by slavery merely existing or not existing, but instead by the Southern states seceding, making the entire war about secession in the first place. This also tracks with the fact that several states only seceded after the start of the war (such as Arkansas), after President Lincoln ordered all states to mobilize troops. Now, with that in mind, I have a challenge for the esteemed posters of this venerable Forum: without changing the cause, nor the trigger for the war (it has to be over slavery, and it must be triggered by secession), complicate the sides of the war. For example, a free state siding with the Confederacy counts as a complication, and so does a slave state siding with the Union. Note that the latter already happened, in the form of Delaware and Maryland - now let's be clear, I'm not talking about this being a "make Maryland secede" challenge: the weirder the pick, the better - I'm talking Confederate Michigan and Union Mississippi tier. You may, however, shift when the war occurs. Good luck, and happy imagining!

items.model_answer:
If the U.S. Civil War had been “complicated” further, the most important question is: complicated in what way? The war was already driven by slavery, secession, constitutional conflict, economics, regional identity, and military strategy. But several additional factors could have made it much longer, bloodier, and more politically unstable.

The biggest complication would have been foreign intervention. If Britain or France had formally recognized the Confederacy, or even pressured the Union strongly enough, the South might have gained diplomatic legitimacy, loans, naval assistance, or trade protection. That would not necessarily have guaranteed Confederate independence, but it could have prolonged the war and made Union victory much harder. European powers were cautious, though, especially after the Emancipation Proclamation turned the conflict more clearly into a war against slavery, which made open support for the Confederacy politically dangerous.

Another major complication would have been broader internal division within the North. The Union was not politically unified. There were Democrats who opposed the war, feared federal power, or resisted emancipation. If antiwar sentiment had grown stronger—because of casualties, economic strain, or military defeats—Lincoln might have faced overwhelming pressure to negotiate peace. In that case, the Union could have fractured politically even if it remained stronger militarily.

The border states were also crucial. If states like Kentucky or Missouri had fully joined the Confederacy, the strategic map would have changed dramatically. These states were important for rivers, railroads, manpower, and geography. Their loss would have made it harder for the Union to invade the South and easier for the Confederacy to defend itself. Likewise, if Maryland had seceded, Washington, D.C. would have been nearly surrounded, creating a severe political and military crisis.

Complication could also have come from slave uprisings or larger-scale guerrilla warfare. Enslaved people already resisted in many ways and fled to Union lines, undermining the Southern economy and war effort. If resistance had become more coordinated and violent on a large scale, the Confederacy would have been forced to divert more manpower internally. On the other hand, irregular warfare across the border regions—as happened in places like Missouri—could have spread more widely and made the war even more chaotic and harder to end.

A weaker Union military leadership early in the war could have complicated things too. The North had more resources, but poor coordination and hesitant generals repeatedly delayed victory. If the Union had suffered more major defeats, or if Confederate leaders had translated battlefield success into diplomatic recognition or Northern political collapse, the outcome could have become uncertain. The Civil War was not inevitable in its exact result; Union victory depended on sustaining military pressure and political will over time.

Finally, Reconstruction shows how the war remained complicated even after the battlefield conflict ended. Even with Union victory, the country did not smoothly resolve the issues beneath the war. Racial inequality, white supremacist violence, sectional resentment, and disputes over federal authority continued for decades. So if the war itself had been further complicated—through foreign intervention, deeper Northern division, border-state secession, or prolonged guerrilla conflict—the aftermath would likely have been even more unstable, perhaps leaving the United States permanently divided or producing a much weaker postwar union.

So the short answer is that additional complications would likely have made the Civil War longer, more international, more politically fragile, and potentially less likely to end in a clear Union victory.

edus.text: If the U.S. Civil War had been “complicated” further, the most important question is: complicated in what way?
The war was already driven by slavery, secession, constitutional conflict, economics, regional identity, and military strategy.
But several additional factors could have made it much longer, bloodier, and more politically unstable.
The biggest complication would have been foreign intervention.
If Britain or France had formally recognized the Confederacy, or pressured the Union strongly enough, the South might have gained diplomatic legitimacy, loans, naval assistance, or trade protection.
That would not necessarily have guaranteed Confederate independence,
but it could have prolonged the war and made Union victory much harder.

European powers were cautious, especially after the Emancipation Proclamation turned the conflict more clearly into a war against slavery, which made open support for the Confederacy politically dangerous.
Another major complication would have been broader internal division within the North.
The Union was not politically unified.
There were Democrats who opposed the war, feared federal power, or resisted emancipation.
If antiwar sentiment had grown stronger—because of casualties, economic strain, or military defeats—Lincoln might have faced overwhelming pressure to negotiate peace.
In that case, the Union could have fractured politically even if it remained stronger militarily.
The border states were also crucial.
If states like Kentucky or Missouri had fully joined the Confederacy, the strategic map would have changed dramatically.
Their loss would have made it harder for the Union to invade the South and easier for the Confederacy to defend itself.
Likewise, if Maryland had seceded, Washington, D.C. would have been nearly surrounded, creating a severe political and military crisis.
Complication could also have come from slave uprisings or larger-scale guerrilla warfare.
Enslaved people already resisted in many ways and fled to Union lines, undermining the Southern economy and war effort.
If resistance had become more coordinated and violent on a large scale, the Confederacy would have been forced to divert more manpower internally.
On the other hand, irregular warfare across the border regions could have spread more widely and made the war even more chaotic and harder to end.
A weaker Union military leadership early in the war could have complicated things too.
If the Union had suffered more major defeats, or if Confederate leaders had translated success into diplomatic recognition or Northern political collapse, the outcome could have become uncertain.
The Civil War was not inevitable in its exact result; Union victory depended on sustaining military pressure and political will over time.
Finally, Reconstruction shows how the war remained complicated even after the battlefield conflict ended.
Even with Union victory, the country did not smoothly resolve the issues beneath the war.
Racial inequality, white supremacist violence, sectional resentment, and disputes over federal authority continued for decades.

So if the war itself had been further complicated, the aftermath would likely have been even more unstable, perhaps leaving the United States permanently divided or producing a much weaker postwar union.

So the short answer is that additional complications would likely have made the Civil War longer, more international, more politically fragile, and potentially less likely to end in a clear Union victory.

items.question: What If Break the British-Russian Alliance
human_answers: A some things that could happen.: During the Russo-Japanese War you have: - the 2nd Pacific Sqn hit something with their guns in British waters - When they do get to Pacific the French assist them and they do a bit better - Russia as they did a bit better demand more and more from Japan - Japan moves closer to the UK sphere as they feel like both Russia and France is ganging up on them - Russia demands that UK to not get involved - the Royal Navy parks some ships just outside Port Arthur for "training" - Japanese diplomats don't make crazy demands and sour some of the Anglo-Japanese relationship. In Germany - The Kaiser see that they will not be able to out build the Royal Navy but sees that France and Russia are what they need to prepare for - The German navy decides that they need a pile of fast cruisers to protect any overseas holdings that they have and leaves the battleship race - As people suggested Kaiser Wilhelm II does not have a disability In the Middle East and Asia - Russia and Britain have even greater cold war on Persian control - Russia is found to be assisting the start of Indian independence groups (not 100% sure on time line with that ) - Russia is seen to be making demands on China and trade I am sure there are more PoD but this just popped in my head

Three major factors were at play in the Russo-British diplomatic relations at the turn of the century. 1. Generational change at the Foreign Office, with the rise of more eurocentric and anti-German key decisionmakers. 2. The failed French attempts to form an anti-British coalition during Second Boer War. This more or less forced Britain to come to terms with France, or accept the fact that von Holstein had been right, and that by merely waiting Germany could indeed ultimately dictate terms for her new treaties with Britain. 3. The Eastern Question and the Boxer war were drawing new powers in to the old Great Game in Asia, and Britain had to react to the rising power of Japan and their genuine attempts to strike a bargain with expansionist Russia that had just occupied northern Manchuria and was viewing the Korean peninsula as the logical next target. Combined with the determined naval buildup of Franco-Russian alliance and Germany, the international status quo of the late 1800s was becoming untenable. While France was fumbling, her governments were also pouring in vast amounts of money and building a naval force explicitly tailored to counter the Royal Navy. Russian naval buildup also seemed most formidable on paper before the Russo-Japanese war, and first and foremost her land armies seemed poised to sweep to northern India at any moment in the prewar fears of the Committee of Imperial Defence. Lansdowne tried to sort out this challenge out by solving all outstanding imperial disputes on a case-by-case basis, which led him to support both the Anglo-Japanese alliance and reconciliation with France. And after that, only Russia and Germany were left - and Russia seemed so weak after 1905 that Britain sought to strike a bargain with Nicholas II not out of fear of Russian power, but because it seemed like a real risk that humiliated Russia would reapproach Germany instead! Because of these decisions Sir Edward Grey inherited a much more fixed diplomatic board. He, in turn, fatally fumbled it all by trying to build a new balancing act to maintain some sort of strategic ambiguity, when pre-existing treaties and commitments meant that the only way to deter German expansionism and a new major war was through clear and determined military posture. But then again, such a commitment to building a large land army was outside of the realm of political possibilities in the pre-1914 British politics of the day. So, you'll need a really early POD, or alternatively a WW1-analogy has to be delayed long enough.

There are a multitude of butterflies that could prevent the July Crisis. The plan to assassinate Franz Ferdinand could have failed to materialize in the first place, it seems like at one point it was called off and then put back on. Maybe the "back on" message gets lost or delayed and it doesn't go forward, and Franz goes to Bosnia unimpeded. There would still be Black Hand terrorism against higher ranking members of the AH government, as their had been prior to the assassination IOTL, but it wouldn't be big enough to cause a July Crisis equivalent. Here's what I'm thinking: In 1915, Russia sours British opinion by demanding much, much more influence in Persia and makes it obvious that they want some sort of naval access in the Persian Gulf, but they aren't explicit about it and it's not part of the renegotiated treaty. It's enough to sour British opinion, but not make them rethink relations altogether. However, things get worse when Greece and the Ottomans escalate tensions over the Aegean islands (this was thought to be the realistic catalyst for a European conflict prior to the July Crisis) and Russia gives full throated support to Greece and observers know that Russia is clearly eyeing to firmly control the Dardanelles either directly or through a proxy like Greece or Bulgaria. Keeping the Ottomans around wasn't a key part of British policy, but the possibility of total Russian dominance in the Middle East is too much for Britain to bare. Finally, AH + Germany clearly favor the Ottomans right in time for the Home Rule Crisis to get even worse, forcing the British to keep more soldiers home. So here we have a Britain that's tied up at home and frazzled abroad. IOTL it was the Ottomans that declared war on Russia, which brought in France and Britain. But here, it's Russia declaring war on the Ottomans, meaning that Britain (and France) don't have a clear entry into this aggressive war.
items.original_question:
AHC: Break the British-Russian Alliance

Hello all. I've been reading up a lot on the buildup to WW1, and one of the more interesting aspects I found was the frayed relations between Russia and Britain. It seems like they were on another sort of collision course over Persia as their agreement over spheres of influence was up for renegotiation in 1915, and Russia was in a much better position to negotiate terms than it was in the aftermath of the Russo-Japanese War. Your challenge is to create a plausible scenario where Russia and Britain can no longer even pretend to be allies. For me, I think an overzealous Russia that asks for too much in 1915 Persia talks could torpedo the alliance, but Russian overreach with regards to the Straits of Constantinople could be another pain point for Britain. A scenario where Britain can't bring itself to support Russia, and Britain itself finds itself completely embroiled in the Home Rule Crisis, would make a very interesting TL.

criteria.3-4: Covers a few relevant issues but misses most central mechanisms such as Persia, India, Japan, France, Germany, or the Ottoman/Straits question.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several important mechanisms but leaves major gaps or treats them as disconnected events.
criteria.7-8: Connects most major mechanisms, including Asian imperial rivalry, naval balance, Franco-Russian obligations, German strategy, and Ottoman or Balkan implications.
criteria.9-10: Comprehensively integrates the Great Game, Russo-Japanese consequences, Anglo-Japanese relations, French diplomacy, German calculations, Persian Gulf/India security, and potential WWI alignment effects.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer traces consequences over time from the initial rupture through later alliance patterns, crises, and possible war outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected events with no causal chain or chronology.
criteria.3-4: Offers a rough sequence but relies on leaps, unexplained reversals, or arbitrary outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly understandable chain from rupture to downstream effects, though some links are underexplained.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent multi-stage timeline showing how British, Russian, German, French, Japanese, and Ottoman choices interact.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a robust long-range scenario where each stage follows from prior incentives, constraints, and perceptions, with clear handling of second- and third-order effects.

criteria.name: Historical Constraint and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids contradictions with known capabilities, treaty commitments, domestic politics, and strategic priorities of the pre-WWI powers.
criteria.1-2: Contains major factual errors or contradictions, such as impossible alliances, anachronistic policies, or ignoring binding commitments entirely.
criteria.3-4: Has several historical inaccuracies or assumes states act against core interests without explanation.
criteria.5-6: Mostly respects historical constraints but includes some questionable assumptions about diplomacy, military capacity, or domestic politics.
criteria.7-8: Generally consistent with known treaties, naval and land capabilities, imperial priorities, and political limits, with only minor issues.
criteria.9-10: Carefully controls for constraints such as British reluctance for a continental army, Russian post-1905 weakness, French dependence on Russia, German naval choices, and Japanese security interests.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Counterfactual Modesty
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer appropriately distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes in an open-ended counterfactual scenario.
criteria.1-2: Presents deterministic claims with no acknowledgment of uncertainty or alternative paths.
criteria.3-4: Uses some hedging but still asserts highly speculative outcomes as inevitable.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty and offers at least one alternative, though likelihoods are not well differentiated.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates probable consequences from contingent possibilities and notes key decision points that could redirect the timeline.
criteria.9-10: Shows excellent calibration by weighing multiple plausible branches, explaining why some outcomes are more likely, and avoiding overconfident claims about WWI, alliance blocs, or imperial collapse.

items.model_answer:
If the British–Russian alliance were broken, the effects would depend on which historical moment you mean, but in general it would have destabilized the balance of power in Europe and Asia and likely changed both diplomacy and war planning in major ways.

If we are thinking about the early 20th century, especially the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 and the broader alignment that fed into the Triple Entente, breaking that relationship would have weakened the anti-German bloc. Britain, France, and Russia were not a formal single alliance in the same way as the Triple Alliance, but their cooperation mattered enormously. Without British–Russian understanding, Germany and Austria-Hungary would have faced a less coordinated opposition. Russia might have been more isolated diplomatically, Britain might have hesitated to support continental commitments, and France would have lost part of the strategic advantage of encircling Germany with allies on both east and west.

That could have altered the path to World War I in several ways. It might have reduced immediate tensions in some imperial regions, since Britain and Russia had long competed in Central Asia and Persia. But it also could have made crises in Europe more dangerous by increasing uncertainty. Germany might have felt freer to pressure France or Russia if it believed Britain and Russia were divided. Alternatively, Britain, fearing Russian expansion without any agreement in place, might have focused more on imperial defense than on European commitments. In that case, the formation of the wartime coalition against the Central Powers would have been slower, weaker, or less certain.

In Asia and the Middle East, a broken British–Russian relationship would likely have revived the “Great Game.” Competition over Afghanistan, Persia, Tibet, and routes toward India would have intensified. Britain’s main fear was Russian movement toward India; Russia’s goal was influence and security along its southern frontier. Without cooperation, both empires would probably have increased military and diplomatic rivalry in those buffer zones. That could have led to proxy conflicts, stronger local resistance movements being courted by one side or the other, and greater instability in Persia and Afghanistan.

Economically and politically, a break would also have encouraged each side to seek new partners. Britain might have leaned more heavily on Japan, the Ottoman Empire, or even sought some accommodation with Germany under certain conditions. Russia might have moved closer to France alone, or tried to repair ties with Germany if possible. Such a realignment could have reshaped alliance systems across Eurasia.

If the alliance broke during World War I itself, the consequences would have been even more dramatic. Britain depended on Russia to tie down German and Austro-Hungarian forces in the east, while Russia benefited from British finance, supplies, and naval pressure on Germany. A rupture would have relieved pressure on Germany, potentially allowed greater concentration of German force on the Western Front, and weakened the Allies’ overall strategic position. It might have shortened the war or changed its outcome.

So, in the broadest sense, breaking the British–Russian alliance would probably have produced more rivalry in Asia, more uncertainty in Europe, and a weaker counterweight to Germany and Austria-Hungary. Rather than creating a stable peace, it would most likely have made the international system less predictable and more dangerous.

items.question: What If Netherlands being invaded in WW1
human_answers: The Netherands was one of the first nations to declare full mobilisation. This resulted that the Dutch army was fully mobilized and on their positions. The field army, the mobile part, was for 1914 conditions, modern. The other half of the army, the older echelons, manned the forts. The chalange in August was to delay the Germans so the waterline inundations could be set. Considering the beautiful summer of 1914, resulting in low water levels of the rivers, this could be a chalange. The Germans probaly would use 3rd or 4rd welle, erzats units for attacking mid and north netherlands, same training level or below as the Dutch coscript soldiers. If troop movements will take place at the same time as the main attack south? Only 1st and 2nd welle of the 1st Army will cross Limburg and Brabant, which is in the path of advance for the main objective, Paris, France

Evacuation is an option. OTL the English evacuated all the children from London and other cities facing Blitz bombing to the countryside; the RN can well secure the crossing to England for a pretty large number of Dutch noncombatants who aren't deemed more useful staying in the bastion to sustain what production is possible in the circumstances. The only thing the Germans can do to interfere would be to attempt to place their U-boats to interdict, but I believe the subs would be terribly vulnerable to the most elementary ASW methods the RN is inventing on the fly in those narrow waters with their limited channels of access north and south. If this eventually amounts to evacuating half the population or more, it might be a problem to have that many refugees in Britain itself--but from there, there are more options for farther relocation. As far as moving people who otherwise would pose too much a logistic burden without being useful to the war economy even in Britain, Canada is not too far on; during WWII that is where German and other Axis POWs wound up being sent until the USA entered and more of them went to American camps where they generally were employed as farm labor. Free allies of the Commonwealth will be welcome enough, plus the Dutch have their own colonies as well. The Netherlands being all in as Entente allies pretty much from the get-go is bad news for Germany too as others noted. To add to such basic concerns as the Germans losing their major back door to try to circumvent the blockade OTL, not to mention losing such resources as the Fokker airplane works, I suppose the DEI forces, such as they are, will move immediately to attack nearby German colonies in their region, which means first of all German New Guinea; in the ATL Japan will acquire fewer of the German Pacific possessions as the Dutch will be taking some of them instead. Short run, the Entente will have little trouble rushing in food and other vital supplies, longer run they sort out the population in the bastion to maximize their effectiveness in holding and pushing back their siege while evacuating people less useful there, many of whom will be useful elsewhere such as in British war industries. None of them need be left to starve! Meanwhile the Entente has an excellent complex of ports and the Germans have another front to worry about. It is pretty obvious why the Germans had the wit not to open this door OTL, and if it was only a matter of chance they avoided it--well that was a lucky chance indeed. It seems pretty clear to me they just knew better and would avoid doing this unless handed an industrial strength Idiot Ball with a lead paint chaser.

Hmmm, I am curious as to if the Dutch are given a mandate over any bit of New Guinea at the end of this war. Maybe it is like with the French and British giving up claims of land in Egypt to Italy, with French and British Guiana having their borders changed in the interior in favor of Dutch claims? The British are going to be unable to get the Japanese to give up anything they get, and they believed IOTL that taking away areas from the Dominions to give back to the Germans would poison relations with them, and that they would need to find land elsewhere to pay off the Germans, if needed for a peace. The land wasn't exactly the most valuable anyways. The Dutch are unlikely to want colonies that are too out of the way of Indonesia that would make e them split their manpower in the future. Getting some land from Germany in Europe would be ideal, though the Germans had already Germanized the area a lot. How brutal the invasion is will have an effect.

items.original_question: What if Netherlands being invaded in WW1 Suppose the Netherlands is invaded in WW1, does the Netherlands stand a chance of withstanding such an attack? Most likely, the Dutch army will retreat behind the New Dutch Waterline ( Nieuwe Hollandse Waterlinie ). The fortresses are already obsolete, AFAIK. However, the inundation zones may still be an impassable obstacle.... Most obvious POD is that Molkte decides against a coup de main on Liege, but instead decides to bypass Liege to the north. This is consistent with Schlieffen's original "Schlieffen plan". The German army moves roughly between Maastricht and Roermond on its way to northern France.... Assuming that France is not defeated in this ATL either, will attention shift north? Will Germany want to occupy all of the Netherlands? Will the waterline hold? What does it mean for Germany's chances in WW1? It is also fine to discuss other POD's in which the Netherlands is invaded. The Dutch defenses are shown on this map I made:

items.model_answer:
If Germany had invaded the Netherlands in World War I, the effects would likely have been significant both militarily and politically, though probably not enough by themselves to change the ultimate outcome of the war in Germany’s favor.

The most immediate reason Germany might have invaded would have been strategic convenience. In 1914, the Schlieffen-style war planning depended on sweeping through Belgium to outflank French defenses. The Netherlands, especially the southern region around Maastricht and the lower Rhine, could have offered additional routes for troop movement and logistics. Invading it might have made German operations in the west somewhat easier in the opening weeks, at least on paper.

But the costs would have been serious. Dutch neutrality had important value to Germany. As long as the Netherlands stayed neutral, it remained a channel for trade, finance, intelligence, and access to overseas goods despite the British blockade. Rotterdam in particular functioned as a vital economic gateway. If Germany invaded, that neutral outlet would disappear. Britain would almost certainly have tightened its naval and economic pressure even further, and the Dutch colonial empire, especially the Dutch East Indies, would be exposed to Allied seizure or isolation. Germany would gain territory in Europe but lose an important indirect economic lifeline.

An invasion would also have widened the diplomatic shock caused by the attack on Belgium. Britain had already entered the war over Belgium’s neutrality and the broader balance of power. Violating Dutch neutrality too would reinforce the image of Germany as openly disregarding international law. That would strengthen Allied propaganda, make neutral opinion more hostile to Germany, and possibly push fence-sitting countries further toward the Entente sooner.

Militarily, the Dutch army was smaller than the Belgian one and the country might have been overrun relatively quickly in many areas. However, the Netherlands was not easy terrain for large-scale operations. Waterlines, rivers, dikes, and the possibility of deliberate flooding made parts of the country defensible. Even if Germany occupied much of it, that would require troops, occupation forces, and supply commitments at a moment when speed was essential. Any delay in the opening campaign could undermine the very advantage Germany hoped to gain.

There is also the British angle. A German presence on the Dutch coast would alarm Britain greatly. Control, or attempted control, of ports facing the North Sea could be seen as an even greater threat to British security than Germany’s move through Belgium alone. Britain would almost certainly commit to preventing Germany from benefiting from Dutch ports and coastline. The Royal Navy could blockade and attack aggressively, and Britain might support Dutch resistance or seize Dutch colonial possessions.

For the Netherlands itself, the consequences would be severe. Instead of remaining outside the direct fighting while mobilized and economically strained, it would become a battlefield and occupied zone. Civilian hardship, destruction of infrastructure, refugee movements, food shortages, and possibly flooding from defensive measures would all become much worse. Dutch politics after the war would also be transformed, likely with stronger anti-German feeling and deeper domestic trauma.

In terms of the larger war, the most plausible outcome is that Germany gains some short-term operational flexibility in 1914 but pays a larger long-term strategic price. It would lose the benefits of Dutch neutrality, intensify British hostility, and burden itself with another occupied country. So the likely result is not a German victory, but a slightly broader and even more economically damaging war for Germany, while making the Netherlands suffer far more than it did historically.

edus.text: If Germany had invaded the Netherlands in World War I, the effects would likely have been significant both militarily and politically,
though probably not enough by themselves to change the ultimate outcome of the war in Germany’s favor.
The most immediate reason Germany might have invaded would have been strategic convenience.
In 1914, the Schlieffen-style war planning depended on sweeping through Belgium to outflank French defenses.
The Netherlands, especially the southern region around Maastricht and the lower Rhine, could have offered additional routes for troop movement and logistics.
Invading it might have made German operations in the west somewhat easier in the opening weeks, at least on paper.
But the costs would have been serious.
Dutch neutrality had important value to Germany.
As long as the Netherlands stayed neutral, it remained a channel for trade, finance, intelligence, and access to overseas goods despite the British blockade.
Rotterdam in particular functioned as a vital economic gateway.
If Germany invaded, that neutral outlet would disappear.
Britain would almost certainly have tightened its naval and economic pressure even further,
and the Dutch colonial empire, especially the Dutch East Indies, would be exposed to Allied seizure or isolation.
Germany would gain territory in Europe but lose an important indirect economic lifeline.
An invasion would also have widened the diplomatic shock caused by the attack on Belgium.
Britain had already entered the war over Belgium’s neutrality and the broader balance of power.
Violating Dutch neutrality too would reinforce the image of Germany as openly disregarding international law.
That would strengthen Allied propaganda, make neutral opinion more hostile to Germany, and possibly push fence-sitting countries further toward the Entente sooner.
Militarily, the Dutch army was smaller than the Belgian one and the country might have been overrun relatively quickly in many areas.
However, the Netherlands was not easy terrain for large-scale operations.
Waterlines, rivers, dikes, and the possibility of deliberate flooding made parts of the country defensible.
Even if Germany occupied much of it, that would require troops, occupation forces, and supply commitments at a moment when speed was essential.
Any delay in the opening campaign could undermine the very advantage Germany hoped to gain.
There is also the British angle.
A German presence on the Dutch coast would alarm Britain greatly.
Control, or attempted control, of ports facing the North Sea could be seen as an even greater threat to British security than Germany’s move through Belgium alone.
Britain would almost certainly commit to preventing Germany from benefiting from Dutch ports and coastline.
The Royal Navy could blockade and attack aggressively,
and Britain might support Dutch resistance or seize Dutch colonial possessions.
For the Netherlands itself, the consequences would be severe.
Instead of remaining outside the direct fighting while mobilized and economically strained, it would become a battlefield and occupied zone.
Civilian hardship, destruction of infrastructure, refugee movements, food shortages, and possibly flooding from defensive measures would all become much worse.
Dutch politics after the war would also be transformed, likely with stronger anti-German feeling and deeper domestic trauma.
In terms of the larger war, the most plausible outcome is that Germany gains some short-term operational flexibility in 1914 but pays a larger long-term strategic price.
It would lose the benefits of Dutch neutrality, intensify British hostility, and burden itself with another occupied country.
So the likely result is not a German victory, but a slightly broader and even more economically damaging war for Germany,
while making the Netherlands suffer far more than it did historically.
