Similar to the Southern Party, the PCs were formed to protect a specific group of peoples' interests. However, unlike the Southerners, the PCs fight for the rights of minorities, well, actually just those of Hispanic origin. There is also a strong Catholic Socialist faction in the party, most likely due to former leader Dolores Huerta. Currently led by Julian Castro.

I had a rather lengthy idea I've been toying around with for a party system for a work of fiction written in my Power Without Knowledge setting that I might write out today but on an unrelated note I've been mulling over the impact of a more successful Joseph Smith presidential run . I'm not suggesting that he win, or even that he not be assassinated, I'm just trying to puzzle out the consequences of his electoral platform surviving his death. Perhaps some sort of alliance with the Liberty Party ? Smith's platform included provisions shrinking the size of Congress and docking their pay, along with the elimination of courts martial and instituting the death penalty for public officials that didn't defend their constituents' constitutional rights, but what suggests at least some buy-in from the Liberty Party was a program of complete emancipation by 1850, with at least some degree of compensation financed by the sale of public land. Smith also argued for the annexation of Texas and Oregon. I understand it's a gamble of long odds (especially regarding constitutional changes and territorial expansion) but perhaps a pragmatic move to adopt compensation as a way to attract votes in slave states that would otherwise dig in their heels at any mention of abolition? It would also almost certainly require butterflying away the LDS move to Utah, leaving them a powerful swing constituency in Illinois. The idea of an openly abolitionist party arising in and surviving the 19th century and explicitly focused on the rights of minority religious and ethnic groups has a lot of promise. *EDIT- In keeping with my new Strange Bedfellows idea for an alternate American history in party systems here's my reinterpretation of the Second Party System: Federalist Party - The sole survivor of the First Party System and the Era of Good Feelings, the Federalist Party was able to claw its way back from the brink in the wake of the shattering of the National Republican Party following the much maligned 1824 election. Advocating a strong central government, Hamiltonian economics and infrastructure spending, the party was aided in its recovery by the influx of anti-Jacksonians leaving the disintegrating National Republicans. Nullifier Party - Intrinsically rooted in the fallout of the Era of Good Feelings, the Nullifier Party was shaped in it's early history by the rise of Andrew Jackson and the fallout of the Nullification Crisis of 1832. Considering himself cheated out of the presidency in 1824 Jackson had joined the Nullifiers out of a belief in populism and states' rights, though he would oppose the doctrine within the party known as "Hard Nullification" (the right of the states to cancel federal laws), instead advocating a policy of limiting government power at the federal level. While in office Jackson tended to side with Southern interests against abolitionism, opposed (but could not dismantle) the Bank of the United States and defied the Supreme Court in the lead up to the Trail of Tears. Liberty Party - As the 19th century went on, national expansion through the annexation of Texas and the Mexican-American War put the issue of slavery at the forefront of the nation's politics. The Federalists would side with northern industrial interests in opposition to the spread of the Peculiar Institution, while Nullifiers, viewing such attempts as federal overreach, became adamant defenders of it. Despite this focus on the issue it wouldn't be until the 1850's that the Liberty Party, the only explicitly abolitionist party in the Union, would gain traction beyond the local level. A party of minority rights and abolitionism, the Libertarians would lead a coalition of freedmen, Mormons and Owenite socialists of all stripes to political action, parlaying a pivotal influence in several midwestern states into a coalition with the Federalists in 1860.
items.original_question:
AHC: Create an exotic party system

So the challenge, inspired by these two excellent examples (all credit to @Wolfram and @TheNixonator , respectively), is to create an alternate political party system for a country using obscure, defunct or marginal political parties or factions that existed in that country historically. Paramilitaries and secret societies pulling a Know-Nothing are allowed. There was some support for Social Credit in the US so I'm counting it as an example. As for the rules: I'm being pretty loose in my definition of party/faction, but please limit it to historical groups that existed in the country you're writing about, or create a scenario where the that country expands if you want to bring in outside groups. Alternate party mergers are acceptable as long as the names of the current major or third parties aren't used. A heterodox blend of political planks makes it more interesting for all involved. I think that about covers it, have at it and try to have a little fun!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Create an exotic party system

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Divergence Logic
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer establishes a clear alternate-history or institutional premise that plausibly produces an exotic party system rather than merely listing random parties.
criteria.1-2: No clear divergence point or premise; parties appear arbitrary or unrelated to the scenario.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a premise, but the link to party formation is weak, vague, or mostly asserted.
criteria.5-6: Provides a recognizable divergence and explains some direct effects on party development.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible divergence with clear causal links to multiple party origins and alignments.
criteria.9-10: Develops a rich, internally grounded counterfactual premise whose institutional, social, and historical consequences strongly explain the whole party system.

criteria.name: Party System Breadth and Distinctiveness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer creates a varied, exotic, and politically meaningful set of parties with distinct identities, constituencies, ideologies, and roles.
criteria.1-2: Provides too few parties or parties are generic labels with little differentiation.
criteria.3-4: Includes several parties, but many overlap ideologically or lack clear bases of support.
criteria.5-6: Creates a functional multiparty system with some distinct platforms and voter blocs.
criteria.7-8: Offers a diverse party ecology with clear ideological niches, regional bases, factions, and political functions.
criteria.9-10: Presents a vivid, memorable, and exotic party system where each party has a distinctive history, constituency, symbolism, and strategic role.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage and Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms by which the new parties emerge, compete, evolve, and affect governance over time.
criteria.1-2: Little or no explanation of how parties form, gain support, or influence politics.
criteria.3-4: Gives limited mechanisms, mostly party platforms without electoral or social dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic formation causes, voter bases, and some electoral consequences.
criteria.7-8: Covers party origins, coalitions, regional strength, factional drift, electoral incentives, and policy effects.
criteria.9-10: Traces long-range dynamics across generations, including realignments, splinters, alliances, media framing, institutional pressures, and governing consequences.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence and Internal Consistency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the created party system remains coherent across time, geography, ideology, and institutions without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible timelines, or mutually incompatible party claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some coherent elements but frequent inconsistencies in ideology, chronology, or influence.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with minor unexplained jumps or tensions between party traits and outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains strong consistency across party histories, platforms, regions, and electoral status.
criteria.9-10: Shows excellent systemic coherence, with tensions explicitly explained as factions, compromises, historical legacies, or strategic adaptations.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Constraint Awareness
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer balances imaginative exoticism with plausible political sociology and acknowledges uncertainty where appropriate.
criteria.1-2: Wildly implausible or deterministic; ignores political constraints and social realities.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible ideas, but relies heavily on unsupported leaps or overconfident claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible, though some assumptions or long-range outcomes are underjustified.
criteria.7-8: Balances creativity with realistic voter behavior, institutions, regional interests, and contingency.
criteria.9-10: Highly imaginative yet disciplined; clearly distinguishes likely outcomes from speculative ones and explains constraints, tradeoffs, and alternative possibilities.

items.model_answer:
Imagine a party system built not around ideology, class, or region, but around time. In this exotic system, political parties represent different attitudes toward the past, present, and future.

One party, the Preservation Party, believes society should move very slowly. Its members argue that traditions, inherited institutions, and long-tested customs are humanity’s safest guide. They do not reject change completely, but they insist that nearly every reform must prove itself against the wisdom of previous generations.

A second party, the Immediate Party, focuses almost entirely on present conditions. It does not care much whether a policy is ancient or visionary; it asks only whether it improves life now. Its politicians are practical, short-cycle thinkers, often popular in times of crisis because they promise visible results rather than grand theories.

A third party, the Horizon Party, represents the future. It supports experimental policies, long-term planning, and investment in projects that may not pay off for decades. It might champion radical technologies, environmental transformation, or social redesign. Critics would call it reckless; supporters would call it visionary.

Elections in such a system would not just be about left versus right, but about which time horizon should dominate government. During war or economic collapse, voters might turn to the Immediate Party. In culturally anxious periods, they might favor the Preservation Party. In moments of optimism, they might empower the Horizon Party.

This system would be exotic because it reorganizes politics around a basic human tension: whether legitimacy comes from what has endured, what works now, or what could exist tomorrow. It could produce richer debates than many modern party systems, though it might also create conflict, since each party would accuse the others of blindness—one trapped in nostalgia, one in short-termism, and one in fantasy.

items.question: What If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon for crewed lunar missions?
human_answers: I don't think you understand SpaceX very well. The Starship "failures" are the result of rapid design-test-redesign, pushing the hardware to its limits to find out just what those limits actually are. I think they are up to the third generation design. If putting a Starship into orbit was so important to them, they'd have done by now. Still in test phase. Falcon 9 (and Heavy) is not about putting maximum mass into space, it is about putting payloads into space at minimum cost. So yes, a single type of engine and propellant all the way to orbit: the upper stage is just a cut-down version of the launcher and Merlin Vacuum is a Merlin 1D with a longer nozzle for more efficiency. Reusing a booster cuts payload mass by about 40%, but they break-even on the second or third flight. Falcon 9 is so cost-efficient that SpaceX is eating everyone else's lunch at this point. It's no Saturn V, to be sure, but it isn't meant to be. Saturn V was designed with each stage optimized just for its specific part of the mission... which made it extremely expensive to develop and build and totally uneconomic. A diametrically opposite design approach.

I actually like the idea of an improved dragon better than what we have with Starship (assuming it ever carries humans). As for using it for lunar missions. Do we need to recreate the Apollo Mission profile or can we build some sort of transfer craft a sort of tug or booster that can be docked with and used to get to and from the moon. We would need a way to refuel it in earth orbit but it may be one way to get Dragon to the moon. And long term it may be better. I have always thought that we needed some sort of “space craft” vs the way we do everything with the vehicle we use to get up and down from earth. That would I suppose be a big task to build and maintain and refuel this transfer vehicle. But it may allow a less powerful system to do the job. And once you have the hardware it is harder to cancel the thing. So we may actually get some long term use.

All true of course, also fully ignored in most cases and specifically in the articles/videos I cited above The "mantra" is simply that Dragon is cheaper and therefor better than Orion. Similar statements about Falcon versus SLS. One of the videos I didn't cite was in fact one that suggests Lunar HLS "Starship" will be used for ferrying the landing party from LEO to LLO where they would use Dragon to land on the Moon and then return to the HLS "Starship" to be ferried back to LEO where Dragon would be used to land on Earth. Ya, IIRC you lose the core stage. Ya it would be 'neat' but keep in mind the Super Draco's are not actually "throttleable" since they are supposed to be used as abort rockets and not landing rockets. The way the propellants are stored at very high pressures in order to get that high thrust for abort and I think that precludes landing use so they likely would have to be redesigned.. Randy
items.original_question: What if Falcon/Dragon to the Moon? Kind of bouncing off this thread as I've run across some of the usual "hype" sources such as this and this , (nothing from SpaceX though which I think is telling) "bragging" about SpaceX's "great new plan" to send crew Dragon to the Moon "sooner than NASA or China" etc, et-al. (Of course they all simply ignore the issues with Dragon going beyond LEO and the fact Orion and SLS are designed to do exactly that but what would I expect ) So the question is essentially "What if SpaceX had continued to iterate and improve Dragon and Falcon Heavy for use in Lunar missions? Granting that as I pointed out here that there's likely no "place" for such a move since the SpaceX to Mars focus was pretty much baked in since the start and with such a short timeline getting a plausible POD is going to be problematic I do wonder if a bit more focus on "Dear Moon" along with Cargo/Crew Dragon couldn't set up a premise where the eventual "HLS" might end up more realistic? Anyway, open for thoughts and comments Randy

items.model_answer:
If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions, the most likely outcome is that the company could have fielded a limited, commercially driven circumlunar capability earlier than Starship, but a full lunar landing architecture would still have been difficult, expensive, and operationally constrained.

Falcon Heavy plus Dragon was always more plausible for missions around the Moon than for landing on it. A crew-rated Dragon launched by Falcon Heavy could, in principle, support a free-return circumlunar flight if enough performance margin, life support duration, radiation protection, communications, and deep-space reentry capability were added. That kind of mission might have happened in the late 2010s or early 2020s if SpaceX had treated it as a core program rather than a publicity concept. It would probably have resembled an upgraded version of the dearMoon or early tourist circumlunar ideas: a few astronauts or private passengers looping around the Moon and returning to Earth without entering lunar orbit for long or attempting a landing.

Actually landing astronauts on the Moon with Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have been much harder. Dragon was not a lunar lander, and turning it into one would have required major redesign. Even if SpaceX revived a propulsive landing variant, a Moon-capable Dragon would need deep-throttling engines, landing sensors, dust tolerance, surface power, ascent capability, and substantial redundancy for crew safety. Falcon Heavy also would not have been able to send a crewed Dragon and all required lunar landing hardware directly to the Moon in one simple launch. That would have pushed SpaceX toward an architecture involving multiple launches, on-orbit assembly, refueling, or separate transfer and landing stages. At that point, the company would essentially be building a smaller, more complex version of what Starship later aimed to do in a more integrated way.

If SpaceX had committed to this path, NASA’s Artemis era might have looked somewhat different. SpaceX could have offered NASA a commercial circumlunar transport service years before Starship Human Landing System was ready. NASA might have used such missions for crew training, deep-space systems validation, or even as an Orion alternative for some roles, though political and institutional factors would still strongly favor SLS/Orion for flagship government missions. For lunar landings, SpaceX might have competed with a modular architecture: Falcon Heavy launches a crew vehicle, another launch sends a lander, and perhaps a third sends a propulsion stage. That might have made SpaceX a more direct competitor to traditional lunar programs earlier, but probably not a cheaper or faster provider of actual landings than the company hoped.

The tradeoff is that continuing Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar development would likely have slowed Starship. SpaceX has finite engineering capacity, and a serious crewed lunar adaptation of Dragon would have absorbed money, management attention, test flights, and safety certification effort. In return, SpaceX might have achieved an earlier but narrower milestone: getting people around the Moon before Starship was ready. But the company would probably have delayed the fully reusable super-heavy-lift system that underpins its longer-term Mars and lunar ambitions. In that sense, SpaceX might have gained a near-term lunar presence while sacrificing some progress toward the much larger architecture it actually wanted.

Commercially, there may have been a viable niche. Wealthy private customers, space agencies outside NASA, or prestige missions could have paid for circumlunar flights. A lunar Dragon program might also have strengthened SpaceX’s position in human deep-space transportation and given it more flight heritage beyond low Earth orbit. But it is unlikely that Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have become the dominant long-term system for sustained lunar exploration. They would have been too limited in payload, too operationally complex, and too expendable compared with the kind of reusable high-capacity system SpaceX ultimately pursued.

So the clearest counterfactual is this: SpaceX could probably have delivered a real crewed circumlunar program with Falcon Heavy and Dragon if it had stayed focused on that goal, and it might have done so earlier than any Starship-based human lunar mission. But for actual lunar landings, Falcon Heavy and Dragon would probably have led to a stopgap architecture—impressive, technically possible, but cumbersome and strategically inferior to a purpose-built reusable system.

edus.text: If SpaceX had continued developing Falcon Heavy and Dragon specifically for crewed lunar missions,
the most likely outcome is that the company could have fielded a limited, commercially driven circumlunar capability earlier than Starship,
but a full lunar landing architecture would still have been difficult, expensive, and operationally constrained.
Falcon Heavy plus Dragon was always more plausible for missions around the Moon than for landing on it.
A crew-rated Dragon launched by Falcon Heavy could, in principle, support a free-return circumlunar flight
if enough performance margin, life support duration, radiation protection, communications, and deep-space reentry capability were added.
That kind of mission might have happened in the late 2010s or early 2020s
if SpaceX had treated it as a core program rather than a publicity concept.
It would probably have resembled an upgraded version of the dearMoon or early tourist circumlunar ideas:
a few astronauts or private passengers looping around the Moon and returning to Earth without entering lunar orbit for long or attempting a landing.
Actually landing astronauts on the Moon with Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have been much harder.
Dragon was not a lunar lander,
and turning it into one would have required major redesign.
Even if SpaceX revived a propulsive landing variant,
a Moon-capable Dragon would need deep-throttling engines, landing sensors, dust tolerance, surface power, ascent capability, and substantial redundancy for crew safety.
Falcon Heavy also would not have been able to send a crewed Dragon and all required lunar landing hardware directly to the Moon in one simple launch.
That would have pushed SpaceX toward an architecture involving multiple launches, on-orbit assembly, refueling, or separate transfer and landing stages.
At that point, the company would essentially be building a smaller, more complex version of what Starship later aimed to do in a more integrated way.
If SpaceX had committed to this path,
NASA’s Artemis era might have looked somewhat different.
SpaceX could have offered NASA a commercial circumlunar transport service years before Starship Human Landing System was ready.
NASA might have used such missions for crew training, deep-space systems validation, or even as an Orion alternative for some roles,
though political and institutional factors would still strongly favor SLS/Orion for flagship government missions.
For lunar landings, SpaceX might have competed with a modular architecture:
Falcon Heavy launches a crew vehicle, another launch sends a lander, and perhaps a third sends a propulsion stage.
That might have made SpaceX a more direct competitor to traditional lunar programs earlier,
but probably not a cheaper or faster provider of actual landings than the company hoped.
The tradeoff is that continuing Falcon Heavy/Dragon lunar development would likely have slowed Starship.
SpaceX has finite engineering capacity,
and a serious crewed lunar adaptation of Dragon would have absorbed money, management attention, test flights, and safety certification effort.
In return, SpaceX might have achieved an earlier but narrower milestone:
getting people around the Moon before Starship was ready.
But the company would probably have delayed the fully reusable super-heavy-lift system that underpins its longer-term Mars and lunar ambitions.
In that sense, SpaceX might have gained a near-term lunar presence
while sacrificing some progress toward the much larger architecture it actually wanted.
Commercially, there may have been a viable niche.
Wealthy private customers, space agencies outside NASA, or prestige missions could have paid for circumlunar flights.
A lunar Dragon program might also have strengthened SpaceX’s position in human deep-space transportation and given it more flight heritage beyond low Earth orbit.
But it is unlikely that Falcon Heavy and Dragon would have become the dominant long-term system for sustained lunar exploration.
They would have been too limited in payload, too operationally complex, and too expendable compared with the kind of reusable high-capacity system SpaceX ultimately pursued.
So the clearest counterfactual is this:
SpaceX could probably have delivered a real crewed circumlunar program with Falcon Heavy and Dragon if it had stayed focused on that goal,
and it might have done so earlier than any Starship-based human lunar mission.

But for actual lunar landings, Falcon Heavy and Dragon would probably have led to a stopgap architecture—impressive, technically possible, but cumbersome and strategically inferior to a purpose-built reusable system.

items.question: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?
human_answers: The only time Aircraft Carriers carry out multi-day attacks on the same location is when they either are providing air cover to an invasion force or have total air superiority. If Pearl Harbour had been a single raid each day for two days the raid on the second day would have suffered serious losses and the patrol aircraft may have located the Carriers which then becomes a very big question of risking a Carrier. Aircraft Carriers are great at projecting power in that they represent overwhelming firepower from unexpected directions at any time. For example look at the exercises carried out between the cold war Royal Navy and the USA. I think it was HMS Ark Royal which involved HMS Ark Royal being the aggressor and striking US bases on the US Eastern Sea Board. up to a week of operations with strikes on a daily basis and undetected due to sneaky sneaky tactics. Aircraft Carriers are also hideously vulnerable to attrition and easily overwhelmed while in contact with shore based aircraft. Naval Aircraft are compromises due to structural needs and limitations caused by operational environment. The exact same engine in an airframe designed with the same technology will result in a land based aircraft of higher basic capability. The further technology has improved the smaller the difference in performance. During 1940's this difference was massive. Size constraints include wingspan, height and weight. Takeoff distance is also important. Range suffers because you need to hit takeoff speed much sooner. What all of this leads to is the fact the Royal Navy could not safely carry out more than a single night of attacks. The Raid was split into two waves due to time it took to launch the loaded aircraft then spot the next wave on the flight deck. Number of aircraft in an attack is also determined by speed at which aircraft could be launched. Even today the raid count is determined by rate of aircraft launch and form up time. j If the Royal Navy had 4 Fleet Carriers available the raid would still have been a single night. However the number of aircraft in each raid would have changed. With 4 carriers the raid would have likely been 80 Swordfish in two waves and it would also have been possible to attempt to wipe out the local airbases in order to do a daylight follow up. The Fighters from 4 Carriers would have been able to fend of larger opposition. If the aircraft compliment was the same as HMS Ilustrious then you could plan on 60 Fulmar's to be available. The likelihood is however that had 4 Carriers been available the air group would be Swordfish, Fulmar's and Sea Gladiators with 60 fighters in Fleet being impossible at this time of the war. 40 Swordfish with Torpedo's and 40 with bombs and flares equals Taranto being removed as a Naval Base for a full year with few Oil storage tanks remaining and the ships in the harbour being severely damaged and total constructive losses. Photos of Taranto pre war show the ships moored stern in at a the docks and essentially tied together. This being hit by 250 or 500lb bombs would decimate the Italian ships due to very week deck armour. 20 to 50 mm is very light and even a 250lb SAP bomb should go through. If 6 ships and tied together you create a 60m by 140m target square as a minimum with plenty of HE and fuel to burn in the ships. Swordfish Dive Bombing was fairly accurate. 40 Torpedo armed and 32 bombers with 8 Flare dropping aircraft equals insane damage levels.

The Brits achieved miracles with a bunch of obsolete biplanes ... The first wave, 12 aircraft, consisted of 6 Swordfish armed with torpedoes, 2 two with flares plus four 250 lb (110 kg) bombs, and 4 with six bombs. The second wave , 8 aircraft, 5 with torpedoes, 2 with flares pus four bombs. Total attack force, 20 aircraft, of which only 11 actually carried a torpedo ! (contrast Pearl Harbor, Japanese attack force= 353 aircraft) The Brits don't need more 'waves', they need more aircraft and more carriers... Which means a POD of 1 April 1918 (April Fools day === how appropriate ) and a replacement of the 'Bomber will always get through' nonsense with one of 'By 1940 our carrier fleet will sink your battleship fleet' (it's debatable when this would be accepted, HOWEVER :- By 1918, the RN had between 650 and 936 Short 184 torpedo bombers. In 1919, the RN had taken delivery of 90 Sopwith Cuckoo torpedo bombers (the had ordered 230 but then the war ended). So, even in 1918, some-one in the RN was having some 'modern' thoughts
items.original_question: What if the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto? Could the Italian army have been pushed out of Albania, Libya and some of their islands (both in the Dodecanese and at home) in 1940-41 with greater efforts by the Brits to send more surplus men, ships, advanced tanks and aircraft? Remember the Regia Marina was larger than the Kriegsmarine

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Brits had carried out a second attack at Taranto?

criteria.name: Operational feasibility of a second Taranto strike
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically evaluates whether the Royal Navy could mount a second attack on Taranto given 1940 carrier operations, aircraft availability, launch cycles, night operations, fuel, maintenance, and risk to HMS Illustrious.
criteria.1-2: Treats a second attack as trivially possible or impossible with little reference to carrier operations or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some limits such as aircraft numbers or danger but gives a shallow or partly inaccurate feasibility assessment.
criteria.5-6: Explains key constraints, including limited Swordfish numbers, night attack requirements, and carrier vulnerability, with some gaps.
criteria.7-8: Provides a well-grounded assessment of sortie generation, aircraft losses, rearming, scouting risk, and why repeat attacks were difficult.
criteria.9-10: Integrates carrier doctrine, launch/recovery cycles, maintenance, surprise, Italian response, and force protection into a highly plausible feasibility judgment.

criteria.name: Damage mechanisms and immediate military effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains what a second attack would likely damage at Taranto and how that would affect the Italian fleet, harbor infrastructure, oil stores, repair capacity, and naval operations.
criteria.1-2: Gives vague claims such as 'Italy would be destroyed' or 'nothing changes' without explaining damage mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Identifies possible extra ship damage but neglects infrastructure, repair limits, ordnance types, or harbor conditions.
criteria.5-6: Discusses additional torpedo or bomb damage to ships and some operational consequences, though with limited specificity.
criteria.7-8: Covers ships, docks, fuel, repair facilities, anti-air defenses, and how torpedoes, bombs, and flares could alter outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Offers a nuanced damage model tied to aircraft loadouts, target layout, shallow-water torpedo use, deck armor, fires, and Italian recovery timelines.

criteria.name: Causal chain from Taranto to Mediterranean strategy
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces plausible downstream consequences for the Mediterranean war, including Italian fleet availability, British convoy operations, Malta, North Africa, Axis naval behavior, and German intervention.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to broad conclusions about winning the war without a credible chain from the second attack.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Mediterranean consequences but relies on loose speculation or skips major intermediate steps.
criteria.5-6: Connects heavier Taranto damage to Italian naval weakness and some effects on convoys or North Africa, but incompletely.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain involving fleet attrition, convoy security, Malta pressure, Axis logistics, and likely German countermeasures.
criteria.9-10: Sustains a long-range, conditional chain that weighs British gains against Italian adaptation, Luftwaffe deployment, resource limits, and theater-wide feedback effects.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and counterfactual restraint
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes under the counterfactual, avoids overclaiming, and handles dependence on assumptions such as aircraft numbers, timing, surprise, and Italian readiness.
criteria.1-2: Presents a single deterministic outcome with no uncertainty or caveats.

items.model_answer:
If the British had carried out a second major carrier strike on Taranto soon after the first attack in November 1940, the most likely result is that the Italian battle fleet would have been damaged even more severely and forced to withdraw for a longer period, giving Britain a stronger temporary advantage in the central Mediterranean. But it probably would not have transformed the whole war in the Mediterranean on its own.

The first Taranto raid had already shown that the Italian navy was vulnerable at anchor and that shallow-water torpedo attack was practical. A second strike, especially if launched before the Italians could fully reorganize defenses, might have sunk or crippled additional battleships, damaged cruisers and support ships, and further disrupted repair and fuel arrangements. That would have made the Regia Marina even less willing to risk decisive surface action. In the short term, British convoys to Malta, Egypt, and Greece might have moved with somewhat less fear of interception by heavy Italian units.

This could also have had an important psychological effect. Taranto was already a shock. A second successful blow would have reinforced British naval prestige and deepened Italian caution. Italian commanders, already constrained by fuel shortages, air cover problems, and the need to preserve capital ships, might have become even more defensive. The British might then have enjoyed greater operational freedom in the eastern and central Mediterranean during the following months.

However, there are important limits to the counterfactual. First, the British carrier force was small and fragile. Mounting another attack quickly would have required aircraft, trained crews, good weather, and a carrier kept in action despite substantial risk from submarines, surface forces, and land-based airpower. The Royal Navy could not strike repeatedly without exposing itself. A second raid might also have met stronger defenses, because after the first attack the Italians would likely improve torpedo nets, anti-aircraft guns, smoke screens, barrage balloons, dispersal, and readiness. So the second attack may have been less effective than the first.

Second, the Mediterranean balance was not determined by battleships alone. Airpower, submarines, convoy protection, logistics, and Axis support from Germany mattered enormously. Even with the Italian battle fleet weakened further, the British still faced the Luftwaffe, especially once German air units became more active in the theater, and the constant problem of sustaining Malta and Egypt over long distances. Italian naval losses would not automatically stop Axis supply to North Africa, because merchant shipping, escorts, aircraft, and later German involvement remained crucial factors.

Third, strategic priorities mattered. Around this time Britain was also drawn into Greece and other commitments. Even if Taranto had been followed up more aggressively, British gains at sea could have been diluted by broader strategic overreach. A stronger naval position does not necessarily translate into a decisive strategic outcome if army and air commitments are stretched elsewhere.

So the best answer is: a second attack on Taranto would probably have increased British naval superiority for a time, further weakened Italian willingness and ability to contest the Mediterranean by surface action, and perhaps improved convoy operations and pressure on Axis logistics. But it is unlikely by itself to have knocked Italy out of the naval war or radically changed the final course of the Mediterranean campaign. It would have been an important operational success, not a single war-winning stroke.

items.question: What If Vichy France had sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944?
human_answers: When the Allies invaded NW Africa, the French colonies of Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia Kesselrings command was approved to recruit patriotic French to resist the Allies. The proposed infantry division never materialized. Enough men were found for a weak battalion, but after the unhealthy and unreliable were rejected there were enough to form a single over strength company. Given the German shortage of up to date equipment, particularly artillery and motor transport. The extra 100,000 French would be armed with the usual mix of older & obsolescent weapons, often in inferior numbers, like most other ground combat formations in Rundsteadts OB West. Just maybe there would be a SS 'Frankreich' division with good equipment, but otherwise its going to be leftovers, horse drawn artillery, little or no medium and heavy artillery, no supporting armor other than a few obsolescent R35 or D2 tanks, pitiful air support, inferior AT guns, French made MG vs the MG 34 or MG42. Compounding all this is the chronic German shortages of artillery ammunition and fuel. If the 100,000 French soldiers are used to offset other soldiers who are then sent to other front the questions is who? The overaged German reservists of the Bodenstang formations? The Ossies from Poland, Urkraine, Beylo Russ, ect... ? The elite Panzer Truppen? If the French are just added on top of the others, with no transfers, then its just the same inadequate equipment spread across a increase of 5% or 10% of men. A second given is the relatively small number of French soldiers who volunteered for the crusade in the east. The members of the Charlemagne division totaled far less than 100,000 through the entire war. Probably less than 50,000 served in that formation. While volunteers could be found to fight in the east, there was no similar movement in the west. The Milcie managed to recruit young men who wanted to avoid labor service, but that relatively large body failed to volunteer or participate in the battle of France. Most deserted long before the Allied armies over ran the police districts the Milcie units were assigned to.
items.original_question: Impact of French soldiers in the Atlantic Wall? I just read that after the Dieppe Raid Pétain was so enthusiastic and convinced Germany would win that he actually offered French troops to the Reich, only to be turned down by a less than convinced Hitler. But what could have been the impact of let's say 100,000 French soldiers helping Germany on D-Day? I assume they would have to be conscripted from the industrial workforce in Germany? In that case, would that impact production? And what could be the performance of those soldiers fighting clearly for Germany as late as 1944?

items.model_answer:
If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944, the overall result of the war in Western Europe probably would not have changed, but the Normandy campaign likely would have been bloodier, slower, and politically more complicated.

The first thing to note is that this scenario requires a major political break from what actually happened. By 1944, Vichy France had very limited real autonomy, much of France was under direct German occupation, and the French armed forces available to Vichy were tightly constrained. So for 100,000 troops to appear on the Atlantic Wall, Germany would have had to rearm, organize, and trust a very large French collaborationist force. That alone would have been difficult, because the Germans were never fully confident in French loyalty, especially by the late war when resistance activity was growing and Germany was clearly under strain.

If we assume those troops do exist and are deployed in a serious way, their military effect would depend on quality more than raw numbers. One hundred thousand additional men spread along the Atlantic Wall could strengthen coastal defenses, man bunkers, guard roads, patrol rear areas, and free some German units for mobile reserve duties. In the best case for Germany, this could make the initial Allied landings in Normandy more costly. More defended strongpoints, more infantry around beach exits, and more manpower to contain airborne drops might delay Allied consolidation. The Americans at Omaha in particular, or the British and Canadians against fortified villages and coastal batteries, might have faced stiffer resistance.

But these troops would not have solved Germany’s main problems. The Atlantic Wall was never going to stop the Allies by itself if they achieved air and naval supremacy, which they did. Allied warships could still bombard fixed positions, Allied aircraft could still isolate the battlefield, and Allied logistics still dwarfed anything Germany and its collaborators could sustain in France. Even if French collaborationist troops added density to the defense, they would remain vulnerable to massive firepower and to disruption once the landings succeeded.

Their reliability would also be a huge issue. Many might fight poorly, desert, surrender quickly, or switch sides once the invasion began, especially if they were defending French soil against forces that included Free French elements and were clearly backed by the likely victors. Others, especially hardened collaborationists, might fight stubbornly. So the effect would probably be uneven: some sectors might hold longer, while in others the presence of French troops might collapse under pressure or create confusion in command and morale.

Politically, the consequences could be significant. If large French forces openly fought for the German side in Normandy, it would deepen the stigma of collaboration after liberation. Postwar France might see even harsher purges, more civil conflict, and a more difficult effort by de Gaulle to rebuild national unity. The narrative that Vichy was an illegitimate aberration, separate from the “real France” of the Resistance and Free French, would be harder to sustain if 100,000 French troops had visibly fought against the liberation. That could leave a more bitter domestic legacy, even if it did not save Germany militarily.

In operational terms, the most plausible outcome is not that D-Day fails outright, but that Allied casualties rise and the breakout from Normandy is delayed. A stronger infantry screen might slow the seizure of beachheads, complicate linkups between beaches, and increase the time needed to capture Cherbourg, Caen, or key road networks. But once the Allies established themselves ashore, Germany’s wider strategic position would still be dire. The Soviet advance in the east, Allied bombing, fuel shortages, and the imbalance in industrial capacity would remain overwhelming.

So the likely answer is that 100,000 Vichy French troops on the Atlantic Wall would make the liberation of France more costly and perhaps somewhat slower, but they would not prevent it. The deeper effect might be less on the military outcome of the war than on the political memory of France, making collaboration far more central, visible, and traumatic in the country’s postwar history.

edus.text: If Vichy France had somehow sent 100,000 French troops to help defend the Atlantic Wall in 1944,
the overall result of the war in Western Europe probably would not have changed,
but the Normandy campaign likely would have been bloodier, slower, and politically more complicated.
The first thing to note is that this scenario requires a major political break from what actually happened.
By 1944, Vichy France had very limited real autonomy,
much of France was under direct German occupation,
and the French armed forces available to Vichy were tightly constrained.
So for 100,000 troops to appear on the Atlantic Wall, Germany would have had to rearm, organize, and trust a very large French collaborationist force.
That alone would have been difficult,
because the Germans were never fully confident in French loyalty,
especially by the late war when resistance activity was growing and Germany was clearly under strain.
If we assume those troops do exist and are deployed in a serious way,
their military effect would depend on quality more than raw numbers.

One hundred thousand additional men spread along the Atlantic Wall could strengthen coastal defenses, man bunkers, guard roads, patrol rear areas, and free some German units for mobile reserve duties.
In the best case for Germany, this could make the initial Allied landings in Normandy more costly.
More defended strongpoints, more infantry around beach exits, and more manpower to contain airborne drops might delay Allied consolidation.
The Americans at Omaha in particular, or the British and Canadians against fortified villages and coastal batteries, might have faced stiffer resistance.
But these troops would not have solved Germany’s main problems.
The Atlantic Wall was never going to stop the Allies by itself if they achieved air and naval supremacy,
which they did.
Allied warships could still bombard fixed positions,
Allied aircraft could still isolate the battlefield,
and Allied logistics still dwarfed anything Germany and its collaborators could sustain in France.
Even if French collaborationist troops added density to the defense,
they would remain vulnerable to massive firepower and to disruption once the landings succeeded.
Their reliability would also be a huge issue.
Many might fight poorly, desert, surrender quickly, or switch sides once the invasion began,
especially if they were defending French soil against forces that included Free French elements and were clearly backed by the likely victors.
Others, especially hardened collaborationists, might fight stubbornly.
So the effect would probably be uneven:
some sectors might hold longer,
while in others the presence of French troops might collapse under pressure or create confusion in command and morale.
Politically, the consequences could be significant.
If large French forces openly fought for the German side in Normandy,
it would deepen the stigma of collaboration after liberation.
Postwar France might see even harsher purges, more civil conflict, and a more difficult effort by de Gaulle to rebuild national unity.

The narrative that Vichy was an illegitimate aberration, separate from the “real France” of the Resistance and Free French, would be harder to sustain if 100,000 French troops had visibly fought against the liberation.
That could leave a more bitter domestic legacy,
even if it did not save Germany militarily.
In operational terms, the most plausible outcome is not that D-Day fails outright,
but that Allied casualties rise and the breakout from Normandy is delayed.
A stronger infantry screen might slow the seizure of beachheads, complicate linkups between beaches, and increase the time needed to capture Cherbourg, Caen, or key road networks.
But once the Allies established themselves ashore,
Germany’s wider strategic position would still be dire.
The Soviet advance in the east, Allied bombing, fuel shortages, and the imbalance in industrial capacity would remain overwhelming.
So the likely answer is that 100,000 Vichy French troops on the Atlantic Wall would make the liberation of France more costly and perhaps somewhat slower,
but they would not prevent it.
The deeper effect might be less on the military outcome of the war than on the political memory of France,
making collaboration far more central, visible, and traumatic in the country’s postwar history.

items.question: What If World War I had occurred 9 years earlier?
human_answers: In the OTL First World War, aircraft were used only as reconnaissance planes in the early stages, and pilots dropped bombs by hand. However, by the later years of the war, aviation had achieved remarkable progress. Even if they do not appear in the early phase of the First World War in this TL, they could still emerge later in the conflict and be used for roles such as reconnaissance. Germany and its friends would be pleased to hear that. As I understand it, the Haber-Bosch process spread more slowly than people often assume. Fixing nitrogen in a laboratory and mass-producing chemical fertilizer in a factory are entirely different challenges. Building reactors that could withstand pressures of 200 to 300 atmospheres, developing steel alloys that could endure prolonged exposure to high temperature and high pressure, solving catalyst lifespan problems, controlling thermal runaway and explosions, designing continuous processes, and making the system capable of running nonstop for thousands of hours—this was not simply a matter of chemistry, but a comprehensive scientific and engineering project that required physics, materials science, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering as well. In the 1910s, Germany was the only country in the world capable of doing both. In the OTL, once the Haber process had been developed, the First World War broke out almost immediately. During that period, all resources were directed not toward chemical fertilizer production, but toward the development of explosives. Even afterward, BASF maintained its monopoly over the Haber method.

I think .... better diplomatic ties to Russia than Japan, as the US was very wary of the Japanese in relation to the new US occupation of the Philippines. The USN's "Great White Fleet" didn't make it's globe-sailing cruise till 1907, but several of the more modern ships were in the fleet earlier. The most helpful preparation for the OTL WW1 came with the two incursions into Mexico - Veracruz 1914 and the Pancho Villa chase in 1916-17, and their benefit was more getting the organizational an logistical weaknesses identified. The smaller, but more veteran US Regular Army after the DoW had their junior officers and capable NCO's pillaged to become low to middle ranking leaders in new formations and nationalized NG units. The reformation of highly variable quality state militias into a more consistent National Guard format was a relatively new thing by 1905. From an equipment standpoint, the US Army was way behind their European counterparts in quantity of artillery and quality too. TR's good friend, fellow Republican, and military mentor was Gen. Hunter Liggett could be in the next level as a Corps commander? The very capable Tasker Bliss and Peyton March of OTL WW1 Staff posts were still middle ranking officers in 1905-06 Pershing was a great organizer, but he was very stubborn and had a toxic relationship with the other Allied political and military leaders in 1917-1918. The one top Allied leader Pershing apparently got along with, was General Petain! General Tasker Bliss had to be sent over to pinch-hit for Pershing on the Allied War Councils, as Blis had better diplomatic skills, to go along with his superior staff skill.

items.original_question: What if World War I had occurred 9 years earlier? The First Moroccan Crisis occurred between 1905 and 1906 during the Russo-Japanese War. Although this event did not escalate into a full-scale military conflict, it was resolved through the Algeciras Conference. However, tensions between the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente grew stronger. Then, in 1911, the Second Moroccan Crisis took place. At this time, there were talks of a potential war, but ultimately it was resolved through international negotiations. Despite these series of events, in 1914, World War I broke out due to the assassination of the Austrian Archduke and the subsequent invasion of Serbia. This raises an interesting question. During the July Crisis in the OTL, there were numerous efforts to avoid war, but in the end, the arrogance of autocratic monarchs and the complex web of interests caused tensions to escalate and ultimately explode. What if such a chain reaction and explosion had occurred during the First Moroccan Crisis? What if the First Moroccan Crisis had escalated into a full-blown war, leading to World War I happening 9 years earlier than in the OTL? What could have been the consequences of such a scenario? Here are the questions in English: 1. In 1905, how does the military strength of countries such as the United Kingdom, France, the Russian Empire, the German Empire, Austria-Hungary, and the Kingdom of Italy compare to that of 1914 in OTL? Which country would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL when the war begins? 2. In 1905, the ruling party of the United States is the Republican Party, and the president is Theodore Roosevelt. If a world war were to occur during his presidency, what would America's stance be? Would Teddy Roosevelt maintain neutrality throughout, or would he eventually push for involvement? And how would Roosevelt's vision for the post-war world differ from Wilson's? 3. The Russian Empire, after the Russo-Japanese War in OTL, pursued reforms like constitutional monarchy changes and Stolypin’s agricultural reforms. However, in this TL, war breaks out before such reforms happen. What impact do you think this would have on Russia? I believe Russia would be at a disadvantage compared to OTL. However, there is also this possibility: "Unlike in OTL, there would be no Duma, and no legitimate or proper opposition parties. As a result, although there are many opposing forces, they would not form a cohesive alliance, and there would be no single negotiation channel." "This would make it harder for the anti-government factions to gain representation throughout Russia. Therefore, after the revolution, it would be more difficult to quickly take over the government and establish a revolutionary regime." 4. What do you think is the most likely outcome of the world war in this alternate timeline?

items.model_answer:
If World War I had happened in 1905 instead of 1914, the war would likely still have been a major European conflict driven by rival alliances, imperial competition, and nationalism, but its course and consequences would probably have been quite different because the political map, military technology, and internal stability of the great powers were all somewhat different.

The most immediate difference is that a 1905 war would probably have emerged out of a different crisis. In 1905 Europe was in the middle of the First Moroccan Crisis, Russo-Japanese War fallout, and continuing instability in the Balkans, but the alliance blocs were not yet as rigidly mobilized around a Sarajevo-style trigger. Germany was already worried about encirclement, France wanted security, Russia was weakened by defeat against Japan and by the 1905 Revolution, and Britain had only recently aligned more closely with France. So a war in 1905 might still have pitted Germany and Austria-Hungary against France and perhaps Russia, but Russia would have been less ready, and Britain’s role might initially have been more hesitant or limited.

Militarily, a 1905 world war would have been less industrially mature than the one that began in 1914. Machine guns, heavy artillery, rail mobilization, and barbed wire already existed, so the war could still have become very deadly. But tanks did not yet exist, military aviation was in its infancy, and some of the massive artillery and logistical systems of 1914–18 were not yet fully developed. That means the war might have begun with more fluid maneuver and less of the fully developed trench deadlock that came to define the Western Front, though stalemate was still possible. Armies would also generally have been smaller and somewhat less prepared for a total war of attrition on the later scale.

Russia is one of the biggest variables. In 1914 Russia was still flawed but stronger than it had been in 1905. If a general war had broken out in 1905, Russia’s recent defeat by Japan and domestic revolution could have made it militarily and politically weaker. That might have benefited Germany and Austria-Hungary early in the conflict and perhaps made a Central Powers victory more plausible than it was in the actual war. On the other hand, Austria-Hungary was already fragile, and an early war could still have exposed its military weakness and internal ethnic tensions.

Germany’s position would also be different. In 1905 Germany faced a France that had not yet completed all the military reforms and a Russia that was temporarily crippled. From Berlin’s perspective, this was in some ways a better moment for war than 1914. The Schlieffen-style logic of defeating France quickly before turning east might therefore have seemed even more attractive. If Britain stayed out at first or intervened late, Germany’s chances of a favorable outcome would rise sharply.

A key global difference concerns the United States. In 1905 the United States was less likely to play the decisive financial and military role it eventually did after 1917. America was important, but not yet positioned psychologically or diplomatically in relation to Europe in the same way. Without later U.S. intervention, a long war might have ended in a negotiated peace rather than a clear Allied victory. That would dramatically change the twentieth century.

If the war ended earlier or more indecisively, many later historical outcomes might not occur in the same form. There might be no Treaty of Versailles as we know it, no “stab-in-the-back” myth in exactly the same way, and possibly no Hitler or Nazi movement emerging from the specific German resentment and post-1918 crisis that actually happened. The Russian Revolution might also look very different. A war in 1905 could either destroy the tsarist regime earlier, because it was already under huge stress, or it might produce a limited constitutional settlement without the exact chain of disasters that led to the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917. Either way, the Soviet Union might not emerge in the same form, or at least not on the same timetable.

The Ottoman Empire might also fare differently. By 1914 it had already been badly weakened by the Balkan Wars. In 1905 it was still fragile, but somewhat less diminished. Its role in a general European war might therefore be less predictable. The Balkans too would matter differently: nationalism was already dangerous, but the alignment of Serbia, Bulgaria, and the surrounding powers was not yet identical to the pre-1914 situation.

In the colonies, an earlier war would likely weaken European empires, but perhaps not as decisively as the real war did. Since World War I helped accelerate anti-colonial movements by exhausting imperial powers and mobilizing colonial troops, a 1905 version might still push in that direction, but perhaps more slowly if the war were shorter or less total.

So the most plausible broad answer is this: a world war in 1905 would probably still be devastating, but it might be shorter, somewhat less technologically mature, and more favorable to Germany because Russia was weaker and Britain’s commitment was less certain. The biggest historical consequence is that the chain leading from 1914 to Versailles, the Bolshevik Revolution, fascism, and then World War II would be disrupted. Europe might still emerge unstable and violent, but the specific path of the twentieth century could be radically different—possibly with no Nazi Germany, no Soviet Union in its familiar form, and no Second World War as we know it.

items.question: What If A clash between Rockefeller/Cisneros vs Quayle/Alexander in the US 1996 elections
human_answers: Think about it--when Truman lost, it wasn't *just* because Democrats had been in power a long time. It was *also* because Harry Truman never saw a hornet's nest he didn't want to kick, a temperamental flaw that contributed to a sense of chaos in all walks of life. Combine that with the endemic corruption issues that come from twenty years in power, and you've got a recipe for a one term president. A distinct but similar dynamic appears with the coming of Nixon. Nobody believed LBJ about anything by 1968, and that rubbed off on Humphrey, who was (ironically) more upright but much weaker than Johnson, and the Hump never could shake the Credibility Gap issues he inherited. The loss of trust on all fronts created widespread anger and chaos followed in the wake of that anger. Add to that the endemic corruption issues that come from eight years of Kennedy and Johnson, and you've got a recipe for a Nixon win. No surprise, this is basically the exact same setup that takes down Nixon and Ford. What you might notice here is that the personality flaws of the individual in the White House combine with the problems of institutional corruption that arise after years in power to create a scandal unique to the time and place that ends up consuming everyone involved. I would imagine that a Bush I who gets a second term--by *some* miracle--is going to make some similar mistakes to the ones his son made. They had many of the same advisors, after all. Here, Bush I had none of Bush II's cocksure self assurance to distract from whatever Middle East quagmire he drags the US into, and I think he would crash and burn more quickly in terms of public approval. You might imagine a scenario where Clinton's scandals + much better Perot popular vote= an apparent Bush landslide, where Bush makes the error of mistaking his opponents' divisions for his own strength. I won't get into details because it's current politics, but if you want an example of just such an outcome, look at the results of the last UK general election. The bigger question to me is why America would turn to a plutocrat like Rockefeller after 16 years of "Greed is Good."

Okay, the idea is that this story is loosely based on some ideas from other users who wrote their stories*. The general idea is to create a story with some overall meaning using all of this. So, the story is about how, before the 1988 elections, a recession (like the one in the 90s) occurs. This causes Bush to win by a much smaller margin than OTL (301-236 EVs), resulting in the Democrats gaining more seats in the Senate and the House. This leads to Bush panicking, causing him to try to appease both Reaganite Republicans and more moderate Republicans, although I haven't decided what his cabinet would look like. Anyway, because of this, the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait is delayed until August 18, 1991. Furthermore, Iraq decides to invade the east coast of Saudi Arabia on December 26, 1991, that is, 130 days after the invasion of Kuwait. This leads to larger chain reactions overall, but they are not important at this moment. Two important points should also be added: 1. There were no Yugoslav Wars, therefore Bush was perhaps less concerned about the situation developing in the Balkans and set an earlier deadline (than OTL) for a ceasefire in Iraq, which ended on February 24, 1992. 2. The Iraqi Civil War did not end until 1993, so there was an incentive to be more attentive to the problems of other countries. This resulted in a much more effective Gulf War, and Saddam was overthrown a few days before the coalition reached Baghdad, but these are details. What you're probably wondering is... how did Bush win the 1992 election? Well, it was for several reasons. Like the Gulf War, the fact that the Soviet Union was doing stupid things, that the US was able to recover from the recession thanks to contracts with Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and most importantly, that each and every one of Bill Clinton's sex scandals was revealed. Ultimately, the election ended in a landslide victory for Bush (343-195 EVs). Bush's second term was relatively fruitful**. In foreign policy, he had some relative successes, such as Somalia, and some major successes, such as Rwanda. The economy was booming, and everything was going well. But people were starting to get tired of 16 years of Republican presidency and a Democratic option that wasn't showing it could win 4 elections in a row. Therefore, the Democratic primaries would be an opportunity to determine who could win the 1996 election once and for all. I have a vague idea of who the Democratic candidates might be in the primaries; they would be: ● Jay Rockefeller – He would be the one to win because of his establishment base and because he represents a remnant of the New Deal era, making him the best candidate. ● Henry Cisneros – The surprise candidate of the primaries, someone no one expected to win so many states, even though he's a senator who won the 1990 midterm Senate elections. I think he would come in second or third. ● Jesse Jackson – I'm sure he would see this as the perfect opportunity to run in the 1996 elections. He would run with the rainbow coalition and say that the reason they didn't win the last election was because Bill Clinton was a moderate white Southerner and, above all, a womanizer. Therefore, I see him coming in second or third, but I highly doubt the establishment would want him as their candidate. ● Bill Bradley – He would be the progressive candidate the establishment would prefer over Jackson, but I doubt he would win many states, to be honest. ● Joe Biden - Same as Bradley, but being liberal, not progressive. ● Kent Conrad - Okay, I'd have to justify myself here. I'm actually basing this on some hypothetical 1996 primaries , and I thought it would be interesting and funny to add him as a wildcard candidate. I think he could win Iowa, but I doubt it. In the end, Jay Rockefeller won the primaries, with Jackson and Cisneros coming very close to victory. The Democratic national nomination process ended with Jay Rockefeller as the presidential candidate, and, as happened in the 1988 nomination, a Texan (Henry Cisneros) was chosen, while the protesting defectors voted for Jesse Jackson. The Republican primaries and nomination process is simpler. All the candidates who ran in the 1996 primaries OTL are running ITTL, the difference being that Dan Quayle runs and wins the primary and the Republican nomination. Lamar Alexander came in second in the primaries and became Quayle's running mate. Now, some details I'd like to add are that a) Jesse Jackson would say a few words that would unify all racial demographics in the Rockefeller/Cisneros formula, and Dan Quayle would say something so stupid/racist against Chicanos that it would be repudiated by all centrists; that would be very funny. And that's all I could think of for this scenario***. *The stories I use as a base are: New World Empire: The Second Term of George H.W. Bush Al Grito de Guerra: the Second Mexican Revolution The Rise and Fall of the Vlasov's Russia: The last years of the Soviet Union without Boris YeltsinThird Time's The Charm: A World Without The Yugoslav Wars Daltonia's Test Thread Exocet - the Effects of a different Falklands Paper Doves in Flight: Poland & The World After Communism **For those who want to know, the cabinet is: President: George Bush Vice President: Dan Quayle Secretary of State: James Baker Secretary of Treasury: Jack Kemp Secretary of Defense: Dick Cheney Attorney General: William Barr Secretary of the Interior: Manuel Lujan Jr Secretary of Agriculture: C. Boyden Gray Secretary of Commerce: Barbara Franklin Secretary of Labor: Bill Brock Secretary of Health and Human Services: C. Everett Koop Secretary of Housing and Urban Development: Andrew Card Secretary of Transportation: Sam Skinner Secretary of Energy: James Watkins Secretary of Education: Lamar Alexander Secretary of Veteran Affairs: Ed Derwinski Director of the Office of Management and Budget: Nicholas Brady Counselor to the President: Clayton Yuetter National Security Advisor: Brent Scowcroft Press Secretary: Marlin Fitzwater ***This took me I don't know how many hours, I was literally at it from 4 am until 8:11 am, I want to die

items.model_answer:
A 1996 election between Nelson Rockefeller/Cisneros and Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander would require a very different prior history, since Rockefeller died in 1979, but as a counterfactual it points to a very different ideological and demographic contest than the actual Clinton–Dole race.

The broad shape of the election would likely favor Rockefeller/Cisneros, probably by a clear but not overwhelming margin. Rockefeller represented the old liberal-to-moderate Republican establishment: pro-business, internationalist, socially moderate, comfortable with a strong federal government, and appealing to suburban professionals, Wall Street, much of the Northeast, and moderate independents. Adding Henry Cisneros would strengthen the ticket’s appeal to urban voters, Latinos, and Sun Belt moderates, while also signaling generational and ethnic modernization. In effect, this ticket would try to build a coalition of affluent suburbanites, minorities open to pragmatic centrism, and voters tired of ideological polarization.

Quayle/Alexander would be much more purely conservative, though in somewhat different styles. Quayle would bring cultural conservatism, ties to the Reagan-Bush right, and appeal in the South and parts of the Midwest, while Alexander would project a more competent, technocratic, and less combative image than Quayle alone. Still, the ticket would likely struggle with credibility and gravitas. Quayle’s real-world public image in the 1990s was weak; many voters saw him as inexperienced or unserious. Alexander would help, but probably not enough to fully overcome that liability.

The campaign’s main divide would not be Democrat versus Republican in the normal sense, but moderate establishment pragmatism versus movement conservatism. Rockefeller would probably dominate among Northeastern and West Coast moderates, upscale suburbanites, and many independents. Quayle would do well with evangelical voters, rural conservatives, and the South. The Midwest would be mixed: Alexander could help in border-state and upper-South areas, but Rockefeller’s managerial competence and centrist image would likely appeal in major metropolitan regions.

In electoral-college terms, Rockefeller/Cisneros would probably win states like New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, California, Illinois, and likely much of the industrial Northeast. They would also be competitive in places like Florida, where Cisneros’s Hispanic appeal and Rockefeller’s moderate profile could matter. Quayle/Alexander would likely hold much of the Deep South, the Great Plains, and strongly conservative Mountain West states. Texas would become especially interesting: Cisneros could make it closer than expected, but Quayle’s conservatism would still probably keep it in his column unless Rockefeller’s campaign became a major national wave.

Compared with the real 1996 election, this race would probably be more ideologically clarifying. Clinton in reality occupied much of the center and deprived Republicans of moderate suburban space. In this counterfactual, Rockefeller would be the one monopolizing the center, leaving Quayle with fewer paths beyond energizing the right. That is a harder general-election strategy in the 1990s, when the national mood was relatively prosperous, post–Cold War, and not especially hungry for sharp ideological change.

The result, then, is most likely a Rockefeller/Cisneros victory, perhaps something like a solid popular-vote win and a comfortable electoral-college majority, though not necessarily a landslide. Quayle/Alexander would run strongly in conservative America, but Rockefeller’s stature, moderation, and broader coalition would probably make him the favorite in a 1996 national electorate.

nodes.text: A 1996 election between Nelson Rockefeller/Cisneros and Dan Quayle/Lamar Alexander would require a very different prior history, since Rockefeller died in 1979,
but as a counterfactual it points to a very different ideological and demographic contest than the actual Clinton–Dole race.
The broad shape of the election would likely favor Rockefeller/Cisneros, probably by a clear but not overwhelming margin.

Rockefeller represented the old liberal-to-moderate Republican establishment: pro-business, internationalist, socially moderate, comfortable with a strong federal government, and appealing to suburban professionals, Wall Street, much of the Northeast, and moderate independents.
Adding Henry Cisneros would strengthen the ticket’s appeal to urban voters, Latinos, and Sun Belt moderates,
while also signaling generational and ethnic modernization.
In effect, this ticket would try to build a coalition of affluent suburbanites, minorities open to pragmatic centrism, and voters tired of ideological polarization.
Quayle/Alexander would be much more purely conservative, though in somewhat different styles.
Quayle would bring cultural conservatism, ties to the Reagan-Bush right, and appeal in the South and parts of the Midwest,
while Alexander would project a more competent, technocratic, and less combative image than Quayle alone.
Still, the ticket would likely struggle with credibility and gravitas.
Quayle’s real-world public image in the 1990s was weak;
many voters saw him as inexperienced or unserious.
Alexander would help,
but probably not enough to fully overcome that liability.
The campaign’s main divide would not be Democrat versus Republican in the normal sense,
but moderate establishment pragmatism versus movement conservatism.
Rockefeller would probably dominate among Northeastern and West Coast moderates, upscale suburbanites, and many independents.
Quayle would do well with evangelical voters, rural conservatives, and the South.
The Midwest would be mixed:
Alexander could help in border-state and upper-South areas,
but Rockefeller’s managerial competence and centrist image would likely appeal in major metropolitan regions.

In electoral-college terms, Rockefeller/Cisneros would probably win states like New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, California, Illinois, and likely much of the industrial Northeast.
They would also be competitive in places like Florida,
where Cisneros’s Hispanic appeal and Rockefeller’s moderate profile could matter.
Quayle/Alexander would likely hold much of the Deep South, the Great Plains, and strongly conservative Mountain West states.
Texas would become especially interesting:
Cisneros could make it closer than expected,
but Quayle’s conservatism would still probably keep it in his column
unless Rockefeller’s campaign became a major national wave.
Compared with the real 1996 election, this race would probably be more ideologically clarifying.
Clinton in reality occupied much of the center and deprived Republicans of moderate suburban space.
In this counterfactual, Rockefeller would be the one monopolizing the center,
leaving Quayle with fewer paths beyond energizing the right.
That is a harder general-election strategy in the 1990s,
when the national mood was relatively prosperous, post–Cold War, and not especially hungry for sharp ideological change.
The result, then, is most likely a Rockefeller/Cisneros victory,
perhaps something like a solid popular-vote win and a comfortable electoral-college majority,
though not necessarily a landslide.
Quayle/Alexander would run strongly in conservative America,
but Rockefeller’s stature, moderation, and broader coalition would probably make him the favorite in a 1996 national electorate.
