items.question: What If Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest
human_answers: I would think that you would see a Nelsonian style of celebration and loss. Assuming that the weather was clear enough to allow for Odell, who was alone, to witness their summit and subsequent descent and deadly fall, the MAJOR issue is that Odell does not have a camera on him. The one thing that would irrefutably prove that Mallory and Irvine summited the mountain and then died on their decent would be a photograph, even a distant one, of them on or practically at the summit. Now, Irvine or Mallory did have a camera on them, the near legendary Kodak that is still missing to this day and may hold the truth of whether or not they made it. Assuming that Odell witnessed the summit and the subsequent fall, AND he could record where their bodies fell or near where they fell, then it becomes an issue of finding their bodies and the Kodak. Odell was a respected and trusted witness so i do not think that many would dispute his claim, but finding their remains and the camera would be a major point of corroborating his account. If their bodies and the camera were found, with photographic proof that they did make the summit found in it, it would be both widely celebrated and mourned. Mallory and Irvine would be national heroes in Britain and probably recognized across the world for their achievement. They were historically given a memorial service at St Paul's in London, which was widely attended by many people up to an including the then Prince of Wales, the future Edward VIII. Unlike Franklin or Scott, who were either not found or left where they died, Mallory's body at the least was in a location that its recovery was certainly possible, an Irvine's body may have ended up in a similar location if their death was witnessed. If their bodies were recovered, probably with a sponsored expedition, i could easily see a joint funeral for both in St. Paul's, potentially even reaching a State Funeral with full Royal attendance. Then you have the lasting impact that this would have on the psyche of Britain and the world. After the 1924 Expedition there was a major underswell in mountaineering circles, especially British ones, and to a lesser extent in the greater British populace, that Everest was "unfinished business." While there was a drop off in attempts after the 1924 failure, there was a massive resurgence in the 1930s, a pause during the war for obvious reasons, and then a similar surge in the 1950s culminating in the 1953 success. If Mallory and Irvine reached the top in 1924, that would greatly decrease the interest in Everest. Ironically, Mallory's and Irvine's death, and the debate that raged and still rages over whether they made the summit or not, drove the popularity and allure of the mountain far beyond what it would be if they succeeded but died on the way down. There probably would be several more attempts in the aftermath, at least one of which would probably be sponsored by groups like the British Alpine Club or the Royal Geographic Society as a symbolic summit and successful decent in tribute to Mallory and Irvine. I wouldn't be surprised if they hauled a plaque all the way up there to set up a memorial for them. But Everest probably wouldn't have the same level of mystique is has today. By provably succeeding and dying in the aftermath, Mallory and Irvine would probably completely reshape how we see Everest. Edit: Having gone over this again, the nerd in me now wants the Kodak to be a legendary item in a video game OR an SCP entry. would be a fun nod to an event few people would ever know about.

Yes ! I didn't knew they had had found Irvine (well, his foot at last). https://www.nationalgeographic.com/adventure/article/sandy-irvine-body-found-everest Unbelievable. And then there is this Holly cow they were so close - less than 400 meters to 8848 ! I understand better why so many people are confident they made it to the summit. Also the missing photography of Mallory wife. Unfortunately poor Irvine was found much lower and inside a melting glacier. Hopefully they will found more remains within the next few years. And that infamous camera. What we know for sure: the cylinder, the ice axe and Mallory's body tells us they were roped together at a minimum of 8475 metres, before they fell. Bummers, that's 2133 meters below. Talk about a fall, even if the glacier probably lowered the body on the moutain, along the years. The remaining question is: did the fall happened while climbing, less than 400 m from glory - or descending, having done it ? And there, is the missing photography of Mallory wife. AAAAARGH we are so close from knowing the truth.

So I can tell you that summit fever is very real. I have never climbed anything like Everest obviously but I have scaled (as in hiked) a few 14,000 footers in Colorado and even with that I can state with authority that due to the combination of being tired and euphoric on the way down along with the general feeling that the mission has been accomplished, the brain is not working quite right. That's just reality. Plus, you now have gravity pulling you along. Given that I agree that it is far more likely Mallory and Irvine fell on the descent, either after making the summit or deciding to turn back for whatever reason. While it is unlikely they would have turned back that close to the summit we can't dismiss it either. 400 meters from the summit may not sound like much but at that altitude is actually a very long distance and maybe the combination of bad weather, declining oxygen supplies, or overall uncertainty caused them to turn around. My personal opinion - they made it to the top (it part because I want it to be true) and fell badly on the way down but until we can get actual physical evidence that clearly shows they made the summit that's all it is, an opinion.

Interestingly a lot of practical research has gone into trying to answer the question of whether or not the clothing worn by Mallory and Irvine would have been sufficient to enable them to survive the extreme environment. This has included tests in weather chambers and even a 2006 Everest expedition with climbers wearing exact replicas of Mallory's clothing. The overall conclusion of these tests in generally that the clothing itself was actually quite comfortable and well insulated and that provided Mallory and Irvine kept moving and didn't stop for any length of time or encounter any serious deterioration in weather conditions they could have continued to "operate effectively". Weather chamber tests showed that with the clothing they had Mallory and Irvine could have survived temperatures of −30 °C. Although it was also found that if wind speed picked up the insulation of the clothing would only just be sufficient to −10 °C. While a lot of luck would have been required its not beyond the realms of possibility that Mallory and Irvine could have succeeded in the right conditions. A bigger factor would have probably been whether or not they were carrying sufficient oxygen and if their relatively primitive breathing apparatus could be relied on not to fail (One of the reasons why Mallory chose the relatively inexperienced Irvine to accompany him on his summit attempt was due to the latter's expertise with the breathing apparatus).

They never intended to climb the second step. In fact, no one knew the second step existed in 1924. And Mallory wrote that he considered the NE ridge route impossible. Odell's sighting put them at the base of the summit pyramid, above the third step, anyway. Mallory very clearly explained his intended route in his letters, which was to bypass the steps and either take the zig-zag or the couloir. Anker is ... a controversial source on anything 1924. He has a habit of disregarding any evidence that contradicts his theories on Mallory/Irvine. It's more likely than not that they summited and died on the way down, by virtue of the fact that they died . The vast majority of climbers who've died on Everest got summit fever and died on the descent because they pushed themselves way too hard to reach the peak. Michael Tracy is a grump, but he's done more to shed light on the truth of 1924 Mallory/Irvine than basically anyone else. This video is one of his that cover's their intended routes. We'll never know what actually happened of course – the '99 team utterly botched their investigation upon finding Mallory, and given Irvine's foot was found in the Rongbuk Glacier, his body probably fell clean off the mountain below Mallory in '24 so we're unlikely ever find it. But barring new evidence, the most plausible theory is that they made the summit and died on the descent that evening/night.
items.original_question: What if Mallory and Irvine Summited & Survived Everest In 1953 the New Zealand Mountaineer Edmund Hillary and Nepalese Sherpa Tenzing Norgay became the first people to reach the summit of Mount Everest (8.849m). However there remains to this day an enduring question about whether or not Hillary and Norgay actually were the first people to reach the summit of Everest or simply the first to do so and survive the experience. In 1924 during the second British expedition to attempt to conquer Everest British climbers George Mallory and Sandy Irvine set off on the expeditions third attempt to reach the summit. An attempt from which neither man would return. On the morning of the 6th of June Mallory and Irvine had set off for the summit from their final camp (8,138 m on the North Ridge). Their progress was tracked and filmed by expedition leader Noel Oddell who had positioned himself on a ridge further down the mountain to observe and record the expected first summit of the mountain. Mallory and Irvine were last spotted through a gap in the clouds approximately 240 metres from the summit still proceeding onwards. After this the pair simply disappeared. Despite many searches in the days and years following their disappearance the pair would not be seen again for another 75 years when Mallory's remarkably well preserved body would be discovered at an altitude of 8,156m. In the 1933 expedition an ice axe that could only have belonged to Mallory or Irvine was discovered at an altitude of 8,380m proving that the pair had reached at least this altitude. The location and state of Mallory's body (Irvine's partial remains in the form of a detached foot would later emerge from a glacier at a much lower altitude) indicated that he had suffered a fall which had resulted in his death either as a direct result or by later exposure likely during a decent of the mountain. The body revealed circumstantial evidence that suggests Mallory might have successfully reached the summit. Mallory carried a photo of his wife with the intention of leaving it on the summit. No such photo was found on the body. Given the excellent preservation of the body and personal possessions, the absence of the photo suggests he may have reached the summit and deposited it there. Mallory's snow goggles were in his pocket, indicating he may have died at night; that he and Irvine had made a push for the summit and were descending very late in the day. Given their known departure time and movements, had they not made the summit, it is unlikely they would have still been out by nightfall. Perhaps the one artefact that may put the mystery to bed is the Kodak pocket camera that Irvine was known to be carrying and which he presumably would have used to take a photo of the first successful ascent had such a thing occurred and may still contain useable photographs of the attempt. Assuming that Mallory had been successful in reaching the summit and managed to avoid whatever calamity befell on their decent and are able to survive the whole ordeal what would the the effects have been of Mount Everest having been summited for the first time by George Mallory in 1924? How would this have affected the history of Everest and expeditions to climb the mountain after 1924? How would Mallory and Irvine's achievement have been received and remembered?

items.model_answer:
If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and then survived to tell the story, it would likely have changed both the history of exploration and the cultural meaning of Everest in major ways.

First, the British Empire would have claimed one of the greatest exploration victories of the age. In 1924 Everest was not just a mountain challenge; it was tied to national prestige. Britain had failed to be first to the poles in the most triumphant way and still valued heroic exploration as proof of national character. A successful and surviving Mallory and Irvine would have become instant global celebrities, probably among the most famous men in the English-speaking world. Their ascent would have been framed as a triumph of courage, discipline, and imperial science. That would have mattered especially because Everest was then approached from Tibet, under conditions shaped by diplomacy and empire rather than modern mountaineering tourism.

Second, the mythology of Everest would be very different. In our history, Mallory’s disappearance helped create the mountain’s central legend: the unresolved question of whether they were first. That mystery gave Everest a haunting quality. If they had summited and survived, there would be no great “did they make it?” debate. Instead of being remembered as tragic, semi-mythic figures, they would be remembered as clear victors and pioneers. The mountain’s symbolic history would shift from one of fatal obsession and ambiguity to one of early human conquest through improvisation and boldness.

Third, the 1953 ascent by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay would still have been important, but not as the “first ascent.” It might instead have been celebrated as the first ascent by a new route variation, the first fully documented modern ascent, or the first postwar ascent. Hillary and Tenzing would still likely be famous because of the quality of their climb and the era’s media coverage, but their place in global memory would probably be reduced. Tenzing in particular might not have become quite the same symbol of Himalayan mountaineering achievement, because the defining “first” would already belong to two Britons from the interwar period.

Fourth, mountaineering technique and risk culture might have evolved differently. A successful 1924 oxygen-assisted ascent would have validated high-altitude climbing technology much earlier. It might have encouraged faster acceptance of supplemental oxygen, clothing systems, and siege-style expedition planning. At the same time, because Mallory and Irvine would have succeeded with equipment far cruder than later climbers used, their climb might have reinforced a heroic ideal that boldness and endurance mattered more than technical refinement. Future expeditions may have felt both inspired and pressured to emulate them, possibly leading to more attempts in the 1920s and 1930s if political access to Tibet had allowed it.

Fifth, their survival would have had a large effect on how the story was told because they could explain what actually happened near the top. Historians and climbers would know whether the Second Step was climbed, how effective their oxygen gear was, what route choices they made, and what conditions they faced. That knowledge could have advanced Himalayan climbing earlier by replacing speculation with practical experience. Their testimony would also have shaped debates about human limits at extreme altitude.

There would also be consequences for the culture of heroism. Mallory’s famous reply, “Because it’s there,” became iconic partly because he died and was turned into a symbol of pure, fatal aspiration. A living Mallory might have become not just a legend but a public intellectual of climbing—lecturing, writing, advising expeditions, perhaps influencing generations of mountaineers directly. Irvine, who was young and technically gifted, might have gained recognition as more than Mallory’s junior partner; he could have become an important figure in expedition engineering or oxygen-system design.

Politically and culturally, Britain might have woven the ascent into a broader story of imperial endurance during a period of weakening global dominance. It would not have reversed imperial decline, but it would have offered a potent symbolic victory. Schoolbooks, newspapers, and public ceremonies would likely have enshrined the ascent as a quintessential British achievement. The fact that Everest was later first climbed in the age of decolonization gave the 1953 ascent a different tone; a 1924 success would have been more straightforwardly imperial in its meaning.

At the same time, some longer-term effects would be surprisingly limited. Everest would still eventually become a global obsession. Nepal’s later opening, advances in aviation, postwar media, and commercial expedition culture would still transform the mountain. Mallory and Irvine’s success would not stop Everest from becoming crowded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. But the origin story of that obsession would be different: Everest would have been “won” much earlier, and perhaps seen less as the final unconquered summit of the modern world than as an interwar masterpiece of exploration.

So the biggest change is this: Everest would lose one of history’s greatest mysteries and gain one of history’s clearest heroic victories. Britain would likely have owned the symbolic first ascent, Mallory and Irvine would stand beside the greatest explorers of any age, and the later history of mountaineering would unfold under the shadow not of their disappearance, but of their success.

edus.text: If George Mallory and Andrew “Sandy” Irvine had reached the summit of Everest in 1924 and then survived to tell the story, it would likely have changed both the history of exploration and the cultural meaning of Everest in major ways.
First, the British Empire would have claimed one of the greatest exploration victories of the age.
In 1924 Everest was not just a mountain challenge; it was tied to national prestige.
Britain had failed to be first to the poles in the most triumphant way and still valued heroic exploration as proof of national character.
A successful and surviving Mallory and Irvine would have become instant global celebrities, probably among the most famous men in the English-speaking world.
Their ascent would have been framed as a triumph of courage, discipline, and imperial science.
That would have mattered especially because Everest was then approached from Tibet, under conditions shaped by diplomacy and empire rather than modern mountaineering tourism.
Second, the mythology of Everest would be very different.
In our history, Mallory’s disappearance helped create the mountain’s central legend: the unresolved question of whether they were first.
That mystery gave Everest a haunting quality.
If they had summited and survived, there would be no great “did they make it?” debate.
Instead of being remembered as tragic, semi-mythic figures, they would be remembered as clear victors and pioneers.
The mountain’s symbolic history would shift from one of fatal obsession and ambiguity to one of early human conquest through improvisation and boldness.
Third, the 1953 ascent by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay would still have been important, but not as the “first ascent.”
It might instead have been celebrated as the first ascent by a new route variation, the first fully documented modern ascent, or the first postwar ascent.
Hillary and Tenzing would still likely be famous because of the quality of their climb and the era’s media coverage, but their place in global memory would probably be reduced.
Tenzing in particular might not have become quite the same symbol of Himalayan mountaineering achievement, because the defining “first” would already belong to two Britons from the interwar period.
Fourth, mountaineering technique and risk culture might have evolved differently.
A successful 1924 oxygen-assisted ascent would have validated high-altitude climbing technology much earlier.
It might have encouraged faster acceptance of supplemental oxygen, clothing systems, and siege-style expedition planning.

At the same time, because Mallory and Irvine would have succeeded with equipment far cruder than later climbers used, their climb might have reinforced a heroic ideal that boldness and endurance mattered more than technical refinement.
Future expeditions may have felt both inspired and pressured to emulate them, possibly leading to more attempts in the 1920s and 1930s if political access to Tibet had allowed it.
Fifth, their survival would have had a large effect on how the story was told because they could explain what actually happened near the top.
Historians and climbers would know whether the Second Step was climbed, how effective their oxygen gear was, what route choices they made, and what conditions they faced.
That knowledge could have advanced Himalayan climbing earlier by replacing speculation with practical experience.
Their testimony would also have shaped debates about human limits at extreme altitude.
There would also be consequences for the culture of heroism.
Mallory’s famous reply, “Because it’s there,” became iconic partly because he died and was turned into a symbol of pure, fatal aspiration.
A living Mallory might have become not just a legend but a public intellectual of climbing—lecturing, writing, advising expeditions, perhaps influencing generations of mountaineers directly.

Irvine, who was young and technically gifted, might have gained recognition as more than Mallory’s junior partner; he could have become an important figure in expedition engineering or oxygen-system design.
Politically and culturally, Britain might have woven the ascent into a broader story of imperial endurance during a period of weakening global dominance.
It would not have reversed imperial decline, but it would have offered a potent symbolic victory.
Schoolbooks, newspapers, and public ceremonies would likely have enshrined the ascent as a quintessential British achievement.
The fact that Everest was later first climbed in the age of decolonization gave the 1953 ascent a different tone; a 1924 success would have been more straightforwardly imperial in its meaning.
At the same time, some longer-term effects would be surprisingly limited.
Everest would still eventually become a global obsession.
Nepal’s later opening, advances in aviation, postwar media, and commercial expedition culture would still transform the mountain.
Mallory and Irvine’s success would not stop Everest from becoming crowded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

But the origin story of that obsession would be different: Everest would have been “won” much earlier, and perhaps seen less as the final unconquered summit of the modern world than as an interwar masterpiece of exploration.
So the biggest change is this: Everest would lose one of history’s greatest mysteries and gain one of history’s clearest heroic victories.

Britain would likely have owned the symbolic first ascent, Mallory and Irvine would stand beside the greatest explorers of any age, and the later history of mountaineering would unfold under the shadow not of their disappearance, but of their success.

Irvine, who was young and technically gifted, might have gained recognition as more than Mallory’s junior partner; he could have become an important figure in expedition engineering or oxygen-system design.
Politically and culturally, Britain might have woven the ascent into a broader story of imperial endurance during a period of weakening global dominance.
It would not have reversed imperial decline, but it would have offered a potent symbolic victory.
Schoolbooks, newspapers, and public ceremonies would likely have enshrined the ascent as a quintessential British achievement.
The fact that Everest was later first climbed in the age of decolonization gave the 1953 ascent a different tone; a 1924 success would have been more straightforwardly imperial in its meaning.
At the same time, some longer-term effects would be surprisingly limited.
Everest would still eventually become a global obsession.
Nepal’s later opening, advances in aviation, postwar media, and commercial expedition culture would still transform the mountain.
Mallory and Irvine’s success would not stop Everest from becoming crowded in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

But the origin story of that obsession would be different: Everest would have been “won” much earlier, and perhaps seen less as the final unconquered summit of the modern world than as an interwar masterpiece of exploration.
So the biggest change is this: Everest would lose one of history’s greatest mysteries and gain one of history’s clearest heroic victories.

Britain would likely have owned the symbolic first ascent, Mallory and Irvine would stand beside the greatest explorers of any age, and the later history of mountaineering would unfold under the shadow not of their disappearance, but of their success.

items.original_question: What if Pop Culture gets 1st Amendment and Union Protections for Production and Distribution Early From 1930 to 1968, the Motion Picture Production Code ("Hays Code") governed the production and distribution of motion picture content in the United States of America - a self-imposed by movie studios and exhibitors set of guidelines about what could and could not be shown/mentioned/referred to in film (be it a feature whether live-action or animated, a short whether live-action or animated, a serial chapter, or a documentary newsreel). Similar sets of guidelines governed graphic novels, comic books and newspaper comic strips (the Comics Code from 1954 to 2011), the National Association of Broadcasters' Code of Practices for Television Broadcasters (the so-called Television Code from 1952 to 1983) with a similar set of guidelines for radio, and the near-censorship of video games by the North American nations' governments before the Entertainment Software Association came up with the voluntary, self-regulating Entertainment Software Rating Board to inform consumers about content. There were various religious and secular moralistic censorship groups across the United States at the time dedicating themselves to preserving morality and good taste in American culture of the time through literature, music, sports, comic strips, motion pictures and radio. Various Tinseltown scandals led up to the 1915 U.S. Supreme Court case Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio which unanimously held that free speech protections of the U.S. Constitution's 1st Amendment did not extend to motion pictures. But for our purposes, let's examine what if instead the Supreme Court ruled unanimously that radio, literature, comic strips, music and motion pictures were in fact protected by the 1st Amendment. If the Supreme Court were to decide that no local, state, or federal political body had the right to regulate or censor the production and distribution of any work of radio, film, literature, music within reason and neither did any religious or business organization within reason, then what? If the National/Catholic Legion of Decency, the National Board of Review and the Motion Picture Association (then the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America) were ordered by the Supreme Court to within reason allow for almost any type of motion pictures to be created so long as no people (especially children) and or animals were harmed by the making of a film, where should they go from here? I would suggest that instead of restrictive production/distribution codes, film distributors would possibly make an early version of the Film Rating System which would check film patrons' identifications at the box office against a film's rating. This would give many makers and distributors of motion pictures more creative freedom to explore the kinds of topics and subject matter they want to explore as well as spur various technological developments of all sorts. For our purposes, let's explore firstly what if the MPPDA Film Rating System established in the late 1910s is the one of today. Rating Indicator ​ Rating Description ​ G ​ General Audiences - All Ages Admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children whether viewing together with parents or by themselves. PG ​ Parental Guidance Suggested - Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their youngest children. PG-13 ​ Parents Strongly Cautioned - Some material may be inappropriate for children under the age of 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers and should be discussed before viewing decision. R ​ Restricted - Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them with proper legal identification at the box office. NC-17 ​ Adults Only - No One 17 Years And Under Admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not legally admitted and all adults must have legal identification at the box office. With the Film Rating System in place to ensure film producers and film distributors have the creative freedom to pursue the projects they want to make, there could be other ways for the Legion of Decency and various religion and social rights groups could clean up Hollywood for film, radio and eventually television without hampering creative freedom. One of those ways would be to convince studios, distributors and talent agencies to unionize and have their own unions so to ensure fairer treatment and hiring of prospective workers and talents, safe business practices and work hazard safety management, and fair/equal compensation for equal work for all kinds of work. This would involve the Directors Guild, Writers Guild, American Cinema Editors, Producers Guild, American Society of Cinematographers, Screen Actors Guild, Animation Guild and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees with membership being encouraged or socially pressured to watchdog for mistreatment. With creative and editorial freedom enshrined for radio and motion pictures in the Constitution, there could also be movements to establish an alliance of the Christian churches, Jewish synagogues, Islamic mosques and other religious institutions' collective motion picture production and distribution systems as a single studio called the Holy Light Studios Alliance which would be dedicated to the production and distribution of motion pictures approved by the moral standard guidelines of various local, state, national and international Christian, Jewish and Muslim faith doctrines. Entertainment, education and information fit for religious viewers. They would take in the various technological and artistic talents and know-how from the secular Hollywood studios and apply them towards delivering motion pictures (narrative feature and even the documentaries) with high production standards and quality to deliver their messages to the masses while showing religion on the side of freedom versus tyranny. This would also filter down to local radio stations (and eventually television stations starting in the late 1940s) that would choose to become affiliates of the religious non-denominational Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) which would be listener and eventually viewer-supported to broadcast religious services, national and international news along with news analysis and commentary, local community sports highlights and commentary, charity events, and even motion pictures from the Holy Light library after they finish their original theatrical runs come the advent of television. Local, state and federal non-partisan movements and educational institutions such as colleges, universities, trade schools and public schools would take advantage of the creative and editorial freedoms to organize radio (and eventually television) stations under one coast-to-coast network to provide listener/viewer-supported entertainment/culture, public affairs, educational and community outreach programming for the masses. National Public Radio (NPR) and the Trinity Broadcasting Network (TBN) would both provide alternatives to the commercial broadcast radio (and eventually television) networks found in the American Broadcasting Company (ABC - formerly NBC Blue), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS) and the National Broadcasting Company (NBC - formerly NBC Red). All of them would agree, however, that their news reporting standards were to be "factual, fair and without bias" and any commentary and analysis from a partisan political viewpoint should be "clearly defined as such". While NPR and TBN were listener and eventually viewer-supported from the beginning; ABC, CBS and NBC would ensure that commercial time would be limited during hours when children and teenagers would be most likely to be tuning in. The commercial networks would choose to give fair and equal time, coverage and analysis of viewpoints and educational/informative programs to keep up with NPR and TBN's higher standards. However, there was another effect of the Mutual Film Corp. v. Industrial Commission of Ohio decision - the major movie studios could not buy and own the cinema companies that their films would be released to. This would be an antitrust compromise with the governments so that no corporate body could block the release of a film in a release slot that could pose a risk to another company's releases. What would the ripple effects of all this combined be on the motion picture and radio studios and distributors of the time (20th Century-Fox, Columbia, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Paramount, RKO, Republic, United Artists, Universal, Walt Disney and Warner Brothers) on the content in the films they would release to the public? How might some of your favorite films and other pop culture installments from the early 20th Century and beyond have gone if all their makers and distributors were given maximum creative freedom within reason to make what they wanted to? Feel free to discuss this entire ATL in the comments.

If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had gained strong First Amendment protection and stable union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American mass culture would likely have developed into a more openly political, more artistically diverse, and more labor-stable system much sooner. The biggest effects would probably appear in censorship, labor relations, representation, and the political role of media.

In actual history, each of these media developed under constraints that limited both content and working conditions. Film faced censorship and the Production Code; comics were shaken by moral panic and the Comics Code; broadcasting operated under heavy political scrutiny and the logic of licensing, which encouraged caution. At the same time, labor protections in these industries were uneven, delayed, or contested, leaving writers, actors, animators, technicians, and later broadcasters vulnerable to studio control and blacklisting. If constitutional and union protections had arrived earlier and been more secure, media industries would likely have matured differently.

In film, earlier First Amendment protection would probably have weakened the legitimacy of state and local censorship boards and reduced the power of the Hays Code. Hollywood films in the 1920s, 1930s, and 1940s might have addressed sexuality, race, labor conflict, poverty, fascism, and political corruption more directly. The sharp boundary between “respectable” studio entertainment and more daring independent or foreign work might have been less pronounced. American cinema could have resembled postwar European film earlier in its willingness to treat controversial themes as normal subjects rather than dangerous exceptions.

In comics, earlier legal and cultural protection would have mattered enormously. Comics were treated as low-status and suspect, especially by midcentury critics who blamed them for juvenile delinquency. If they had enjoyed robust First Amendment protection earlier, the anti-comics panic of the 1950s might have had far less power. The Comics Code Authority may never have become as dominant, or it might have emerged in a much weaker form. That would likely have allowed horror, crime, political satire, adult drama, and autobiographical comics to flourish decades earlier. The idea of comics as a medium for all ages, rather than primarily for children, might have become mainstream by the mid-twentieth century instead of much later.

Broadcasting is a more complicated case because it was tied to public spectrum regulation. Even with stronger First Amendment protection, radio and television would still likely have remained subject to some licensing rules. But earlier constitutional protection could have reduced the climate of caution that made networks vulnerable to advertiser pressure, anti-radical campaigns, and government intimidation. News and public affairs programming might have become more adversarial earlier. There may have been more room for dissenting political viewpoints, stronger investigative journalism, and less fear-driven self-censorship during periods such as the Red Scare and McCarthy era.

The labor side is equally important. Earlier and stronger union protections in film, comics, and broadcasting would likely have shifted power away from studio heads, publishers, and network executives. Writers, performers, animators, camera crews, radio workers, and comic artists could have secured better pay, credit, residuals, job security, and control over working conditions much earlier. In comics especially, where creators often lost ownership of characters and received little compensation, stronger unions might have transformed the economics of the field. Creator rights and royalties might have become standard long before the late twentieth century, changing not only artists’ livelihoods but also the kinds of works they were willing to produce.

This would also likely have reduced the effectiveness of blacklisting. If media workers had both stronger labor institutions and stronger speech protections, anti-communist purges in Hollywood and broadcasting might still have occurred, but they would have been harder to enforce and easier to challenge. Careers destroyed by political suspicion might have survived. As a result, American media culture in the 1940s and 1950s might have contained more openly left-liberal, labor-oriented, and anti-racist perspectives.

Representation would probably have changed as well. Earlier freedom from censorship and stronger collective organization could have opened more space for women, racial minorities, immigrants, and queer creators and characters. This would not automatically eliminate prejudice, since industries and audiences still reflected broader social inequalities. But institutional barriers would have been lower. More creators from marginalized groups might have found sustainable careers, and more stories about minority experiences might have reached mass audiences earlier.

There would also be economic consequences. Stronger unions often raise labor costs, so the big studios, publishers, and networks might have produced fewer works at certain points or resisted innovation more aggressively. Some executives would likely have argued that heavy labor protections reduced flexibility. At the same time, more secure workers and freer creators often produce more durable and ambitious cultural products. So the result might not have been less media, but a different mix: fewer disposable, tightly controlled products and more works with distinctive authorial voices.

Politically, earlier constitutional and labor protection for these media could have made the United States more accustomed to mass media as a site of democratic contest rather than moral regulation. Public debates over media harm would not disappear, but the presumption might shift from “control dangerous media” to “protect expressive freedom unless there is clear harm.” That would have broader implications for American political culture, making it harder to suppress controversial ideas simply because they were popular, visual, or aimed at mass audiences.

Overall, if film, comics, and broadcasting had gained First Amendment and union protections much earlier, twentieth-century American culture would likely have been less censored, less hierarchical, and more politically and artistically pluralistic. The United States probably would have seen earlier development of adult comics, more daring studio films, more independent broadcasting, stronger creator rights, and weaker blacklists. The central tradeoff would have been greater conflict between labor and management and fewer mechanisms for elite control, but the likely long-term result would have been a richer and more democratic media landscape.

edus.text: If film, comics, and broadcasting in the United States had gained strong First Amendment protection and stable union protection much earlier in the twentieth century, American mass culture would likely have developed into a more openly political, more artistically diverse, and more labor-stable system much sooner.
The biggest effects would probably appear in censorship, labor relations, representation, and the political role of media.
In actual history, each of these media developed under constraints that limited both content and working conditions.
Film faced censorship and the Production Code.
Comics were shaken by moral panic and the Comics Code.
Broadcasting operated under heavy political scrutiny and the logic of licensing, which encouraged caution.
At the same time, labor protections in these industries were uneven, delayed, or contested.
This left writers, actors, animators, technicians, and later broadcasters vulnerable to studio control and blacklisting.
If constitutional and union protections had arrived earlier and been more secure, media industries would likely have matured differently.
In film, earlier First Amendment protection would probably have weakened the legitimacy of censorship boards and reduced the power of the Hays Code.
Hollywood films might have addressed controversial topics more directly.
The boundary between “respectable” studio entertainment and more daring independent or foreign work might have been less pronounced.
American cinema could have resembled postwar European film earlier in its treatment of controversial themes.
In comics, earlier legal and cultural protection would have mattered enormously.
Comics were treated as low-status and suspect, especially by critics who blamed them for juvenile delinquency.
If they had enjoyed robust First Amendment protection earlier, the anti-comics panic of the 1950s might have had far less power.
The Comics Code Authority may never have become as dominant.
That would likely have allowed diverse genres to flourish decades earlier.
The idea of comics as a medium for all ages might have become mainstream much earlier.
Broadcasting is a more complicated case because it was tied to public spectrum regulation.
Even with stronger First Amendment protection, radio and television would still likely have remained subject to some licensing rules.
But earlier constitutional protection could have reduced the climate of caution.
News and public affairs programming might have become more adversarial earlier.
There may have been more room for dissenting viewpoints and less self-censorship.
Earlier and stronger union protections would likely have shifted power away from executives.
Workers could have secured better pay, credit, residuals, job security, and control much earlier.
In comics especially, stronger unions might have transformed the economics of the field.
Creator rights and royalties might have become standard long before the late twentieth century.
This would also likely have reduced the effectiveness of blacklisting.
Anti-communist purges might still have occurred, but they would have been harder to enforce and easier to challenge.
As a result, American media culture might have contained more openly left-liberal and anti-racist perspectives.
Earlier freedom and stronger organization could have opened more space for marginalized creators and characters.
This would not automatically eliminate prejudice.
But institutional barriers would have been lower, enabling more diverse careers and stories.
Stronger unions often raise labor costs.
So studios and networks might have produced fewer works or resisted innovation.
At the same time, more secure workers often produce more ambitious cultural products.
So the result might have been a different mix of media rather than less media.
Politically, earlier protections could have made mass media more accepted as a site of democratic contest.
The presumption might shift toward protecting expressive freedom unless there is clear harm.
Overall, earlier First Amendment and union protections would likely have made American culture less censored and more pluralistic.
The United States probably would have seen earlier development of diverse media forms and stronger creator rights.
The central tradeoff would have been greater labor-management conflict and fewer mechanisms for elite control.
But the likely long-term result would have been a richer and more democratic media landscape.

items.question: What If the Haber process is never invented?
human_answers: there are very very very few inventions that are so dependent on one person or group or situation that they wont get invented without them. Frankly i am not sure i can think of any. Yes it may get delayed but never invented? seams doubtful Now this isn't my area of expertise but. Usually when it is time to railroad you can pretty much count n somene inventing and building a railroad. This is why we often get similar inventions in multiple locations. Even back in the day a lot of inventions that get credited to one country and that other counties then “stole them” probably had more then a few cases of contry B finally get to the same level of knowledge in that area and this leads to someone figuring it out. The differencecis that as we get to more modern times the knowledges of 1st world countries gets closer and closer and spreads thoughout . This is why things like nuclear science, jet engines and radar were all “sort of” being looked at in multiple countries with a relatively short time span. So unless there are some very unusual circumstances odds are someone will eventually figure it out.

Luigi Casale develops the Casale process after WWI. Italy had a deficit of fertilizers pre-war; it didn't have the trade networks or finances of other nations to purchase Chilean saltpeter in large amounts, and they invested heavily in nitrogen fixation as a result. WWI worsened that deficit, compounded by the loss of wheat imports from Russia, so Casale started work in 1917 on a more efficient method of nitrogen fixation. Said research continued in the postwar, because BASF refused to license the Haber-Bosch process elsewhere, and the Haber-Bosch process would have required modification anyways because Italy didn't have sufficient coal to use it to produce hydrogen gas in the original Haber-Bosch process. So Italy has the incentive to develop efficient nitrogen fixation processes for strategic autonomy, and Casale has the means to do so. Casale did postgraduate research in Berlin under Walter Nernst, whose research into physical chemistry mirrored that of Haber's, before returning to Italy. Casale then works near the Terni steelworks, which provided the steel to build pressure reactors able to stand pressures more than 3 times that of the Haber-Bosch process (notably by providing an unused battleship gun barrel). Even if we assume some sort of inexplicable theft or espionage on the part of Casale not mentioned in these histories and somehow nobody else thinks to apply Le Chatelier's Principle or try different catalysts, that just means the Frank-Caro process dominates. Sure, the 3x difference in energy usage is going to be difficult to bear, but between that and losing a total war/starving, people will just build more power plants and mine more fossil fuels or mineral nitrates/phosphates. Sources: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0920586121004831 (might be paywalled) https://riviste.fupress.net/index.php/subs/article/download/2809/2057/21510 The Social Side of a Scientific Breakthrough: Fritz Haber, Walther Nernst, and the Discovery of Ammonia Synthesis 1830–1930 | MPIWG Ammonia synthesis. Central to the mass production of fertilizer and explosives. It has been billed as the most consequential scientific breakthrough of the twentieth century. Historical perspectives on ammonia range from technological development to natural resource use, geopolitics, wartime... www.mpiwg-berlin.mpg.de

Arguably the only hard bit of the Haber process is the need for pressurisation to encourage the reaction to react in the right direction. The rest is more or less basic chemistry. So initially the other less efficient methods get adopted (because the nitrates are useful and profitable) and when suitable pressure vessels become available someone discovers the alt-Haber process. Unlike OTL, there will be more opportunity to refine and improve the other less efficient methods of manufacture. Pressure vessels themselves are relatively easy once you have late 19th century naval guns to adapt or inspire: durable pressure vessels are a bit harder [1], but any ferrous vessel will tend to provide iron catalyst even if nobody thought of using it beforehand. So in short, it's just delayed a few years - maybe up to a decade - and meanwhile other less efficient processes get used more than OTL. [1] As of about 20 years ago, the detailed mechanism of metal corrosion in high temperature reducing environments was still poorly understood and under investigation.

items.model_answer:
If the Haber process is never invented, the modern world is much poorer, smaller, and more politically unstable.

The core reason is nitrogen. Plants need usable nitrogen to grow, but most of the nitrogen in the air is chemically inaccessible to them. Before Haber-Bosch, agriculture depended on natural nitrogen sources like manure, crop rotation with legumes, compost, and mined nitrate deposits such as Chilean saltpeter and guano. Those sources are limited. Without industrial nitrogen fixation, global food production would hit a hard ceiling much earlier.

The biggest consequence is population. In real history, synthetic fertilizer supported the huge agricultural gains of the twentieth century. Without it, yields would be much lower almost everywhere, especially for cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize. The world population would almost certainly be far smaller than today, perhaps by billions. Many countries that in reality underwent rapid population growth would instead face chronic food scarcity, stronger pressure to limit family size, or repeated famine.

Agriculture would look different. Farmers would devote much more land to maintaining soil fertility, especially through legume rotations and livestock manure. More people would have to work in farming because productivity per worker would be lower. Meat production would also be constrained, since livestock both consume grain and produce manure, creating a tighter agricultural balance. Forests and grasslands would likely be converted to cropland more aggressively in some regions to compensate for lower yields, though in other regions population limits might reduce total pressure on land. So the environmental outcome is mixed: less synthetic fertilizer pollution, but potentially more deforestation and habitat loss per unit of food.

Economically, industrialization would still happen, but with a lower ceiling on urbanization and growth. Modern economies rely on a small farming sector feeding a huge non-farming population. Without synthetic fertilizer, many more workers stay tied to the land, slowing the expansion of cities, education, heavy industry, and service economies. Standards of living rise more slowly, especially in densely populated countries with poor soils or limited access to natural nitrates.

Geopolitically, the world changes sharply. Access to natural nitrate deposits becomes strategically crucial. Countries with nitrate resources, especially Chile, become much more important. Major powers would compete intensely over fertilizer and explosives precursors, because fixed nitrogen matters not just for farming but also for munitions. Germany’s situation in World War I is a classic example: the Haber-Bosch process helped it keep producing explosives despite blockade. Without it, Germany would likely run short sooner, which could shorten the war or alter its course. More broadly, states would be more vulnerable to blockades and resource chokepoints.

There is also a dark military tradeoff. No Haber process means less large-scale domestic production of nitrates for explosives, which could reduce the intensity or duration of some wars. But it would not eliminate industrial warfare, and it would increase competition for natural nitrate supplies. So military effects would be significant but not straightforwardly peaceful.

Public health and society would also be different. Chronic malnutrition would be more common. Political systems would face repeated crises over bread prices and harvest failures. Governments might invest much earlier in birth control, land reform, rationing systems, agricultural science, and alternative nitrogen-fixation methods. In fact, strong pressure would exist to develop some substitute process sooner or later, because the demand is so overwhelming. If Haber specifically never invents his process, someone else might eventually discover another scalable route to synthetic ammonia, though perhaps later, more expensively, or less efficiently. If we assume no equivalent process emerges at all, then the long-run constraint on human society is severe.

So the simplest answer is this: without the Haber process, there is no Green Revolution in anything like the form we know, global population stays much lower, famines are more frequent, economic development is slower, and international politics revolve more heavily around scarce natural nitrogen. The world is less chemically intensive, but also less prosperous and less capable of feeding itself.

edus.text: If the Haber process is never invented, the modern world is much poorer, smaller, and more politically unstable.
The core reason is nitrogen.
Plants need usable nitrogen to grow.
But most of the nitrogen in the air is chemically inaccessible to them.
Before Haber-Bosch, agriculture depended on natural nitrogen sources like manure, crop rotation with legumes, compost, and mined nitrate deposits such as Chilean saltpeter and guano.
Those sources are limited.
Without industrial nitrogen fixation, global food production would hit a hard ceiling much earlier.
The biggest consequence is population.
In real history, synthetic fertilizer supported the huge agricultural gains of the twentieth century.
Without it, yields would be much lower almost everywhere, especially for cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize.
The world population would almost certainly be far smaller than today, perhaps by billions.
Many countries that in reality underwent rapid population growth would instead face chronic food scarcity, stronger pressure to limit family size, or repeated famine.
Agriculture would look different.
Farmers would devote much more land to maintaining soil fertility, especially through legume rotations and livestock manure.
More people would have to work in farming because productivity per worker would be lower.
Meat production would also be constrained, since livestock both consume grain and produce manure, creating a tighter agricultural balance.
Forests and grasslands would likely be converted to cropland more aggressively in some regions to compensate for lower yields.
In other regions population limits might reduce total pressure on land.
So the environmental outcome is mixed: less synthetic fertilizer pollution, but potentially more deforestation and habitat loss per unit of food.
Economically, industrialization would still happen, but with a lower ceiling on urbanization and growth.
Modern economies rely on a small farming sector feeding a huge non-farming population.
Without synthetic fertilizer, many more workers stay tied to the land, slowing the expansion of cities, education, heavy industry, and service economies.
Standards of living rise more slowly, especially in densely populated countries with poor soils or limited access to natural nitrates.
Geopolitically, the world changes sharply.
Access to natural nitrate deposits becomes strategically crucial.
Countries with nitrate resources, especially Chile, become much more important.
Major powers would compete intensely over fertilizer and explosives precursors, because fixed nitrogen matters not just for farming but also for munitions.
Germany’s situation in World War I is a classic example.
The Haber-Bosch process helped it keep producing explosives despite blockade.
Without it, Germany would likely run short sooner, which could shorten the war or alter its course.
More broadly, states would be more vulnerable to blockades and resource chokepoints.
There is also a dark military tradeoff.
No Haber process means less large-scale domestic production of nitrates for explosives, which could reduce the intensity or duration of some wars.
But it would not eliminate industrial warfare, and it would increase competition for natural nitrate supplies.
So military effects would be significant but not straightforwardly peaceful.
Public health and society would also be different.
Chronic malnutrition would be more common.
Political systems would face repeated crises over bread prices and harvest failures.
Governments might invest much earlier in birth control, land reform, rationing systems, agricultural science, and alternative nitrogen-fixation methods.
Strong pressure would exist to develop some substitute process sooner or later, because the demand is so overwhelming.
If Haber specifically never invents his process, someone else might eventually discover another scalable route to synthetic ammonia.
If we assume no equivalent process emerges at all, then the long-run constraint on human society is severe.

So the simplest answer is this: without the Haber process, there is no Green Revolution in anything like the form we know, global population stays much lower, famines are more frequent, economic development is slower, and international politics revolve more heavily around scarce natural nitrogen.
The world is less chemically intensive, but also less prosperous and less capable of feeding itself.

items.question: What If one people, two nation-states
human_answers: Italy would be easy to do, even with a recent-ish POD: there were proposals floating around in the mid-19th century, concerning Victor Emmanuel II crowning himself king of the Two Sicilies rather than annexing the place outright, while keeping the local government around; since Cavour himself was hesitant to annex the South, and only did so because Garibaldi was becoming too much of a loose cannon, if things had gone slightly differently, this could've happened, and since the South had its own distinct identity and history (even though it used Tuscan as its own official language, as every other state in the peninsula did), this could've stuck, with northern and southern Italy becoming kind of like Australia and New Zealand, independent countries closely tied to each other and under the same monarch. Ironically, the Third War of Independence could've gone better for northern Italy, since northern and southern troops couldn't integrate well IRL, and Italy could've gained Trento and Trieste before World War I, butterflying away the need for intervention; the Two Sicilies could have eventually gained a protectorate of sorts over Albania (history would rhyme there, since Skanderbeg had ties to the Neapolitan royals of his era and fled to Naples when his anti-Turkish uprising failed) and would've surely annexed the Papal enclaves once the north annexes Rome. Garibaldi's OTL expedition to Trento might instead take place in Pola or even Fiume but, as I stated earlier, northern Italy could be more willing to just accept territorial bribes from Austria here, since most of the Irredenta would've been gained already.

Faroese should linguistic be seen as a dialect of Western Norwegian. You could pretty much write Faroese with Nynorsk (the written standard the dialects in this region use) and vice versa. Where Faroese differ from Icelandic is that like Norwegian it have seen near complete replacement of vocabulary with Danish vocabulary thanks to the use of Danish Bibles, while on Iceland the Bible was translated into Icelandic early on and the Danish state supported the existence of a distinct Icelandic language for ideological reasons.. The main reason why Danes and Norwegians have trouble reading Faroese is because it use a it own variation of the Latin alphabet which is different from the one Danes and Norwegians use, while even if Icelandic was written using Danish or the different Norwegian written standards, it would be hard to understand it because of the difference in vocabulary. If the Danish-Norwegian Union had survived the Faroese Island would simply have been seen as part of Western Norway.

If the Prussians had done a better job containing the Great Northern War plague, then there might have been far more Prussian Lithuanians, who differ from Lithuanians in that they are Lutheran, strongly influenced by German culture, and speak a Germanized register of Lithuanian. While they kept the Lithuanian language alive during the Russian repression, the Prussian Lithuanians actually opposed Lithuaniation nationalism and explicitly refused to live in an independent Lithuanian state, accepting nothing else than German rule. Thus, when the Memel Territory was established, the Prussian Lithuanians declared themselves to be "Memellanders". Subsequently, after WW2, the Soviets saw them as Germans and expelled them from East Prussia. IOTL, the GNW plague absolutely decimated the Prussian Lithuanians, who comprised nearly 90% of its victims. Had it been contained effectively, and a butterfly net used afterwards, there would've been far more Prussian Lithuanians in East Prussia, perhaps enough to cause a national awakening. The Soviets likely would've propped up "Prussia" as a separate SSR from Lithuania while still expelling the Germans, and supported Prussian Lithuanian nationalism to divide and conquer (having just annexed resistive Lithuania). Basically Moldovenism, though in this case with genuine religious and cultural differences (plus a very different standard language).
items.original_question:
AHC: one people, two nation-states

There have been plenty of cases where one people with a common language and ancestry are separated into two nation-states. I'm not talking about ideological reasons like in the case of Germany and Korea, but in terms of centuries-long division of religion (Catholic Croats and Orthodox Serbs or Catholic Austrians and Protestant Germans) or geopolitics (Montenegro and Ottoman-dominated Serbia, Russia-dominated Moldova and Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia). And this explains why I specifically use the term "nation-state", as one people separated for long enough by the aforementioned factors would eventually evolve into different nation-states with their own ethnic identities. Is there any other scenario where this can happen?

items.model_answer:
If one people are divided between two nation-states, the result is usually a tension between shared identity and separate political loyalty. A single people may still have the same language, history, religion, ethnicity, or collective memory, but once they live under two different states, each state begins shaping them through its own laws, institutions, education system, economy, and foreign policy.

Over time, several outcomes are possible. The two states may remain closely connected, treating themselves as parts of a broader national community despite political separation. This can produce cooperation, cross-border solidarity, and even movements for reunification or confederation. But separation can also harden. Each state may cultivate its own version of history and patriotism, so that the one people gradually become two politically distinct nations in practice, even if they still claim common origins.

This situation can also create conflict. If both states claim to represent the same people, they may compete for legitimacy. Minorities on each side of the border may face pressure to prove loyalty. Questions of citizenship, migration, military service, and sovereignty become sensitive. In extreme cases, one state may seek unification by force, or outside powers may exploit the division.

So “one people, two nation-states” generally means that cultural nationhood and political statehood do not perfectly match. It does not automatically lead to war or unity, but it almost always creates an unstable relationship in which identity, sovereignty, and belonging are continuously negotiated.

items.question: What If Reverse Cuba and the Philippines
human_answers: American interest in Cuban had been more or less secured after the Span-Am War, so it'll be difficult for them to justify annexation, which could earn the ire of the Cuban independentists and the Southern States. But the Philippines presented some once in a lifetime opportunity for the US to finally gain their own foothold in the China market, instead of lurking around ports under the jurisdiction of other great powers. In a relatively practical POV, the US didn't need to annex the whole islands. Why waste men and money against the people that's prepared to fight to the last man to preserve their freedom (some historians even claimed that the Fil-Am War was the US first taste of a Vietnam scenario)? They could just let them be, make some economic agreements with them, get some ports, etc. and voila, they've got themselves a permanent presence in the Pacific without too much blood. Heck they could even convince the Brits to recognize the Republic and establish relations hoping to have Germany (or Japan) to back down from doing anything funny (although that may be a long shot).

Well, these few regions can try to secede. The issue is if they can maintain status quo. Malolos Republic controlled the navy or whatsoever left of the Spanish Navy. The government also controlled majority of the population of the Philippines. The Malolos republic can raise 100k men while your local provinces seceding have that same or lower population than the opposing army with your army having no or minimal rifles whatsoever. Your opponents have also better and well educated generals compared to you. You got also the issue of loyalty of your populace if they are more loyal to your seceding province or Malolos Republic. It is simple reality of warfare, you can try but the question is if you can succeed. It is pure imagination that civil war is because some or one provinces seceded. The only way that Civil war will happen is if Luna or Aguinaldo or anyone in the army fights among themselves. Or if you got a PoD that will butterfly away anything the resembles OTL 1890s Philippines.

Not really. The mood in the US was generally fairly pro-Cuban, and many of the Yellow Journalists of the time were agitating for Cuban independence. Plus, the labor unions in the US were also tied pretty closely to the Cubans. The whole reason the Maine was in Cuba was because the US had much more vested in what happened there than in the Philippines, due to the proximity to Florida. They were very concerned that the violence in the island might damage US investments further, and they were determined that either Cuba would remain Spanish or that Cuba would be in the US sphere somehow. Given that 6 decades later, human civilization nearly ended with a foreign threat got a foothold on that island, that was a fairly prescient concern. The US didn't care much about the Philippines until they managed to sink the Spanish fleet and realized that nothing was stopping them from taking the islands, so they did. So, in summation, if you want the US to annex Cuba and liberate the Philippines, you'd have to change things much earlier than the war.

Your mission is to reverse the fate of Cuba and the Philippines after the Spanish-American War. That means Cuba getting annexed and the Philippines being made a protectorate. Puerto Rico can be either.

items.model_answer:
If Cuba and the Philippines had been “reversed” in the sense that the United States annexed Cuba as a long-term territory while granting the Philippines rapid independence, the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century history of U.S. imperialism would likely have looked quite different, though not completely transformed.

Cuba was much closer to the United States, deeply tied to the U.S. economy, and already central to American strategic thinking because of the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and the future Panama Canal zone. If the U.S. had kept Cuba outright instead of treating it as a nominally independent protectorate, it probably would have become a much more integrated part of the American sphere, perhaps closer to Puerto Rico in status, though its large population, strong nationalism, and plantation economy would still have made annexation politically contentious. American investors would likely have expanded even faster there, and Washington might have intervened even more directly in Cuban politics rather than relying on devices like the Platt Amendment. Cuban nationalism, in turn, might have become more sharply anti-colonial earlier, because formal annexation would have removed even the symbolic promise of sovereignty.

If, on the other hand, the Philippines had been granted early independence after Spain’s defeat, the United States would have avoided the Philippine-American War or greatly reduced it. That would have meant fewer casualties, less domestic controversy over overseas empire, and a weaker test case for large-scale American colonial rule in Asia. The anti-imperialist movement in the United States might have been stronger politically, because the U.S. would have been able to claim it had liberated rather than conquered a former Spanish colony. At the same time, an independent Philippines in 1898 or shortly after would have faced serious problems: factional conflict, limited state capacity, possible vulnerability to Japan, Germany, or other powers, and heavy continued U.S. economic and naval influence. So independence would not necessarily have meant full autonomy.

Strategically, this reversal would have made U.S. empire look more Caribbean-centered and less Pacific-Asian. The United States still would have pursued Asian trade, but without direct control of the Philippines its military and diplomatic role in East Asia might have been weaker. That could have reduced later American leverage in the western Pacific and slightly altered the buildup to U.S.-Japanese rivalry. Meanwhile, stronger formal control over Cuba would have underscored the Monroe Doctrine style of regional domination in the Americas.

Politically and ideologically, the reversal would have exposed a major contradiction even more clearly. Americans often justified intervention in Cuba in the language of liberation, while rule in the Philippines was defended through “civilizing” arguments. If Cuba had been annexed and the Philippines freed, the U.S. might have appeared more honest in Asia and more blatantly imperial in the Caribbean. Race would have remained central: many U.S. policymakers were more comfortable dominating nearby tropical territories indirectly, and many were uneasy about annexing large nonwhite populations as full parts of the Union. So annexing Cuba might still have stopped short of statehood and produced a colonial arrangement marked by legal inequality.

Overall, reversing Cuba and the Philippines would probably have reduced the scale of U.S. imperial war in Asia, intensified formal American domination in the Caribbean, and shifted the symbolism of 1898. The United States would still have emerged as an imperial power, but one more focused on nearby hemispheric control than on transpacific colonial expansion.

edus.text: If Cuba and the Philippines had been “reversed” in the sense that the United States annexed Cuba as a long-term territory while granting the Philippines rapid independence,
the late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century history of U.S. imperialism would likely have looked quite different,
though not completely transformed.

Cuba was much closer to the United States, deeply tied to the U.S. economy, and already central to American strategic thinking because of the Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, and the future Panama Canal zone.
If the U.S. had kept Cuba outright instead of treating it as a nominally independent protectorate,
it probably would have become a much more integrated part of the American sphere, perhaps closer to Puerto Rico in status,
though its large population, strong nationalism, and plantation economy would still have made annexation politically contentious.
American investors would likely have expanded even faster there,
and Washington might have intervened even more directly in Cuban politics rather than relying on devices like the Platt Amendment.
Cuban nationalism, in turn, might have become more sharply anti-colonial earlier,
because formal annexation would have removed even the symbolic promise of sovereignty.
If, on the other hand, the Philippines had been granted early independence after Spain’s defeat,
the United States would have avoided the Philippine-American War or greatly reduced it.
That would have meant fewer casualties, less domestic controversy over overseas empire, and a weaker test case for large-scale American colonial rule in Asia.
The anti-imperialist movement in the United States might have been stronger politically,
because the U.S. would have been able to claim it had liberated rather than conquered a former Spanish colony.

At the same time, an independent Philippines in 1898 or shortly after would have faced serious problems: factional conflict, limited state capacity, possible vulnerability to Japan, Germany, or other powers, and heavy continued U.S. economic and naval influence.
So independence would not necessarily have meant full autonomy.
Strategically, this reversal would have made U.S. empire look more Caribbean-centered and less Pacific-Asian.
The United States still would have pursued Asian trade,
but without direct control of the Philippines its military and diplomatic role in East Asia might have been weaker.
That could have reduced later American leverage in the western Pacific and slightly altered the buildup to U.S.-Japanese rivalry.
Meanwhile, stronger formal control over Cuba would have underscored the Monroe Doctrine style of regional domination in the Americas.
Politically and ideologically, the reversal would have exposed a major contradiction even more clearly.
Americans often justified intervention in Cuba in the language of liberation,
while rule in the Philippines was defended through “civilizing” arguments.
If Cuba had been annexed and the Philippines freed,
the U.S. might have appeared more honest in Asia and more blatantly imperial in the Caribbean.
Race would have remained central:
many U.S. policymakers were more comfortable dominating nearby tropical territories indirectly,
and many were uneasy about annexing large nonwhite populations as full parts of the Union.
So annexing Cuba might still have stopped short of statehood and produced a colonial arrangement marked by legal inequality.

Overall, reversing Cuba and the Philippines would probably have reduced the scale of U.S. imperial war in Asia, intensified formal American domination in the Caribbean, and shifted the symbolism of 1898.
The United States would still have emerged as an imperial power,
but one more focused on nearby hemispheric control than on transpacific colonial expansion.
