nodes.text: If modern music had developed without Elvis Presley and The Beatles, it would still exist,
but it would likely look and sound very different in pace, style, and cultural reach.
Elvis mattered because he helped bring together rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and pop into a form that became early rock and roll for mainstream white America.
Without him, that crossover still probably happens,
because the musical forces behind it were already there in Black American music, Southern radio, independent labels, and youth culture.
But it likely happens more slowly and through a wider group of performers rather than one giant symbol.
Artists like Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino, Buddy Holly, Jerry Lee Lewis, and others might have had even greater historical weight.
The social shock of rock and roll would still come,
but perhaps with less of a single face attached to it.
The Beatles mattered in a different way.
They did not invent rock, pop songwriting, studio experimentation, youth fandom, or the album as an artistic statement by themselves,
but they accelerated all of those.
Without them, the 1960s music scene would probably be more fragmented.
The British Invasion might still occur through bands like The Rolling Stones, The Kinks, The Who, and The Animals,
but perhaps not as explosively or globally.
American pop and rock might remain more dominant in the early 1960s,
and British bands might have broken through more gradually.
Songwriting and recording would likely evolve differently too.
The Beatles helped normalize the idea that a pop group could write its own material, reinvent its sound repeatedly, and use the studio as a creative instrument.
Without that model, the separation between songwriters, performers, and producers might have lasted longer in mainstream pop.
The shift from singles toward albums as major artistic and commercial units might also have been delayed.
Psychedelic pop, baroque pop, and experimental studio rock would still emerge,
but perhaps less quickly or under different leaders, such as Brian Wilson, Phil Spector, Frank Zappa, or later progressive rock musicians.
Culturally, both Elvis and The Beatles were symbols as much as musicians.
Elvis represented generational rebellion, sexuality, and the mainstreaming of sounds rooted in Black music, though often in unequal ways.
The Beatles represented modern youth culture becoming international, self-conscious, and artistically ambitious.
Without them, music would likely remain important,
but it might have had a weaker role as a single global language for youth identity in the 1950s and 1960s.
One of the biggest changes would be in influence chains.
Countless later artists were shaped directly by Elvis or The Beatles.
Without them, the paths leading to classic rock, power pop, folk rock, psychedelic rock, Britpop, singer-songwriter pop, and even some strands of heavy metal and indie music would shift.
Bob Dylan’s turn toward rock might happen differently.
The Byrds, Beach Boys, David Bowie, Oasis, ELO, and many others might sound different or perhaps not emerge in the same form at all.
Still, modern music would not disappear.
The deeper engines of change—Black American innovation, recording technology, postwar prosperity, radio, television, teenage consumer culture, and transatlantic exchange—would still be there.
So the most likely outcome is not a world without modern popular music,

but a world where it becomes less centralized around a few icons, develops more unevenly, and perhaps gives greater credit to a broader range of artists who were overshadowed by Elvis and The Beatles.
In short, without Elvis and The Beatles, modern music would probably be less unified, less quickly transformed, and less centered on a few legendary figures.
It would still become modern music,
but through a more scattered and slower revolution.

items.question: What If the Royal Navy had deployed carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward?
human_answers: Far too big Even with folding wings I don't think they would fit on the elevators and would take up too much room in the hanger even of they fit which again I suspect not Its landing on performance of he Beaufighter is about the same as an avenger (60 knots?) but its much heavier than the TBF so I am not sure the arrestor cables of the day could handle such a plane. Its a nice idea but its too much of a plane for the carriers of the day - might work on an Audacious class but not the carriers built in the late 30s. The Whispering Death is already doing sterling work as a land based anti shipping aircraft during the war and it has great range - not quite 'Rikko' (G3m and G4m Japanese bombers) range, but close too it, but still a scourge where ever it operated.

In the last thread on the subject I mentioned, given any wing-break would have to be somewhat outboard the engines*, that you could probably take one up and down on Implacable's forward lift but the hangar height would preclude you rolling it off. You could store one in Illustrious's hangar, if you made it from a kit of parts, as the lift is too narrow. So deck parks only. You could use some form of depressing oleos to lower the Beaufighter's resting angle. You might just scrape it into Implacable's hangar but clearances would be marginal. Any kind of seaway would make deck handling tricky to impossible. You could also only load a torpedo on the flight deck with the aircraft back up to full height. I also suggested an increased-chord rudder and handed props because the Beaufighter could be a handful with all the room in the world. Operating a Beau on/off of a carrier is an expensive way to give a pilot a coronary... ETA: The wing-breaks are going to be in the order of 25ft apart and Illustrious's elevators are only 22ft across. Folding the wings is also going to involve re-siting the cooling ducts from the outboard leading edge.
items.original_question: What if Sea Beaufort and Sea Beaufighters used on Royal Navy aircraft carriers? What if the Royal Navy used a possible Bristol Sea variant of both Beauforts and Beaufighters on their carriers starting in 1940 replacing Fairy Swordfish aircraft in the torpedo attack role for example? Would this be possible design wise? Would they be better than the bomb and torpedo attack aircraft available at the time? Would the aircraft actually be able to be used like this or would they be too large? How effective would they be if used on aircraft carriers? Regards

criteria.name: Carrier suitability and physical feasibility of Sea Beauforts/Sea Beaufighters
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately reasons through whether carrier-capable Beauforts and Beaufighters could physically operate from Royal Navy carriers from 1940, including size, weight, folding wings, elevators, hangar limits, deck parks, arrestor gear, landing speeds, and sea-state handling.
criteria.1-2: Treats carrier operation as straightforward or impossible with little technical reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions size or weight issues but omits key constraints such as lifts, hangars, arrestor loads, or deck handling.
criteria.5-6: Identifies several major feasibility constraints but with limited carrier-class specificity or unclear severity.
criteria.7-8: Explains most relevant constraints and distinguishes marginal deck operation from practical sustained carrier use.
criteria.9-10: Provides a technically coherent assessment tied to 1940 RN carrier designs, showing why operation would be marginal, deck-park dependent, or impractical despite possible modifications.

criteria.name: Aircraft modification and integration requirements
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the changes needed to navalize Beauforts and Beaufighters, including folding wings, strengthened undercarriage and arrestor hooks, corrosion protection, propeller/rudder handling changes, torpedo loading, maintenance burden, and performance penalties.
criteria.1-2: Assumes existing aircraft could simply be placed on carriers with no meaningful changes.
criteria.3-4: Lists generic navalization changes without linking them to Beaufort/Beaufighter design problems.
criteria.5-6: Covers basic navalization needs and some performance or maintenance tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Connects specific modifications to likely operational problems such as wing-fold location, deck clearance, torpedo loading, and low-speed handling.
criteria.9-10: Gives a detailed, plausible integration pathway and explains how each change affects space, weight, reliability, sortie rate, and carrier safety.

criteria.name: Operational and tactical effects on Royal Navy air warfare
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly evaluates how carrier Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters would affect RN strike, fighter, reconnaissance, anti-shipping, and convoy operations from 1940 onward.
criteria.1-2: Makes broad claims of decisive success or no impact without operational mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions possible stronger strike or fighter capability but does not analyze how it would be used.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some tactical benefits and drawbacks, such as range or payload versus sortie rate and deck capacity.
criteria.7-8: Balances improved long-range strike/firepower against fewer embarked aircraft, slower handling, and carrier vulnerability.
criteria.9-10: Explains theater-specific operational consequences in the Atlantic, Mediterranean, Arctic, or Far East while accounting for sortie generation, air-group composition, and mission suitability.

criteria.name: Long-range counterfactual chain coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer builds a causally connected timeline from 1940 deployment through later war outcomes, avoiding isolated claims and showing how early technical choices propagate into doctrine, procurement, carrier design, and campaign results.

items.model_answer:
If the Royal Navy had fielded genuinely effective carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, the result would probably have been a noticeable but not war-winning increase in British naval striking power, especially in the Mediterranean and against Axis shipping. It would not have transformed the war at sea overnight, because British carriers, doctrine, radar integration, escort strength, and pilot training still imposed hard limits. But it could have made Fleet Air Arm carriers much more dangerous much earlier.

The key change would be that the Royal Navy would have had a better torpedo and strike capability at sea before aircraft like the Barracuda and before American carrier practices and aircraft began to influence Allied operations. Historically, the Fleet Air Arm relied heavily on the Swordfish and later the Albacore—slow, vulnerable biplanes that were excellent for some niche tasks but increasingly obsolete in daylight against strong opposition. A navalized Beaufort would have offered a faster, more survivable torpedo bomber with greater range and payload. A navalized Beaufighter would have added a powerful long-range strike fighter and anti-shipping aircraft, capable of suppressing flak, escorting strikes, and attacking lighter vessels directly.

In the Mediterranean, this could have mattered a great deal. British carriers often operated within reach of strong Italian and later German air power. A faster strike wing could have improved attacks on Italian convoys to North Africa and perhaps increased the attrition imposed on Axis supply lines to Libya. Even modest improvements here could have had real strategic effects, because Rommel’s forces were chronically supply-constrained. If carrier-based Beauforts had been available in useful numbers in 1941–42, British naval air strikes against merchant shipping, escorts, and port targets might have been more frequent and more lethal. Sea Beaufighters, in particular, could have made British carrier strikes less dependent on surprise and darkness, since they could provide heavy suppressive fire and better self-defense than Swordfish-type aircraft.

The most obvious comparison is Taranto and Bismarck. At Taranto, slower biplanes actually worked well because of surprise, night attack, and weak fighter opposition. Sea Beauforts would not necessarily have made Taranto dramatically better, and they may even have been less suitable for that specific shallow-water, low-speed torpedo role unless properly adapted. Against Bismarck, however, the Royal Navy might have benefited more clearly from faster torpedo bombers. Swordfish succeeded partly because bad weather and low speed disrupted German fire control, but they were also extraordinarily vulnerable. Sea Beauforts could have offered a better chance of repeated attacks with fewer losses, assuming crews were trained for deck operations and torpedo delivery.

In the Atlantic, the impact would have been more limited but still meaningful. Fleet carriers and especially escort carriers were constrained by deck size and aircraft handling. The Beaufort and Beaufighter were relatively large, heavy twin-engined aircraft. Even if navalized successfully, they would have been difficult to operate from many British carriers, particularly the smaller ones. So this counterfactual only works if we assume not just arrestor hooks and folding wings, but a whole set of successful naval adaptations and carrier operating procedures. If that hurdle is fully cleared, then convoy escort carriers might still struggle to use them efficiently, meaning the biggest beneficiaries would be the larger fleet carriers. This limits the scale of the transformation.

Against the Kriegsmarine surface fleet and coastal shipping, Sea Beaufighters could have been valuable. The land-based Beaufighter became an effective strike aircraft in anti-shipping work later in the war. Putting that capability to sea earlier could have improved attacks on German naval units in Norway or on supply traffic in confined waters. But carrier availability was always a bottleneck. The Royal Navy never had enough fleet carriers to maintain constant pressure everywhere. Better aircraft would improve each strike opportunity, but not solve the basic shortage of decks.

There are also real tradeoffs. Twin-engined naval aircraft generally demanded more deck space, more maintenance, and more fuel. British armored carriers had relatively small hangars and air groups compared with American carriers. So a Sea Beaufort or Sea Beaufighter air group might have reduced total aircraft numbers carried. That could produce a paradox: each individual aircraft is more capable, but the carrier’s overall striking cycle may become less flexible. A carrier packed with large twin-engined strike aircraft might have fewer fighters for combat air patrol, reconnaissance planes, or reserve aircraft. In 1940–42 especially, that could be dangerous.

Another major issue is development burden. Making either aircraft carrier-capable from 1940 onward would have required engineering effort, testing, and production capacity that Britain was already stretching to the limit. Strengthened landing gear, naval corrosion protection, arrestor gear compatibility, folding wings or compact stowage arrangements, low-speed handling improvements, torpedo gear, and deck-landing training would all have taken time and resources. If Britain diverts effort into this, something else likely slips. The payoff could be worthwhile, but it would not come for free.

So the most plausible overall outcome is this: the Royal Navy gets an earlier and more modern carrier strike arm, Axis convoys in the Mediterranean suffer more heavily, some major naval operations become less risky and more effective, and British carriers gain a better daylight anti-shipping punch. But there is no clean revolution. The aircraft would be hard to operate, carrier capacity would still be limited, and the Fleet Air Arm’s broader institutional and logistical constraints would remain.

In short, if the Royal Navy had deployed Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward, Britain would likely have fought a sharper, more lethal carrier war at the tactical and operational level, especially in the Mediterranean. The effect could have been significant enough to worsen Axis supply problems and improve British naval striking options, but not so great as to fundamentally overturn the larger balance of naval power by itself.

edus.text: If the Royal Navy had fielded genuinely effective carrier-capable Sea Beauforts and Sea Beaufighters from 1940 onward,
the result would probably have been a noticeable but not war-winning increase in British naval striking power, especially in the Mediterranean and against Axis shipping.
It would not have transformed the war at sea overnight,
because British carriers, doctrine, radar integration, escort strength, and pilot training still imposed hard limits.
But it could have made Fleet Air Arm carriers much more dangerous much earlier.
The key change would be that the Royal Navy would have had a better torpedo and strike capability at sea before later aircraft and American influence.
Historically, the Fleet Air Arm relied heavily on the Swordfish and later the Albacore.
These were slow, vulnerable biplanes that were increasingly obsolete in daylight against strong opposition.
A navalized Beaufort would have offered a faster, more survivable torpedo bomber with greater range and payload.
A navalized Beaufighter would have added a powerful long-range strike fighter and anti-shipping aircraft.
In the Mediterranean, this could have mattered a great deal.
British carriers often operated within reach of strong Italian and later German air power.
A faster strike wing could have improved attacks on Italian convoys to North Africa and increased attrition on Axis supply lines.
Even modest improvements here could have had real strategic effects.
Rommel’s forces were chronically supply-constrained.
If carrier-based Beauforts had been available in useful numbers in 1941–42,
British naval air strikes might have been more frequent and more lethal.
Sea Beaufighters could have made British carrier strikes less dependent on surprise and darkness.
The most obvious comparison is Taranto and Bismarck.
At Taranto, slower biplanes worked well because of surprise, night attack, and weak fighter opposition.
Sea Beauforts would not necessarily have made Taranto dramatically better.
Against Bismarck, the Royal Navy might have benefited more clearly from faster torpedo bombers.
Sea Beauforts could have offered a better chance of repeated attacks with fewer losses.
In the Atlantic, the impact would have been more limited but still meaningful.
Fleet and escort carriers were constrained by deck size and aircraft handling.
The Beaufort and Beaufighter were relatively large, heavy twin-engined aircraft.
Even if navalized successfully, they would have been difficult to operate from many British carriers.
This counterfactual requires extensive successful naval adaptations and procedures.
Even then, escort carriers might struggle to use them efficiently.
This limits the scale of the transformation.
Against the Kriegsmarine and coastal shipping, Sea Beaufighters could have been valuable.
Carrier availability was always a bottleneck.
Better aircraft would improve each strike opportunity.
They would not solve the basic shortage of decks.
There are also real tradeoffs.
Twin-engined naval aircraft demanded more deck space, maintenance, and fuel.
British armored carriers had relatively small hangars and air groups.
A Sea Beaufort or Sea Beaufighter air group might have reduced total aircraft numbers carried.
Each individual aircraft would be more capable.
The carrier’s overall striking cycle might become less flexible.
That could be dangerous in 1940–42.
Another major issue is development burden.
Making these aircraft carrier-capable would have required major engineering effort and resources.
If Britain diverted effort into this, something else would likely slip.
The payoff could be worthwhile.
It would not come for free.
The most plausible overall outcome is that the Royal Navy gains an earlier, more modern carrier strike arm and achieves heavier Axis losses with somewhat more effective operations.
But there is no clean revolution.
The aircraft would be hard to operate, carrier capacity limited, and institutional constraints persistent.
In short, Britain would likely have fought a sharper, more lethal carrier war at the tactical and operational level.
The effect would not have fundamentally overturned the larger balance of naval power by itself.

items.question: What If : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944
human_answers: The only Southerner who got any serious support at the DNC in 1944 was Alabama Senator John H. Bankhead II, who came in a distant third with 98 votes (8.33%) on the first ballot. The only other (non Alben W. Barkley) Southerners who got even one vote were: J. Melville Broughton (Governor of North Carolina), Prentice Cooper (Governor of Tennessee), Robert S. Kerr (Senator from Oklahoma), Herbert O'Conor (Governor of Maryland), Claude Pepper (Senator from Florida), Sam Rayburn (Speaker of the House), and Bascom N. Timmons (D.C. based newspaperman who grew up in Texas). Of these, only Bankhead II, Barkley, Broughton, Cooper, Kerr, and O’Conor got double digits. So your best case scenario is Roosevelt and/or the convention see a need to nominate a Southerner, and go with Bankhead II who IOTL died on June 12, 1946 following a stroke on May 24, 1946, which means you end up with three Presidents in little over a year. Based on the 1886 Succession Act, Bankhead II’s successor would be none other than… James F. Byrnes. IOTL, Truman appointed him in July of 1945, and it’s pretty likely Bankhead II does similarly, wanting to support a follow Southerner. (Prior to the Succession Act of 1947, neither the Speaker of the House nor the President pro tempore of the Senate were in the line of succession.) So in a roundabout way, you do end up with Byrnes as President…

Right. Byrnes thought he was Roosevelt's choice. Truman went to the DNC planning to make a nominating speech for Byrnes. If Byrnes does get the nod... FDR wins in 1944 anyway. But things diverge after that. IMO the Republicans sweep in 1946 as OTL. Byrnes was a very capable man and won't make any big missteps, so IMO he will be renominated in 1948. There may be a feeling that the 1948 nomination is a poisoned chalice, what with the 1946 GOP sweep and general public fatigue with 16 years of Democrat Presidents. The "Humphreyite" liberals may still try to push a civil rights plank at the DNC, but against Byrnes' at least tacit opposition will fail. They won't bolt to support Wallace overtly. Instead they may sit back to watch Byrnes crash and burn in November, while they regroup for 1952. Byrnes will lose a fair number of voters to Wallace outside the South. Also, AIUI, Dewey chose to soft-pedal civil rights OTL in the vain hope of winning some Upper South states with the Democrats divided. TTL that ignis fatuus isn't around, so Dewey probably emphasizes civil rights to draw the increasingly important black vote in the North and also some white liberals. This should be enough for Dewey to win. The next question is whether he has enough "coat tails" for Republicans to hold Congress. Another question is how the civil rights issue shapes across the next decade. OTL, leadership on the issue was taken by liberal non-Southern Democrats, with the low-key support of Republicans. The first cracks in the "Solid South" came in the 1950s, as a few white Southerners who could no longer rely on the national Democratic party to protect Jim Crow found they could vote Republican. If under Dewey, Republicans claim the leading role, that's not going to happen. The "Humphreyites" will gain control of the Democrats by 1952; there may be a Dixiecrat ticket that year. Dewey will be re-elected, barring some debacle in Korea or whatever. Warren won't be Chief Justice, but the Court will still be making rulings like Brown .
items.original_question: What if : FDR picks a Segregationist VP in 1944 In 1944, after intense pressure, President Franklin Delano Roosevelt would drop Vice President Henry Asgard Wallace from the ticket but due to his initial choice of James F. Byrnes being rejected due to his conversion from Catholicism, he would ultimately be convinced to go with Missouri Senator Harry S. Truman. Truman, as President, proved to be a liberal on racial issues and on labor rights, seeing as his SCOTUS Appointments sealed the deal on Brown v Board of Education being unanimous. However, what if ultimately, FDR went with a strict segregationist who was in favor of the New Deal at least early in their career? What happens when he becomes President and any ideas who this could be (one idea is Russell and another is Connally but both might say no to the offer)? Who do they appoint to SCOTUS instead of Burton and Vinson in 1945 and 1946 and Clark and Minton if they won a full term in 1948? What would 1948 look like in this TL? I suspect the southern president would probably appoint segregationist justices or lawyers to the court who make it through thanks to the Conservative Coalition being aligned on this one issue, though I admit I am unsure how they would handle the post war time frame, especially with 1945-1949. Furthermore, I could see a case for Dewey not being nominated ittl as in 1948 iotl, his nomination wasn't guaranteed but his wing of the party was able to get things to align with him by the convention. Here, with a more conservative leaning court and administration, the Republicans may pick a Conservative who can bring stability to both the party and the nation as long as it isn't Taft Sr. Also, I imagine the effects this has on American politics, specifically the civil rights movement, especially if Brown v Board goes the other way, if this has happened with perhaps more radical actions being taken and maybe an earlier Black Panther Party if things get really bad, but that's up in the air for the first decade of this period in time.

criteria.9-10: Closely anchors the premise in 1944 vote totals, factional pressures, FDR’s preferences, labor/liberal opposition, and the narrow pathways by which a segregationist VP could be nominated.

criteria.9-10: Integrates domestic and foreign policy mechanisms over a decade, including likely non-changes, path dependence from WWII institutions, Brown-era judicial implications, and limits on what a segregationist president could actually change.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent multi-step causal chain from 1944 onward, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, avoids contradictions with established facts, and handles alternate branches responsibly.
criteria.1-2: Presents a deterministic or incoherent timeline full of factual contradictions.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible pieces but jumps between claims, overstates certainty, or contradicts its own assumptions.

criteria.7-8: Maintains clear causal continuity across multiple election cycles and flags major contingent points such as candidate choice, Korea, court appointments, and party splits.

items.model_answer:
If Franklin Roosevelt had chosen an openly segregationist running mate in 1944, the most important consequence is that the vice presidency would suddenly matter far more than anyone expected, because Roosevelt was visibly frail and likely to die in office. In real history, that is exactly what happened with Harry Truman’s succession in 1945. So in this scenario, the central question is not just campaign optics, but who becomes president after Roosevelt’s death and what that does to the end of World War II and the opening phase of postwar America.

Politically, Roosevelt might have had some short-term reasons to do it. The Democratic coalition still depended heavily on the white South, and by 1944 there was growing tension inside the party over race, labor, and federal power. Picking a segregationist could have been an attempt to reassure Southern conservatives who disliked New Deal centralization but remained Democratic out of habit and regional loyalty. It might also have been meant to block the renomination of Henry Wallace, who many party leaders thought too left-wing and eccentric. So as a convention maneuver, a Southern segregationist might have looked like a compromise: anti-Wallace, acceptable to party bosses, and useful for holding the South.

In the election itself, Roosevelt probably still wins. The war was going well by late 1944, Roosevelt remained an immense political figure, and Republican Thomas Dewey was not in a position to easily overturn the Democratic advantage. A segregationist vice-presidential nominee might have alienated Black voters in northern cities, labor liberals, and some urban ethnic Democrats, but many of those groups were still strongly attached to Roosevelt and the New Deal. Since African Americans outside the South had only recently begun shifting into the Democratic column in large numbers, the move would likely slow that realignment rather than immediately reverse it. It could narrow Roosevelt’s margin, but probably not cost him the presidency.

The real divergence begins in April 1945, when Roosevelt dies. A segregationist vice president becomes president in the final months of the war. On foreign policy, there may be less change than people sometimes assume. The basic machinery of wartime policy was institutional by then: the military, the State Department, the Allied agreements, and the Manhattan Project were already in motion. Any Democratic successor would probably still oversee Germany’s defeat, continue war against Japan, and face the atomic bomb decision in a broadly similar framework. There could be differences in style, administrative competence, and relations with advisers, but not necessarily a completely different outcome in the war itself.

Domestic politics, though, could change sharply. Truman, despite all his limitations, eventually desegregated the armed forces and endorsed a modest civil-rights agenda in 1948, helping trigger the Dixiecrat revolt and beginning the Democratic Party’s long break with the white South. A segregationist president in 1945 would likely do the opposite. He would probably resist civil-rights pressure, avoid federal anti-lynching or anti-poll-tax efforts, and try to keep the Democratic coalition anchored in white Southern dominance. That would postpone a major turning point in party history. The federal government’s early postwar signal in favor of civil rights would be delayed, perhaps by years.

That delay matters because the late 1940s were a formative period. Black veterans returned from war expecting greater citizenship. Civil-rights organizations were gaining strength. Northern Black voting power was growing. If the White House were openly hostile rather than cautiously supportive, civil-rights activists would likely redirect more energy toward courts, grassroots organizing, and pressure on Congress rather than expecting executive action. The civil-rights movement would still come, because its underlying forces were powerful, but it might emerge with a more oppositional, less Democratic-party-centered character in the immediate postwar years.

The party system could also shift differently. In real history, Truman’s civil-rights stance fractured the Democratic coalition in 1948, with Strom Thurmond’s Dixiecrat campaign signaling the South’s growing estrangement from the national party. If the president himself were a segregationist, there might be no Dixiecrat revolt at that moment because the South would feel represented inside the administration. Instead, the strain would move northward: liberals, labor, Black voters, and civil-rights advocates might become more restless within the Democratic Party. Some could defect to Henry Wallace’s Progressive campaign in 1948 in larger numbers, or pressure for a convention fight against the incumbent. The party might split, just not along the same line as in actual history.

That creates an opening for Republicans. A Republican Party that sensed Democratic weakness among northern liberals and Black voters might move earlier and more confidently toward a civil-rights posture, not necessarily out of principle alone but out of electoral opportunity. Since the GOP still had a meaningful liberal and moderate wing in the 1940s, especially in the Northeast and Midwest, it could try to reclaim its older image as the party of Lincoln more aggressively. If so, African American partisan realignment might become more competitive and less one-directional than it became in real history.

There is also a constitutional and institutional angle. Truman was inexperienced in foreign affairs, but he was not a regional ideological outlier in the same way an uncompromising segregationist would have been. If Roosevelt knowingly elevated a man unacceptable to large portions of his own coalition, his final political judgment would later be seen as a major blunder. Historians would likely treat the 1944 convention not as a pragmatic compromise that produced an unexpectedly consequential successor, but as the moment when Roosevelt sacrificed the future of postwar liberalism to preserve temporary party unity.

Everything would depend somewhat on which segregationist he chose. Someone like James Byrnes, for example, was deeply conservative on race but also highly experienced and influential in national governance; under him, policy might be more effective administratively even while remaining reactionary on civil rights. A more purely sectional figure, such as a politician in the mold of Theodore Bilbo, would be far more destabilizing and far less acceptable nationally. So the scale of divergence depends on whether Roosevelt picked a “respectable” Southern conservative or an inflammatory racial demagogue. But in either case, the broad effect is the same: the transition from New Deal liberalism to postwar liberalism becomes much less favorable to civil rights.

So the most likely overall answer is this: Roosevelt probably still wins in 1944, the war abroad ends in roughly similar fashion, but Roosevelt’s death in 1945 puts a segregationist in the White House at exactly the moment when the federal government was beginning to define the postwar order. That would likely delay Democratic support for civil rights, postpone the break between the national party and the white South, unsettle Black and liberal loyalty to the Democrats, and potentially give Republicans a bigger opening in northern and Black politics. In short, the immediate military history might not change dramatically, but the racial and partisan history of postwar America could change a great deal.

edus.text: If Franklin Roosevelt had chosen an openly segregationist running mate in 1944, the most important consequence is that the vice presidency would suddenly matter far more than anyone expected,
because Roosevelt was visibly frail and likely to die in office.
In real history, that is exactly what happened with Harry Truman’s succession in 1945.

So in this scenario, the central question is not just campaign optics, but who becomes president after Roosevelt’s death and what that does to the end of World War II and the opening phase of postwar America.
Politically, Roosevelt might have had some short-term reasons to do it.
The Democratic coalition still depended heavily on the white South,
and by 1944 there was growing tension inside the party over race, labor, and federal power.
Picking a segregationist could have been an attempt to reassure Southern conservatives who disliked New Deal centralization but remained Democratic out of habit and regional loyalty.
It might also have been meant to block the renomination of Henry Wallace, who many party leaders thought too left-wing and eccentric.
So as a convention maneuver, a Southern segregationist might have looked like a compromise: anti-Wallace, acceptable to party bosses, and useful for holding the South.
In the election itself, Roosevelt probably still wins.
The war was going well by late 1944,
Roosevelt remained an immense political figure,
and Republican Thomas Dewey was not in a position to easily overturn the Democratic advantage.
A segregationist vice-presidential nominee might have alienated Black voters in northern cities, labor liberals, and some urban ethnic Democrats,
but many of those groups were still strongly attached to Roosevelt and the New Deal.
Since African Americans outside the South had only recently begun shifting into the Democratic column in large numbers, the move would likely slow that realignment rather than immediately reverse it.
It could narrow Roosevelt’s margin,
but probably not cost him the presidency.
The real divergence begins in April 1945, when Roosevelt dies.
A segregationist vice president becomes president in the final months of the war.
On foreign policy, there may be less change than people sometimes assume.
The basic machinery of wartime policy was institutional by then: the military, the State Department, the Allied agreements, and the Manhattan Project were already in motion.
Any Democratic successor would probably still oversee Germany’s defeat, continue war against Japan, and face the atomic bomb decision in a broadly similar framework.
There could be differences in style, administrative competence, and relations with advisers,
but not necessarily a completely different outcome in the war itself.
Domestic politics, though, could change sharply.

Truman, despite all his limitations, eventually desegregated the armed forces and endorsed a modest civil-rights agenda in 1948, helping trigger the Dixiecrat revolt and beginning the Democratic Party’s long break with the white South.
A segregationist president in 1945 would likely do the opposite.
He would probably resist civil-rights pressure, avoid federal anti-lynching or anti-poll-tax efforts, and try to keep the Democratic coalition anchored in white Southern dominance.
That would postpone a major turning point in party history.
The federal government’s early postwar signal in favor of civil rights would be delayed, perhaps by years.
That delay matters because the late 1940s were a formative period.
Black veterans returned from war expecting greater citizenship.
Civil-rights organizations were gaining strength.
Northern Black voting power was growing.

If the White House were openly hostile rather than cautiously supportive, civil-rights activists would likely redirect more energy toward courts, grassroots organizing, and pressure on Congress rather than expecting executive action.
The civil-rights movement would still come, because its underlying forces were powerful,
but it might emerge with a more oppositional, less Democratic-party-centered character in the immediate postwar years.
The party system could also shift differently.
In real history, Truman’s civil-rights stance fractured the Democratic coalition in 1948, with Strom Thurmond’s Dixiecrat campaign signaling the South’s growing estrangement from the national party.
If the president himself were a segregationist, there might be no Dixiecrat revolt at that moment because the South would feel represented inside the administration.
Instead, the strain would move northward: liberals, labor, Black voters, and civil-rights advocates might become more restless within the Democratic Party.
Some could defect to Henry Wallace’s Progressive campaign in 1948 in larger numbers, or pressure for a convention fight against the incumbent.
The party might split, just not along the same line as in actual history.
That creates an opening for Republicans.

A Republican Party that sensed Democratic weakness among northern liberals and Black voters might move earlier and more confidently toward a civil-rights posture, not necessarily out of principle alone but out of electoral opportunity.

Since the GOP still had a meaningful liberal and moderate wing in the 1940s, especially in the Northeast and Midwest, it could try to reclaim its older image as the party of Lincoln more aggressively.
If so, African American partisan realignment might become more competitive and less one-directional than it became in real history.
There is also a constitutional and institutional angle.
Truman was inexperienced in foreign affairs,
but he was not a regional ideological outlier in the same way an uncompromising segregationist would have been.
If Roosevelt knowingly elevated a man unacceptable to large portions of his own coalition, his final political judgment would later be seen as a major blunder.

Historians would likely treat the 1944 convention not as a pragmatic compromise that produced an unexpectedly consequential successor, but as the moment when Roosevelt sacrificed the future of postwar liberalism to preserve temporary party unity.
Everything would depend somewhat on which segregationist he chose.
Someone like James Byrnes, for example, was deeply conservative on race but also highly experienced and influential in national governance;
under him, policy might be more effective administratively even while remaining reactionary on civil rights.
A more purely sectional figure, such as a politician in the mold of Theodore Bilbo, would be far more destabilizing and far less acceptable nationally.
So the scale of divergence depends on whether Roosevelt picked a “respectable” Southern conservative or an inflammatory racial demagogue.
But in either case, the broad effect is the same: the transition from New Deal liberalism to postwar liberalism becomes much less favorable to civil rights.

So the most likely overall answer is this: Roosevelt probably still wins in 1944, the war abroad ends in roughly similar fashion, but Roosevelt’s death in 1945 puts a segregationist in the White House at exactly the moment when the federal government was beginning to define the postwar order.

That would likely delay Democratic support for civil rights, postpone the break between the national party and the white South, unsettle Black and liberal loyalty to the Democrats, and potentially give Republicans a bigger opening in northern and Black politics.
In short, the immediate military history might not change dramatically, but the racial and partisan history of postwar America could change a great deal.

If Roosevelt knowingly elevated a man unacceptable to large portions of his own coalition, his final political judgment would later be seen as a major blunder.

Historians would likely treat the 1944 convention not as a pragmatic compromise that produced an unexpectedly consequential successor, but as the moment when Roosevelt sacrificed the future of postwar liberalism to preserve temporary party unity.
Everything would depend somewhat on which segregationist he chose.
Someone like James Byrnes, for example, was deeply conservative on race but also highly experienced and influential in national governance;
under him, policy might be more effective administratively even while remaining reactionary on civil rights.
A more purely sectional figure, such as a politician in the mold of Theodore Bilbo, would be far more destabilizing and far less acceptable nationally.
So the scale of divergence depends on whether Roosevelt picked a “respectable” Southern conservative or an inflammatory racial demagogue.
But in either case, the broad effect is the same: the transition from New Deal liberalism to postwar liberalism becomes much less favorable to civil rights.

So the most likely overall answer is this: Roosevelt probably still wins in 1944, the war abroad ends in roughly similar fashion, but Roosevelt’s death in 1945 puts a segregationist in the White House at exactly the moment when the federal government was beginning to define the postwar order.

That would likely delay Democratic support for civil rights, postpone the break between the national party and the white South, unsettle Black and liberal loyalty to the Democrats, and potentially give Republicans a bigger opening in northern and Black politics.
In short, the immediate military history might not change dramatically, but the racial and partisan history of postwar America could change a great deal.

items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise definition and historical anchoring
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what it means for the Allies/Entente to lose on the Salonica/Macedonian front and anchors the divergence in the real military, political, and logistical conditions of 1917-1918.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise vaguely or anachronistically; confuses WWI with WWII or ignores the Salonica/Macedonian context.
criteria.3-4: Identifies the front but gives an unclear or implausible Allied defeat with little reference to real 1918 conditions.
criteria.5-6: Defines a plausible defeat, such as failed Entente offensive or withdrawal, with some correct historical anchors.
criteria.7-8: Specifies a credible point of divergence tied to Doiran, Vardar, Bulgarian morale, Greek participation, or Entente logistics.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes limited tactical defeat from strategic collapse, and grounds it in documented constraints of the Macedonian front.

criteria.name: Causal fidelity to Balkan military mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the military mechanisms by which an Allied loss could occur and what immediate effects it would have on Bulgaria, Greece, Serbia, and Central Powers operations.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported claims of easy conquest or collapse; ignores terrain, supply, morale, and force composition.
criteria.3-4: Mentions military outcomes but with weak or inaccurate causal links, such as assuming Salonica alone decides the war instantly.
criteria.5-6: Addresses some relevant mechanisms, including defensive terrain, Bulgarian forces, Entente reserves, or Greek involvement.
criteria.7-8: Connects battlefield outcomes to Bulgarian morale, Serbian recovery, Greek politics, supply bottlenecks, and Central Powers priorities.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust operational chain showing how Allied defeat affects withdrawals, lines of communication, Balkan armies, and feasibility of further Central Powers advances.

criteria.name: Integration of Bulgarian domestic collapse and alliance constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for Bulgaria’s internal war weariness, food shortages, manpower exhaustion, mutiny risk, relations with Germany, and the limits these imposed even after an Allied defeat.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Bulgaria as either effortlessly triumphant or inevitably collapsing without explaining domestic conditions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Bulgarian morale or politics only superficially and misses why Bulgaria sought an armistice historically.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some domestic pressures such as shortages, war weariness, or agrarian unrest but underdevelops their implications.
criteria.7-8: Explains how an Allied defeat could delay or alter, but not automatically remove, Bulgaria’s morale and political crisis.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs military success against structural exhaustion, minority troop issues, Radomir-style unrest, Malinov’s policy, and German failure to meet Bulgarian expectations.

criteria.name: Long-range strategic consequences for World War I
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the coherence and plausibility of the answer’s downstream chain from an Allied loss at Salonica to wider outcomes for the Central Powers, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Italy, Germany, and the 1918 armistices.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to sweeping conclusions such as Central Powers victory or unchanged history with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Gives a broad outcome but neglects key theaters or timing, especially the Western Front and Austria-Hungary’s collapse.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several downstream effects, such as delayed Bulgarian surrender or altered pressure on Austria-Hungary, with partial coherence.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible sequence linking the Balkan result to Serbia, Greece, Ottoman communications, Danube/Balkan security, and Germany’s worsening overall position.
criteria.9-10: Balances local Central Powers gains against decisive global constraints, showing how Salonica might delay or reshape armistices without overclaiming reversal of Germany’s strategic defeat.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes, avoids internal contradictions, and handles ambiguous terms such as 'Allies lose' with appropriate caveats.
criteria.1-2: States speculative outcomes as certain, contradicts itself, or ignores the ambiguity of the premise.
criteria.3-4: Uses some caveats but still makes deterministic or mutually inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Shows moderate uncertainty awareness and mostly avoids contradictions, though some assumptions remain unstated.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates immediate, medium-term, and long-term probabilities and flags dependencies such as scale of defeat or German reinforcement levels.
criteria.9-10: Maintains consistent assumptions throughout, compares multiple plausible branches, and calibrates confidence in each major causal claim.

items.model_answer:
If the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the most immediate consequence is that Bulgaria and the Central Powers secure the Balkans more firmly, at least for a time. Historically, the Allied offensive from Salonica in September 1918 helped force Bulgaria out of the war, which opened the way for the collapse of the Central Powers in southeastern Europe. If instead the Allied army at Salonica is defeated or fails badly enough to be driven back, that chain of collapse is interrupted.

The first major effect is that Bulgaria probably stays in the war longer. That matters because Bulgaria was the weakest and most exposed of the Central Powers by late 1918. Its surrender historically shattered the strategic position of both the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary. If Bulgaria holds, Germany and Austria-Hungary preserve their land connection to the Ottoman Empire, and the Central Powers avoid a dangerous breach in the Balkans. Serbia is not liberated in 1918, and Allied pressure from the south against Austria-Hungary is reduced or eliminated.

This would also strengthen the Ottoman position temporarily. The Ottoman Empire was already in serious trouble in Palestine and the Middle East, so a Salonica victory would not magically save it, but it would reduce the sense of total encirclement and delay political collapse. Supplies and communications through the Balkans remain more viable. The Ottomans might hold out somewhat longer, and the armistice at Mudros could be delayed.

Austria-Hungary also benefits in the short run. Historically, the Balkan collapse added to the empire’s internal disintegration and military hopelessness. If the Salonica front is secure, Vienna faces one less crisis. That does not solve the empire’s enormous ethnic, economic, and military problems, but it may delay surrender and perhaps delay the final breakup by weeks or months. The empire was probably still doomed by late 1918 because of internal nationalist revolts, hunger, and defeat elsewhere, but the timing could shift.

For Germany, a lost Allied campaign at Salonica would be useful politically and strategically, but probably not war-winning by itself. By late 1918 Germany’s decisive problem was the failure of its spring offensives in France and the overwhelming superiority of the Allies on the Western Front. Even if the Balkans remain intact, Germany is still being pushed back in the west, its population is exhausted, and its allies are weakening. So a defeat at Salonica likely prolongs the war rather than reverses the final outcome. It may encourage Berlin to hope for better armistice terms or to fight on longer, but it does not remove the core reasons Germany lost.

There are two broad plausible versions of this scenario. In the milder version, the Allies simply fail to break through. In that case, Bulgaria survives into late 1918 or even 1919, the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian collapses are delayed, and the war may last somewhat longer. In the more dramatic version, the Allies are heavily defeated and forced to evacuate Salonica. That would be a major political shock. It would vindicate critics who had long mocked the Salonica expedition as a sideshow, damage Allied prestige in Greece and the Balkans, and possibly strengthen pro-Central or neutralist forces in the region. Even so, unless this defeat frees major Central Power forces to decisively alter the Western Front, it still probably changes the timing and shape of the ending more than the ultimate winner.

The postwar Balkans would also look different. Serbia, having failed to be liberated by Allied action in 1918, emerges in a weaker position. The creation of Yugoslavia might still happen if Austria-Hungary collapses, but Serbian bargaining power would be reduced and local political dynamics could shift. Bulgaria, instead of being a defeated state forced into the Treaty of Neuilly under the same circumstances, might negotiate from a somewhat stronger position if the broader Central Power defeat comes later and under more confused conditions. Greece might experience even harsher political recriminations over the war, since the Salonica front was tied directly to the National Schism and the Venizelist decision to join the Allies.

So the best overall answer is: if the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the Central Powers gain a temporary but meaningful reprieve in southeastern Europe. Bulgaria likely stays in the war longer, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary may collapse later, Serbia remains occupied longer, and the First World War could be prolonged. But unless this Balkan victory somehow produces a major knock-on effect on the Western Front, it probably does not save Germany or overturn the final Allied victory; it mainly delays and reshapes the end of the war.

edus.text: If the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the most immediate consequence is that Bulgaria and the Central Powers secure the Balkans more firmly, at least for a time.
Historically, the Allied offensive from Salonica in September 1918 helped force Bulgaria out of the war,
which opened the way for the collapse of the Central Powers in southeastern Europe.
If instead the Allied army at Salonica is defeated or fails badly enough to be driven back, that chain of collapse is interrupted.
The first major effect is that Bulgaria probably stays in the war longer.
That matters because Bulgaria was the weakest and most exposed of the Central Powers by late 1918.
Its surrender historically shattered the strategic position of both the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary.
If Bulgaria holds, Germany and Austria-Hungary preserve their land connection to the Ottoman Empire,
and the Central Powers avoid a dangerous breach in the Balkans.
Serbia is not liberated in 1918,
and Allied pressure from the south against Austria-Hungary is reduced or eliminated.
This would also strengthen the Ottoman position temporarily.
The Ottoman Empire was already in serious trouble in Palestine and the Middle East,
so a Salonica victory would not magically save it,
but it would reduce the sense of total encirclement and delay political collapse.
Supplies and communications through the Balkans remain more viable.
The Ottomans might hold out somewhat longer,
and the armistice at Mudros could be delayed.
Austria-Hungary also benefits in the short run.
Historically, the Balkan collapse added to the empire’s internal disintegration and military hopelessness.
If the Salonica front is secure, Vienna faces one less crisis.
That does not solve the empire’s enormous ethnic, economic, and military problems,
but it may delay surrender and perhaps delay the final breakup by weeks or months.
The empire was probably still doomed by late 1918 because of internal nationalist revolts, hunger, and defeat elsewhere,
but the timing could shift.
For Germany, a lost Allied campaign at Salonica would be useful politically and strategically, but probably not war-winning by itself.
By late 1918 Germany’s decisive problem was the failure of its spring offensives in France and the overwhelming superiority of the Allies on the Western Front.
Even if the Balkans remain intact, Germany is still being pushed back in the west, its population is exhausted, and its allies are weakening.
So a defeat at Salonica likely prolongs the war rather than reverses the final outcome.
It may encourage Berlin to hope for better armistice terms or to fight on longer,
but it does not remove the core reasons Germany lost.
There are two broad plausible versions of this scenario.
In the milder version, the Allies simply fail to break through.
In that case, Bulgaria survives into late 1918 or even 1919, the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian collapses are delayed, and the war may last somewhat longer.
In the more dramatic version, the Allies are heavily defeated and forced to evacuate Salonica.
That would be a major political shock.
It would vindicate critics who had long mocked the Salonica expedition as a sideshow,
damage Allied prestige in Greece and the Balkans,
and possibly strengthen pro-Central or neutralist forces in the region.
Even so, unless this defeat frees major Central Power forces to decisively alter the Western Front, it still probably changes the timing and shape of the ending more than the ultimate winner.
The postwar Balkans would also look different.
Serbia, having failed to be liberated by Allied action in 1918, emerges in a weaker position.
The creation of Yugoslavia might still happen if Austria-Hungary collapses,
but Serbian bargaining power would be reduced and local political dynamics could shift.

Bulgaria, instead of being a defeated state forced into the Treaty of Neuilly under the same circumstances, might negotiate from a somewhat stronger position if the broader Central Power defeat comes later and under more confused conditions.
Greece might experience even harsher political recriminations over the war, since the Salonica front was tied directly to the National Schism and the Venizelist decision to join the Allies.
So the best overall answer is: if the Allies lose on the Salonica front, the Central Powers gain a temporary but meaningful reprieve in southeastern Europe.
Bulgaria likely stays in the war longer, the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary may collapse later, Serbia remains occupied longer, and the First World War could be prolonged.
But unless this Balkan victory somehow produces a major knock-on effect on the Western Front, it probably does not save Germany or overturn the final Allied victory;
it mainly delays and reshapes the end of the war.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.

items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin from the start, it probably would have been a noticeably better fighter, but not a transformational one on the level of the best late-war designs.

Historically, the P-40 began with the Allison V-1710, which was sturdy and worked well at low and medium altitude, but its single-stage supercharging limited high-altitude performance. Later Merlin-powered P-40 variants showed that the airframe benefited from the British engine. If Curtiss had designed the aircraft around the Merlin from the beginning rather than adapting the existing P-36/P-40 line, the gains could have been somewhat larger than what was actually achieved.

The biggest improvement would likely have been in high-altitude performance. A Merlin-based P-40 would have climbed better, held its power better at altitude, and been more competitive in European-style air combat where altitude mattered greatly. That would have made it a stronger interceptor and escort fighter in 1940–42, and perhaps more appealing to the RAF in the Battle of Britain era than the Allison-powered Tomahawk was. It also might have reduced one of the aircraft’s major criticisms: that it was durable and fast in a dive, but simply outclassed higher up.

Designing around the Merlin from the outset could also have improved the aircraft’s overall integration. The nose, cooling system, center of gravity, and drag profile could have been optimized instead of modified later. That might have produced somewhat better speed, handling balance, and reliability than the Merlin P-40s actually achieved. In the best case, you could imagine a cleaner, lighter, more refined P-40 that closed part of the gap with the Spitfire V or early Bf 109F, especially at medium altitude.

But there were real limits. The P-40 airframe was rooted in an older design philosophy than the top European fighters. It was relatively heavy, not especially aerodynamically advanced, and had more drag than the best contemporaries. Even with a Merlin, it likely still would not have matched the Spitfire or Bf 109 in climb, ceiling, or agility. It might have become a very solid second-tier fighter: rugged, fast enough, better at altitude, and more versatile, but still not the premier dogfighter of the war.

There would also have been production and strategic complications. Merlin engines were in intense demand for Spitfires, Hurricanes, and later Mustangs. If the P-40 had depended on Merlins from the beginning, engine supply could have constrained production unless Packard-built Merlins came online quickly. One reason the Allison-powered P-40 mattered was precisely that it used an engine available in large numbers. In wartime, a slightly inferior fighter produced in volume can matter more than a better one bottlenecked by engine supply.

So the most likely counterfactual outcome is that a Merlin-designed P-40 would have been a better and more balanced fighter, especially at altitude, and might have enjoyed a stronger reputation in Europe. It could have been more effective in RAF and perhaps early USAAF service. But it probably still would not have become the dominant Allied fighter. Its improvement would have been meaningful rather than revolutionary, and the engine supply question might have limited how much that better design could actually matter.
