items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

items.model_answer:
If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943, in the PT-109 episode, the most important consequence is that there would have been no President Kennedy in 1961–63, and that would likely have changed the course of Cold War politics, U.S. domestic reform, and the symbolism of American liberalism in the 1960s.

At the most immediate level, Kennedy’s death in wartime would probably have made him a naval hero remembered within his family and in wartime memory, but it would have removed the particular son whom Joseph Kennedy Sr. eventually treated as the family’s political standard-bearer after the death of the older brother, Joseph Jr., in 1944. Without JFK, the Kennedy family might still have remained politically active, but it is much less likely that any other sibling would have assembled the same combination of charisma, ambition, media skill, war-hero status, and electoral appeal. Robert Kennedy might still have had a major political career, but probably not on the same timetable and probably not as the center of a presidential dynasty in the same way.

The 1960 election is the first major turning point. Without JFK, Richard Nixon becomes the strong favorite to win the presidency in 1960, unless another Democrat somehow unites the party and defeats him. Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Adlai Stevenson, or Stuart Symington might have competed for the Democratic nomination, but none had Kennedy’s particular ability to bridge northern liberals, urban Catholics, and parts of the South while also projecting youth and vigor on television. A Nixon presidency beginning in 1961 is therefore a plausible baseline outcome.

That shift alone would matter enormously for the Cold War. Kennedy’s handling of the Bay of Pigs, the Vienna summit, the Berlin crisis, and especially the Cuban Missile Crisis shaped the period. A President Nixon might have been more experienced in foreign affairs but also potentially more hawkish. It is possible that a Nixon administration would have avoided some of Kennedy’s missteps, such as authorizing the Bay of Pigs under inherited CIA assumptions. But it is also possible that in a Cuba or Berlin confrontation Nixon would have been less restrained than Kennedy was in October 1962. Kennedy’s combination of toughness and caution during the missile crisis is one reason the world avoided nuclear war. In this counterfactual, the risk of a more dangerous superpower clash is real.

On the other hand, if a Democrat such as Johnson had somehow won in 1960, some domestic outcomes might actually have come faster. Kennedy’s record on civil rights and social legislation was mixed: rhetorically important, but often cautious and constrained by Congress. Johnson, had he reached the presidency earlier, might have pushed major civil rights and anti-poverty legislation sooner because he understood congressional power better than Kennedy did. But that also depends on timing, party balance, and whether the political shock of Kennedy’s actual assassination in 1963—which helped propel the Civil Rights Act—would still exist. Without that martyrdom effect, even Johnson might have had a harder time moving landmark legislation.

Space policy is another area where Kennedy’s absence matters. The moon commitment was deeply associated with his presidency. A different president might still have expanded the space race, especially after Soviet successes, but the famous decision to land a man on the moon before the decade was out might have been delayed, reframed, or never made in the same dramatic way.

Vietnam would also likely change, though not in a simple direction. Kennedy increased U.S. involvement, so his absence does not automatically mean less intervention. Nixon in 1961 might have escalated differently or earlier; Johnson in 1961 might also have deepened involvement. The common argument that Kennedy would have avoided full-scale war remains speculative. The safer conclusion is that JFK’s death in 1943 would not guarantee a less violent Vietnam, but it would make the path into war different, because the key decisions would have been made by someone else under different political pressures.

Culturally and symbolically, the United States would lose “Camelot” as a defining myth. Kennedy’s presidency, and then his assassination, became central to the way Americans understood generational change, national promise, and political tragedy in the 1960s. Without him, there is no Kennedy assassination in Dallas, no immediate LBJ succession under those circumstances, and no comparable fusion of glamour, reformist language, Cold War brinkmanship, and martyrdom. The emotional landscape of the decade would be noticeably different.

So the best concise answer is this: if JFK had died in the PT-109 incident, he would have been remembered as a wartime hero, but the larger consequence is that he almost certainly would never have become president. That would most likely have opened the way for a different winner in 1960, probably Nixon, and in turn altered the handling of Cuba, Berlin, civil rights, the space race, Vietnam, and the political mythology of the 1960s. Some policies later associated with Kennedy might still have happened under others, but the specific trajectory of modern American history would have been substantially different.

edus.text: If John F. Kennedy had died on July 2, 1943, in the PT-109 episode,
the most important consequence is that there would have been no President Kennedy in 1961–63,
and that would likely have changed the course of Cold War politics, U.S. domestic reform, and the symbolism of American liberalism in the 1960s.
At the most immediate level, Kennedy’s death in wartime would probably have made him a naval hero remembered within his family and in wartime memory,
but it would have removed the particular son whom Joseph Kennedy Sr. eventually treated as the family’s political standard-bearer after the death of the older brother, Joseph Jr., in 1944.
Without JFK, the Kennedy family might still have remained politically active,
but it is much less likely that any other sibling would have assembled the same combination of charisma, ambition, media skill, war-hero status, and electoral appeal.
Robert Kennedy might still have had a major political career,
but probably not on the same timetable and probably not as the center of a presidential dynasty in the same way.
The 1960 election is the first major turning point.
Without JFK, Richard Nixon becomes the strong favorite to win the presidency in 1960,
unless another Democrat somehow unites the party and defeats him.
Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Adlai Stevenson, or Stuart Symington might have competed for the Democratic nomination,
but none had Kennedy’s particular ability to bridge northern liberals, urban Catholics, and parts of the South while also projecting youth and vigor on television.
A Nixon presidency beginning in 1961 is therefore a plausible baseline outcome.
That shift alone would matter enormously for the Cold War.
Kennedy’s handling of the Bay of Pigs, the Vienna summit, the Berlin crisis, and especially the Cuban Missile Crisis shaped the period.
A President Nixon might have been more experienced in foreign affairs but also potentially more hawkish.
It is possible that a Nixon administration would have avoided some of Kennedy’s missteps, such as authorizing the Bay of Pigs under inherited CIA assumptions.
But it is also possible that in a Cuba or Berlin confrontation Nixon would have been less restrained than Kennedy was in October 1962.
Kennedy’s combination of toughness and caution during the missile crisis is one reason the world avoided nuclear war.
In this counterfactual, the risk of a more dangerous superpower clash is real.
On the other hand, if a Democrat such as Johnson had somehow won in 1960,
some domestic outcomes might actually have come faster.
Kennedy’s record on civil rights and social legislation was mixed: rhetorically important, but often cautious and constrained by Congress.
Johnson, had he reached the presidency earlier, might have pushed major civil rights and anti-poverty legislation sooner because he understood congressional power better than Kennedy did.
But that also depends on timing, party balance, and whether the political shock of Kennedy’s actual assassination in 1963 would still exist.
Without that martyrdom effect, even Johnson might have had a harder time moving landmark legislation.
Space policy is another area where Kennedy’s absence matters.
The moon commitment was deeply associated with his presidency.
A different president might still have expanded the space race, especially after Soviet successes,
but the famous decision to land a man on the moon before the decade was out might have been delayed, reframed, or never made in the same dramatic way.
Vietnam would also likely change, though not in a simple direction.
Kennedy increased U.S. involvement,
so his absence does not automatically mean less intervention.
Nixon in 1961 might have escalated differently or earlier;
Johnson in 1961 might also have deepened involvement.
The common argument that Kennedy would have avoided full-scale war remains speculative.
The safer conclusion is that JFK’s death in 1943 would not guarantee a less violent Vietnam,
but it would make the path into war different,
because the key decisions would have been made by someone else under different political pressures.
Culturally and symbolically, the United States would lose “Camelot” as a defining myth.
Kennedy’s presidency, and then his assassination, became central to the way Americans understood generational change, national promise, and political tragedy in the 1960s.

Without him, there is no Kennedy assassination in Dallas, no immediate LBJ succession under those circumstances, and no comparable fusion of glamour, reformist language, Cold War brinkmanship, and martyrdom.
The emotional landscape of the decade would be noticeably different.
So the best concise answer is this: if JFK had died in the PT-109 incident, he would have been remembered as a wartime hero,
but the larger consequence is that he almost certainly would never have become president.
That would most likely have opened the way for a different winner in 1960, probably Nixon,
and in turn altered the handling of Cuba, Berlin, civil rights, the space race, Vietnam, and the political mythology of the 1960s.
Some policies later associated with Kennedy might still have happened under others,
but the specific trajectory of modern American history would have been substantially different.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing still would have happened, but it likely would have been slower, more fragmented, and organized around different standards.

The biggest effect of the IBM PC was not that it invented the personal computer. Machines like the Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80, and later CP/M systems already existed. What IBM did was legitimize the microcomputer for business and create a hardware-software platform that others could copy. Without that machine, there is a good chance the early 1980s PC market would have remained divided among incompatible systems for much longer.

In business, IBM’s brand mattered enormously. Many companies that might have considered microcomputers risky or toy-like were reassured by the IBM name. Without that reassurance, large firms probably would have stuck longer with terminals, minicomputers, and centralized systems, while adopting personal computers more cautiously. Apple, Tandy, Commodore, and various CP/M vendors might have gained more ground, but none had IBM’s authority in corporate procurement. Business standardization around one dominant desktop platform would likely have been delayed.

Microsoft would probably still have become important, but in a different way and perhaps less quickly. The IBM PC helped make MS-DOS the core operating system of business computing. Without IBM, Microsoft may have remained more of a language and software supplier across many hardware platforms, or it might have tied itself more strongly to another manufacturer. Its eventual dominance is less certain, and the path to Windows becoming the default desktop environment would have been much less direct.

Intel also might not have become so dominant as early as it did. The IBM PC and especially the huge clone market reinforced the x86 architecture. Without that platform, competing processors from Motorola, Zilog, or others could have stayed more competitive for longer. The desktop world might have evolved around a more varied set of CPU families instead of coalescing around x86.

A major consequence involves the clone market. Because the IBM PC used relatively open, off-the-shelf components and could be reverse-engineered, it enabled “IBM-compatible” computers from Compaq, Dell, and many others. If IBM had never launched the PC, there might not have been a single dominant clone standard to unify the market. That could have meant less price competition, slower commoditization, and a computer industry shaped more like the early home computer era: many brands, many formats, poor compatibility.

Apple might have been the biggest beneficiary. The Macintosh, released in 1984, could have entered a world with no entrenched IBM-compatible business standard. In that scenario, Apple might have had a better chance of becoming the main integrated personal computing platform for both professionals and homes, especially if it had adjusted pricing and software strategy effectively. Still, Apple’s habit of maintaining tight hardware control means it might not have generated the same broad low-cost ecosystem that PC clones eventually did.

Software development would have looked different too. In our timeline, developers increasingly targeted the IBM PC standard because it offered the largest installed base in business. Without that focal point, software markets might have stayed split across Apple, CP/M descendants, Unix workstations, and other proprietary platforms. That fragmentation would likely have made it harder for spreadsheets, word processors, databases, and games to achieve universal reach quickly. Some applications might have become platform-specific power centers rather than cross-industry standards.

Networking and the internet era might also have changed. By the 1990s, masses of cheap IBM-compatible PCs helped put networked computing on millions of desks. Without that standard, the spread of networked desktops probably still occurs, but perhaps with more influence from workstations, terminals, or alternative personal computer platforms. The web still likely emerges, but the client side of the internet may be more diverse and less centered on Windows PCs.

At the industry level, the absence of the IBM PC could have reduced the “Wintel” era or prevented it from taking the same shape. Instead of Microsoft and Intel becoming the central pair in desktop computing, power might have been distributed among Apple, Motorola-based systems, Unix vendors, and possibly a different mass-market business platform. The center of gravity in computing might have remained less standardized and more vertically integrated.

So the most plausible answer is not “no personal computer revolution,” but “a messier one.” Personal computing would still grow because the underlying technology and demand were real. But without the IBM PC, the industry likely would have lacked the early common business standard that accelerated adoption, lowered prices through cloning, and helped make Microsoft and Intel dominant. The result would probably have been a more diverse but less unified computer world, with different winners and slower convergence.

edus.text: If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, personal computing still would have happened,
but it likely would have been slower, more fragmented, and organized around different standards.
The biggest effect of the IBM PC was not that it invented the personal computer.
Machines like the Apple II, Commodore PET, TRS-80, and later CP/M systems already existed.
What IBM did was legitimize the microcomputer for business and create a hardware-software platform that others could copy.
Without that machine, there is a good chance the early 1980s PC market would have remained divided among incompatible systems for much longer.
In business, IBM’s brand mattered enormously.
Many companies that might have considered microcomputers risky or toy-like were reassured by the IBM name.
Without that reassurance, large firms probably would have stuck longer with terminals, minicomputers, and centralized systems,
while adopting personal computers more cautiously.
Apple, Tandy, Commodore, and various CP/M vendors might have gained more ground,
but none had IBM’s authority in corporate procurement.
Business standardization around one dominant desktop platform would likely have been delayed.
Microsoft would probably still have become important,
but in a different way and perhaps less quickly.
The IBM PC helped make MS-DOS the core operating system of business computing.
Without IBM, Microsoft may have remained more of a language and software supplier across many hardware platforms,
or it might have tied itself more strongly to another manufacturer.
Its eventual dominance is less certain,
and the path to Windows becoming the default desktop environment would have been much less direct.
Intel also might not have become so dominant as early as it did.
The IBM PC and especially the huge clone market reinforced the x86 architecture.
Without that platform, competing processors from Motorola, Zilog, or others could have stayed more competitive for longer.
The desktop world might have evolved around a more varied set of CPU families instead of coalescing around x86.
A major consequence involves the clone market.
Because the IBM PC used relatively open, off-the-shelf components and could be reverse-engineered, it enabled “IBM-compatible” computers from Compaq, Dell, and many others.
If IBM had never launched the PC, there might not have been a single dominant clone standard to unify the market.
That could have meant less price competition, slower commoditization, and a computer industry shaped more like the early home computer era:
many brands, many formats, poor compatibility.
Apple might have been the biggest beneficiary.
The Macintosh, released in 1984, could have entered a world with no entrenched IBM-compatible business standard.
In that scenario, Apple might have had a better chance of becoming the main integrated personal computing platform for both professionals and homes,
especially if it had adjusted pricing and software strategy effectively.
Still, Apple’s habit of maintaining tight hardware control means it might not have generated the same broad low-cost ecosystem that PC clones eventually did.
Software development would have looked different too.
In our timeline, developers increasingly targeted the IBM PC standard because it offered the largest installed base in business.
Without that focal point, software markets might have stayed split across Apple, CP/M descendants, Unix workstations, and other proprietary platforms.
That fragmentation would likely have made it harder for spreadsheets, word processors, databases, and games to achieve universal reach quickly.
Some applications might have become platform-specific power centers rather than cross-industry standards.
Networking and the internet era might also have changed.
By the 1990s, masses of cheap IBM-compatible PCs helped put networked computing on millions of desks.
Without that standard, the spread of networked desktops probably still occurs,
but perhaps with more influence from workstations, terminals, or alternative personal computer platforms.
The web still likely emerges,
but the client side of the internet may be more diverse and less centered on Windows PCs.
At the industry level, the absence of the IBM PC could have reduced the “Wintel” era or prevented it from taking the same shape.

Instead of Microsoft and Intel becoming the central pair in desktop computing, power might have been distributed among Apple, Motorola-based systems, Unix vendors, and possibly a different mass-market business platform.
The center of gravity in computing might have remained less standardized and more vertically integrated.
So the most plausible answer is not “no personal computer revolution,”
but “a messier one.”
Personal computing would still grow because the underlying technology and demand were real.

But without the IBM PC, the industry likely would have lacked the early common business standard that accelerated adoption, lowered prices through cloning, and helped make Microsoft and Intel dominant.
The result would probably have been a more diverse but less unified computer world,
with different winners and slower convergence.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.

criteria.3-4: Understands the broad premise but gives a shaky or oversimplified baseline, with notable errors about P-51, P-47, P-38, or bomber offensive chronology.
criteria.5-6: Establishes a mostly accurate baseline, mentioning P-51 range/escort importance and German fighter opposition, but misses key timing or role distinctions.
criteria.7-8: Accurately frames the ETO escort problem, P-51 arrival, P-47/P-38 roles, Big Week context, and bomber-loss pressures with only minor omissions.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the counterfactual in the 1943-45 air war, distinguishing aircraft capabilities, theater priorities, escort doctrine, and the actual shift enabled by long-range P-51 operations.

criteria.name: Substitute Escort Mechanisms: P-47, P-38, Tactics, and Fuel
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and plausibility of mechanisms by which the Allies might compensate for no P-51 escort, especially through P-47 range modifications, drop tanks, P-38 deployment, escort relays, routing changes, and operational tradeoffs.
criteria.1-2: Assumes either total failure or no change without explaining substitute escorts, fuel constraints, or tactical adaptation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions replacements such as P-47s or P-38s but treats them generically and ignores range, altitude, maintenance, and drop-tank issues.
criteria.5-6: Explains some substitute mechanisms, such as P-47 drop tanks or P-38 use, but with limited attention to feasibility, timing, logistics, or performance tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Covers multiple compensation paths, including P-47 high-altitude strengths, range limits, external tanks, P-38 theater/logistics issues, and adjusted bomber tactics.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced feasibility analysis of substitute escort systems, including production capacity, internal fuel/rack modifications, tank availability, pilot training, altitude performance, maintenance burden, and opportunity costs across theaters.

criteria.name: Causal Chain Through the Bomber Offensive and Luftwaffe Attrition
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer builds a coherent long-range causal chain from no P-51 escort to bomber survivability, mission selection, Luftwaffe fighter attrition, air superiority, and timing of Allied air dominance.
criteria.1-2: Provides disconnected claims with no credible causal chain linking escort absence to air-war outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Gives a simple causal story, such as 'more bombers die' or 'Germany survives longer,' without tracing intermediate mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Links reduced escort quality to higher bomber losses and slower Luftwaffe attrition, but the chain is short or misses feedback effects.
criteria.7-8: Shows how escort range affects deep raids, bomber losses, German interception choices, fighter pilot attrition, Big Week-style operations, and the pace of air superiority.
criteria.9-10: Develops a detailed, temporally coherent chain with feedback loops: altered target selection, escort availability, German fighter concentration, attrition rates, bomber-force morale/replacement pressures, and likely delays or adaptations in Allied air dominance.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Downstream Military and Strategic Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly covers downstream consequences beyond air combat, including strategic bombing effectiveness, D-Day preparation, oil/transport attacks, ground campaigns, aircraft production priorities, and theater tradeoffs.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or makes sweeping claims about the war outcome without support.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two downstream effects but exaggerates them or fails to connect them to the escort counterfactual.
criteria.5-6: Discusses plausible effects on bombing effectiveness and invasion preparation, but coverage is incomplete or only loosely causal.
criteria.7-8: Covers several major consequences, such as delayed deep penetration raids, oil/transport campaign impacts, D-Day air superiority risks, and greater reliance on P-47/P-38 production or deployment.
criteria.9-10: Balances military, industrial, and strategic consequences across 1943-45, explaining likely changes in bombing tempo, German recovery windows, invasion support, tactical airpower allocation, aircraft procurement, and why the overall war outcome may or may not change.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Counterfactual Discipline, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids deterministic overclaiming; and remains internally consistent with aircraft capabilities, production realities, and Allied resource advantages.

items.model_answer:
If there had been no P-51 Mustang bomber escort, the air war over Europe would likely have gone much worse for the Allies, at least for a significant period.

The core issue is that long-range escort was essential for daylight strategic bombing. Before effective escorts could accompany bombers deep into Germany, US bombers suffered very heavy losses. Unescorted or partially escorted formations were vulnerable to concentrated attacks by German fighters, especially once they passed beyond the range of earlier escorts like the P-47 and Spitfire. The P-51 changed that because it could go all the way to distant targets and back while still performing well in combat.

Without the P-51, several outcomes become more likely. First, the US Eighth Air Force would probably have had to reduce or suspend deep-penetration daylight raids more often, especially after costly missions like Schweinfurt-Regensburg. Second, bombing strategy might have shifted toward more limited targets near the coast, more night bombing, or a greater reliance on the RAF’s area-bombing campaign. Third, the Luftwaffe would have remained stronger for longer, because one of the most important effects of the P-51 was not just protecting bombers but helping destroy German fighters in the air and on the ground. That mattered enormously before D-Day.

This does not mean the Allies would have lost the war. Germany was still being squeezed by the Soviet advance in the east, Allied industrial superiority, naval blockade, fuel shortages, and the cumulative effects of bombing of transport and oil. Other escort solutions might also have expanded eventually, such as longer-range P-47 variants or drop-tank improvements for existing fighters. So the war in Europe probably still ends in Allied victory.

But the likely counterfactual is that victory comes more slowly and at greater cost. Strategic bombing would be less effective in 1943–44, bomber losses would be higher, German aircraft production and air defenses would suffer less disruption for longer, and preparations for the invasion of Western Europe would be riskier because Allied air superiority would arrive later or less completely. In short: no P-51 escort probably does not save Germany, but it likely prolongs the war and increases Allied casualties substantially.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. It doesn't need to be very successful, as they only had about 2000 inhabitants and Argentina had a population of about 30 million. As long as 3000 people move in, the locals become a minority. That may lead to ethnic tensions down the line, but they are just too few people in a too isolated place and facing a country that earned a reputation by going against one of the world's leading military powers and winning IITL.

Argentina would have gone as far as She could (and probably beyond) to accommodate them. It is of course possible that someone in the Islands would misbehave. That person would be crushed. The whole Argentina (Anaya) assumption was the Goa* Hypothesis. They are not going to come, there is not going to be a war, AND our US friends** shall help us. They were very, as in very, very, conscious of their international public reputation. Had they won the situation of the Kelpers and what the world was shown would be one of their primary preoccupations. items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.

items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won in 1982, the Falkland Islanders almost certainly would not have been physically exterminated or expelled en masse, but they also would not have been allowed to continue as a self-determining British community in the way they did after the British victory. The most likely outcome is a combination of political subordination, pressure to accept Argentine sovereignty, and gradual demographic and cultural assimilation.

The key point is that Argentina’s claim treated the islands as Argentine territory under illegal British occupation, not as a separate people with a right to decide their future. So if Buenos Aires had consolidated control, it likely would have regarded the existing population as residents to be incorporated, not as a sovereign community whose wishes were decisive. Islanders would probably have been offered Argentine citizenship or residency under Argentine administration, schools and official life would have shifted toward Spanish and Argentine national symbols, and local institutions would have been remade to fit Argentine law and governance.

At the same time, the military regime in 1982 was authoritarian and had a very poor human-rights record. That matters. Even if there were no plan for mass deportation, any islander resistance, pro-British political activity, or refusal to cooperate could have been met with surveillance, intimidation, detention, or restrictions on civil liberties, especially in the short term under military rule. The population was small enough that tight administrative control would have been feasible.

In the longer term, much would have depended on whether Argentine democracy returned quickly and on how secure Argentine control was internationally. Under a post-junta civilian government, treatment might have become less repressive, but the underlying aim would still likely have been integration into Argentina rather than recognition of the islanders’ preference to remain British. Immigration from the mainland might also have been encouraged over time, which could have diluted the existing islander community politically and culturally.

So the best concise answer is: they probably would have been kept on the islands, but as a population expected to become Argentine, with their British identity, political wishes, and local autonomy progressively weakened—and, under the 1982 dictatorship at least, dissent could have faced serious repression.

nodes.text: If Argentina had won in 1982, the Falkland Islanders almost certainly would not have been physically exterminated or expelled en masse,
but they also would not have been allowed to continue as a self-determining British community in the way they did after the British victory.
The most likely outcome is a combination of political subordination, pressure to accept Argentine sovereignty, and gradual demographic and cultural assimilation.
The key point is that Argentina’s claim treated the islands as Argentine territory under illegal British occupation,
not as a separate people with a right to decide their future.
So if Buenos Aires had consolidated control, it likely would have regarded the existing population as residents to be incorporated,
not as a sovereign community whose wishes were decisive.
Islanders would probably have been offered Argentine citizenship or residency under Argentine administration,
schools and official life would have shifted toward Spanish and Argentine national symbols,
and local institutions would have been remade to fit Argentine law and governance.
At the same time, the military regime in 1982 was authoritarian and had a very poor human-rights record.
That matters.
Even if there were no plan for mass deportation,
any islander resistance, pro-British political activity, or refusal to cooperate could have been met with surveillance, intimidation, detention, or restrictions on civil liberties,
especially in the short term under military rule.
The population was small enough that tight administrative control would have been feasible.
In the longer term, much would have depended on whether Argentine democracy returned quickly
and on how secure Argentine control was internationally.

items.question: What If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank?
human_answers: Let’s first think about the hypothetical scenarios that fit the “conditions” you mentioned. 1. Joseon modernizes before or at the same time as Japan. The relationship between Korea and Japan isn’t bad, but Japan is unable to colonize Korea because Korea becomes strong enough to resist. 2. Japan loses the First Sino-Japanese War or the Russo-Japanese War, and therefore fails to expand into Korea. For each of these conditions, Japan’s situation would be drastically different. In particular, if Japan were to lose a war, the "extent of its defeat" would make a huge difference. However, in my view, if Japan had developed in this way, there’s a high chance that the "Pacific War and other major conflicts" would never have occurred. There wouldn’t have been such "dramatic growth" as in real history—but there also wouldn’t have been such "catastrophic destruction" either. Ultimately, this is something that depends on the imagination of whoever envisions it. Honestly, I think it’s quite possible that Japan could still have developed to the level of a "modern G7 nation". Of course, it’s not inevitable.

East Asia would be completely different without Japanese expansion. Just to keep this in 1900 let's say they beat China but lose to Russia in 1905. I think that a Japan that doesnt even fight the 1894 war with China would be in too alien a modern world for a comparison with OTL to be very useful (mainly since no Chinese defeat in the 1894 war could lead to among other things a surviving Qing dynasty IMO). The Japanese public is highly demoralized by the loss against Russia, Korea remains an idependent country playing off Russian and Japanese influence, and Japan maintains an alliance with the UK and US. Japan not getting militarily or colonially involved in mainland Asia probably reduces the level of overall "momentum" that Japan is able to sustain as a growing world power. Many types of industries go hand in hand in their development and a Japan that does not pursue a world-class navy is probably also not going to be able to justify a world-class heavy industry to go with it. A weaker Japan is also taken less seriously and most importantly takes itself less seriously. I believe they would be somewhat simil啊r to Thailand or the modern day Philippines. Maybe they'd end up like OTL Taiwan and get really deep into some high tech sectors like semiconductors.

You are absolutely right, and it would be a natural effect to expect. Looking at your chart reminds of peculiarities of public opinion in the region in OTL however: Notice the contrast between China and Korea's Favorable-Unfavorable ratios and the opposing ratios of the South Asian and Southeast Asian countries, including 3 Southeast Asian countries Japan occupied in WWII? I have often heard people assert Japan is hated "throughout Asia" because of WWII, or is hated wherever its Army occupied anyplace during the war, but a closer inspection shows this is mainly a China and Korea thing. And for China, while with real historical basis, it's a generationally cultivated and amplified 21st century thing-- Polls were not so lopsidedly negative in the China of the 70s, 80s, and most of the 90s. There may even be some of that in South Korea also, with Japan a highly partisan issue amplified by the left-leaning party since the democratization of the late 80s, development of competitive partisan politics, and Kim Dae-Jung's breakthrough to political power, because the South Korean left's best revenge against supporters of former military dictators is to characterize them as part of continued lineage of 'collaborators' with Japan. items.original_question: If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank? If Meiji Japan still "Meiji's" but never expands, or fails to expand at China or Russia's expense, could it have grown to G7 rank in the twentieth century? In other words, it takes all the modernization and technological upgrade steps it can to protect its sovereignty in the late 19th century world, but either is deterred or self-deters from annexing Chinese or Russian territory, or territory possibly in their sphere, like Korea, or if attempting to do so, because such attempts were rather fashionable among *many* (but not all) modern industrial states, they fail, would the same things constraining Japanese aggression or success *also* doom Japan's ability to increase its economic productive capacity and standard of living over most of the decades of the 20th century? Or not? Could Japan do as well, or better, in absolute GDP growth, per capital GDP growth, PPP measured GDP growth, and GDP global rank, by, for instance, 1920, 1940, or 1960 or 1980, without having any expansionary success beyond consolidating control over the Ryukyu Kingdom and diplomatically clarifying its ownership of the Kurile and Bonin Islands and never having won a territory in a foreign war? I think I can illustrate it best using this graphic. This helpfully long term chart of real GDP growth of Japan, Britain and the US shows Japan's growth curve in * red *. Would Japan's line be higher, lower, or about the same, without Japan's early successful wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, WWI absorption of Micronesia, 1930s exploitation of Manchuria and then occupied China, followed by the ultimately futile and highly destructive Pacific War, and the Cold War alliance arrangement the US and Japan set up to deal with the Soviet Union and avoid the recurrence of mutual war? Maybe the red line in the alternate history of an alternate Japan would have lower at some points and higher at others, but if so, please specify roughly when, and where do you think things would be stabilizing by the 1960 through present-day era. It may be tempting to call a Meiji (and beyond) Japan, with this type of foreign policy record that lacks success at military-naval territorial expansion as a Japan "pulling a Thailand" or analogous to a Thailand. But I would urge caution in making such an analogy. Sure, Thailand protected its sovereignty uniquely within its Southeast Asian neighborhood, while not being able to clash with colonial powers head on. But that's as far as the analogy would apply. Thailand's technological advancement and industrialization was for long, until the 1960s, pretty weak, and a Japan on Thailand's *economic* trajectory would be *categorically* poorer and less technologically, industrially, scientifically, and financially sophisticated than OTL's Japan. Thailand also only *began* experiments with constitutional government about fifty years later than Japan, even though Japan in the mid-20th century had some spectacular democratic and especially liberal failures and has some democratic deficits to this day. But their internal political cultures and societies are quite different.

items.model_answer:
Yes—quite possibly, but with a different profile and probably on a slower, less dramatic path.

If “still Meiji” means Japan still carries out the core Meiji transformations—centralization of the state, abolition of the old feudal order, land-tax reform, mass education, conscription, legal modernization, infrastructure building, and active industrial policy—then the biggest drivers of long-run economic growth are still there. Those domestic reforms mattered more to eventual great-power status than empire did. Japan’s rise was not created from scratch by conquest; it was built on state capacity, literacy, social discipline, industrial learning, and successful adaptation of Western institutions and technology.

So in principle, a non-expansionist Meiji Japan could still have become a first-rank industrial economy, and eventually something like a G7-level country. In fact, post-1945 Japan is strong evidence for this. The Japan that actually became an economic superpower after World War II did so after losing its empire, under severe constraints on military power, and with growth driven by exports, technology absorption, high savings, industrial coordination, and human capital. That suggests empire was not necessary for becoming rich.

But the counterfactual has to be handled carefully, because imperial expansion did provide some real advantages. Victories over China and Russia raised Japan’s international prestige, improved treaty revision, increased access to Taiwan, Korea, and later Manchuria, and gave strategic depth and some access to resources and captive markets. Expansion also strengthened domestic nationalist coalitions and military influence. Without those gains, Japan might have faced tighter resource constraints, less geopolitical leverage, and perhaps more vulnerability to Western pressure. It might have remained respected but not feared, commercially integrated but diplomatically less equal for longer.

The key question is what “G7 rank” means. If it means military-great-power status by the early twentieth century, then probably no: without defeating China or Russia, Japan likely does not break into the top rank as quickly or as unmistakably. Those wars were crucial signals to the world that Japan had arrived as a great power. If it means becoming one of the world’s leading advanced industrial economies by the later twentieth century, then yes, that seems very plausible. A Japan that stayed focused on domestic industrialization, shipping, textiles, machinery, chemicals, education, and trade could well have become rich without colonial empire—perhaps richer per capita sooner, because it would avoid the enormous fiscal, political, and eventually catastrophic military costs of imperial overstretch.

In some ways, non-expansion might even improve the long-run outcome. Empire drew Japan into increasingly destructive continental commitments, intensified military dominance in politics, worsened relations with major powers, and culminated in a disastrous war that destroyed much of the country. A Japan that remained reformist, commercially ambitious, and strategically cautious might have looked more like a Northeast Asian version of a highly developmental trading state: less glamorous in hard-power terms before 1914, but potentially more stable and more prosperous over the long run.

So the best direct answer is: yes, Meiji Japan could likely still have reached G7-level economic status without expanding at China’s or Russia’s expense, provided its internal modernization remained intact and it retained access to world markets, capital, and technology. It probably would not have become as quickly or as visibly a military great power, but it may have had a better long-term path to wealth precisely because it avoided the burdens and disasters of empire.

edus.text: Yes—quite possibly, but with a different profile and probably on a slower, less dramatic path.

If “still Meiji” means Japan still carries out the core Meiji transformations—centralization of the state, abolition of the old feudal order, land-tax reform, mass education, conscription, legal modernization, infrastructure building, and active industrial policy—then the biggest drivers of long-run economic growth are still there.
Those domestic reforms mattered more to eventual great-power status than empire did.
Japan’s rise was not created from scratch by conquest;
it was built on state capacity, literacy, social discipline, industrial learning, and successful adaptation of Western institutions and technology.
So in principle, a non-expansionist Meiji Japan could still have become a first-rank industrial economy, and eventually something like a G7-level country.
In fact, post-1945 Japan is strong evidence for this.

The Japan that actually became an economic superpower after World War II did so after losing its empire, under severe constraints on military power, and with growth driven by exports, technology absorption, high savings, industrial coordination, and human capital.
That suggests empire was not necessary for becoming rich.
But the counterfactual has to be handled carefully,
because imperial expansion did provide some real advantages.

Victories over China and Russia raised Japan’s international prestige, improved treaty revision, increased access to Taiwan, Korea, and later Manchuria, and gave strategic depth and some access to resources and captive markets.
Expansion also strengthened domestic nationalist coalitions and military influence.
Without those gains, Japan might have faced tighter resource constraints, less geopolitical leverage, and perhaps more vulnerability to Western pressure.
It might have remained respected but not feared, commercially integrated but diplomatically less equal for longer.
The key question is what “G7 rank” means.
If it means military-great-power status by the early twentieth century, then probably no:
without defeating China or Russia, Japan likely does not break into the top rank as quickly or as unmistakably.
Those wars were crucial signals to the world that Japan had arrived as a great power.
If it means becoming one of the world’s leading advanced industrial economies by the later twentieth century, then yes, that seems very plausible.
A Japan that stayed focused on domestic industrialization, shipping, textiles, machinery, chemicals, education, and trade could well have become rich without colonial empire—
perhaps richer per capita sooner, because it would avoid the enormous fiscal, political, and eventually catastrophic military costs of imperial overstretch.
In some ways, non-expansion might even improve the long-run outcome.

Empire drew Japan into increasingly destructive continental commitments, intensified military dominance in politics, worsened relations with major powers, and culminated in a disastrous war that destroyed much of the country.
A Japan that remained reformist, commercially ambitious, and strategically cautious might have looked more like a Northeast Asian version of a highly developmental trading state:
less glamorous in hard-power terms before 1914, but potentially more stable and more prosperous over the long run.
So the best direct answer is: yes, Meiji Japan could likely still have reached G7-level economic status without expanding at China’s or Russia’s expense,
provided its internal modernization remained intact and it retained access to world markets, capital, and technology.
It probably would not have become as quickly or as visibly a military great power,
but it may have had a better long-term path to wealth precisely because it avoided the burdens and disasters of empire.

items.question: What If the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed?
human_answers: Define failed - do you just mean the fighter planes are sitting armed in their revetments, the AA guns (both fleet and land based) are manned, the ships are at condition ZED, the radar stations are manned, and the Air Information Center has been set up (probably not fully manned but at least some minimal level of staffing). This gets you raid warning, fighters get into the air in time to meet the raid, and the ships in port and ready to take the punch. That is not done due any specific intelligence about an attack it is simply done as a response to the war warnings of late November. Between fighter defenses and AA fire and planes not making it back to the carriers the Japanese lose somewhere between 1/3 and 1/2 of their attacking aircraft. Damage to the Pacific Fleet is a lot less because the ships are buttoned up and a lot less planes are destroyed on the ground because they are either in the air or in protected revetments or at least dispersed. Losses to fighter pilots are higher because of more guys getting shot down but they also take their measure of the Japanese. That constitutes failure for the Japanese, particularly given the losses in trained air crews. What it means going forward I'm not sure but it sure is an ugly start. Or, do you mean by failure the US does all of the above but also has knowledge a Japanese carrier task force is going to attack Oahu during the morning of 7 December from a position between 200-250 miles north of Oahu. This means every available attack aircraft on Oahu is bombed up and ready to go (6 B-17s, 21 B-18s, 5 A-20s, 23 SBDs, 8 SB2Us) and Kimmel is able to position Enterprise and Lexington 150 miles to the southwest of where the KB is expected to be operating as well as sending the small number of submarines he has in port to the north as well. By the way, Kimmel also has a moment of profound insight and realizes the safest place for his fat slow battleships is sitting in port at Condition ZED. That scenario has the US forces on island ready to take the punch and the US has about 180 attack aircraft of various types ready to throw at the KB to include roughly the equivalent of seven squadrons of US Navy and US Marine Corps dive bombers the most effective weapon in the US arsenal. Scenario One is quite realistic and only needs some fairly minor PODs to make it work. Scenario Two is a lot less realistic but if you squint hard enough you can probably come up with some PODs that still make it work. Scenario One the attacking aircraft get butchered but the KB likely gets away clean. Scenario Two the attacking aircraft get butchered and Nagumo loses at least two carrier maybe as many as four depending on the breaks.

I do not disagree with the analysis above, but I would take a different path in logical application from the same starting point. Define failure. What if the Japanese failed to attack Pearl Harbor at all. What if on the morning of 7 December the seas were unexpectedly, and unseasonably rough enough to preclude any launch of aircraft. The invasion of Malaya started four hour earlier, and it is too late to cancel attacks on US possession in the western Pacific. Conditions are not much better on the eighth. Kido Butai trundles back home to Japan, undetected by US aircraft.. This may seem like a "what if Japan declared war, and did not attack Pearl Harbor" scenario but it is not. The key difference is, what if Japan launched surprise attacks all over Asia without declaring war, and its most powerful naval assets were non-combat effective for the first 25 days of the war? Comments?

I'm not too familiar either with how much intelligence the US had on Japan pre-Pearl Harbor, but I do know that a Japanese submarine was sunk by the US just hours before Pearl Harbor, and the message either was ignored or received too late to mobilize the dock. I could totally see an early warning, through this incident, cause Pearl Harbor to mobilize and allow for Japanese pilots to lose the element of surprise. Assuming the Japanese ships aren't found and only the planes are destroyed, this would make Japan more cautious against the US, since the Pacific Fleet wouldn't be as weak as it was after Pearl Harbor in our timeline. Additionally, because of the warning, there might be less civilian causalities and so, in the United States, there is anger at being attacked, there wouldn't be the rallying cry of "OMG THEY MURDERED A BUNCH ON INNOCENT AMERICANS!" But, overall, Pearl Harbor not being totally destroyed is definitely an interesting and plausible scenario that would have an impact on WWII.
items.original_question: What if the attack on Pearl Harbor completely failed? This was something that popped into my head. What if the USA has gained early warning of Pearl Harbor and had managed to defeat the attack? I am not too familiar with the intelligence background of it but I do believe I heard that there were some potential early signs before the attack that were ignored. If say the USA had received information a few days in advance and was able to crush the japanise attack and keep many of their best ships in a strong position in Hawaii now much would it change the pacific campaign? Would America be able to defeat Japan early maybe before the Nazis even fall?

criteria.7-8: Specifies a plausible point of divergence, such as radar response, submarine warning, war-warning readiness, or bad seas, and explains why it could occur.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes multiple plausible meanings of failure, such as failed surprise versus carrier losses versus aborted strike, and evaluates their different implications.

Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in order to cripple the U.S. Pacific Fleet long enough to secure its conquests in Southeast Asia and the western Pacific. If the attack had completely failed—meaning the carriers, battleships, aircraft, fuel depots, repair facilities, and personnel were largely unharmed, while Japan lost many planes and perhaps some carriers or elite aviators—then Japan would have achieved the opposite of its goal. Militarily, the Pacific War would likely become much harder for Japan much sooner. Historically, Japan gained several months of freedom of action because the U.S. battleships were sunk or damaged and the Pacific Fleet was temporarily disorganized. If Pearl Harbor failed, the U.S. Navy would retain much more immediate striking power. That does not mean the United States could

items.question: The Highest Patriotism: What If George McGovern became President in 1968
human_answers: The one thing that keeps coming to me is Nixon would have the greatest meltdown in political history, screaming bloody murder then the Eastern Establishment has screw him for a third and final time. Even in OTL 68 a lot of the GOP had in fact become very weary over backing Nixon over his defeats in 1960, and 1962 in California. Now this last minute scandal, Nixon messing with the peace talks, cost him and the Republicans the election for a third time. At the very best, Tricky Dick might become a Secretary of State under a future Republican president and a Statesman, but the White House is forever gone. GOP swings back to the Rockefeller Republicans like George Romney and Nelson Rockefeller himself, but could also swing to Reagan. McGovern quickly makes a peace deal for Vietnam and pulls out. The South eventually falls. But we wash our hands of that conflict. McGovern would see to a second wind of the Great Society and likely see to a very liberal and Leftist Supreme Court along with many other Judges and at least some mild liberal reforms passed in Congress.
