items.question: What If the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out?
human_answers: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? The Holy Roman Empire was the legacy of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire (as opposed to the HOLY Roman Empire) plunged Western Europe into the Middle Ages, from 476 CE (the razing of Rome by the Goths/ the collapse of Rome/ the retrenchment of Rome) to 1266 CE Marco Polo (goes to China) to 1492 CE (the discovery of the Americas by Spain/ starting Mercantilism & Colonialism). It is hard to put a firm date on the latter time when the Middle Ages ended. The role of the Roman Empire. The Roman Empire provided a conduit for a Pax Romana, that, in turn, provided for a common culture and trade from Wales in the West to Asia Minor in the East. From Germania in the North to Numidia in the South. The Roman Empire essentially lined the Mediterranian Sea. When the Roman Empire came apart, we saw the balkanization of Europe, EXCEPT for the Holy Roman Empire. We see the various raiding groups causing the fortification and (for the Roman Catholic Church the Monasticism, of Europe, as the social order broke down and people’s view of their then-world became increasingly insular! The exception of the Holy Roman Empire and the Church of Rome were the phoenix that arose out of ashes of the Roman Empire and that was the Roman Catholic Church, aka The Vatican, and that formed the Holy Roman Empire (the geopolitical extension of the Catholic Church.) Which was basically Italy and Germany. There will those who will bring up the Byzantine Empire. You are right but let’s keep this simple, shall we? I believe the questioner was asking about Western Europe and it is that, to which I am addressing my comments. You are free to write your own answer for the Moorish perspective. The Vatican itself had a bigger, but weaker, hold over Western Europe. in contrast to the Holy Roman Empire. In large part, that is that a King needed the Pope’s support & backing to rule. Excommunication was a death sentence to a King’s reign. Power flowed from the Vatican to the King and down thru the nobles. Less is Moor! It is at this point, that I must bring in the Moors, so I might mention that the Middle East was blockaded, as a route to the Orient. Columbus was hired to find a western route to the Orient, by the Spanish royal couple, Ferdinand & Isabella, to end-run that blockade of the Middle East, the Moors having just expelled from Spain! Columbus’s success drew the rulers and merchant of many West Europeans outlook of the world into a more colonial view of the world. Mercantilism & Colonialism. Mercantilism is the economic view of getting resources from colonies and selling finished goods to those colonies. Colonies are a political view of establishing colonies. This race for territory caused a lot, A LOT, of tensions between the nations of Western Europe, not to mention the colony and mother country. The land grab leads to navies, armies, and the settlements to protect trade routes and exploit the resources of those colonies in the Americas, Africa, and Asia. This leads, in turn, to mutual defense treaties (the bifurcation of us vs them. In 1517 CE, Martin Luther & his 95 Thesis’s which begins the beginning of the Reformation. The Vatican begins to lose its grip over Western Europe. Competing Churches no longer recognize the Pope as the supreme authority and Governments rapidly follow suit, leading to even more tension. In 1806 CE, Napolean puts an end to the Holy Roman Empire. Italy and Germany split into principalities, that eventually evolved into modern nations of Italy and Germany. Nationalism took root! The modern era summarized. This tensions reached a flashpoint when a Serbian nationalist assassinated the Archduke of Austria and his wife! All those mutual defense treaties came in to play and WW I began. This led to the Czar and his family being overthrown in Russia, leading in turn to communism and the Soviet Union. The land grab and mutual defense treaties, after WW II, which encouraged colonies to break away and assert their independence. The Cold War. The dissolution of the USSR. Modern times. When it is all said and done. How would it be without the Holy Roman Empire? In a word “Different!” The social and historical order would be changed. Like dominos falling into each other into each other, the dominions of Europe would be reprioritized. We got the history we got because things happened as they did. You start to tug on the woof and weave of time, time will unravel like a cheap sweater, and then all bets are off, about how that history evolves. You can hate the Roman Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Vatican, but they got us where we are and none can say if an alternative would be better or worse!

Question: What if the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out? Details: Would Europe perhaps have had 1 or 2 Super States comparable to China in the Middle East? I’m not sure I ‘get’ the question. Charlemagne’s empire, often regarded as the origin of the Holy Roman Empire, was the nearest Western Europe came to a super state. If the Pope had not decided to crown Charlemagne Emperor in 800, so he continued as King of the Franks, as he had been since 774, I can’t really see that would have made much difference. The break-up, shortly after Charlemagne’s death, had nothing to do with his title of Emperor. Partible inheritance had a lot to do with, but even with primogeniture, the Empire might not have been very stable. We know, from the Oaths of Strasbourg (842) that France and Germany already had well established separate languages by then, even though the ruling classes were all of German origin. They also had very distinct cultural histories, with France’s institutions inherited from the old Roman Empire, which Germany had always stood outside. The Holy Roman Empire was refounded as a powerful state by Otto the Great in 962. This incarnation never included France, but did include Germany (plus some surrounding lands) and what contemporaries called Italy (the northern half of what we call Italy). This empire held together as a powerful and, by the standards of the day, quite co-ordinated entity, until the fall of the Hohenstaufen in 1254. I can see how, had the Hohenstaufen not fallen, there was a potential for it to develop into a superstate bestriding much of Western Europe, perhaps by conquest, but more likely by inheritance. Something like Charles V’s empire, but sooner, and based on a much more powerful and united Germany. Its contemporaries could see that potential too, especially when it inherited and took over Sicily (including the southern half of today’s Italy). That is one reason why some of them combined to bring it down when the opportunity presented itself. How the Empire not existing could help that process, though, I’m really not sure. Eastern Europe, of course, had and has its superstate, Russia.

Counterfactual premise A world without the Holy Roman Empire (HRE) means removing a political entity that, from roughly 800–1806, linked a patchwork of central European duchies, bishoprics, free cities and principalities under an elective imperial crown claiming Roman continuity. “Never existed” can be interpreted in two ways: (A) Charlemagne never unified Francian/German lands into an empire in 800, so no imperial tradition develops; or (B) a united central-imperial polity is attempted but fails early and never reconstitutes. Both lead to similar broad consequences: a much weaker supra‑regional institution in Central Europe, earlier fragmentation or alternative unifiers, different church–state relations, altered balance among France, Poland, Italy, the Baltic and the Ottoman frontier, and big effects on state formation, law, religion and culture. Core structural consequences (high level) Greater political fragmentation in the German-speaking lands for longer, accelerating emergence of numerous small sovereign states or city-states with stronger local sovereignty. Without an imperial crown as a focal institution, imperial law, imperial diets and the symbolic framework that mediated overlordship are gone. Earlier consolidation by other regional powers. France would face a more fragmented eastern neighbor; Brandenburg/Prussia, Poland, Bavaria, and Austria would compete to fill the power vacuum. That competition would likely produce a different map: some larger territorial states (Prussia or Poland–Lithuania) could expand sooner and further; alternatively, many microstates persist under shifting suzerainties. Different Church–state dynamics. The HRE’s peculiar relationship with the papacy (lay investiture conflict, imperial coronations, imperial protection of papal interests at times) disappears, changing ecclesiastical politics in Italy and Central Europe. Local princes may gain ecclesiastical autonomy faster; church reform movements and the timing/location of conflicts with Rome shift. Italy’s fragmentation intensifies long-term. The HRE historically provided a counterweight to papal and northern Italian city ambitions. Without imperial intervention, northern Italian communes and the papacy consolidate power in different patterns; the peninsula could see an earlier and more decisive rise of maritime republics or stronger papal states. The map of colonization, warfare and alliances in the later early modern period shifts, because a major central European diplomatic player is missing. European coalitions against France, the Ottomans, or in colonial rivalry form differently. Political and military consequences Rise of alternative hegemonies: Brandenburg/Prussia or Austria might either not arise as single hegemonic states or would develop different identities. If no imperial legitimacy constrains them, dynasties could centralize quicker or be absorbed by neighbors. A strong Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth could expand west into Silesia and Bohemia absent imperial claims, creating a large Poland-centered bloc. The balance against the Ottomans alters: the HRE’s patchwork provided troops, fortresses and political organization to resist Ottoman expansion in Hungary and the Balkans. Without a coordinating imperial structure, response to Ottoman advance could be slower and more regionally uneven; the Ottomans might consolidate greater gains in Central Europe earlier, or conversely local powers could carve defensive coalitions independent of an emperor. Warfare and military innovation diffuse differently. Habsburg dynastic networks that used imperial offices to bind Central Europe would be less effective; their dynastic power would need other bases (landed holdings, marriage alliances), shifting the locus of Habsburg power possibly more toward Spain/Italy earlier or less central in German lands. Religion and the Reformation Protestant Reformation dynamics change substantially. In the historical HRE, the refusal or acceptance of imperial enforcement, the Peace of Augsburg (1555) and the Thirty Years’ War (1618–48) were mediated by imperial institutions. Without an empire: Local rulers might adopt confessional changes with fewer supra‑regional constraints, producing a more mosaic religious map more quickly. Continental confessional wars might be less sweeping but more localized; or they might be replaced by prolonged border conflicts between rising states (e.g., Sweden, Poland, France) rather than an empire-centered Thirty Years’ War. The Peace of Westphalia’s state-sovereignty principles would arise differently or later; the concept of sovereign territorial states might develop earlier as local rulers assert final authority over religion and law. Legal, economic and cultural effects Legal fragmentation and local autonomy accelerate. The imperial legal framework (Imperial Chamber Court, Reichstag) that moderated disputes and preserved rights for imperial estates is absent, so legal pluralism strengthens and regional customary law matters more. Urban and mercantile development. Free imperial cities were historically important nodes. Without imperial status, some cities either fall under territorial princes faster (reducing urban autonomy) or secure different international protections (alliances with Venice, Hanseatic League, or France). The Hanseatic League and Italian maritime republics may gain or lose relative influence depending on territorial pressure from expanded states. Cultural and intellectual flows persist but different patronage networks emerge. Universities, monastic orders and the printing press continue to diffuse ideas; without imperial patronage, cultural centers may cluster more strongly in distinct courts (Prussia, France, Poland, Italian states) and in free cities that find other patrons. Colonial and global consequences Central European absence as a unified actor likely does not dramatically alter early Iberian and later British/Dutch colonization because those were maritime powers. However: A weaker or more fragmented Habsburg base could reduce Spanish/Habsburg coordination across Europe, affecting Habsburg capacities in the 16th–17th centuries. Migration patterns to the Americas and colonies may change: German-speaking emigration might be more regionally driven by small principalities rather than imperial policy, altering settlement patterns in North America and the Caribbean. Military manpower supply for colonial wars differs; mercenary markets in Central Europe could expand, influencing wars abroad. Long-term nation-building and modern map (plausible scenarios) Scenario A — Early microstate Europe Persistent extreme fragmentation: dozens of sovereign German-speaking principalities and city-states survive into the 19th century. France and a stronger Prussia (or a stronger Austria that never consolidated imperial claims) dominate; German unification is delayed or takes a different form (confederation under French or Austrian influence, or a northern confederation led by Prussia emerges later as in real history but with different borders). Industrialization in German lands is uneven; some city-states industrialize quickly, others lag. Scenario B — Alternative unifier rises Prussia (Brandenburg) or a Polish–Silesian union becomes the dominant central European state earlier. If Prussia unifies German lands sooner without an imperial counterweight, a unified German nation-state might appear before 1871, changing the Napoleonic era and the 19th-century balance. If Poland expands west, a large Central European Commonwealth alters Russo‑Prussian dynamics. Scenario C — Stronger regional empires elsewhere Without imperial symbolic legitimacy in Central Europe, dynasties like the Habsburgs pivot toward Italy/Spain and build more coherent maritime/peninsular empires, or they lose ground to France and the Ottomans. The Ottoman Empire may hold more territory in Hungary and the Balkans for longer. Effects on modern Europe (concise) Germany’s path to nationhood changes: the German Empire of 1871 might not exist as known; German-speaking unity could be delayed, achieved under different leadership, or remain fragmented into smaller states in the 20th century. Borders of modern states shift: Poland, Czech lands (Bohemia), Silesia, Bavaria and the Austrian core could belong to different polities or be partitioned differently in the 18th–19th centuries. The ideological legacy of the HRE (mixed sovereignty, legal pluralism, imperial law) that influenced Western legal thought is weaker; the Westphalian state system might crystallize differently, potentially strengthening territorial sovereignty earlier. European wars of the 17th–19th centuries reconfigure: alliances without an imperial center produce different coalition patterns against France, Britain, and the Ottomans, producing alternative outcomes in the Napoleonic and world wars. Key takeaway Removing the Holy Roman Empire shifts Europe from a semi‑centralized, symbolic imperial order to a more fragmented or differently united Central Europe. The most probable outcomes are stronger competition among regional powers (Prussia, Austria, Poland, France, the Ottomans), earlier and deeper political fragmentation in German lands, altered religious and legal settlements, and a different timeline for European state consolidation and balance of power. Exact borders and events are highly sensitive to contingent decisions—small dynastic marriages, battles, or success of a single ambitious ruler could produce radically different maps—so the counterfactual space is wide, but the themes above are robust across plausible variants.

There is no such thing as a total polity vacuum. As an example: defeated Germany in 1945 was occupied, divided and ruled by the victors in specific zones. Lower level German administration (in villages, cities) and courts of justice, never ceased to exist. Similarly, without the Holy Roman Empire, another polity would have taken the place. A confederation of German states, perhaps, with or without a loose central authority. Nothing really different from the HRE, except for one point: there would be much less friction with the East Roman Empire (Constantinople), which always claimed exclusivity in the use of “Roman” and supremacy in title and political protocol. Could such a better understanding between Byzantium and Central Europe have avoided the Schism of the Church in 1054 ? Probably. A united Christianity, under increased influence of the Byzantine ecclesiastic model, might have avoided the struggle between Papacy and European kings, might also have avoided the Protestant Reformation. Last but not least, crusades in much better coordination with Constantinople, better and lasting results. And no Turks in Europe , not even in Asia Minor…

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Holy Roman Empire never existed? How would Europe have turned out?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Definition and Historical Grounding
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what it means for the Holy Roman Empire to have never existed and grounds the counterfactual in accurate baseline history from Charlemagne/Otto I through 1806.
criteria.1-2: Leaves the premise vague or treats the HRE as simply the ancient Roman Empire; contains major chronological or factual errors.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes the HRE as a medieval/early modern central European polity but gives an unclear removal point or relies on oversimplified history.
criteria.5-6: Defines a plausible removal scenario, such as no imperial coronation or no Ottonian refoundation, with mostly accurate baseline facts.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes Charlemagne, the Ottonian HRE, papal legitimacy, German and Italian components, and the empire's long institutional lifespan.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames multiple plausible versions of 'never existed' and explains how each affects the causal starting conditions without anachronism.

criteria.name: Central European State Formation and Fragmentation Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains likely effects on German-speaking lands, Austria, Bohemia, northern Italy, free cities, principalities, and possible alternative unifiers.
criteria.1-2: Makes unsupported claims such as Europe inevitably becoming one or two superstates without explaining central European mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions fragmentation or unification but does not connect it to imperial institutions, dynasties, inheritance, or local sovereignty.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the absence of imperial authority would alter German and Italian fragmentation, though with limited detail on actors or pathways.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes competing outcomes involving Austria, Brandenburg/Prussia, Bavaria, Bohemia, Poland-Lithuania, free cities, or northern Italian states.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced, mechanism-rich account of how the loss of imperial law, elective kingship, princely rights, and dynastic politics could produce several plausible state-formation trajectories.

criteria.name: Church, Law, Reformation, and Institutional Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how the absence of the HRE would affect papal-imperial relations, investiture politics, imperial law, the Reformation, confessional settlement, and concepts of sovereignty.
criteria.1-2: Ignores religion and law or falsely assumes the Catholic Church and Reformation would proceed unchanged in all respects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions the Church or Reformation only generally, with little connection to the HRE's specific institutional role.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some likely changes to papal authority, Protestantism, or legal pluralism but treats them as isolated effects.
criteria.7-8: Connects the absence of imperial structures to altered papal politics, local religious autonomy, Augsburg/Westphalia-like settlements, and legal fragmentation.
criteria.9-10: Explains in detail how the Investiture Controversy, imperial courts/diets, prince-bishoprics, Peace of Augsburg, Thirty Years' War dynamics, and sovereignty norms might be transformed.

criteria.name: Long-Range Geopolitical and Global Ripple Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces coherent downstream effects on France, Poland-Lithuania, the Habsburgs, the Ottomans, Italy, Russia, colonial competition, and later European wars.
criteria.1-2: Provides only vague statements that Europe would be 'different' with no long-range causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Lists possible affected powers or wars but gives little explanation of how the absence of the HRE changes them.
criteria.5-6: Traces some plausible regional consequences, such as stronger France or altered German unification, but omits major neighboring powers or later periods.
criteria.7-8: Covers multiple downstream arenas, including Franco-German balance, Habsburg power, Ottoman frontier, Italian politics, and nineteenth-century nation-building.
criteria.9-10: Builds coherent long-range chains from medieval institutional absence to early modern alliances, Ottoman resistance, Habsburg-Spanish dynamics, colonial-era power balances, Napoleonic outcomes, and modern borders.

criteria.name: Plausibility, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids deterministic overclaiming, acknowledges contingency, maintains internal consistency, and distinguishes robust effects from speculative scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Presents a single deterministic outcome with contradictions or impossible claims, such as unchanged modern Europe despite removing the HRE.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of uncertainty but mixes incompatible claims or asserts speculative outcomes as certain.
criteria.5-6: Offers plausible outcomes with occasional overconfidence or weak handling of alternative branches.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely structural effects from uncertain contingencies and keeps causal claims internally consistent.
criteria.9-10: Uses calibrated language, multiple scenario branches, explicit uncertainty, and strong contradiction control while preserving a coherent overall assessment of Europe's altered development.

items.model_answer:
If the Holy Roman Empire had never existed, Europe would still have been politically fragmented in the center, but the shape of that fragmentation—and the balance of power across the continent—would likely have been quite different.

The first big effect would be on Germany and northern Italy, because those were the core lands gathered, however loosely, under the imperial title. The Holy Roman Empire was never a strong centralized state, but it did provide a legal and symbolic framework that tied hundreds of princes, bishops, cities, and nobles into a recognized order. Without it, central Europe would probably have broken into either a patchwork of fully sovereign regional kingdoms much earlier, or else into a smaller number of larger territorial states competing for dominance. In other words, the empire often preserved fragmentation while also regulating it. Remove that structure, and the political map of the German lands could have become either more chaotic in the short run or more consolidated in the long run.

A likely possibility is that some stronger duchies or kingdoms—Saxony, Bavaria, Austria, Bohemia, or perhaps a revived Lotharingian-type middle kingdom—would have emerged as major states much earlier. The absence of an emperor would also remove one of the main legitimizing authorities in medieval Europe. That would matter because the empire was not just a government; it was part of the idea that Christendom should have both a pope and an emperor. Without it, the papacy might initially have had more room to act politically, but in the longer term kings in France, England, and elsewhere would probably have claimed greater autonomy even sooner, since there would be no universal secular rival to them.

France would likely be one of the main beneficiaries. Historically, the Holy Roman Empire acted as a broad eastern counterpart that limited French expansion into the Rhine region and Italy. Without an empire, France might have expanded eastward earlier and more deeply, especially into Burgundy, Lorraine, and the Rhineland. That could have made France stronger sooner, perhaps producing an earlier and more pronounced French predominance in western Europe.

Italy would also be transformed. The empire’s intermittent claims over northern and central Italy helped prevent durable political unification but also checked both papal and purely local ambitions. Without imperial involvement, northern Italian city-states might have developed more independently, and regional powers like Milan, Venice, or the papacy might have dominated larger parts of the peninsula. Alternatively, a stronger French or even Aragonese-Spanish influence in Italy could have appeared earlier, since there would be no imperial claimant to contest them. So Italy might have either unified under a regional power earlier than in real history or become even more clearly a battlefield for outside monarchies.

The Habsburgs, in particular, would probably have been much less important, or at least important in a very different way. Their rise depended heavily on acquiring and holding the imperial crown as well as their dynastic possessions in Austria and beyond. Without the empire, they might remain a regional Austrian dynasty rather than becoming one of Europe’s great ruling houses. That would have major consequences for Spain, the Low Countries, Bohemia, Hungary, and the long Habsburg-Valois and Habsburg-Bourbon rivalries that shaped early modern Europe.

The Reformation would also likely unfold differently. The empire’s decentralized constitutional order gave reformers and sympathetic princes room to survive. Martin Luther benefited from the fact that no single centralized authority could easily crush him across all German lands. Without the empire, two different outcomes become plausible. If central Europe were divided into several stronger monarchies, one or more of them might suppress Protestantism more effectively, reducing its spread. On the other hand, if the region were even more politically splintered but without imperial institutions, religious division could become even less manageable. Still, the specific pattern of “cuius regio, eius religio,” formalized in the empire, would probably not emerge in the same way.

The Thirty Years’ War would almost certainly not happen in the form we know. That conflict depended on the empire’s constitutional and religious tensions, especially in Bohemia and the German principalities, while also drawing in outside powers. Without the empire, there might still be major wars in central Europe over religion, dynastic claims, and territory, but they would be organized around different states and alliances. Europe might avoid the particular devastation that Germany suffered in the seventeenth century, or that devastation might instead fall on a different geopolitical zone.

There would also be long-term consequences for the formation of Germany. The Holy Roman Empire lasted so long that it delayed the emergence of a unified German nation-state while at the same time preserving a sense that the German lands formed some kind of common political space. Without it, “Germany” might have unified earlier under one dominant kingdom, or it might never have emerged as a single state at all. A Europe with no nineteenth-century German Empire, or with a much earlier German kingdom, would look radically different. The balance of power that eventually produced the Franco-Prussian War, World War I, and even parts of World War II might never take the same form.

More broadly, the idea of Europe itself would shift. The Holy Roman Empire embodied a medieval universalist vision: many peoples under a shared Christian political order, however imperfectly realized. Its disappearance from history from the outset would likely accelerate the rise of fully sovereign territorial monarchies and a state system more like the modern one. In that sense, Europe might have become “Westphalian” earlier: less centered on universal claims, more on borders, dynasties, and national kingdoms.

So the most likely overall answer is not that Europe would become simpler, but that central Europe would lose the loose framework that held it together for a millennium. France might become stronger earlier, Italy and Germany would develop along very different lines, the Habsburgs might never become a continental super-dynasty, the Reformation and the wars of religion would take different forms, and the modern European balance of power might emerge much earlier—but around very different states. The Holy Roman Empire was weak as an empire, yet enormously important as a structure. Without it, Europe would probably be less medieval sooner, but also potentially more unstable in different ways.

edus.text: If the Holy Roman Empire had never existed, Europe would still have been politically fragmented in the center,
but the shape of that fragmentation—and the balance of power across the continent—would likely have been quite different.
The first big effect would be on Germany and northern Italy,
because those were the core lands gathered, however loosely, under the imperial title.
The Holy Roman Empire was never a strong centralized state,
but it did provide a legal and symbolic framework that tied hundreds of princes, bishops, cities, and nobles into a recognized order.

Without it, central Europe would probably have broken into either a patchwork of fully sovereign regional kingdoms much earlier, or else into a smaller number of larger territorial states competing for dominance.
In other words, the empire often preserved fragmentation while also regulating it.
Remove that structure,
and the political map of the German lands could have become either more chaotic in the short run or more consolidated in the long run.
A likely possibility is that some stronger duchies or kingdoms would have emerged as major states much earlier.
The absence of an emperor would also remove one of the main legitimizing authorities in medieval Europe.
That would matter
because the empire was not just a government;
it was part of the idea that Christendom should have both a pope and an emperor.
Without it, the papacy might initially have had more room to act politically,
but in the longer term kings in France, England, and elsewhere would probably have claimed greater autonomy even sooner,
since there would be no universal secular rival to them.
France would likely be one of the main beneficiaries.
Historically, the Holy Roman Empire acted as a broad eastern counterpart that limited French expansion into the Rhine region and Italy.
Without an empire, France might have expanded eastward earlier and more deeply.
That could have made France stronger sooner,
perhaps producing an earlier and more pronounced French predominance in western Europe.
Italy would also be transformed.
The empire’s intermittent claims over northern and central Italy helped prevent durable political unification
but also checked both papal and purely local ambitions.
Without imperial involvement, northern Italian city-states might have developed more independently,
and regional powers like Milan, Venice, or the papacy might have dominated larger parts of the peninsula.
Alternatively, a stronger French or Aragonese-Spanish influence in Italy could have appeared earlier,
since there would be no imperial claimant to contest them.
So Italy might have either unified under a regional power earlier than in real history
or become even more clearly a battlefield for outside monarchies.
The Habsburgs would probably have been much less important, or at least important in a very different way.
Their rise depended heavily on acquiring and holding the imperial crown as well as their dynastic possessions.
Without the empire, they might remain a regional Austrian dynasty rather than becoming one of Europe’s great ruling houses.
That would have major consequences for Spain, the Low Countries, Bohemia, Hungary, and the long rivalries that shaped early modern Europe.
The Reformation would also likely unfold differently.
The empire’s decentralized constitutional order gave reformers and sympathetic princes room to survive.
Martin Luther benefited from the fact that no single centralized authority could easily crush him.
Without the empire, two different outcomes become plausible.
If central Europe were divided into several stronger monarchies, one or more might suppress Protestantism more effectively,
reducing its spread.
On the other hand, if the region were even more politically splintered but without imperial institutions, religious division could become even less manageable.
Still, the specific pattern of “cuius regio, eius religio” would probably not emerge in the same way.
The Thirty Years’ War would almost certainly not happen in the form we know.
That conflict depended on the empire’s constitutional and religious tensions,
while also drawing in outside powers.
Without the empire, there might still be major wars in central Europe,
but they would be organized around different states and alliances.
Europe might avoid the particular devastation that Germany suffered in the seventeenth century,
or that devastation might instead fall on a different geopolitical zone.
There would also be long-term consequences for the formation of Germany.
The Holy Roman Empire lasted so long that it delayed the emergence of a unified German nation-state
while at the same time preserving a sense of common political space.
Without it, “Germany” might have unified earlier under one dominant kingdom,
or it might never have emerged as a single state at all.
A Europe with no nineteenth-century German Empire, or with a much earlier German kingdom, would look radically different.
The balance of power that eventually produced major wars might never take the same form.
More broadly, the idea of Europe itself would shift.
The Holy Roman Empire embodied a medieval universalist vision: many peoples under a shared Christian political order.
Its disappearance from history from the outset would likely accelerate the rise of fully sovereign territorial monarchies and a more modern state system.
In that sense, Europe might have become “Westphalian” earlier.
So the most likely overall answer is not that Europe would become simpler,
but that central Europe would lose the loose framework that held it together for a millennium.

France might become stronger earlier, Italy and Germany would develop differently, the Habsburgs might never become a super-dynasty, the Reformation and wars of religion would take different forms, and the modern balance of power might emerge much earlier—but around very different states.
The Holy Roman Empire was weak as an empire,
yet enormously important as a structure.
Without it, Europe would probably be less medieval sooner,
but also potentially more unstable in different ways.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?
human_answers: Note: Parts of this answer will be copied from this one . However, this is a different scenario than that one. Note: I do not claim that this answer is realistic, nor that everything would happen the way I say it would. This is, of course, impossible to predict. Anyway, the point of divergence here is 378 AD, with the battle of Adrianople. Battle of Adrianople You see, Rome could have won this battle quite decisively. They had numerical parity, if not superiority, to the Gothic forces. They had great heavy cavalry. Valens had a large amount of additional reinforcements marching in from the west as well. They likely would have arrived within the next few days. Had the two forces linked up, they would have likely beaten the Goths. Why did I have the Romans win at Adrianople? The Roman defeat at Adrianople and the resulting Gothic invasions devastated the Balkans, to the point where they were somewhat depopulated. This is avoided in this timeline. This also avoids the Goths rising up in revolt within the Empire later on. With the Balkans in a much better position, the Romans are able to largely keep the Huns at bay, forcing them west. The Huns were defeated in battle by the Western Romans and their allies in 451 AD, so I could see the Eastern Romans doing the same here. Next, Theodosius the Great recognizes Eunegius as Emperor in 394, rather than killing and deposing him. This avoids the problem of Honorius becoming Emperor and also doesn’t kill over a third of the western army. Eunegius agrees to let Flavius Stilicho become Magister Militum of the west in exchange for being recognized as Emperor. Stilicho would survive longer in this timeline due to Honorius not rising to power, allowing him to better contain the barbarians invading the Empire. He would represent a bridge between the barbarians living within the Empire, allowing them to be more easily assimalated and showing that the two could coexist. Flavius Aetius would also survive longer, giving Rome a strong military leader to hold the Empire together. Next, Majorian is not betrayed in 460 AD, and his fleet is not destroyed. This allows him to retake North Africa, giving Western Rome fresh sources of manpower, taxes, food, and resources. Majorian finds out about Ricimier’s plots and has him executed. His replacement would be loyal and competent. Majorian would stabalize Italy and North Africa, and implement his reforms to the imperial administration. This would make the Empire more stable. Majorian would implement laws to whip the decedant and lazy upper class back into shape, reinvigorate pride in the Roman state, and reintroduce native Italians into the army. Majorian’s successor, likely Julius Nepos, would continue his reforms, enforcing and expanding upon them. Roman Empire in 460 AD. In this timeline, Carthage is under Roman rule as well. Under Majorian’s successors, Gaul and most of Hispania would still be lost, but the Empire would survive. Julius Nepos comes to power in the mid-late 470s, continuing the reforms of Majorian and strengthening the Empire. He would fortify the borders and choose a competent successor, who would continue the reforms of Majorian and Nepos. Majorian, Nepos, and their successors would recognize that the Empire could not rely on slavery, and that it needed to bolster its population in order to survive. Therefore, they would implement more efficient farming practices and the use of technology such as water wheels and mills in order to make the production of flour more efficient. They would also update architectural codes and improve living standards in order to increase stability and keep more people alive and healthy. They would massively revamp sanitation systems to reduce the risk of disease and improve healthcare for pregnant mothers in order to bolster the population further. They would also choose a competent successor, who would likely free most remaining slaves to increase the conscriptable, taxable population. Barbagel water mill complex During this time monuments and architecture would be restored. Propaganda would hearken back to the old days and the resilience of the Roman people, reinvigorating pride in the Empire. Leo I in the East would die a few years later than in our timeline, helping out the West. The West largely goes on as a regional power until Justinian comes along. He would officially reunify the East and West, although there would still be two emperors. Without Italy being devastated by the Gothic wars, its population thrives, and the Roman spirit is reignited in the East as well. Justinian implements the reforms of the West all across the Empire, and Rome reaches a new technological golden age. Hispania and southern Gaul are retaken for the Empire, and the whole of North Africa up to the Atlantic is under Roman control as well. The Justinian Plague is still devastating, but with the improved sanitation and without the devastation of the Gothic wars, Rome is still going strong. The Plague would drive demand for labor up as the population declines, allowing the middle class to grow and seeing the further implementation of technology into the everyday lives of Romans. Women would be allowed to hold more jobs and to work in factories, and would slowly gain more power and rights in society from there. In this timeline, with the Balkans secured and giving Rome much greater manpower than it had in our world, Germanus would be able to destroy the Persians at Antioch, making Persia rethink Rome’s weakness. The Persians would sue for peace, restoring the “Eternal Peace” they had signed with Rome not long before. They would have to make several concessions, allowing Rome to fortify the border. In this timeline, Germanus would not have to fight the Ostrogoths in Italy, and would thus not fall ill. He would become Emperor after Justinian, and after him would be Justin Germanus, who would be another competent ruler. These two would further expand on the reforms of their predecessors, upholding them and giving them time to stick. IRL Rome under Justinian With large sources of manpower from North Africa, the Balkans, and Italy, Rome is not percieved as weak by Persia. In this timeline, Phokas would not rise to power and severely weaken the Empire, as Justin Germanus would not order him to camp north of the Danube for the winter. Maurice would still rise to power after Justin, and would be a fairly competent Emperor as he was in our timeline. After Maurice, Heraclius would not want to see the Empire split between Maurice’s sons and would rise to power. Heraclius was also fairly competent. Without Phokas, and with Persia having been stopped by Germanus decades earlier, the Persians wouldn’t attack the Romans. rubrics.question_focus: What If the Roman Empire never fell and lived to the year 2020?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise and Roman survival mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines how the Roman Empire avoids collapse and whether that survival path is historically plausible for late antiquity rather than simply assuming uninterrupted Roman power.
criteria.1-2: Gives no concrete divergence point or relies on magic, vague inevitability, or an unchanged empire lasting effortlessly to 2020.
criteria.3-4: Names a broad reason Rome survives but gives little connection to real late Roman crises such as succession, fiscal strain, military pressure, or administrative division.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible divergence or reform path addressing some key causes of decline, though with gaps or oversimplified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Builds survival from historically grounded changes in military, fiscal, succession, frontier, and administrative systems, with mostly plausible tradeoffs.
criteria.9-10: Defines a precise, well-justified survival pathway that addresses Western and Eastern Roman vulnerabilities, barbarian integration, internal legitimacy, economy, and frontier defense without making Roman success automatic.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence from antiquity to 2020
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer sustains a coherent sequence of cause and effect across major eras instead of jumping from ancient Rome to a modern superstate without intermediate mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Skips most historical development or presents disconnected claims about the modern world.
criteria.3-4: Includes some chronological stages but relies on large unexplained leaps, anachronisms, or unmotivated outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several eras with a recognizable causal chain, though some transitions are thin or overly deterministic.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a mostly coherent timeline through late antiquity, medieval, early modern, industrial, and modern periods, showing how earlier changes constrain later outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust, era-by-era causal chain where demographic, military, institutional, religious, technological, and geopolitical developments interact plausibly over fifteen centuries.

criteria.name: Coverage of major downstream historical effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores the main consequences of a surviving Roman Empire for Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, religion, language, colonialism, industrialization, and global power by 2020.
criteria.1-2: Mentions only one or two superficial effects, such as everyone speaking Latin or Rome being powerful.
criteria.3-4: Covers a few downstream effects but omits several central domains such as Christianity, Islam, medieval Europe, colonialism, or modern geopolitics.
criteria.5-6: Addresses multiple major domains, though some are brief, generic, or not clearly tied to Roman survival.
criteria.7-8: Substantively covers most major domains, including religion, languages, state formation, warfare, trade, colonization, technology, and modern international order.
criteria.9-10: Explores a broad and balanced set of downstream effects, including second-order consequences for Islam, the papacy, Slavic/Germanic states, European colonial powers, nationalism, world wars, decolonization, and the 2020 balance of power.

criteria.name: Plausibility of institutional, economic, technological, and social evolution
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explains how a Roman state could adapt its institutions, economy, technology, and society over time rather than remaining a static ancient empire.
criteria.1-2: Depicts Rome as essentially unchanged for 1,500 years or assumes implausible technological/social outcomes without explanation.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges some adaptation but treats Roman institutions, slavery, citizenship, urban life, or technology in a simplistic or anachronistic way.
criteria.5-6: Gives reasonable mechanisms for some changes, such as bureaucracy, military reform, language shifts, trade, sanitation, or industrialization, but leaves key tensions unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Shows credible institutional and social adaptation, including changing imperial authority, military recruitment, taxation, religion, urban systems, labor, and economic modernization.
criteria.9-10: Presents a nuanced model of Roman transformation into a modern state, explaining constitutional change, identity formation, labor systems, technological diffusion, industrialization, public health, and economic integration with historically plausible constraints.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, contradiction control, and avoidance of overdetermined history
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the speculative nature of the scenario responsibly, avoids internal contradictions, and does not simply replay real-world history unchanged despite a radically altered Roman survival.
criteria.1-2: States outcomes with unjustified certainty, contains major contradictions, or copies real history wholesale despite the changed premise.
criteria.3-4: Shows occasional caution but includes many deterministic claims, inconsistent borders/events, or real-world events that occur without plausible causes.
criteria.5-6: Generally coherent and acknowledges uncertainty, though some events are too conveniently preserved or contradicted by earlier assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, flags alternative possibilities, and keeps most claims internally consistent with the altered Roman geopolitical landscape.
criteria.9-10: Consistently distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradiction; explains why familiar events would change or persist; and treats long-range history as contingent rather than inevitable.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire had never fallen and survived to 2020, the modern world would probably be far more politically unified around the Mediterranean and much of Europe, North Africa, and the Near East, but also much more shaped by continuity than by the fragmentation that created medieval and modern Europe. The biggest change is that “Rome” would not just be an ancient influence; it would be the central state tradition of the Western world, perhaps of a large part of Afro-Eurasia.

The first major consequence would be the absence, or at least severe weakening, of the medieval breakup that followed the collapse of the Western Empire. Historically, Rome’s fall opened the way for Germanic kingdoms, feudalism, the political independence of the papacy, and the emergence of separate nations like France, Spain, and eventually Germany and Italy. If Rome remained intact, these identities might still develop as regional cultures, but not necessarily as fully sovereign nation-states. Europe could look more like a vast imperial federation: provinces with local languages and customs, but under one imperial legal and administrative system.

Language would likely be transformed. Latin would almost certainly remain the prestige language of government, law, education, and perhaps science, much as English functions globally today. Over time, spoken Latin would still evolve, so regional dialects might emerge into something like modern Romance languages. But because of constant state administration, roads, military service, education, and media, those dialects might stay much closer together. In some areas, especially if Rome remained strong enough to integrate local elites, Latin could spread even further into regions where Germanic or Slavic languages later dominated. English as we know it might never exist, or would be a provincial hybrid at the edge of the empire’s influence.

Religion would also be very different. Christianity would still likely become central, since the empire had already been Christianizing before the Western collapse, but the relationship between church and state would be transformed. In our history, the weakening of imperial authority let the Roman Church become an independent power and eventually helped produce a split between Catholic and Orthodox worlds. In a continuous empire, that split might be reduced, delayed, or take another form. The emperor might remain the dominant authority over the church, as in Byzantine caesaropapism, producing a more centralized imperial Christianity. The Protestant Reformation might never happen, or would appear less as a revolt of separate princes and more as an internal constitutional crisis of the empire.

Economically, a surviving Rome could create a long-lasting common market across three continents. Stable roads, ports, coinage, and law would encourage trade on a massive scale. The empire might industrialize earlier if internal peace and accumulated administrative knowledge supported large-scale investment, or later if elite conservatism discouraged disruptive change. That is an important uncertainty: a long-lived empire could be remarkably adaptive, or it could become so bureaucratic and status-bound that innovation slowed. So by 2020, Rome could either be a technologically advanced superstate or a huge but uneven empire forced into modernization by internal pressures and foreign rivals.

The development of science and modern politics would depend heavily on whether Rome remained centralized in an authoritarian sense or evolved constitutional institutions. One reason modern Europe became so innovative was competition among many states. Rival kingdoms and republics financed voyages, armies, trade networks, and scientific development. If Rome monopolized power, that competition would be internal rather than international. That might reduce warfare between European powers but also lessen the pressure that drove rapid military and technological change. On the other hand, if the empire developed rival cities, senatorial blocs, commercial regions, and semi-autonomous provinces competing within a common system, it could preserve innovation without political disintegration.

Colonialism would likely be altered dramatically. A Roman Empire surviving into the age of oceanic navigation would probably become a major colonial power, perhaps the dominant one. If it controlled Iberia, Gaul, Italy, North Africa, and the eastern Mediterranean, it would have the manpower, ports, and wealth to explore the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. The Americas might be colonized under Roman banners or by imperial chartered provinces rather than by Spain, Portugal, England, and France. Much of the world might therefore know Roman law, Latin-derived languages, and imperial institutions even more widely than they know European ones today.

Modern nationalism would be weaker or at least delayed. In our timeline, people came to think of themselves as French, Spanish, Greek, or Serbian citizens partly through the breakup of empires and the rise of popular sovereignty. In a world where Rome never fell, identity might be layered: one could be African, Iberian, Gallic, Syrian, and Roman at once. The 19th century might bring reform movements demanding representation for provinces rather than independence from the empire. Rome in 2020 might resemble a hybrid of the European Union, the United States, and imperial China: ancient legitimacy, continental scale, legal universalism, and deep regional diversity.

Its capital might not even be Rome itself. A durable empire may have shifted its administrative center over time to places like Constantinople, Ravenna, Milan, Carthage, or a dual-capital arrangement. By 2020, “Roman Empire” might refer less to a city-centered monarchy and more to a civilizational state with a parliament, emperor, constitution, and vast bureaucracy. The emperor could be a symbolic figure like a constitutional monarch, or still an executive ruler if imperial reforms never democratized fully.

Globally, such an empire would be one of the dominant powers on Earth, perhaps rivaling China, India, or a separate American superpower if the Americas eventually formed independent post-colonial states. International law might be more heavily influenced by Roman legal concepts than it already is. Ideas like citizenship, sovereignty, civil rights, and imperial membership would likely descend more directly from Roman institutions rather than from the nation-state system created after Westphalia.

So by 2020, a never-fallen Roman Empire would most likely produce a world that is less nationally fragmented, more legally and linguistically Romanized, and more politically centered on a long-lasting imperial system. Whether that world would be freer, richer, or more peaceful is less clear. It could be a stable multicultural superstate with deep infrastructure and shared citizenship, or a massive, hierarchical empire whose very longevity suppressed the pluralism that helped create modern democracy and scientific dynamism. The most plausible outcome is not “ancient Rome with smartphones,” but a profoundly transformed modern civilization in which Rome remained the main vessel of state continuity from antiquity to the present.

edus.text: If the Roman Empire had never fallen and survived to 2020, the modern world would probably be far more politically unified around the Mediterranean and much of Europe, North Africa, and the Near East, but also much more shaped by continuity than by the fragmentation that created medieval and modern Europe.
The biggest change is that “Rome” would not just be an ancient influence;
it would be the central state tradition of the Western world, perhaps of a large part of Afro-Eurasia.
The first major consequence would be the absence, or at least severe weakening, of the medieval breakup that followed the collapse of the Western Empire.

Historically, Rome’s fall opened the way for Germanic kingdoms, feudalism, the political independence of the papacy, and the emergence of separate nations like France, Spain, and eventually Germany and Italy.
If Rome remained intact, these identities might still develop as regional cultures, but not necessarily as fully sovereign nation-states.
Europe could look more like a vast imperial federation: provinces with local languages and customs, but under one imperial legal and administrative system.
Language would likely be transformed.
Latin would almost certainly remain the prestige language of government, law, education, and perhaps science, much as English functions globally today.
Over time, spoken Latin would still evolve, so regional dialects might emerge into something like modern Romance languages.
But because of constant state administration, roads, military service, education, and media, those dialects might stay much closer together.
In some areas, Latin could spread even further into regions where Germanic or Slavic languages later dominated.
English as we know it might never exist, or would be a provincial hybrid at the edge of the empire’s influence.
Religion would also be very different.
Christianity would still likely become central, since the empire had already been Christianizing before the Western collapse,
but the relationship between church and state would be transformed.
In our history, the weakening of imperial authority let the Roman Church become an independent power and eventually helped produce a split between Catholic and Orthodox worlds.
In a continuous empire, that split might be reduced, delayed, or take another form.
The emperor might remain the dominant authority over the church, producing a more centralized imperial Christianity.
The Protestant Reformation might never happen, or would appear less as a revolt of separate princes and more as an internal constitutional crisis of the empire.
Economically, a surviving Rome could create a long-lasting common market across three continents.
Stable roads, ports, coinage, and law would encourage trade on a massive scale.
The empire might industrialize earlier if internal peace and accumulated administrative knowledge supported large-scale investment, or later if elite conservatism discouraged disruptive change.
That is an important uncertainty: a long-lived empire could be remarkably adaptive, or it could become so bureaucratic and status-bound that innovation slowed.
So by 2020, Rome could either be a technologically advanced superstate or a huge but uneven empire forced into modernization by internal pressures and foreign rivals.
The development of science and modern politics would depend heavily on whether Rome remained centralized in an authoritarian sense or evolved constitutional institutions.
One reason modern Europe became so innovative was competition among many states.
Rival kingdoms and republics financed voyages, armies, trade networks, and scientific development.
If Rome monopolized power, that competition would be internal rather than international.
That might reduce warfare between European powers but also lessen the pressure that drove rapid military and technological change.
On the other hand, if the empire developed rival cities and semi-autonomous provinces competing within a common system, it could preserve innovation without political disintegration.
Colonialism would likely be altered dramatically.
A Roman Empire surviving into the age of oceanic navigation would probably become a major colonial power.
If it controlled key Mediterranean regions, it would have the manpower, ports, and wealth to explore the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
The Americas might be colonized under Roman banners rather than by Spain, Portugal, England, and France.
Much of the world might therefore know Roman law, Latin-derived languages, and imperial institutions even more widely than today.
Modern nationalism would be weaker or at least delayed.
In our timeline, people came to think of themselves as national citizens partly through the breakup of empires and the rise of popular sovereignty.
In a world where Rome never fell, identity might be layered.
The 19th century might bring reform movements demanding representation rather than independence.
Rome in 2020 might resemble a hybrid of the European Union, the United States, and imperial China.
Its capital might not even be Rome itself.
A durable empire may have shifted its administrative center over time.
By 2020, “Roman Empire” might refer to a civilizational state with a parliament, emperor, constitution, and vast bureaucracy.
The emperor could be symbolic or still an executive ruler.
Globally, such an empire would be one of the dominant powers on Earth.
International law might be more heavily influenced by Roman legal concepts.
Ideas like citizenship and sovereignty would likely descend more directly from Roman institutions.
So by 2020, a never-fallen Roman Empire would most likely produce a world that is less nationally fragmented, more Romanized, and more politically centered on a long-lasting imperial system.
Whether that world would be freer, richer, or more peaceful is less clear.
It could be a stable multicultural superstate with shared citizenship,
or a massive, hierarchical empire whose longevity suppressed pluralism.
The most plausible outcome is not “ancient Rome with smartphones,”
but a profoundly transformed modern civilization in which Rome remained the main vessel of state continuity from antiquity to the present.

items.question: What If the Roman Empire never fell? How would this change most of our history today?
human_answers: The problem with the previous answer is that it is ahistorical. The Roman Empire did not fall until 1453, when the Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople. Emperor Constantine had moved the capitol to the Greek city of Byzantium because of its excellent geographic, strategic, and central location, calling it New Rome, although at that point the empire was then split between eastern and western halves until the west collapsed in the fifth century. Subsequently renamed Constantinople, it then became the center of the world and continued long after the city of Rome itself declined sharply as the locus of empire shifted. Attempts, sometimes successful, were made to reclaim parts of the west. Indeed the name of the city itself continued until the cataclysm of World War I. In addition, Justinian was the last Emperor to use Latin rather than Greek, which prevailed for another eight centuries, or far longer than Rome itself. There was never a “Byzantine Empire.” That was a far later German concoction in order to legitimate their own “Holy Roman Empire, which, as Voltaire once said, was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire, What actually existed, as I have suggested elsewhere, was not something “Byzantine,” but rather a Greco-Roman Empire that lasted for a millennium. This is still confused and not well known due to the ignorance and prejudice of northwestern Europeans towards the south. Thus, the Roman Empire did not fall or disappear the way you have been led to believe. In fact, if the empire began with Augustus, the Rome-based portion only lasted for a bit more than four centuries, while the Eastern Roman Empire continued for another thousand years, and all the people in the empire, including the Greeks, referred to and considered themselves Romans until the very end. The empire itself was polyglot as it always was, but the dominant language was Greek. Thus, while the “Middle Ages” or medieval period happened in the west, which was still backward, that was not the case in the east, in what in fact was the bulk of the empire, which continued a thriving, but heavily Christianized civilization. Thus, in the year 1000 Constantinople had a population of over a million people. The original Roman Empire was far better at practical things, particularly organization, administration, functional engineering, etc. than the quarrelsome Greeks, who otherwise brilliantly developed and dominated culture, art, science, philosophy, etc. Romans provided the critical stability, legal and social infrastructure that was previously lacking in an otherwise largely Greek world that had been established by Alexander and his successors. As a result, Roman law, justice and organization provided the framework which sustained an otherwise largely Greek cultural entity. The empire would not have fallen had it not been for the Fourth Crusade (1202–1204) which, instead of going to Jerusalem to fight Muslims attacked other Christians via Venetian ships and encouragement. The barbarian Knights/Crusaders literally destroyed the city of Constantinople, pillaging and worse, burning down much of the city while the Venetians, at least having some artistic sense, carted off a lot of treasures that you still see in St. Marks to this day. The crusaders took over what was left of the city setting up their own “empire” for a few decades until the Romans finally reclaimed it, but in a much-weakened state. Thus, by the time the Turks finally conquered the city in 1453 with new long-range cannons, there were only about 50,000 people left there. That is when the Roman Empire finally fell, in its Greco-Roman-Christian incarnation. Given true history then, if the empire hadn’t fallen it is quite possible that Greek would still be the common language, you might be speaking it, and the European world would be very different. The “old” nations of Europe after all, have only existed for around five centuries. They really ascended after the fall of the City and the “renaissance” that followed, (another retroactively coined term), instilled to a considerable extent by Greek refugee scholars who fled to the Italian city-states, which welcomed then as teachers, given their thirst for knowledge and ancient manuscripts. Many other things would be different, starting with religion. In the empire the church was subordinate to the Emperor, and less powerful than in the west, where given the power vacuum, the Bishop of Rome, or Pope, was able to claim supremacy. Consequently, if the empire had continued the church would not have had so much power, and it is likely there would never have been a Protestant Reformation. Regions would have had their own Patriarchs. There is no way to know how geography would have taken shape, given uncertainty as to how far the empire might have reached, or how competent it would have been, but at its maximum it could have stretched over all of Europe. Alternatively, it could have been smaller, as it continued to fend of endless barbarian invasions from the east, allowing other powers to emerge in the west anyway, but possibly without the virulent nationalism that eventually developed and led to catastrophic wars and mass murder in the last century. Much would depend on whether the empire could regain Italy, which was essential to the emergence of modern Europe. (In 1500 Italy was richer than all of western Europe combined and more culturally advanced). Since it was then divided into competing city-states in the fashion of ancient Greece, that might have transpired if the empire was relatively free from barbarian invasions. Slavs, at least in the south were already being absorbed before the fall of the empire and thus would likely still be integrated. Unknowns are how the Russians, or more importantly the Germans might have emerged. But generally, the empire had always done a great job of absorbing and integrating other peoples, until the rise of Islam. If the empire had remained strong it is unlikely that the Arabs would have conquered what was then European Christian north Africa and Egypt, or even much of what is now called the “middle east,” which would have remained Christian and Roman, linked to the west via Constantinople. The empire took the brunt of Muslim invasion, thus protecting the west for centuries, and if not for the Fourth Crusade could have grown stronger and more powerful and Europe would not have been threatened or invaded. In addition, Persian culture might still exist, possibly as yet another empire. Greek rationalism did not disappear as the church in the east largely reconciled itself with it and focused on spiritual matters. Consequently, the church would not have been able to significantly thwart scientific progress. Europe, including a good portion of the east would still dominate the world. and remain centered in Constantinople. They would likely still have found the Americas, but development might have been different, possibly without African slavery, among other things. The culture would be more advanced and sophisticated, but economic growth might not be as robust, given a different emphasis and outlook, and without a “Protestant ethic” but rather a sort of merchant mentality. Higher education might not have been found in universities as we know them, but rather closer to the academic format of the ancient world, more focused on the development of the mind and learning. Ultimately we cannot know because of vicissitudes of one-man rule. There can be a great ruler and then a terrible ruler. You can have a Marcus Aurelius or a Caligula. So given different personalities there is no way to know, and that can be precarious and lead to instability or conflict until someone else consolidates power. What we can learn clearly from history is the less power we surrender to others over us the better off we are. Finally, the Fourth Crusade was clearly the worst disaster in western history even beyond World War I if only because the latter might never have happened if the empire hadn’t fallen. Such a general and vague question can lead to endless possibilities and alternatives, but in the end all that is left is what actually happened.

items.model_answer:
If the Roman Empire never “fell,” most of history would change not because everything would become permanently Roman in a simple way, but because the political fragmentation of Europe would be much weaker. The biggest consequence would be that a single imperial system would continue to shape law, language, religion, trade, and identity across much of Europe and the Mediterranean. That would affect almost everything that came later: the rise of nation-states, the power of the Church, colonial expansion, scientific development, and even the modern idea of citizenship.

The first major change would be political. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Europe split into many kingdoms, and that fragmentation helped create medieval feudalism. If Rome remained intact, Europe might have stayed under a large bureaucratic state with professional administration, taxation, roads, and standing armies. Local lords would likely be weaker, and the medieval castle-based, feudal order might never dominate in the same way. Instead of France, Spain, and perhaps even parts of Germany and Italy emerging as separate sovereign powers so early, they might remain provinces or semi-autonomous regions inside a larger imperial framework. Modern nationalism could be delayed by centuries or take a very different form.

The second major change would be cultural and linguistic. Latin would almost certainly remain far more dominant as a spoken and administrative language across the West, and the divergence into separate Romance languages might be slower or less extreme. A unified Roman educational system could preserve classical literacy much more broadly. That would mean fewer sharp breaks between “ancient” and “medieval” learning. The Renaissance, which in our history involved rediscovering parts of classical culture, might not happen in the same way because much of that culture would never have been so deeply lost in the West.

Religion would also develop differently. In actual history, the collapse of imperial authority in the West helped the Christian Church become a major independent source of order and legitimacy. If the Empire stayed strong, the Church might remain more tightly controlled by imperial institutions, more like the Byzantine pattern in the East. The Pope might never gain the same independent political power that he did in medieval Europe. That would likely reshape the entire history of Catholicism, the Holy Roman Empire, the Investiture Controversy, and even the Protestant Reformation. If there were no strong divide between secular rulers and an autonomous Western Church, the conditions that produced Reformation-era conflicts might be much weaker or simply different.

Economically, a surviving empire could preserve large-scale Mediterranean trade networks and urban life more successfully. Instead of the economic contraction that followed the Western collapse, cities, roads, ports, and long-distance commerce might continue with less interruption. Europe could become richer earlier, with stronger markets and more centralized public works. On the other hand, a powerful empire might also suppress local experimentation and competition. In real history, Europe’s political fragmentation sometimes encouraged innovation because rival states competed militarily, commercially, and technologically. A long-lasting Roman superstate might bring greater stability but less competitive dynamism.

That leads to science and technology. A continuous Roman order might preserve engineering and administrative knowledge better, but it is not certain that this would produce an earlier industrial revolution. Rome was highly organized, but it was also conservative and heavily dependent on hierarchy and coerced labor. If slavery remained deeply embedded and the imperial elite had little incentive to mechanize work, technological change might actually slow in some areas. So a surviving Roman Empire might produce a world that is more orderly and urban earlier, but not necessarily more modern in the industrial sense. It could be advanced in roads, law, architecture, and administration while lagging in the kind of disruptive innovation that came later in early modern Europe.

The global balance of power would also be transformed. A united Roman Mediterranean would be a much stronger rival to powers in Persia, the Islamic world, and later the Ottoman Turks. The rise of Islam in the seventh century would still matter enormously, but its expansion into former Roman territories might face a more coordinated opponent. If Rome held North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean more successfully, then the religious and cultural map of the Middle East, North Africa, and southern Europe could look very different. That would in turn affect trade with Asia, the Crusades, and the transmission of mathematics, medicine, and philosophy.

Colonialism might emerge differently too. In our history, Atlantic empires were built by competing kingdoms such as Spain, Portugal, England, and France. If those regions remained integrated into one imperial system, overseas expansion might either happen earlier through coordinated state power or later if the empire remained focused on the Mediterranean. If colonization did happen under a Roman framework, the Americas could be shaped not by several European languages and rival empires but by one dominant imperial culture, likely Latin-derived in law and administration. The modern map of the world could be far less national and far more provincial-imperial.

The modern state itself would look different. Many ideas we take for granted—sovereign nations, national armies, national languages, and national histories—grew out of post-Roman Europe. If Rome endured, people might identify more with empire than with nation. “European civilization” might be less a collection of separate peoples and more the continuation of a single imperial commonwealth. Modern legal systems would probably be even more deeply Roman than they already are. Citizenship might develop earlier as a broader imperial status, but democracy might develop later if imperial hierarchy remained strong.

So the biggest overall change is this: instead of a Europe shaped by fragmentation, feudalism, competing kingdoms, and later nation-states, much of the West might develop under a continuous imperial order. That would probably make the world more unified in language, law, and administration, but less politically diverse. Some things we associate with “modernity” might arrive sooner—urban continuity, legal rationality, infrastructure—while others, especially nationalism, parliamentary government, and perhaps industrial capitalism, might arrive later or in a very different form. In short, if Rome never fell, today’s world might be less national, less linguistically divided, more legally standardized, and more Mediterranean-centered—but not necessarily freer, more innovative, or more democratic.
