items.question: What If You Detonated a Nuclear Bomb at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: Surprisingly little—especially compared to what would happen if you put it just under the surface. Evin isn’t the first person to think of setting off nuclear weapons underwater. In fact, we’ve actually tried it a bunch of times. This (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ggH-ObiUWEE) is what it looks like. Most of the tests, however, involved either small bombs or shallow water. Evin’s scenario concerns neither. At 53 megatons, the Tsar Bomba was the most powerful nuclear weapon ever detonated, and at 11 kilometers, the Mariana(s) Trench is the deepest part of the ocean. No underwater test has involved bombs anywhere near that size, nor depths anywhere near that deep. In 1962, physicist Freeman Dyson wrote a memo discussing eight possible novel weapon systems, all of which looked like they’d be possible in the near future, and outlined the potential military uses and dangers of each. This memo has been declassified, but was never published. Freeman’s son, science historian George Dyson, got a paper copy of the memo from his father, and was kind enough to show it to me. In the memo, one of the eight ideas Freeman discusses is the use of gigaton nuclear weapons as wave generators. It includes this rather terrifying passage describing the detonation of a submerged gigaton mine off the North American coast: “Quantitative study of the destructive effects has not been made. Rough estimates indicate that the inundation would reach to a height of 200-300 feet above sea level, or a distance of 200-300 miles inland, whichever limit is reached first.” [Image: image] Luckily for the coast, later research paints a less dire picture. The seminal work in the field of nuclear ocean waves is Water Waves Generated By Underwater Explosions (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?Location=U2&doc=GetTRDoc.pdf&AD=ADA304244), a sprawling 400-page report produced for the Department of Defense by Bernard Le Mehaute and Shen Wang. The report, published in 1996, exhaustively examines and summarizes all available research about the ocean waves created by nuclear explosions. The report outlines how when a nuclear weapon goes off underwater, it produces a cavity of hot gasses, which then collapses. If the explosion happens near the surface, it can create some pretty big waves—under some circumstances, they can be hundreds of feet high near ground zero. [Image: image] Or is it ocean zero? Fortunately for the coast, these waves are fundamentally different from tsunamis. It turns out that if the waves are very large, they break early, and expend most of their energy creating a narrow surf zone on the continental shelf. This is potentially hazardous to some ships, but much less catastrophic than a direct nuclear attack. When they reached the coast, the waves would be no worse than those from a bad storm. But those are waves from an explosion close to the surface. A nuke set off deep underwater acts a bit differently. The explosion at the bottom of the Mariana Trench will create a quickly-expanding spherical cavity of hot steam. To figure out how big it gets, we can try a formula from the 1971 paper Evaluation of Various Theoretical Models For Underwater Explosion (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/737271.pdf): \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right )^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx580\text{ meters}\] The bubble grows to about a kilometer across in a couple of seconds. The water above bulges up, though only slightly, over a large area. Then the pressure from that six miles of water overhead causes it to collapse. Within a dozen or so seconds, the bubble shrinks to a minimum size, then ‘bounces’ back, expanding outward again. It goes through three or four cycles of this collapse and expansion before disintegrating into, in the words of the 1996 report, “a mass of turbulent warm water and explosion debris.” According to the report, as a result of such a deep-water closed bubble creation and dissipation, “no wave of any consequence will be generated.” That “turbulent warm water” is actually quite substantial. The rising column of heat creates a hot spot in the ocean—many degrees warmer than the surrounding water—that lingers for some time. [Image: image] Earlier this year, Severe Tropical Storm Sanvu passed over the Mariana Trench. The column of deep, hot water from our nuke could conceivably have been enough to strengthen it into a typhoon, much as the deep warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico’s Loop Current sometimes cause hurricanes to rapidly intensify. In addition to the heat energy from the water, Sanvu could whip up a spray containing fallout from the blast, and approach Iwo Jima as a radioactive whirlwind. Of course, that’s getting a little far-fetched. In the absence of an improbable typhoon interaction, the overall effect of the bomb isn’t quite as dramatic as Evin might have imagined. ... But. All that changes when this cat enters the equation: [Image: image] Literally. Let’s say that when I’m typing the above equation, the cat hops onto my desk and steps on the “0” key, which inserts six extra zeroes: \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right) ^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53000000\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx35\text{ miles}\] If there was enough water, and if the model held up, this blast would expand into a bubble 70 miles across. In reality, the oceans aren’t that deep. Instead, it blows a hole in the Earth’s crust dozens of miles across, leaving a hole through which briefly glows the magma of the mantle. Around the early 1990s, scientists started discovering jumbled fields of petrified wood mixed with sand buried beneath the Louisiana and Texas coast. These turned out to be the remains of North American forests swept out to sea by a massive tsunami. The culprit was a comet or asteroid hitting the Yucatan—the impact that killed most of the dinosaurs. The debris played a key role in identifying the 65-million-year-old Chicxulub impact site—this book (http://www.amazon.com/Crater-Doom-Princeton-Science-Library/dp/0691131031) provides a wonderful account of the unraveling of that mystery. 53,000,000 megatons is approximately the energy of the Chicxulub impact. A blast this size in the Mariana Trench creates kilometer-high waves that engulf the forests of Indonesia, California, and the Pacific Northwest, along with most of coastal China and the rest of the Pacific rim. Huge volumes of rock and water are blasted into space. The debris takes less than an hour to encircle the Earth. As the chunks of rock fall back into the atmosphere, they heat to a glow—like meteors—igniting global firestorms. The hole fills in, with huge columns of steam and great convulsions. The Mariana Trench is gone, and with it Guam and the Mariana Islands. The area is now marked by a 100-kilometer-wide scar of magma sizzling beneath the waters of the Pacific. The majority of the world’s plants die and the food chain collapses completely. Between the famine and the fires, most life on Earth is wiped out. Stupid cat. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a nuclear bomb were detonated at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the result would be dramatic locally but not apocalyptic globally.

The bottom of the trench is about 11 kilometers underwater, where the pressure is enormous, around 1,100 times atmospheric pressure. A nuclear weapon would still detonate; that pressure would not “crush” the bomb before it went off if it were properly designed to survive the descent. The explosion would create an intensely hot plasma bubble and a powerful shock wave in the surrounding water. Because water is dense and nearly incompressible compared with air, the blast would couple very efficiently into the ocean, producing a very strong local shock.

However, the water pressure at that depth would also strongly confine the explosion bubble. The fireball would be much smaller than in air, and the bubble would expand and collapse rapidly. A lot of the weapon’s energy would go into vaporizing water, generating shock waves, and heating the surrounding ocean, rather than producing the huge atmospheric blast effects people usually imagine from nuclear explosions.

If the bomb were large enough, it could excavate sediment, trigger underwater landslides, and damage or destroy anything nearby. Marine life in the immediate area would be killed. There would also be radioactive contamination of local water and sediments, especially if the weapon touched the seafloor and sucked up trench material into the explosion products. But the trench contains an enormous volume of water, so the heat would dissipate relatively quickly on a global scale, and the contamination would be diluted over time, though it could persist in sediments and food webs regionally.

It would not boil the ocean. It would not crack Earth’s crust. It would not set off the mantle or trigger planet-scale geologic catastrophe. Even the largest nuclear weapons are tiny compared with the energies involved in tectonic processes.

Could it cause a tsunami? Probably not a major ocean-wide one from the explosion alone. Nuclear explosions are very energetic, but tsunamis require moving an enormous mass of water over a large area, usually by displacing the seafloor in an earthquake or landslide. The direct blast bubble from a bomb, even a very large one, is too localized to create the sort of broad displacement needed for a giant tsunami. A secondary underwater landslide might generate a more meaningful local or regional wave, but still not likely a civilization-ending event.

At the surface, you might see a disturbed patch of ocean, perhaps bubbling, uplift, or wave activity depending on yield, but because the detonation is so deep, much of the energy would be absorbed before reaching the atmosphere. There would be no giant mushroom cloud rising straight from the trench in the familiar above-ground sense. If the weapon were extremely large, some effects might eventually reach the surface, but they would be far less visually spectacular than an atmospheric blast of the same yield.

So the short answer is: a nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench would produce a violent but mostly localized underwater explosion, kill nearby organisms, contaminate the local environment, and possibly trigger local seafloor disturbance, but it would not cause a global disaster.

edus.text: If a nuclear bomb were detonated at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, the result would be dramatic locally but not apocalyptic globally.
The bottom of the trench is about 11 kilometers underwater, where the pressure is enormous, around 1,100 times atmospheric pressure.
A nuclear weapon would still detonate.
That pressure would not “crush” the bomb before it went off if it were properly designed to survive the descent.
The explosion would create an intensely hot plasma bubble and a powerful shock wave in the surrounding water.
Because water is dense and nearly incompressible compared with air, the blast would couple very efficiently into the ocean, producing a very strong local shock.
However, the water pressure at that depth would also strongly confine the explosion bubble.
The fireball would be much smaller than in air, and the bubble would expand and collapse rapidly.

A lot of the weapon’s energy would go into vaporizing water, generating shock waves, and heating the surrounding ocean, rather than producing the huge atmospheric blast effects people usually imagine from nuclear explosions.
If the bomb were large enough, it could excavate sediment, trigger underwater landslides, and damage or destroy anything nearby.
Marine life in the immediate area would be killed.
There would also be radioactive contamination of local water and sediments, especially if the weapon touched the seafloor and sucked up trench material into the explosion products.

But the trench contains an enormous volume of water, so the heat would dissipate relatively quickly on a global scale, and the contamination would be diluted over time, though it could persist in sediments and food webs regionally.
It would not boil the ocean.
It would not crack Earth’s crust.
It would not set off the mantle or trigger planet-scale geologic catastrophe.
Even the largest nuclear weapons are tiny compared with the energies involved in tectonic processes.
Could it cause a tsunami?
Probably not a major ocean-wide one from the explosion alone.
Nuclear explosions are very energetic, but tsunamis require moving an enormous mass of water over a large area, usually by displacing the seafloor in an earthquake or landslide.
The direct blast bubble from a bomb, even a very large one, is too localized to create the sort of broad displacement needed for a giant tsunami.
A secondary underwater landslide might generate a more meaningful local or regional wave, but still not likely a civilization-ending event.
At the surface, you might see a disturbed patch of ocean, perhaps bubbling, uplift, or wave activity depending on yield.
But because the detonation is so deep, much of the energy would be absorbed before reaching the atmosphere.
There would be no giant mushroom cloud rising straight from the trench in the familiar above-ground sense.
If the weapon were extremely large, some effects might eventually reach the surface, but they would be far less visually spectacular than an atmospheric blast of the same yield.

So the short answer is: a nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench would produce a violent but mostly localized underwater explosion, kill nearby organisms, contaminate the local environment, and possibly trigger local seafloor disturbance, but it would not cause a global disaster.

items.question: What If You Stayed in a Swimming Pool During a Thunderstorm?
human_answers: Before we go any further, I want to emphasize something: I am not an authority on lightning safety. I am a guy who draws pictures on the internet. I like when things catch fire and explode, which means I do not have your best interests in mind. The authorities on lightning safety are the folks at the US National Weather Service: http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/ (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/) (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/) Ok. With that out of the way ... To answer these questions, we need to get an idea of where lightning is likely to go. There’s a cool trick for this, and I’ll give it away right here at the start: Roll an imaginary 60-meter sphere across the landscape and look at where it touches. They say lightning strikes the tallest thing around. That’s the kind of maddeningly inexact statement that immediately sparks all kinds of questions. How far is “around”? I mean, not all lightning hits Mt. Everest. But does it find the tallest person in a crowd? The tallest person I know is probably Ryan North (paleontologists estimate he stood nearly five meters tall at the shoulder). Should I try to hang around him for lightning safety reasons? What about other reasons? (This is probably why you people ask the questions on this blog, not me.) But how does lightning pick its targets? This video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1mB5rM8WHU), captured by Tom A. Warner, might be the single coolest piece of footage I’ve ever seen. It shows a bolt of lightning recorded at 7,207 frames per second. The 33-second video represents barely a tenth of a second of real time. There are lots of slow-motion videos of lightning, but this is by far the best I’ve found. Tom’s video gives an idea of how lightning moves. It starts with a branching bundle of charge—the “leader”—descending from the cloud. This is what you see in the first part of the video. It spreads downward at speeds of tens to hundreds of kilometers per second, covering the few kilometers to the ground in a few dozen milliseconds. The leader carries comparatively little current—on the order of 200 amps. That’s still enough to kill you, but it’s nothing compared to what happens next. Once the leader makes contact with the ground, the cloud and the ground equalize with a massive discharge of more like 20,000 amps. This is the blinding flash you see. It races back up the channel at a significant fraction of the speed of light, covering the distance in under a millisecond—all within a single frame of that video. (Technical detail: while it’s called a “return stroke”, charge is still flowing downward. However, the discharge appears to propagate upward. This effect similar to how when a traffic light turns green, or whatever (http://xkcd.com/1116/) color, the cars in front start moving, then the cars in back, so the movement appears to spread backward.) So the place on the ground where we see a bolt “strike” is the spot where the leader first makes contact with the surface. The leader moves down through the air in little jumps. It’s ultimately feeling its way toward the (usually) positive charge in the ground. However, it only “feels” charges within a few tens of meters of the tip. If there’s something connected to the ground within that distance, the bolt will jump to it. Otherwise, it jumps out in a semi-random direction and repeats the process. [Image: image] This is where the 60-meter sphere comes in. It’s a way to imagine what spots might be the first thing the leader senses—the places it might jump to in its next (final) step. To figure out where lightning is likely to hit, you roll the imaginary 60-meter sphere across the landscape (for safety reasons, do not use a real sphere). This sphere climbs up over trees and buildings without passing through anything (or rolling it up). Places the surface makes contact—treetops, fenceposts, and golfers in fields—are potential lightning targets. This means you can calculate a lightning “shadow” around an object of height h on a flat surface. [Image: image] The shadow is the area where the leader is likely to hit the tall object instead of the ground around it: \[\text{Shadow Radius}=\sqrt{-h(h-2r)}\] Now, that doesn’t mean you’re safe on the ground around it—often, it means the opposite. After the current hits the tall object, it flows out into the ground. If you’re touching the ground nearby, it can travel through your body. Of the 28 people killed by lightning so far this year, 13 were standing under or near trees (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/fatalities.htm). With all this in mind, let’s look at possible lightning paths for the scenarios in the questions. How dangerous is it, really, to be in a pool during a thunderstorm? Pretty dangerous. Water is conductive, but that’s not the biggest problem—the biggest problem is that if you’re swimming, your head is poking up from a large flat surface. But lightning striking the water near you would still be bad. The 20,000 amps spread outward—mostly over the surface (http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/earth/dwyer-lightning.html)—but how much of a jolt it will give you at what distance is hard to calculate My guess is that you’d be in significant danger anywhere within a minimum of a dozen meters—and further in fresh water, because the current will be happier to take a shortcut through you. What would happen if you were taking a shower when you were struck by lightning? Or standing under a waterfall? [Image: image] You’re not in danger from the spray—it’s just a bunch of droplets of water in the air. It’s the tub under your feet, and the puddle of water in contact with the plumbing, that’s the real threat. What would happen if you were in a boat or a plane that got hit by lightning? Or a submarine? [Image: image] A boat without a cabin is about as safe as a golf course. A boat with a closed cabin and a lightning protection system is about as safe as a car. A submarine is about as safe as a submarine safe (a submarine safe is not to be confused with a safe in a submarine—a safe in a submarine is substantially safer than a submarine safe). What if you were changing the light at the top of a radio tower and lightning struck? Or what if you were doing a backflip? Or standing in a graphite field? Or looking straight up at the bolt? [Image: image] What would happen if lightning struck a bullet in midair? The bullet won't affect the path the lightning takes. You'd have somehow to time the shot so the bullet was in the middle of the bolt when the return stroke happened. The core of a lightning bolt is a few centimeters in diameter (http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/1968/JB073i006p01889.shtml). A bullet fired from an AK-47 is about 26 mm long and moves at about 700 millimeters every millisecond. The bullet has a copper coating over a lead core. Copper is a fantastically good conductor of electricity, and much of the 20,000 amps could easily take a shortcut through the bullet. [Image: image] Surprisingly, the bullet handles it pretty well. If it were sitting still, the current would quickly heat and melt the metal. But it’s moving along so quickly that it exits the channel before it can be warmed by more than a few degrees. It continues on to its target relatively unaffected. There are some curious electromagnetic forces created by the magnetic field around the bolt and the current flow through the bullet, but none of the ones I examined changed the overall picture very much. What if you were flashing your BIOS during a thunderstorm and you got hit by lightning? [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you stayed in a swimming pool during a thunderstorm, you could be seriously injured or killed.

Lightning does not need to hit you directly. If it strikes the pool, the water, nearby deck, metal ladder, plumbing, or electrical equipment, the electric current can spread through the water and surrounding area. Because your body is in contact with the water, you can be shocked, suffer cardiac arrest, burns, muscle damage, or drowning if you lose consciousness.

A common misconception is that “water attracts lightning.” The bigger issue is that pool water conducts electricity well enough for a lightning strike nearby to become dangerous. This is true for outdoor pools, especially those with metal components and connected pump systems. Indoor pools can also be risky if the building is struck and the electrical or plumbing systems carry current.

So the practical answer is: you should get out of the pool immediately at the first sound of thunder or sign of lightning, and stay out until at least 30 minutes after the last thunder.

items.question: What If Cows Could Photosynthesize?
human_answers: In a way, they already do. A field of grass sits there all day soaking up energy from the sun and storing it chemically. A grazing animal can then come along and absorb weeks of accumulated energy in a matter of minutes. [Image: image] A Jersey cow presents in the neighborhood of nearly two square meters of usable space to the sun if it stands right. (Cows would have to be trained to stand optimally, but we might not have too far to go; research suggests they already align themselves north-south (http://www.pnas.org/content/early/2008/08/22/0803650105). Chlorophyll photosynthesis extracts 3%-6% of the total energy from sunlight. If we figure on any given day the cow gets the equivalent of about six hours of peak sunlight, it works out to less than two million joules of usable energy each day. [Image: image] Is that a lot? Well, a 450-kilogram cow just wandering around in a field might eat about 10 kilograms of dry matter a day, extracting on the order of 50 million joules of metabolic energy. So photosynthesis could only make up about 4% of the required intake—saving only a few handfuls of grain. If we could equip cows with solar panels, which can be several times more energy-efficient than photosynthesis, we could improve that number—but not by much. [Image: image] The basic problem facing cows is the same one facing solar cars—they're too small. If you saw the world's cattle population in silhouette, they'd have an overall cross-sectional area of about two thousand square kilometers. This means that if they were migrating through the air over Rhode Island (biology is not my strong suit), they'd blot out the sun over barely half the state. They'd only catch enough sunlight to produce a daily average of about 40 gigawatts of power (two megayodas (http://what-if.xkcd.com/3/)). By contrast, about 3% of the world's surface area is cultivated, which means that (given rough estimates of geographic distribution of farmland) our crops easily intercept over a thousand times more sunlight than our cattle—which is why grazing is a good strategy. I'd like to conclude with this quote, which I found in the Cedara Agricultural Development Institute's Applied Ruminant Nutrition for Dairy Cows: Cows on a typical dairy ration can produce 80 to 100 litres of saliva per day. This has nothing to do with photosynthesis, but I wanted to share anyway. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If cows could photosynthesize, they would still not be able to live “like plants,” but it would change their biology, behavior, and ecology in major ways.

The first key point is energy. Photosynthesis is a relatively weak way to power a large animal. A cow is big, warm-blooded, and metabolically expensive to run. Even if its skin or fur contained chlorophyll-like structures, the surface area of a cow is far too small to capture enough sunlight to meet all of its energy needs. Roughly speaking, the sunlight falling on a cow’s body over a day would provide only a fraction of the chemical energy the cow gets from eating. So a photosynthetic cow would almost certainly still need to eat, but probably less than a normal cow.

That would mean cows might spend less time grazing and could survive better when food is scarce, as long as sunlight is available. They might evolve thinner coats, broader bodies, darker or greener skin, or even behavior that maximizes sun exposure, such as standing still in open fields for long periods. Calves and lactating cows would still need especially high energy, so photosynthesis would help but not replace feeding.

Their digestive system might shrink somewhat if they relied less on grass fermentation. If they ate less plant matter, they might also produce less methane, since methane in cows mostly comes from microbes breaking down cellulose in the rumen. That could reduce their climate impact. On the other hand, if photosynthesis required new tissues, pigments, or symbiotic microbes, cows might become more physiologically complex and vulnerable to different diseases.

Ecologically, photosynthetic cows would compete a bit less with other herbivores for food, and livestock farming might become more land-efficient in terms of feed production. But they would need access to sunlight, so dense housing or indoor feedlot systems would be less suitable. Their daily routines might look partly plant-like: more basking, less roaming.

At that point it would be much less cow-like.

So the most realistic outcome is not a cow that stops eating and lives on sunlight, but a hybrid organism that still grazes while getting a useful energy supplement from the sun. edus.text: If cows could photosynthesize, they would still not be able to live “like plants,”
but it would change their biology, behavior, and ecology in major ways.
The first key point is energy.
Photosynthesis is a relatively weak way to power a large animal.
A cow is big, warm-blooded, and metabolically expensive to run.
Even if its skin or fur contained chlorophyll-like structures, the surface area of a cow is far too small to capture enough sunlight to meet all of its energy needs.
Roughly speaking, the sunlight falling on a cow’s body over a day would provide only a fraction of the chemical energy the cow gets from eating.
So a photosynthetic cow would almost certainly still need to eat,
but probably less than a normal cow.
That would mean cows might spend less time grazing
and could survive better when food is scarce,
as long as sunlight is available.
They might evolve thinner coats, broader bodies, darker or greener skin, or even behavior that maximizes sun exposure,
such as standing still in open fields for long periods.
Calves and lactating cows would still need especially high energy,
so photosynthesis would help but not replace feeding.
Their digestive system might shrink somewhat
if they relied less on grass fermentation.
If they ate less plant matter, they might also produce less methane,
since methane in cows mostly comes from microbes breaking down cellulose in the rumen.
That could reduce their climate impact.
On the other hand, if photosynthesis required new tissues, pigments, or symbiotic microbes, cows might become more physiologically complex and vulnerable to different diseases.
Ecologically, photosynthetic cows would compete a bit less with other herbivores for food,
and livestock farming might become more land-efficient in terms of feed production.
But they would need access to sunlight,
so dense housing or indoor feedlot systems would be less suitable.
Their daily routines might look partly plant-like:
more basking, less roaming.
There would also be biological tradeoffs.
Plants can photosynthesize well partly because they are stationary, have huge leaf area, and tolerate slow energy income.
Cows are mobile mammals with high demands.
To make photosynthesis truly important, a cow might need dramatic redesign:
much larger surface area, reduced fur, slower metabolism, maybe even lower activity levels.
At that point it would be much less cow-like.
So the most realistic outcome is not a cow that stops eating and lives on sunlight,
but a hybrid organism that still grazes while getting a useful energy supplement from the sun.
It would eat less, emit less methane, behave differently, and probably look quite different,
but sunlight alone would not be enough to power an ordinary cow.

items.question: What If You Had to Stop a Runaway Freight Train with a BB Gun?
human_answers: First of all, for the record, shooting asteroids with lasers is a great (http://proceedings.aip.org/resource/2/apcpcs/664/1/509_1?bypassSSO=1) way to deflect them. Stopping a train with a BB gun might be harder. A Red Ryder spring-piston lever-action air rifle fires a standard 0.177-caliber 0.33g steel BB at a muzzle velocity of 100 meters per second. The GE Genesis Series I locomotive weighs 12 metric tons and travels at around 45 meters per second. If you bounce a single BB off the front of the locomotive from point blank range, you slow it down by about a foot per day. [Image: image] At one shot per second, it’d take over two days and nearly 200,000 BBs to bring the train to a halt—and by that point it would’ve stopped on its own anyway. (Based on the formulas on this page (https://pantherfile.uwm.edu/horowitz/www/PropulsionResistance.html) for the drag forces on a train, a back-of-the-envelope differential equation for the locomotive's motion suggests that on a flat track with no brakes, it would slow down on its own from 100 to 20 mph in ten or fifteen minutes). Clearly, the Red Ryder isn’t cutting it. It’s time to wade into the terrifying world of hardcore air rifle enthusiasts. The Tactical Edition Drozd Blackbird (http://www.drozdmax.com/bb-machine-guns/tactical-edition-blackbird.html) is a high-end BB machine gun (of course there are BB machine guns). It fires 1200 rounds a minute at a muzzle velocity of over 200 meters per second. At those speeds, standard BBs are capable of fracturing bone. Unfortunately, even instantaneously emptying the full 600 rounds into the front of the train would only reduce its speed by a small fraction of a percent. A single person with a BB gun can't do it. But what if we had an army? [Image: image] We’ll give each person a patch of ground two feet by four feet. This is a little cramped, but it should give them room to fire in an arc over the shoulder of the person in front of them. If we restrict them to 45 degrees in front of the train on either side of the track, we can pack about 100 people within 10 meters, 300 more within 20 meters, 550 more within 30 meters, and another 750 within 40 meters. [Image: image] Most of the shooters are able to hit the train fairly straight-on. Integrating the momentum from all the different shooting angles shows that the fanned-out arrangement exerts on the train over 90% of the force that an ideal arrangement (with every gun directly in front of the train) would. BBs experience a lot of drag, so the shots from those further away will reach the train at a lower speed. This page (http://www.swatairsoft.eu/37.html) gives estimates for the drag forces on a BB at various speeds. I love the internet. With all that in mind, let’s look at what happens when a crowd of people with BB machine guns try to stop a train. In fact, people have two arms, so let’s have them all dual-wield. At t=0, the people within 50 meters of the train—all 2,500 of them—pull the triggers, unleashing 100,000 BBs per second. As the train plows ahead, people in front magically fly sideways off the tracks. This is unrealistic, but we can’t let them slow down the train with their bodies—that would be cheating. As those people stop firing, people further down the tracks come into range and start shooting. The train is moving so quickly that any one person only gets off a few dozen rounds before the target moves past (or through) them. [Image: image] At any given time, there are 45,000 BBs in the air. But there’s a problem: When the steel balls bounce off the front of the train, they don’t disappear. They fly back at the shooters (who’ll probably shoot their eyes out) and into the line of fire. At its peak, this cloud of ricochets deflects nearly 1% of incoming shots via BB-BB collisions. This is a neat effect, but it doesn’t substantially interfere with our operation. Unfortunately, even this hail of steel takes several excruciating minutes—and almost two kilometers of track—to stop the train. That means we’d need over 100,000 shooters lined up along the track, and arming them would cost in the neighborhood of $50 million. We can do better, but we’ll have to relax the BB gun requirement. The AK-47 has a muzzle velocity of 715 meters per second and fires a bullet which outweighs a steel BB by a factor of 25. The bullets go so fast that they penetrate into the body of the train (which means they’re a little less efficient at transferring momentum, but it doesn’t really matter). Calculations show a crowd of 2,500 people firing two AK-47s each would be able to stop our runaway locomotive within the space of 30 meters—in only a second and a half. Mission accomplished. [Image: image] ... well. The greatly reduced drag coefficient of machine gun ammo compared to steel ball bearings means we can shoot from a much greater distance. Let’s make the crowd 200 meters deep instead of 50. At t=0, 40,000 people open fire. The AK-47 typically has a 30-round magazine and fires 10 shots per second. Within a third of a second, a quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Stray shots no doubt cause a lot of fatalities in the front of the crowd, but with a trained and disciplined group of shooters, the bulk of the shots could actually manage to hit the target. At t=15 ms, the locomotive has inched forward by half a meter and encounters the leading edge of the bullet cloud. By t=30 ms, the locomotive is being hit by a half dozen new bullets every millisecond. At t=150 ms, the locomotive has crawled forward about six meters, but it’s absorbing several hundred bullets each millisecond. This has begun to slow its forward momentum (and tear it apart—let’s assume it’s loaded full of some kind of lightweight material that distributes the shock of the bullet evenly). At around t=300ms, the full quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Most people have gotten off a total of six shots between their two guns. Interestingly, the bullets from the front rows of shooters occasionally catch up with—and collide with—slower bullets from the shooters behind them. This doesn’t happen a lot, but it does happen. The locomotive creeps forward to seven meters, seven and a half, seven and three quarters … and then seven and a half again. Success. But the shooters have only fired about a dozen rounds so far. Their magazines are still mostly full. At t=1s, almost a million shots have been fired. The locomotive is sliding backward at about 100 m/s (220 mph). At t=2s, the locomotive’s backward acceleration slows down quite a bit. This is partly because it’s starting to get out of range of the shooters. But it’s also because the locomotive is traveling at nearly the speed of sound, and the bullets are having a harder and harder time catching up. When they do, they have so little relative velocity that they can’t accelerate it much more. By this point, drag from the atmosphere is the dominant force on the locomotive’s motion. The rear end lifts from the tracks, the locomotive starts to tumble, and finally disintegrates into a cloud of shrapnel and spent bullets. Now bring on that asteroid. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Train Motion, Drag, and Natural Deceleration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of the runaway train as a moving physical system, including inertia, rolling/aerodynamic resistance, time and distance to slow, and whether BB effects are compared to natural slowing.

criteria.3-4: Mentions inertia but omits drag, distance, or time-scale consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains that the train would slow only gradually and that BBs add little beyond normal resistance.
criteria.7-8: Connects BB impulse, train speed, drag, and stopping distance in a coherent causal chain.
criteria.9-10: Clearly compares forced deceleration to natural deceleration and explains why BB-only stopping takes impractical time and track length.

criteria.name: Escalation Scenarios and Crowd/Weapon Logistics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores plausible escalations from one BB gun to many shooters, high-rate BB guns, or stronger firearms, while tracking geometry, firing windows, ammunition, costs, and staffing.
criteria.1-2: Considers only a single shot or jumps to an unsupported solution.
criteria.3-4: Mentions needing many guns or people but gives no workable spatial or logistical reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Discusses multiple shooters or automatic BB guns with rough but incomplete estimates.
criteria.7-8: Models crowd size, firing rate, range, train passage time, and ammunition needs with plausible scaling.
criteria.9-10: Provides a detailed escalation chain showing why BB armies are impractical and how firearm-level momentum changes the outcome.

criteria.name: Projectile Interaction Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of physical mechanisms after firing: impact, bounce versus penetration, momentum transfer efficiency, air drag on BBs, angle of fire, ricochets, collisions among projectiles, and hazards to shooters.
criteria.1-2: Treats projectiles as magically stopping the train without impact physics.
criteria.3-4: Mentions impacts but ignores bounce, penetration, drag, or firing angle effects.
criteria.5-6: Includes some relevant mechanisms such as ricochet or air drag, but unevenly or qualitatively.
criteria.7-8: Explains most important projectile mechanisms and their effects on stopping force.
criteria.9-10: Integrates drag, angles, ricochets, projectile collisions, penetration, and safety consequences into the causal analysis.

criteria.name: Long-Range Counterfactual Coherence and Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains the counterfactual premise while avoiding contradictions, clearly marking assumptions, uncertainty, absurd extrapolations, and downstream consequences such as destruction of the train or danger to people.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise, ignores feasibility limits, or gives a fantastical answer as fact.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but contains major internal contradictions or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent scenario with basic assumptions and some uncertainty acknowledged.
criteria.7-8: Builds a consistent long-range chain from BB gun to massed fire to consequences, with calibrated caveats.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly coherent counterfactual analysis, explicitly bounds assumptions, controls contradictions, and traces major downstream effects.

items.model_answer:
A BB gun would not realistically stop a runaway freight train.

A freight train has enormous mass and momentum. Even a relatively short train can weigh thousands of tons, and if it is moving at speed, the amount of energy involved is far beyond what a BB gun can affect. A BB has tiny mass and relatively low velocity compared with firearms or industrial equipment, so its impact on the train itself would be negligible. Shooting the locomotive, wheels, or cars would not meaningfully slow it down.

The only remotely plausible way a BB gun could matter is indirectly, by hitting some very specific vulnerable control or sensor in just the right way, causing the train to shut down or trigger braking. But in practice, modern freight trains are built to withstand harsh conditions, and their critical systems are not exposed in a way that a BB gun could reliably exploit from outside. If anything, you would be more likely to damage something useless or make the situation worse.

So if you truly had to stop a runaway freight train, a BB gun is essentially not a viable physical stopping tool. The real options would be things like emergency braking systems, derailers in controlled conditions, routing the train onto a safer track, cutting power, or coordinated intervention by rail operators and emergency crews.

items.question: What If It Were Actually a Tie?
human_answers: In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane. Nate Silver flippantly posted his 'tie' question on Twitter during the tallying of the extremely close 2012 Republican Iowa Caucus results. In that case, an exact tie was averted—Santorum ended up winning by 34 votes out of 121,503. And since it was a non-binding nominating vote, the Iowa Republican Party could handle a tie any way they wanted. But since it’s Election Day, let’s apply his question to the current contest. What will happen if there's a tie? I don't mean an electoral college tie. There’s probably about a 1 in 500 chance of one of those this year, and the consequences are thoroughly explored (http://blog.constitutioncenter.org/2012/11/an-electoral-college-tie-explained/). Instead, the question concerns both candidates getting the same number of votes in a state. Several researchers—including Silver himself (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/probdecisive2.pdf)—have calculated the odds of a state winner being decided by a single vote, which is effectively the same as the probability of a tie vote. For typical close states, the linked article calculates the probabilities to be in the neighborhood of 1 in 100,000—which makes intuitive sense, since 100,000 is the sort of vote margin by which swing state elections are typically decided. So what if there's a tie in a close state this year? [Image: image] For that matter, what if there’s a tie in every battleground state? [Image: image] Well, for starters, recounts happen. But since recounts happen in close elections in general, these are just as likely to create ties as to break them. They don’t change the underlying probability. So let’s assume that after all recounts, there’s a tie. What then? The short answer is that it’s up to the state’s laws. I went through the general laws of nine competitive states to see how they handle popular vote ties. In most of them, the tie is broken by “drawing lots”—that is, randomly. (If you’re curious, here are links to some tie vote laws in each state: Virginia (http://leg1.state.va.us/cgi-bin/legp504.exe?000+cod+24.2-674), North Carolina (http://law.onecle.com/north-carolina/163-elections-and-election-laws/163-182.8.html), Florida (http://election.dos.state.fl.us/publications/pdf/2012/2012_Election_Laws.pdf), Ohio (http://codes.ohio.gov/orc/3505.33), New Hampshire (http://www.gencourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/lxiii/667/667-17.htm), Wisconsin (http://docs.legis.wi.gov/statutes/statutes/5/I/01), Colorado (http://www.state.co.us/gov_dir/leg_dir/olls/sl1999/sl_154.htm), Iowa (http://search.legis.state.ia.us/nxt/gateway.dll/ic/1/13/2174/2175/2582/2629?f=templates$fn=document-frameset.htm$q=[field%2050.44]$x=Advanced), Nevada (http://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec400)). [Image: image] “Drawing lots” can mean a coin toss, drawing straws, or picking a name from a hat. Most states leave the details up to the Secretary of State or an electoral board, although Iowa Code 50.44 specifies that the names be written on pieces of paper and placed in a “receptacle”. In North Carolina, however, a tie vote (when more than 5,000 votes are cast) results in a new election. (Which could potentially itself result in a tie ...) But let’s imagine that there’s not just one state that’s tied—instead, the nine most competitive states are tied (and the rest go as expected). If North Carolina held a runoff to break the tie, and the other eight states flipped coins (or picked from Iowa’s receptacle), Obama would be reelected in 431 out of 512 cases (http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2012/11/02/us/politics/paths-to-the-white-house.html)—about 84% of the time. But how likely is a nine-state tie? If we ballpark the odds of a tie vote in each close state at 1 in 100,000, then the odds of a tie vote in all nine states is in the neighborhood of one in a quattuordecillion—1 followed by 45 zeroes. (This ignores vote correlation between states, but it’s good enough for a first-order estimate). Florida is hit by an average of 66 tornadoes per year (http://www1.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/cmb/images/tornado/clim/ann-avg-torn1991-2010.gif). If each tornado is 50 yards wide and has a path 1.5 miles long (which is typical (http://www.crh.noaa.gov/lmk/soo/docu/tornado_faq.php), if not necessarily the mean), we can calculate that a typical location in Florida experiences an average 1.4 picotornados per second: \[66\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{year}}\times\frac{1.5\text{ miles}\times50\text{ yards}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx1.4\times10^{-12}\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{second}}\] Astronomer Alan Harris calculates that a person’s lifetime odds of death from a comet or meteorite impact are about 1 in 700,000. If a typical person in the calculation lives 70 years, this suggests a Florida resident suffers an average of 0.64 femtodeaths per second from meteorite impacts: \[\frac{\tfrac{1}{700,000}\text{deaths}}{70\text{ years}}\approx6.4\times10^{-16}\tfrac{\text{deaths}}{\text{second}}\] In 1994, drug smugglers fleeing the authorities dropped an estimated 20 bales of cocaine from an airplane over Florida—one of which crashed through the roof of a Crime Watch meeting and narrowly missed the Homestead Chief of Police (http://www.deseretnews.com/article/392575/ONLY-IN-FLORIDA-DOES-COCAINE-DROP-FROM-SKY.html?pg=all). If Florida has been hit by 20 bales of cocaine over the last 20 years, then the average person in Florida is struck by an average of 29 zeptobales of cocaine per second: \[\frac{20\text{ bales}}{20\text{ years}}\times\frac{\left (\tfrac{75\text{ kg}}{\text{Density of cocaine}} \right )^\tfrac{2}{3}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\tfrac{\text{bales}}{\text{second}}\] (By the way—this means that given a street price of $20,000 per kilogram, a typical acre of Florida land produces an average revenue of three cents per year in falling cocaine bales). Putting all this together: The probability that every battleground state is exactly tied is roughly equal to the probability that, when one of the Florida electors reaches into the hat to draw a name, he or she is struck by a falling cocaine bale, the hat is hurled away within the next few seconds by a tornado, and the elector is obliterated minutes later by a meteorite impact. [Image: image] If you’re in the US, don’t forget to vote—your vote could make or break a tie. And if you’re voting in Florida, keep an eye on the sky.

items.model_answer:
If it were actually a tie, then neither side would count as the unique winner under the usual rules. The outcome would depend on the system being used.

In a scientific or mathematical context, a true tie usually means the measurement or comparison does not distinguish between the options at the required precision. Then you would either report them as equal, use more precise measurement, or apply a predefined tie-breaking rule.

In an election, game, or competition, a tie would mean both sides finished with the same result. Then the rules might call for a recount, overtime, a runoff, shared victory, or some other tie-break procedure.

So the key idea is: if it were actually a tie, you could not honestly say one side won unless there were additional rules that resolve ties.

items.question: What If a 100-Foot Diamond Meteor Hit Earth at Light Speed?
human_answers: Nothing made of matter can go at the speed of light. But that’s ok—we can get close enough! No matter how fast you push something, it will never quite get up to light speed. This seems like it can’t be right, but it is. Our universe has some weird rules. But the closer something gets to the speed of light, the more energy and momentum it has—and this energy and momentum go up without limit. We’ll start slow and work our way up. 1 kilometer per second: If we drop the meteor from the edge of space, 100 kilometers up, it’ll punch through the atmosphere without slowing down too much and hit the ground moving about Mach 3—over a kilometer a second. As it falls, it compresses the air in front of it. When the air is compressed, it heats it up. (This is the same thing that heats up spacecraft and meteors—actual air friction has little to do with that.) By the time it reaches the ground, the lower surface will have heated to over 500℃, which is enough to glow visibly. When it hits the ground, two minutes after it was released, it makes a crater 300 meters across—the size of a school, shattering into fragments in the process. [Image: image] 11 kilometers per second: If we set the diamond in space a little ways away from the Earth, and let it fall toward us, it will hit at about 11 kilometers per second. This is Earth’s escape velocity, and anything that hits the Earth from space will—thanks to gravity—be going at least that fast. At 11 kilometers per second, the brief descent would be visible as a fireball. The energy of the impact would be comparable to a small atomic bomb, and the crater it would create would be a kilometer across—a little smaller than Meteor Crater in Arizona. [Image: image] 72 kilometers per second: This is just about the fastest that anything can hit the Earth if it’s orbiting the Sun. The Leonid meteor shower hits at this speed. Oddly, the speed that something is going doesn’t really affect how deeply it digs into the ground. Isaac Newton came up with a very clever idea (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) for estimating how deeply projectiles will go in their targets before stopping. It turns out that no matter how fast a projectile is going, if it hits something that’s about the same density, it will only go about one body-length in. [Image: image] However, it will make quite a splash. The 72-kilometer-per-second diamond sphere blasts out a crater over two kilometers across, with an energy release comparable to that of the biggest fusion bombs. Here’s where things get weird. 3,000 kilometers per second = 0.01c: This would be pretty bad. The thing that makes this a little unpredictable is the fact that at speeds in the range of hundreds of kilometers per second, the air begins to undergo nuclear fusion (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0032063389900305) (Google that paper title to find the full text). This, combined with plain old plasma heating, may manage to eat apart the diamond sphere completely before it reaches the ground. But it doesn’t do the ground much good. The sphere doesn’t spread out enough to make a difference, and it still hits the ground in roughly one spot. The blast releases a thousand times more energy than the largest nuclear weapon, devastating whatever region it came down over. It gouges out a massive crater—though not the biggest one Earth has ever seen. [Image: image] 0.99c: This is where relativity kicks in. At these speeds, the bonds holding the sphere together are completely irrelevant. It’s just a collection of carbon atoms moving so fast that Lorentz contraction flattens the whole thing into a pancake (although we wouldn’t be able to see that visually (http://www.math.ubc.ca/~cass/courses/m309-01a/cook/terrell1.html)). The SRIM (http://www.srim.org/) particle physics simulation tool can help answer some questions about what happens when it hits. The carbon atoms in the ball carry about 70 GeV of energy each. They’re actually moving too fast to fuse directly with the air—they just pass through it completely. The air molecules punch three meters into the face of the ball before coming to a rest inside it, and it arrives at the ground with a bunch more matter in it than it started with. It’s also expanding rapidly. When it hits the surface, it disintegrates completely, digging downward and outward, carving a cone-shaped path down through the bedrock. The impact depth equation no longer applies, since the atoms are literally passing through each other. The energy cracks a hole in the crust and blows open a crater so big you can see the molten mantle. This delivers the energy of 50 dinosaur-killing Chicxulub impacts—enough to cause a mass extinction, if not end life completely. [Image: image] I’ve always thought that one of the the great things about physics is that you can add more digits to any number and see what happens and nobody can stop you. 0.9999999c: At this speed, every carbon molecule carries 25 TeV of energy, comparable to particles in the beam of the Large Hadron Collider. A little faster, and we might spot Higgs bosons in the impact debris. As it stands, the whole thing hits the planet with about the kinetic energy of the orbiting Moon. It’s enough to punch a gaping hole in the mantle and shake up the surface across the whole planet, turning it molten. This probably ends all life on and around Earth. Oops, cat stepped on my keyboard again and I added a bunch more 9s. 0.9999999999999999999999951c The fastest object (with mass) in recorded history might be the Oh-My-God particle (no relation to the God particle), a proton from space that plowed into the atmosphere over Utah in 1991. It was moving at 99.99999999999999999999951% of the speed of light, which meant it packed the kinetic energy of a baseball—in a single proton. The cascade of particles it blasted apart dwarfed anything the LHC could produce. Nobody knows how it got to be moving so fast. Particles moving that fast hit the Earth a handful of times a year. They seem to come from the general direction of exploding galaxies, but what happened to to make them leave in such a hurry—and why they haven’t slowed down more before they got here—is something of a mystery. Let’s give Aidan’s diamond meteor the speed of the Oh My God particle. These speeds are so high that my copy of SRIM flatly refuses to simulate them. However, we can get some idea from looking at how cosmic rays cascade through rock. The diamond sweeps out a column of atmosphere without seeming to notice and disappears into the crust. A cloud of expanding plasma and radiation grows around the entry point as the energy ripples outward through the body of the planet. Forty milliseconds later the entire far side expands outward in an incandescent cloud. The diamond meteor, and the cascade of particles it created as it collided with the crust, is spread out throughout the body of our planet. The superheated planet glows brighter than the sun. The momentum would be enough to knock the Earth into a different orbit—but the Earth is no more. The energy deposited is ten thousand times greater than the planet’s gravitational binding energy, and the planet is blown into an expanding cloud of plasma, with a particularly energetic streamer extending away from the far side of the impact site, out into space. The Sun hiccups and flares as it absorbs waves of dust. The surfaces of Mars and Venus are scoured clean by the waves of incredibly high-energy plasma. [Image: image] And in the distant future, an alien astronomer on a world hundreds of light-years from Earth frowns at a beeping detector, and wonders what violent event would make a particle move so fast.

items.model_answer:
If a 100-foot diamond meteor hit Earth at the speed of light, the realistic answer is that ordinary physics breaks down before the impact ever happens, because no object with mass can actually reach light speed. But if we take the question as a counterfactual and treat it as though a roughly 30-meter-wide diamond object somehow did strike Earth at nearly or exactly light speed, the result would be unimaginably catastrophic—far beyond any normal asteroid impact.

A 100-foot diamond meteor is about 30 meters across. Diamond has a density of about 3,500 kilograms per cubic meter, so such an object would have a mass on the order of 50 million kilograms. At everyday cosmic speeds, that would already be a dangerous impactor. But at light speed, the kinetic energy in the classical sense becomes nonsensical, and in relativity the energy tends toward infinity. That means the premise implies effectively unlimited impact energy. In other words, there is no meaningful “crater size” estimate under standard physics, because the event would not resemble an ordinary meteor strike at all.

If you soften the question slightly and imagine “very close to light speed,” then the answer is still extreme. The meteor would release far more energy than the largest nuclear arsenals, likely exceeding asteroid-impact scales by many orders of magnitude. Long before it touched the ground, it would generate intense radiation, a superheated shock front, and probably a violent cascade of particle interactions with the atmosphere. The atmosphere in front of it would be compressed and heated so intensely that the object might effectively create a massive plasma channel. To an observer, the event would not look like a rock falling from the sky; it would look more like a planet-striking beam of catastrophic energy.

At exact light speed, under the counterfactual premise, the impact would be best described as a physically impossible event with effectively infinite destructive energy. Locally, it would vaporize the impact region instantly. On a larger scale, if we take the premise literally, the damage could range from sterilizing much of Earth’s surface to completely disrupting the planet, depending on how one chooses to handle the “infinite energy” absurdity.

The “diamond” part barely matters. Diamond is just carbon, and at these energies the material composition is irrelevant. It would not stay a recognizable diamond; the energies involved would overwhelm any chemical or crystal structure almost immediately.

So the direct answer is: if a 100-foot diamond meteor somehow hit Earth at light speed, Earth would suffer essentially unsurvivable, possibly planet-destroying devastation, and the scenario lies outside real physics because a massive object cannot actually travel at light speed.

edus.text: If a 100-foot diamond meteor hit Earth at the speed of light, the realistic answer is that ordinary physics breaks down before the impact ever happens,
because no object with mass can actually reach light speed.
But if we take the question as a counterfactual and treat it as though a roughly 30-meter-wide diamond object somehow did strike Earth at nearly or exactly light speed,
the result would be unimaginably catastrophic—far beyond any normal asteroid impact.
A 100-foot diamond meteor is about 30 meters across.
Diamond has a density of about 3,500 kilograms per cubic meter,
so such an object would have a mass on the order of 50 million kilograms.
At everyday cosmic speeds, that would already be a dangerous impactor.
But at light speed, the kinetic energy in the classical sense becomes nonsensical,
and in relativity the energy tends toward infinity.
That means the premise implies effectively unlimited impact energy.
In other words, there is no meaningful “crater size” estimate under standard physics,
because the event would not resemble an ordinary meteor strike at all.
If you soften the question slightly and imagine “very close to light speed,”
then the answer is still extreme.
The meteor would release far more energy than the largest nuclear arsenals,
likely exceeding asteroid-impact scales by many orders of magnitude.
Long before it touched the ground, it would generate intense radiation, a superheated shock front, and probably a violent cascade of particle interactions with the atmosphere.
The atmosphere in front of it would be compressed and heated so intensely
that the object might effectively create a massive plasma channel.
To an observer, the event would not look like a rock falling from the sky;
it would look more like a planet-striking beam of catastrophic energy.
At exact light speed, under the counterfactual premise, the impact would be best described as a physically impossible event with effectively infinite destructive energy.
Locally, it would vaporize the impact region instantly.
On a larger scale, if we take the premise literally, the damage could range from sterilizing much of Earth’s surface to completely disrupting the planet,
depending on how one chooses to handle the “infinite energy” absurdity.
The “diamond” part barely matters.
Diamond is just carbon,
and at these energies the material composition is irrelevant.
It would not stay a recognizable diamond;
the energies involved would overwhelm any chemical or crystal structure almost immediately.
So the direct answer is:
if a 100-foot diamond meteor somehow hit Earth at light speed, Earth would suffer essentially unsurvivable, possibly planet-destroying devastation,
and the scenario lies outside real physics
because a massive object cannot actually travel at light speed.

items.original_question: 中国有没有考虑过拼音文字系统？我惊讶地了解到以下有关日语和韩语的信息：日语在其语言中使用了大量汉字，并且没有语音系统，直到公元 800 年左右他们创造了第一个假名。 （他们仍然使用大量汉字，但关键是他们最初没有语音系统，然后创建了一个。）韩国人在他们的语言中也使用了很多汉字，直到1443年左右他们创造了韩文时才没有语音系统。 （我不确定他们是否仍然使用大量汉字，但要点与日本相同。）所以你可以看到这是如何提出我的问题的。中国有没有考虑过拼音文字系统？换句话说，是否有任何皇帝、学者、宫廷太监或其他官员，或者只是儒家或道家之类的某个学派的智者……写下一些关于考虑拼音文字系统的想法？他们中是否有人至少注意到日本和韩国的做法并明确拒绝？最关键的是，他们是否说明了拒绝的理由？我感兴趣的时期是前现代中国。 换句话说，从远古时代到 1912 年。编辑：分析很有趣，但是

criteria.1-2: Makes false claims such as 'Chinese cannot be written phonetically' or ignores linguistic structure entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions homophones or dialects superficially but draws simplistic or incorrect conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Explains some linguistic obstacles and benefits, but misses key issues such as cross-dialect writing or literary continuity.
criteria.7-8: Accurately connects phonetic spelling to Mandarin dominance, dialect loss, ambiguity management, and textual conversion problems.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of how different phonetic systems, tones, word spacing, standardization, and regional languages would reshape written communication.

criteria.name: Long-Range Social, Political, and Educational Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects on literacy, schooling, bureaucracy, national integration, regional identity, censorship, publishing, migration, and cultural capital over decades.
criteria.1-2: Lists isolated effects with no causal chain or focuses only on literacy.
criteria.3-4: Provides a few plausible consequences but lacks depth or timeframe.
criteria.5-6: Covers education and state-building effects with some causal links, but omits major social or political tradeoffs.
criteria.7-8: Traces credible multi-decade consequences across literacy, governance, regional languages, and cultural identity.
criteria.9-10: Integrates education, politics, class, regionalism, nationalism, and institutions into coherent long-range chains with tradeoffs and feedback loops.

criteria.name: Cultural, Technological, and International Ripple Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer addresses broader effects on literature, calligraphy, historical texts, dictionaries, computing and typing, publishing, East Asian cultural ties, overseas Chinese communities, and global perceptions of China.

items.model_answer:
If modern China had replaced Chinese characters with a fully phonetic script, the effects would have been far-reaching: literacy probably would have become easier to achieve, printing and typing would have become simpler sooner, and mass education might have expanded even faster. But the change would also have carried major cultural and political costs, and it would have created new linguistic problems rather than simply solving old ones.

On the practical side, a phonetic script usually lowers the burden of learning to read and write. Chinese characters require memorizing thousands of distinct forms, while a phonetic system can represent speech with a much smaller set of symbols. In that world, children might have learned basic literacy faster, adult literacy campaigns might have been more effective, and the state could have spread propaganda, laws, and technical knowledge more quickly. Administrative modernization may also have accelerated, especially in the twentieth century, because typewriters, telegraphy, and early computing all handled alphabetic systems more easily than character-based writing.

But China’s linguistic situation makes the issue more complicated than it first appears. Chinese characters historically allowed people speaking very different Sinitic languages or dialects to share a written standard even when their speech was not mutually intelligible. A phonetic script forces the question: phonetic for which pronunciation? If based on Mandarin, it would likely have strengthened the dominance of standard Mandarin and further marginalized Cantonese, Hokkien, Shanghainese, Hakka, and other speech communities. If different regions wrote phonetically according to local speech, written unity across China might have weakened. So replacing characters could have promoted spoken standardization, but at the cost of regional linguistic diversity and perhaps some national cohesion.

The cultural consequences would have been enormous. Chinese characters are not just a writing tool; they are deeply tied to China’s historical continuity, literature, calligraphy, and elite culture. A phonetic replacement would have made the classical written tradition much less accessible to ordinary readers unless texts were extensively transliterated or translated. In effect, the modern population might have been cut off more sharply from premodern texts, inscriptions, and aesthetic traditions. Calligraphy, seal carving, and character-based visual culture would either have declined dramatically or survived only as specialist arts. China would still have had a rich culture, but it would have felt less visibly continuous with its imperial past.

Politically, such a reform would likely have served state-building. A phonetic script tied to standard Mandarin could have functioned as a powerful nation-making tool, similar to script reforms in other countries that used language policy to centralize authority. The Communist state in particular might have found this useful for education, military mobilization, and ideological unification. At the same time, opponents could have viewed it as an assault on heritage or as a northern imposition on non-Mandarin regions. So while the reform might have strengthened the modern state, it could also have provoked resistance from scholars, traditionalists, and regional communities.

Economically and technologically, a phonetic script might have given China some short-term advantages earlier in the twentieth century, especially in clerical work and early machine processing. However, many of the old disadvantages of characters faded with digital technology. Once computers, predictive input systems, and smartphones emerged, character use became much less of a barrier. So the long-run technological gain may have been smaller than reformers once imagined.

The biggest historical tradeoff is that phoneticization would probably have made China easier to educate and govern, but less connected to its own textual past and less tolerant of linguistic plurality. It might have produced a more standardized, centralized, and accessible modern culture, yet one with a sharper break from traditional civilization. In short, modern China with a phonetic script would likely be more linguistically uniform and initially more efficient, but also culturally more discontinuous and politically more homogenizing.

nodes.text: If modern China had replaced Chinese characters with a fully phonetic script,
the effects would have been far-reaching:
literacy probably would have become easier to achieve,
printing and typing would have become simpler sooner,
and mass education might have expanded even faster.
But the change would also have carried major cultural and political costs,
and it would have created new linguistic problems rather than simply solving old ones.
On the practical side, a phonetic script usually lowers the burden of learning to read and write.
Chinese characters require memorizing thousands of distinct forms,
while a phonetic system can represent speech with a much smaller set of symbols.
In that world, children might have learned basic literacy faster,
adult literacy campaigns might have been more effective,
and the state could have spread propaganda, laws, and technical knowledge more quickly.
Administrative modernization may also have accelerated,
because typewriters, telegraphy, and early computing all handled alphabetic systems more easily than character-based writing.
But China’s linguistic situation makes the issue more complicated than it first appears.
Chinese characters historically allowed people speaking very different Sinitic languages or dialects to share a written standard
even when their speech was not mutually intelligible.
A phonetic script forces the question: phonetic for which pronunciation?
If based on Mandarin, it would likely have strengthened the dominance of standard Mandarin
and further marginalized Cantonese, Hokkien, Shanghainese, Hakka, and other speech communities.
If different regions wrote phonetically according to local speech,
written unity across China might have weakened.
So replacing characters could have promoted spoken standardization,
but at the cost of regional linguistic diversity and perhaps some national cohesion.
The cultural consequences would have been enormous.
Chinese characters are not just a writing tool;
they are deeply tied to China’s historical continuity, literature, calligraphy, and elite culture.
A phonetic replacement would have made the classical written tradition much less accessible to ordinary readers
unless texts were extensively transliterated or translated.
In effect, the modern population might have been cut off more sharply from premodern texts, inscriptions, and aesthetic traditions.
Calligraphy, seal carving, and character-based visual culture would either have declined dramatically or survived only as specialist arts.
China would still have had a rich culture,
but it would have felt less visibly continuous with its imperial past.
Politically, such a reform would likely have served state-building.
A phonetic script tied to standard Mandarin could have functioned as a powerful nation-making tool,
similar to script reforms in other countries that used language policy to centralize authority.
The Communist state in particular might have found this useful for education, military mobilization, and ideological unification.
At the same time, opponents could have viewed it as an assault on heritage
or as a northern imposition on non-Mandarin regions.
So while the reform might have strengthened the modern state,
it could also have provoked resistance from scholars, traditionalists, and regional communities.
Economically and technologically, a phonetic script might have given China some short-term advantages earlier in the twentieth century,
especially in clerical work and early machine processing.
However, many of the old disadvantages of characters faded with digital technology.
Once computers, predictive input systems, and smartphones emerged,
character use became much less of a barrier.
So the long-run technological gain may have been smaller than reformers once imagined.
The biggest historical tradeoff is that phoneticization would probably have made China easier to educate and govern,
but less connected to its own textual past and less tolerant of linguistic plurality.
It might have produced a more standardized, centralized, and accessible modern culture,
yet one with a sharper break from traditional civilization.
In short, modern China with a phonetic script would likely be more linguistically uniform and initially more efficient,
but also culturally more discontinuous and politically more homogenizing.

items.question: What If Japan Had Attacked the Panama Canal Instead of Pearl Harbor?
human_answers: > So I want to know, did the Japanese Navy have the ability to destroy it in a surprise attack, let's say on 1941 Dec 7? I'm asking if the Japanese Navy had the ability.

The Canal is 8400 miles from Tokyo, compared to 4000 miles for Pearl Harbour. The Japanese carriers are stated of having a range of 10,000 miles at a cruising speed of about 16 knots, but remember that drag varies as the square of speed.

Destroying those locks is going to be harder than you think. They are very large, at 110 feet x 1,050 feet, and the lock gates have to have been built to stand up to accidental collisions with large ships (at low speed, admittedly).
items.original_question: 1941 年 12 月 7 日，日本是否可以在突然袭击中瞄准巴拿马运河而不是珍珠港？这个问题来自一个稍微相关的问题。第二次世界大战时，美国大部分工业都位于东海岸，包括所有航母和战列舰的造船业。如果巴拿马运河沉没，将大大减少美国海军在太平洋的后勤保障。所以我想知道，日本海军是否有能力在突然袭击中摧毁它，比如1941年12月7日？到目前为止我所知道的： - 巴拿马运河每条航道有 6 个水闸。这些锁有混凝土墙，但有空心钢门，根据这部纪录片：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d-CaBIKTl4M，在 1:11:00 你可以看到它们是一个空心框架。一枚炸弹或鱼雷可能会在上面炸出一个洞，但可能不足以立即耗尽船闸的水。 - 日本俯冲轰炸机接受过训练，他们在二战早期（珊瑚海、中途岛）遭受的许多航母打击就证明了这一点。注意，我说的是打击，不一定是杀戮。我回顾了这两场战斗，很多次，美国航母都被击中了，但都幸存了（当时美国航母似乎比日本航母坚强得多）。 我只是想指出日本俯冲轰炸机似乎训练有素且准确性良好。 - 编辑：潘

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in late 1941, the immediate shock to the United States would still have been enormous, and war between the two countries would still have been very likely. But the overall strategic effect would probably have been worse for Japan than the historical Pearl Harbor attack.

The main reason is that Pearl Harbor was the center of the U.S. Pacific Fleet. Japan’s real 1941 objective was to cripple American naval power long enough to seize Southeast Asia and build a defensive empire. An attack on the Panama Canal would have struck American logistics and prestige, but not the main concentration of U.S. Pacific battleships, carriers, fuel storage, and naval infrastructure in Hawaii. Unless Japan also attacked Pearl Harbor or otherwise destroyed the Pacific Fleet, the United States would retain much more of its immediate combat power in the Pacific.

Damaging the Panama Canal would certainly matter. The canal was crucial for moving ships quickly between the Atlantic and Pacific. If locks or facilities were badly damaged, the U.S. would have to send ships around South America, adding major transit time. That would complicate reinforcement schedules, naval planning, and merchant shipping. It would also be a dramatic symbolic blow, because the canal was one of the most important strategic assets in the Western Hemisphere. Americans would see it as a direct attack much closer to home than Hawaii.

But Japan would face huge operational problems in carrying out such an attack. Striking Pearl Harbor was already a difficult long-range carrier operation, but Panama was much farther from Japan and deep inside a region where sustaining Japanese naval air power would be much harder. A carrier raid might damage canal facilities, but permanently disabling the canal would be difficult. The locks were robust, and the United States could repair damage relatively quickly unless the attack were repeated or accompanied by sabotage on a large scale. Japan was not well positioned to maintain pressure there. So even a successful raid would likely produce disruption measured in weeks or months, not decisive strategic paralysis.

Politically, the effect on the United States would likely be even more unifying than Pearl Harbor. Pearl Harbor, though devastating, was in a distant Pacific territory. An attack on the Panama Canal would be seen as an assault on the artery connecting America’s two oceans and as a direct threat to the hemisphere. The U.S. declaration of war would almost certainly follow. Germany and Italy might still declare war on the United States if events unfolded similarly, but even if they hesitated, American public anger would be overwhelming.

In military terms, however, Japan would probably gain less time than it did historically. The U.S. Pacific Fleet, if left largely intact at Pearl Harbor, could interfere earlier with Japanese offensives in the Philippines, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies. American carriers and battleships would not have suffered the same initial losses and disruption. Japan’s southern expansion might still succeed in the very short run because of its prepared invasions and local superiority, but U.S. resistance would be stronger sooner. The American Navy could contest sea lanes and launch raids earlier than it did after December 1941.

There is also the question of whether such an attack was even within Japan’s realistic capabilities. In practical terms, it was much less feasible than Pearl Harbor. Japan had limited intelligence, reach, and ability to sustain an operation against Panama. The farther the target from Japan, the greater the chance of detection, navigational error, and logistical strain. So this counterfactual often overstates Japan’s ability to hit the canal hard enough to change the war.

The likely long-term outcome is that the United States still enters the war fully mobilized, but with more of its Pacific striking power intact. The canal might be temporarily out of action, slowing transfers between oceans, yet America’s industrial capacity, shipbuilding, and repair capability would outweigh that setback. Japan would have provoked the same giant enemy while failing to neutralize the fleet it most needed to disable. In that sense, attacking the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor would probably have been a dramatic and provocative move, but strategically a poorer choice for Japan and, if anything, might have led to an earlier and more effective American response in the Pacific.
