edus.text: If Japan had attacked the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor in late 1941,
the immediate shock to the United States would still have been enormous,
and war between the two countries would still have been very likely.
But the overall strategic effect would probably have been worse for Japan than the historical Pearl Harbor attack.
The main reason is that Pearl Harbor was the center of the U.S. Pacific Fleet.
Japan’s real 1941 objective was to cripple American naval power long enough to seize Southeast Asia and build a defensive empire.
An attack on the Panama Canal would have struck American logistics and prestige,
but not the main concentration of U.S. Pacific battleships, carriers, fuel storage, and naval infrastructure in Hawaii.
Unless Japan also attacked Pearl Harbor or otherwise destroyed the Pacific Fleet,
the United States would retain much more of its immediate combat power in the Pacific.
Damaging the Panama Canal would certainly matter.
The canal was crucial for moving ships quickly between the Atlantic and Pacific.
If locks or facilities were badly damaged,
the U.S. would have to send ships around South America,
adding major transit time.
That would complicate reinforcement schedules, naval planning, and merchant shipping.
It would also be a dramatic symbolic blow,
because the canal was one of the most important strategic assets in the Western Hemisphere.
Americans would see it as a direct attack much closer to home than Hawaii.
But Japan would face huge operational problems in carrying out such an attack.
Striking Pearl Harbor was already a difficult long-range carrier operation,
but Panama was much farther from Japan
and deep inside a region where sustaining Japanese naval air power would be much harder.
A carrier raid might damage canal facilities,
but permanently disabling the canal would be difficult.
The locks were robust,
and the United States could repair damage relatively quickly
unless the attack were repeated or accompanied by sabotage on a large scale.
Japan was not well positioned to maintain pressure there.
So even a successful raid would likely produce disruption measured in weeks or months,
not decisive strategic paralysis.
Politically, the effect on the United States would likely be even more unifying than Pearl Harbor.
Pearl Harbor, though devastating, was in a distant Pacific territory.
An attack on the Panama Canal would be seen as an assault on the artery connecting America’s two oceans and as a direct threat to the hemisphere.
The U.S. declaration of war would almost certainly follow.
Germany and Italy might still declare war on the United States if events unfolded similarly,
but even if they hesitated, American public anger would be overwhelming.
In military terms, however, Japan would probably gain less time than it did historically.
The U.S. Pacific Fleet, if left largely intact at Pearl Harbor, could interfere earlier with Japanese offensives in the Philippines, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies.
American carriers and battleships would not have suffered the same initial losses and disruption.
Japan’s southern expansion might still succeed in the very short run because of its prepared invasions and local superiority,
but U.S. resistance would be stronger sooner.
The American Navy could contest sea lanes and launch raids earlier than it did after December 1941.
There is also the question of whether such an attack was even within Japan’s realistic capabilities.
In practical terms, it was much less feasible than Pearl Harbor.
Japan had limited intelligence, reach, and ability to sustain an operation against Panama.
The farther the target from Japan, the greater the chance of detection, navigational error, and logistical strain.
So this counterfactual often overstates Japan’s ability to hit the canal hard enough to change the war.
The likely long-term outcome is that the United States still enters the war fully mobilized, but with more of its Pacific striking power intact.
The canal might be temporarily out of action, slowing transfers between oceans,
yet America’s industrial capacity, shipbuilding, and repair capability would outweigh that setback.
Japan would have provoked the same giant enemy while failing to neutralize the fleet it most needed to disable.
In that sense, attacking the Panama Canal instead of Pearl Harbor would probably have been a dramatic and provocative move,
but strategically a poorer choice for Japan
and, if anything, might have led to an earlier and more effective American response in the Pacific.

items.question: What If Eighteenth-Century European Armies Had Returned to the Crossbow?
human_answers: Yes, a trained archer can probably put more effective shots on an unarmored target than a trained musketman of the 18th century. The problem is that word trained.

One often missed factor is that arrows are delicate and require skilled fletchers to make them. The English invasion of France under Edward IV in 1475 required two years lead time producing enough arrows to supply his troops on campaign.

There have already been some good explanations, regarding relative ease of use for muskets, as well as less training required to use, but I have not seen two constants of campaigning considered: Rain and Disease. Gunpowder and bowstrings both need to be kep...

There's a lot of very good answers already; but I'd like to add on to what @Schwern has said from a Japanese perspective. When the musket was introduced in Japan in the 16th century, it quickly overtook archery in terms of importance.
Schwern had a lot of very good points, but there are other factors as well. - siege warfare.

items.model_answer:
If eighteenth-century European armies had seriously returned to the crossbow, the result would probably not have been a restoration of medieval warfare, but a limited and ultimately unsuccessful attempt to solve some of the weaknesses of early firearms. The crossbow did have a few real advantages over the smoothbore musket: it was quieter, less affected by rain in terms of ignition, potentially more accurate in trained hands at short to moderate ranges, and it did not require gunpowder for every shot. But in the actual military environment of the eighteenth century, those strengths were outweighed by severe practical limits. A widespread return to the crossbow would likely have produced niche uses, some tactical experimentation, and then abandonment in favor of improved firearms.

The biggest issue is rate of effective battlefield fire. Eighteenth-century warfare depended heavily on massed volleys, drilling, and the psychological and physical effect of many projectiles delivered at once. A musket was inaccurate, but thousands of soldiers firing together could still devastate formations, especially at close range. A military crossbow, powerful enough to matter against soldiers wearing coats, leather gear, and sometimes residual armor elements, would generally be slower to reload than a musket unless it was made relatively weak. If it was made weak enough to reload quickly, it lost much of its military value. If it was made strong enough to be dangerous, it often required mechanical spanning devices, which slowed use and complicated drill. That tradeoff made it poorly suited for line infantry.

Another problem is logistics. At first glance, crossbows might seem attractive because they reduce dependence on gunpowder. But eighteenth-century states were actually getting quite good at manufacturing and distributing firearms, powder, and shot on a large scale. Muskets had become standardized military tools. Reintroducing crossbows would mean creating new production systems for bows, strings, bolts, spanning tools, and spare parts. Bolts were bulkier and generally less convenient to carry in very large numbers than musket balls and paper cartridges. Strings were vulnerable to wear and weather, and powerful bows required careful construction. So instead of simplifying supply, crossbows would have introduced a parallel logistics burden.

Training effects are more mixed. One historic advantage of the crossbow over the longbow was that it required less lifelong physical conditioning. In that sense, an army could train crossbowmen more quickly than elite bowmen. But eighteenth-century armies had already built institutions around musket drill, not just individual marksmanship. Soldiers were trained to load and fire in sequence, maneuver in formation, fix bayonets, and function in linear tactics. A return to the crossbow would have required new drill systems and probably encouraged looser formations or more specialized troops. This might have had some value in skirmishing, ambushes, siege defense, and colonial warfare, but it would have fit badly with the dominant battlefield system in Europe.

The bayonet matters a great deal here. One reason muskets became so dominant was that, with a bayonet, they combined ranged and close-combat roles. A line infantryman did not need a separate pike once firearms and bayonets matured. A crossbow does not integrate with melee in the same way. A soldier carrying a crossbow would also need another serious close-combat weapon, adding complexity and reducing flexibility. This alone would have been a major disadvantage in an era when infantry had to withstand cavalry, assault positions, and fight in tightly organized formations.

There are, however, a few areas where crossbows might have found a real role. Light troops could have used them for stealthier shooting in outpost warfare, raids, or sieges. Naval boarding parties might have experimented with them because open powder near sails, rope, and confined spaces was hazardous. Some fortress defenders could have liked a weapon less dependent on powder stores during long sieges. Irregular forces or poorer states might also have considered them if gunpowder supply was unreliable. But these would have been specialized applications, not the basis of mainstream armies.

If major powers had tried to force a general return to the crossbow, they probably would have discovered its shortcomings quickly in wars against musket-armed opponents. Crossbow units would likely have been outranged in practical battlefield terms, outshot in sustained combat, and disrupted before they could achieve decisive effects. Once artillery and musket volleys were already shaping the battlefield, the quieter and somewhat more precise bolt would not compensate for lower volume of fire and weaker integration into line tactics.

The broader strategic effect might have been to slow military modernization slightly in those armies that adopted crossbows too enthusiastically. States that stuck with firearms would likely gain an advantage as muskets improved further, especially with better flintlocks, socket bayonets, lighter guns, and eventually rifled weapons. So a large-scale return to crossbows in eighteenth-century Europe would probably have been remembered as an interesting but misguided detour: useful in a few specialist roles, but incapable of replacing the musket as the core weapon of modern armies.

items.question: What If the Black Death Had Devastated Poland?
human_answers: Poland wasn't actually "spared", it was merely less affected than the rest of Europe. That graphic is incorrect (or rather, incomplete), since a substantial number of both Poland and Milan's population did in fact die of the plague.
There are three types of plague, Pneumonic, Bubonic, and Septicemic all of which are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. People infected by fleas get the bubonic form of the plague.

ANOTHER EXPLANATION REGARDING POLAND IS THAT IT HAD A LOT OF JEWS, PARTICULARLY IN URBAN SETTINGS; NOW, WHY WERE Jews Less Affected? > And even if Jews died at a lesser rate, it can be attributed to the sanitary practices Jewish law.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual against the real historical baseline: Poland was not fully spared by the Black Death, but was generally less affected than many parts of Europe, with regional variation and uncertain evidence.

criteria.7-8: Accurately distinguishes myth from evidence, notes that Poland still suffered plague impacts, and defines a plausible higher-mortality counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual using cautious baseline claims, avoids overreliance on misleading plague maps, and specifies severity, geography, and timing of Poland’s hypothetical devastation.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of how a severe outbreak would affect population, labor, settlement, agriculture, urban life, and minority communities through plausible plague transmission and mortality mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Provides no causal mechanism for devastation or relies on magical, racial, or biologically false explanations.
criteria.3-4: Mentions deaths generally but does not explain transmission, demographic collapse, labor effects, or differential vulnerability.
criteria.5-6: Connects higher mortality to labor shortages, abandoned land, and urban disruption, but mechanisms remain broad or incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Explains plausible bubonic/pneumonic/septicemic plague dynamics, population loss, labor scarcity, migration, and effects on towns, farms, Jews, and elites.
criteria.9-10: Integrates disease biology, trade routes, settlement patterns, sanitation claims with caveats, and differentiated mortality into a coherent demographic mechanism.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces how a devastated Poland could alter state capacity, monarchy, nobility, military power, relations with Lithuania, the Teutonic Order, Bohemia, Hungary, and later regional balance.
criteria.1-2: Ignores politics entirely or makes implausible claims unrelated to medieval Central Europe.
criteria.3-4: Mentions political weakness or collapse vaguely without explaining institutional or geopolitical pathways.
criteria.5-6: Links depopulation to weaker taxation, military recruitment, or noble bargaining power, but downstream effects are thin.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly traces effects on the Piast/Jagiellonian trajectory, Polish-Lithuanian relations, Teutonic conflict, and regional power balances.
criteria.9-10: Builds a nuanced multi-generation chain from mortality to fiscal capacity, elite politics, military outcomes, dynastic unions, and altered Eastern/Central European development.

criteria.name: Economic, Social, and Cultural Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of major long-term societal effects, including serfdom, wages, land use, urbanization, Jewish communities, migration, religious interpretations, and social conflict.
criteria.1-2: Offers only generic catastrophe language with no Poland-specific social or economic consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions economic decline or social unrest but lacks specific mechanisms or medieval Polish context.
criteria.5-6: Discusses labor scarcity, wages, land abandonment, or peasant status, but misses important urban, religious, or minority dimensions.
criteria.7-8: Covers several major effects, including agriculture, towns, labor relations, migration, Jewish communities, and possible scapegoating or legal changes.
criteria.9-10: Explores interacting long-range effects on manorialism, serfdom, urban networks, ethnic/religious minorities, cultural memory, and Poland’s role in European migration and trade.

items.model_answer:
If the Black Death had devastated Poland on the same scale as western Europe, the effects would likely have been profound both for Poland itself and for the broader balance of power in eastern Europe. In actual history, Poland seems to have been less severely affected than many western regions, which helped preserve its population, agricultural output, and political continuity. If instead Poland had suffered catastrophic mortality, several major consequences become plausible.

First, Poland’s demographic and economic development would have been sharply disrupted. A massive population collapse would have reduced the labor force, lowered agricultural production, depopulated villages, and weakened trade networks. Town growth would likely have stalled, and royal revenues would have fallen. The nobility and crown would have faced a much smaller tax base and fewer soldiers. That alone could have made Poland a weaker and less cohesive kingdom in the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

Second, the political consequences could have been large. A severe plague often intensified elite competition, succession instability, and social strain. If Poland had lost a large share of its clergy, administrators, and nobles, state capacity could have declined. The monarchy might have struggled more to consolidate power, enforce law, or maintain border defenses. This could have made Poland more vulnerable to pressure from neighboring powers such as Bohemia, Hungary, the Teutonic Order, and later Lithuania or Muscovy.

Third, one of the biggest counterfactual effects concerns the Polish-Lithuanian union. A plague-ravaged Poland might have entered its union with Lithuania from a position of greater weakness, or perhaps not formed as strong a union at all. Since Poland played a central role in shaping that partnership, a heavily depopulated and economically damaged kingdom might have had less leverage, less military strength, and fewer resources to project influence eastward. The result could have been a looser union, a delayed union, or a more Lithuania-dominated arrangement.

That matters because the Polish-Lithuanian political system became one of the major powers of early modern Europe. If plague had crippled Poland beforehand, the combined state might never have emerged in the same form. This could have changed the outcome of regional struggles with the Teutonic Order, especially conflicts like Grunwald/Tannenberg. A weaker Poland might have been less able to check the Order, altering the political map of the Baltic.

Fourth, eastern Europe more broadly might have developed differently. A weaker Poland would have left more room for rival states to expand. The Teutonic Order might have remained stronger for longer. Bohemia or Hungary might have exercised more influence in central Europe. In the east, Lithuania might have followed a different political path, and Muscovy could have faced a different strategic environment. Over the long term, the absence of a strong Poland or Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth might have accelerated the rise of other regional powers.

There would also likely have been social consequences inside Poland similar to those seen elsewhere, though not necessarily identical. Labor scarcity could have increased peasants’ bargaining power at first, but east-central Europe often responded to late medieval demographic and market pressures by reinforcing noble control over peasants rather than loosening it. So Poland might still have moved toward stronger serfdom, but under conditions of greater instability and economic contraction. The church, urban institutions, and local communities would also have been strained by the loss of personnel and legitimacy.

Culturally, a more devastated Poland might have become less attractive to migrants, settlers, and merchants. That could have reduced the kingdom’s diversity and slowed urban and commercial development. Its role as a relatively stable and expanding realm in later medieval Europe would have been diminished.

In short, if the Black Death had devastated Poland, the most likely result is that Poland would have become poorer, weaker, and less politically influential at a crucial historical moment. That, in turn, could have reshaped the formation of the Polish-Lithuanian union, strengthened some of Poland’s rivals, and significantly altered the political development of central and eastern Europe. The biggest likely difference is not just that Poland would have suffered terribly, but that one of the key states in the region might never have become the major power it later was.

edus.text: If the Black Death had devastated Poland on the same scale as western Europe, the effects would likely have been profound both for Poland itself and for the broader balance of power in eastern Europe.
In actual history, Poland seems to have been less severely affected than many western regions,
which helped preserve its population, agricultural output, and political continuity.
If instead Poland had suffered catastrophic mortality, several major consequences become plausible.
First, Poland’s demographic and economic development would have been sharply disrupted.
A massive population collapse would have reduced the labor force, lowered agricultural production, depopulated villages, and weakened trade networks.
Town growth would likely have stalled, and royal revenues would have fallen.
The nobility and crown would have faced a much smaller tax base and fewer soldiers.
That alone could have made Poland a weaker and less cohesive kingdom in the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.
Second, the political consequences could have been large.
A severe plague often intensified elite competition, succession instability, and social strain.
If Poland had lost a large share of its clergy, administrators, and nobles, state capacity could have declined.
The monarchy might have struggled more to consolidate power, enforce law, or maintain border defenses.
This could have made Poland more vulnerable to pressure from neighboring powers such as Bohemia, Hungary, the Teutonic Order, and later Lithuania or Muscovy.
Third, one of the biggest counterfactual effects concerns the Polish-Lithuanian union.
A plague-ravaged Poland might have entered its union with Lithuania from a position of greater weakness, or perhaps not formed as strong a union at all.

Since Poland played a central role in shaping that partnership, a heavily depopulated and economically damaged kingdom might have had less leverage, less military strength, and fewer resources to project influence eastward.
The result could have been a looser union, a delayed union, or a more Lithuania-dominated arrangement.
That matters because the Polish-Lithuanian political system became one of the major powers of early modern Europe.
If plague had crippled Poland beforehand, the combined state might never have emerged in the same form.
This could have changed the outcome of regional struggles with the Teutonic Order, especially conflicts like Grunwald/Tannenberg.
A weaker Poland might have been less able to check the Order, altering the political map of the Baltic.
Fourth, eastern Europe more broadly might have developed differently.
A weaker Poland would have left more room for rival states to expand.
The Teutonic Order might have remained stronger for longer.
Bohemia or Hungary might have exercised more influence in central Europe.
In the east, Lithuania might have followed a different political path, and Muscovy could have faced a different strategic environment.
Over the long term, the absence of a strong Poland or Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth might have accelerated the rise of other regional powers.
There would also likely have been social consequences inside Poland similar to those seen elsewhere, though not necessarily identical.
Labor scarcity could have increased peasants’ bargaining power at first,
but east-central Europe often responded to late medieval demographic and market pressures by reinforcing noble control over peasants rather than loosening it.
So Poland might still have moved toward stronger serfdom, but under conditions of greater instability and economic contraction.
The church, urban institutions, and local communities would also have been strained by the loss of personnel and legitimacy.
Culturally, a more devastated Poland might have become less attractive to migrants, settlers, and merchants.
That could have reduced the kingdom’s diversity and slowed urban and commercial development.
Its role as a relatively stable and expanding realm in later medieval Europe would have been diminished.
In short, if the Black Death had devastated Poland, the most likely result is that Poland would have become poorer, weaker, and less politically influential at a crucial historical moment.

That, in turn, could have reshaped the formation of the Polish-Lithuanian union, strengthened some of Poland’s rivals, and significantly altered the political development of central and eastern Europe.
The biggest likely difference is not just that Poland would have suffered terribly,
but that one of the key states in the region might never have become the major power it later was.

items.model_answer:
If Europe had unified early in a durable way “like China,” the world would probably have looked much less politically fragmented, but the consequences would depend on what kind of unification happened and when. The short answer is that an early unified Europe likely would have been more internally peaceful and administratively coordinated, but probably less innovative in some areas, less politically pluralistic, and potentially even more formidable abroad.

China’s long periods of imperial unity created a very large, rich, and culturally connected political space. If Europe had developed something comparable—say, a single empire or enduring centralized state after Rome, or a stable continental state in the early medieval period—then many of the defining features of European history would change. There would likely be fewer interstate wars within Europe, because conflicts like the Hundred Years’ War, the Italian Wars, the Thirty Years’ War, and the long rivalry among France, the Habsburgs, Prussia, Britain, and Russia would either not happen in the same way or would become internal power struggles rather than wars among sovereign states. That alone could mean less devastation and more consistent economic integration.

A unified Europe would probably have had a larger internal market earlier. Standardized laws, taxation, roads, coinage, measures, and perhaps language policy could have reduced barriers to trade and state capacity problems. Economic growth might have been steadier. Some things that in actual history emerged only gradually through diplomacy, conquest, and trade could have been imposed from the center much earlier. Infrastructure and administration might have looked more Roman on a permanent basis.

But Europe’s fragmentation was also one of the engines of its dynamism. Because no single ruler controlled the whole continent, merchants, scholars, religious minorities, and political dissidents could often move elsewhere. If one prince censored ideas, another might welcome them. If one state taxed too heavily, capital might flee. If one kingdom lagged militarily or commercially, rivals copied or outcompeted it. This interstate competition helped drive military innovation, state-building, finance, navigation, and in some arguments even the Scientific Revolution. A unified Europe might therefore have been more stable but less experimentally creative. One bad imperial policy could have affected the whole continent, and there would be fewer external European rivals to force correction.

Religion would likely have evolved differently too. The Reformation, for example, depended partly on political fragmentation. Protestant rulers survived because the Holy Roman Empire and wider Europe were too divided for a single authority to crush them everywhere. In a unified Europe, either religious reform would be suppressed more successfully, producing a more religiously uniform continent, or a schism at the center could trigger a massive empire-wide crisis. So Europe might have been more ideologically homogeneous, but also more brittle when challenged.

Overseas expansion is one of the biggest uncertainties. In real history, European maritime empires grew out of fierce competition among Portugal, Spain, the Dutch Republic, France, and Britain. A unified Europe might have expanded overseas more slowly at first if the center focused on land administration rather than naval rivalry. But it also might have expanded even more decisively if a single continental empire could mobilize the resources of all Europe for exploration, conquest, and colonization. In that scenario, the Americas, Africa, and Asia might have faced not competing European empires, but one enormous superstate with greater manpower and coordination.

The balance of world power would likely shift sharply. A unified Europe emerging early, especially if it retained Roman-level Mediterranean integration and then expanded northward, could have become the dominant Old World power far earlier. The Islamic world, Byzantium, steppe empires, India, and later the Ottoman Empire would all face a more consolidated western rival. Russia might either be absorbed, blocked, or shaped very differently. The global system might become bipolar at times—perhaps unified Europe versus unified China—or else dominated by whichever giant state was better at projecting power overseas.

At the same time, unified empires often face classic problems: succession crises, regional revolts, bureaucratic stagnation, frontier overextension, and struggles between center and periphery. Europe is geographically harder to unify and hold than China in some respects. It has peninsulas, mountain ranges, maritime zones, and many historical core regions. So even if unification occurred, maintaining it could require heavy coercion or federal flexibility. A unified Europe might therefore oscillate between unity and fragmentation, more like a recurring empire than a permanently centralized nation-state.

So the most plausible overall result is this: an early unified Europe would likely be less internally war-prone and more economically integrated, but also less politically competitive. That could mean fewer destructive wars and earlier state capacity, yet also fewer of the cross-border rivalries that helped generate Europe’s unusual burst of military, scientific, and commercial expansion. If the unified state stayed effective, Europe might become an even stronger world hegemon than it was historically. If it became rigid, then instead of many competing European powers reshaping the world, you might get one immense empire that is richer and more orderly, but slower to adapt.

edus.text: If Europe had unified early in a durable way “like China,” the world would probably have looked much less politically fragmented,
but the consequences would depend on what kind of unification happened and when.
The short answer is that an early unified Europe likely would have been more internally peaceful and administratively coordinated,
but probably less innovative in some areas, less politically pluralistic, and potentially even more formidable abroad.
China’s long periods of imperial unity created a very large, rich, and culturally connected political space.
If Europe had developed something comparable—say, a single empire or enduring centralized state after Rome, or a stable continental state in the early medieval period—
then many of the defining features of European history would change.
There would likely be fewer interstate wars within Europe,
because conflicts like the Hundred Years’ War, the Italian Wars, the Thirty Years’ War, and long rivalries would either not happen in the same way or would become internal power struggles.
That alone could mean less devastation and more consistent economic integration.
A unified Europe would probably have had a larger internal market earlier.
Standardized laws, taxation, roads, coinage, measures, and perhaps language policy could have reduced barriers to trade and state capacity problems.
Economic growth might have been steadier.
Some developments that emerged gradually in actual history could have been imposed from the center much earlier.
Infrastructure and administration might have looked more Roman on a permanent basis.
But Europe’s fragmentation was also one of the engines of its dynamism.
Because no single ruler controlled the whole continent, merchants and others could often move elsewhere.
If one prince censored ideas, another might welcome them.
If one state taxed too heavily, capital might flee.
If one kingdom lagged, rivals copied or outcompeted it.
This interstate competition helped drive military innovation and other advances.
A unified Europe might therefore have been more stable but less experimentally creative.
One bad imperial policy could have affected the whole continent,
and there would be fewer external European rivals to force correction.
Religion would likely have evolved differently too.
The Reformation depended partly on political fragmentation.
Protestant rulers survived because Europe was too divided for a single authority to crush them everywhere.
In a unified Europe, reform would be suppressed more successfully or a central schism could trigger an empire-wide crisis.
So Europe might have been more ideologically homogeneous, but also more brittle when challenged.
Overseas expansion is one of the biggest uncertainties.
In real history, maritime empires grew out of fierce competition among European states.
A unified Europe might have expanded overseas more slowly at first if the center focused on land administration.
But it also might have expanded more decisively if it mobilized all European resources.
In that scenario, other regions might have faced one enormous superstate.
The balance of world power would likely shift sharply.
A unified Europe emerging early could have become the dominant Old World power far earlier.
Other major powers would face a more consolidated western rival.
The global system might become bipolar or dominated by whichever giant projected power better.
At the same time, unified empires often face classic problems.
Europe is geographically harder to unify and hold than China in some respects.
So even if unification occurred, maintaining it could require heavy coercion or federal flexibility.
A unified Europe might therefore oscillate between unity and fragmentation.
So the most plausible overall result is this:
an early unified Europe would likely be less internally war-prone and more economically integrated,
but also less politically competitive.
That could mean fewer destructive wars and earlier state capacity,
yet also fewer rivalries that helped generate expansion.
If the unified state stayed effective, Europe might become an even stronger hegemon.
If it became rigid, you might get one immense empire that is richer and more orderly, but slower to adapt.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Discipline and Historical Baseline
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately establishes the real historical baseline—Khalkhin Gol/Nomonhan, Japan's north-vs-south strategic debate, the 1941 Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, Soviet force posture in Siberia, and Japan's resource constraints—before reasoning from the altered premise of a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East.
criteria.1-2: Misstates core facts or ignores the actual strategic context; treats the scenario as generic Japan-vs-USSR war.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few relevant facts but with major omissions or inaccuracies about timing, motives, or military conditions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly correct baseline, including Japan's strategic choices and Soviet-Japanese tensions, but lacks detail or nuance.
criteria.7-8: Accurately grounds the counterfactual in the north-south debate, Khalkhin Gol lessons, neutrality pact, and Japanese resource problems.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the divergence point and explains why the real-world decision favored attacking southward rather than Siberia, using the baseline to constrain all later reasoning.

criteria.name: Military Feasibility and Operational Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the plausibility of the military analysis: Japanese Kwantung Army capabilities, Soviet Far Eastern defenses, terrain, logistics, armor/artillery/airpower balance, naval irrelevance or limits, and the likely operational tempo of a campaign in Siberia and Manchuria.
criteria.1-2: Offers implausible military claims, such as easy Japanese conquest of Siberia or Soviet collapse without logistical analysis.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that fighting would be difficult but gives vague or one-sided operational reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Discusses major military factors such as logistics, terrain, and Soviet strength, though some mechanisms remain underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Gives a coherent operational picture showing why Japan would struggle to achieve decisive gains against Soviet Far Eastern forces.
criteria.9-10: Integrates force quality, geography, supply lines, seasonal effects, Soviet reserves, and Japanese strategic limitations into a highly plausible campaign assessment.

criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer reasons through effects on Operation Barbarossa, Stalin's transfer or retention of Siberian divisions, the defense of Moscow, Soviet war production, German strategy, and whether a two-front Soviet war meaningfully changes the Eastern Front.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the German-Soviet war or makes unsupported claims that Germany automatically wins or nothing changes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Moscow or Siberian divisions but treats them simplistically without causal linkage.
criteria.5-6: Explains that a Japanese attack could limit Soviet redeployments and pressure Moscow, but leaves key timing and scale issues vague.
criteria.7-8: Carefully connects Japanese action to Soviet force allocation, Moscow's defense, German opportunities, and limits on Axis coordination.
criteria.9-10: Provides a nuanced, timing-sensitive analysis of whether and how a Far Eastern front could alter Barbarossa, while avoiding deterministic claims.

criteria.name: Pacific, Resource, and Allied Downstream Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of long-range consequences beyond the immediate Soviet front: Japan's oil problem, whether it still attacks Southeast Asia or Pearl Harbor, US embargo and entry into the war, Allied aid to the USSR, Chinese theater effects, and global Axis coordination.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on Siberia and ignores Japan's resource crisis, the United States, China, and the Pacific War.
criteria.3-4: Mentions oil or Pearl Harbor but gives disconnected or contradictory downstream effects.
criteria.5-6: Addresses several major consequences, such as delayed or altered Pacific War and resource shortages, but lacks a full chain.
criteria.7-8: Explains how attacking north would affect Japan's oil strategy, US relations, Southeast Asia, China, and Allied support to the USSR.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent global cascade linking Japan's northern war to Pacific timing, US entry, resource exhaustion, Soviet aid routes, and Axis strategic coordination.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration, Causal Coherence, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Judges whether the answer presents a logically consistent long-range counterfactual with explicit uncertainty, avoids overclaiming, distinguishes likely from possible outcomes, and maintains internal consistency about timing, alliances, and strategic choices.
criteria.1-2: Is deterministic, internally contradictory, or relies on unsupported speculation and hindsight.
criteria.3-4: Shows some causal reasoning but contains major leaps, inconsistent assumptions, or exaggerated certainty.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a plausible main line with moderate uncertainty, though some causal links are thin or underqualified.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes while keeping the chain of events consistent across theaters.
criteria.9-10: Offers a disciplined counterfactual with explicit contingencies, alternative branches, calibrated probabilities, and no significant contradictions.

items.model_answer:
If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II, the most likely result is that the war would have become worse for all sides, but it probably would not have saved Germany from defeat. It could, however, have changed the timing and geography of the war in important ways.

The key issue is when such an attack happens. That matters enormously.

If Japan attacks in 1941, during Germany’s invasion of the Soviet Union, the effect could have been serious. Historically, Stalin was able to transfer well-trained Siberian and Far Eastern divisions westward once he was confident Japan would not strike. Those troops helped stiffen Soviet defenses before Moscow in late 1941. If Japan had attacked instead, Stalin would likely have kept more forces in the east. That would have made the Soviet position around Moscow more dangerous and may have improved Germany’s chances of taking more territory or avoiding its winter setback. Even so, Japan faced huge constraints. Its army in Manchuria was large, but the Soviet Far East was difficult terrain, with long supply lines, harsh weather, and limited infrastructure. Japan had also been badly shaken by its defeat to the Soviets at Khalkhin Gol in 1939, which helped push Tokyo toward expansion southward rather than northward. So a Japanese attack might have tied down Soviet forces, but it is far from certain Japan could have achieved a decisive breakthrough.

If Japan attacks later, after December 1941, the picture changes. Once Japan was already at war with the United States and Britain, opening a major front against the USSR would have stretched Japanese resources even more dangerously. Japan’s main strategic weakness was industrial capacity, especially oil, shipping, and heavy production. Fighting the US Navy and trying to conquer resource-rich areas in Southeast Asia already strained the empire. A Soviet front would have consumed troops, transport, ammunition, and fuel Japan could not easily replace. In that scenario, Japan likely hurts itself more than it helps Germany.

For the Soviet Union, a Japanese attack would have been painful, but not necessarily fatal. The Soviets had significant forces in the Far East, and unlike Germany, Japan was less capable of deep mechanized operations across vast continental space. The USSR might have lost some border areas, ports, or sections of railway, especially around Vladivostok or along the Maritime Provinces, but conquering all of eastern Siberia was beyond Japan’s realistic capacity. The Soviet state was built for absorbing huge losses and shifting resources across vast distances. Unless the Japanese attack coincided with a total German collapse of Soviet defenses in the west, the USSR probably survives.

One important consequence concerns Allied aid. Vladivostok was a major route for Lend-Lease shipments from the United States to the Soviet Union, especially before other routes became fully effective. If Japan attacked the Soviet Far East, this route would be threatened or cut. That would make Soviet logistics worse, especially for trucks, raw materials, and industrial inputs. But Lend-Lease also moved through Persia and the Arctic, so the effect would hurt the USSR without necessarily knocking it out of the war.

For Germany, this is the central question: would a Japanese attack have changed the outcome on the Eastern Front enough to let Hitler win? Probably not. Germany’s larger problems were structural: underestimating Soviet manpower and industry, failing to prepare for a long war, logistical overreach, and Hitler’s own strategic mistakes. Even if the USSR were weakened by a second front, Germany still faced immense Soviet depth and growing Allied industrial power. At best, Japan’s entry against the USSR might have prolonged the war in the east, delayed Soviet offensives, or changed the line at which Germany was finally defeated.

There are also broader consequences. If Japan attacks the USSR instead of striking south against the United States and European colonies, then the Pacific War may look completely different. No Pearl Harbor, or at least a delayed one, would be one of the biggest possibilities. In that version of history, the United States might enter the war later or under different circumstances. Britain and the Netherlands might keep their Asian colonies longer. Japan, however, would then face its oil problem even more sharply, because the drive south was largely about securing resources. A northern strategy against the USSR did not solve Japan’s petroleum shortage. So unless Japan still later moved south, it would be fighting a major war without fixing the resource crisis that drove its expansion.

So the most balanced answer is this: a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East could have significantly complicated Soviet strategy and possibly helped Germany in the short term, especially in 1941, by pinning Soviet divisions in the east and threatening key supply routes. edus.text: If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II, the most likely result is that the war would have become worse for all sides, but it probably would not have saved Germany from defeat.
It could, however, have changed the timing and geography of the war in important ways.
The key issue is when such an attack happens.
That matters enormously.
If Japan attacks in 1941, during Germany’s invasion of the Soviet Union, the effect could have been serious.
Historically, Stalin was able to transfer well-trained Siberian and Far Eastern divisions westward once he was confident Japan would not strike.
Those troops helped stiffen Soviet defenses before Moscow in late 1941.
If Japan had attacked instead, Stalin would likely have kept more forces in the east.
That would have made the Soviet position around Moscow more dangerous and may have improved Germany’s chances of taking more territory or avoiding its winter setback.
Even so, Japan faced huge constraints.
Its army in Manchuria was large, but the Soviet Far East was difficult terrain, with long supply lines, harsh weather, and limited infrastructure.
Japan had also been badly shaken by its defeat to the Soviets at Khalkhin Gol in 1939, which helped push Tokyo toward expansion southward rather than northward.
So a Japanese attack might have tied down Soviet forces, but it is far from certain Japan could have achieved a decisive breakthrough.
If Japan attacks later, after December 1941, the picture changes.
Once Japan was already at war with the United States and Britain, opening a major front against the USSR would have stretched Japanese resources even more dangerously.
Japan’s main strategic weakness was industrial capacity, especially oil, shipping, and heavy production.
Fighting the US Navy and trying to conquer resource-rich areas in Southeast Asia already strained the empire.
A Soviet front would have consumed troops, transport, ammunition, and fuel Japan could not easily replace.
In that scenario, Japan likely hurts itself more than it helps Germany.
For the Soviet Union, a Japanese attack would have been painful, but not necessarily fatal.
The Soviets had significant forces in the Far East, and unlike Germany, Japan was less capable of deep mechanized operations across vast continental space.

The USSR might have lost some border areas, ports, or sections of railway, especially around Vladivostok or along the Maritime Provinces, but conquering all of eastern Siberia was beyond Japan’s realistic capacity.
The Soviet state was built for absorbing huge losses and shifting resources across vast distances.
Unless the Japanese attack coincided with a total German collapse of Soviet defenses in the west, the USSR probably survives.
One important consequence concerns Allied aid.
Vladivostok was a major route for Lend-Lease shipments from the United States to the Soviet Union, especially before other routes became fully effective.
If Japan attacked the Soviet Far East, this route would be threatened or cut.
That would make Soviet logistics worse, especially for trucks, raw materials, and industrial inputs.
But Lend-Lease also moved through Persia and the Arctic, so the effect would hurt the USSR without necessarily knocking it out of the war.
For Germany, this is the central question: would a Japanese attack have changed the outcome on the Eastern Front enough to let Hitler win?
Probably not.
Germany’s larger problems were structural: underestimating Soviet manpower and industry, failing to prepare for a long war, logistical overreach, and Hitler’s own strategic mistakes.
Even if the USSR were weakened by a second front, Germany still faced immense Soviet depth and growing Allied industrial power.
At best, Japan’s entry against the USSR might have prolonged the war in the east, delayed Soviet offensives, or changed the line at which Germany was finally defeated.
There are also broader consequences.
If Japan attacks the USSR instead of striking south against the United States and European colonies, then the Pacific War may look completely different.
No Pearl Harbor, or at least a delayed one, would be one of the biggest possibilities.
In that version of history, the United States might enter the war later or under different circumstances.
Britain and the Netherlands might keep their Asian colonies longer.
Japan, however, would then face its oil problem even more sharply, because the drive south was largely about securing resources.
A northern strategy against the USSR did not solve Japan’s petroleum shortage.
So unless Japan still later moved south, it would be fighting a major war without fixing the resource crisis that drove its expansion.

So the most balanced answer is this: a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East could have significantly complicated Soviet strategy and possibly helped Germany in the short term, especially in 1941, by pinning Soviet divisions in the east and threatening key supply routes.
But Japan was unlikely to conquer deep Soviet territory, and the attack probably would not have been enough to bring down the Soviet Union by itself.
In the larger picture, it might have prolonged the war, increased casualties, and reshaped the Pacific theater, but it probably would not have fundamentally reversed the eventual defeat of the Axis.

nodes.text: If Japan had attacked the Soviet Far East during World War II, the most likely result is that the war would have become worse for all sides, but it probably would not have saved Germany from defeat.
It could, however, have changed the timing and geography of the war in important ways.
The key issue is when such an attack happens.
That matters enormously.
If Japan attacks in 1941, during Germany’s invasion of the Soviet Union, the effect could have been serious.
Historically, Stalin was able to transfer well-trained Siberian and Far Eastern divisions westward once he was confident Japan would not strike.
Those troops helped stiffen Soviet defenses before Moscow in late 1941.
If Japan had attacked instead, Stalin would likely have kept more forces in the east.
That would have made the Soviet position around Moscow more dangerous and may have improved Germany’s chances of taking more territory or avoiding its winter setback.
Even so, Japan faced huge constraints.
Its army in Manchuria was large, but the Soviet Far East was difficult terrain, with long supply lines, harsh weather, and limited infrastructure.
Japan had also been badly shaken by its defeat to the Soviets at Khalkhin Gol in 1939, which helped push Tokyo toward expansion southward rather than northward.
So a Japanese attack might have tied down Soviet forces, but it is far from certain Japan could have achieved a decisive breakthrough.
If Japan attacks later, after December 1941, the picture changes.
Once Japan was already at war with the United States and Britain, opening a major front against the USSR would have stretched Japanese resources even more dangerously.
Japan’s main strategic weakness was industrial capacity, especially oil, shipping, and heavy production.
Fighting the US Navy and trying to conquer resource-rich areas in Southeast Asia already strained the empire.
A Soviet front would have consumed troops, transport, ammunition, and fuel Japan could not easily replace.
In that scenario, Japan likely hurts itself more than it helps Germany.
For the Soviet Union, a Japanese attack would have been painful, but not necessarily fatal.
The Soviets had significant forces in the Far East, and unlike Germany, Japan was less capable of deep mechanized operations across vast continental space.

The USSR might have lost some border areas, ports, or sections of railway, especially around Vladivostok or along the Maritime Provinces, but conquering all of eastern Siberia was beyond Japan’s realistic capacity.
The Soviet state was built for absorbing huge losses and shifting resources across vast distances.
Unless the Japanese attack coincided with a total German collapse of Soviet defenses in the west, the USSR probably survives.
One important consequence concerns Allied aid.
Vladivostok was a major route for Lend-Lease shipments from the United States to the Soviet Union, especially before other routes became fully effective.
If Japan attacked the Soviet Far East, this route would be threatened or cut.
That would make Soviet logistics worse, especially for trucks, raw materials, and industrial inputs.
But Lend-Lease also moved through Persia and the Arctic, so the effect would hurt the USSR without necessarily knocking it out of the war.
For Germany, this is the central question: would a Japanese attack have changed the outcome on the Eastern Front enough to let Hitler win?
Probably not.
Germany’s larger problems were structural: underestimating Soviet manpower and industry, failing to prepare for a long war, logistical overreach, and Hitler’s own strategic mistakes.
Even if the USSR were weakened by a second front, Germany still faced immense Soviet depth and growing Allied industrial power.
At best, Japan’s entry against the USSR might have prolonged the war in the east, delayed Soviet offensives, or changed the line at which Germany was finally defeated.
There are also broader consequences.
If Japan attacks the USSR instead of striking south against the United States and European colonies, then the Pacific War may look completely different.
No Pearl Harbor, or at least a delayed one, would be one of the biggest possibilities.
In that version of history, the United States might enter the war later or under different circumstances.
Britain and the Netherlands might keep their Asian colonies longer.
Japan, however, would then face its oil problem even more sharply, because the drive south was largely about securing resources.
A northern strategy against the USSR did not solve Japan’s petroleum shortage.
So unless Japan still later moved south, it would be fighting a major war without fixing the resource crisis that drove its expansion.

So the most balanced answer is this: a Japanese attack on the Soviet Far East could have significantly complicated Soviet strategy and possibly helped Germany in the short term, especially in 1941, by pinning Soviet divisions in the east and threatening key supply routes.
But Japan was unlikely to conquer deep Soviet territory, and the attack probably would not have been enough to bring down the Soviet Union by itself.
In the larger picture, it might have prolonged the war, increased casualties, and reshaped the Pacific theater, but it probably would not have fundamentally reversed the eventual defeat of the Axis.

items.question: What If Gunpowder-Era Fortresses Were Built as Circles or Squares Instead of Stars?
human_answers: Star forts or bastion forts are designed to enable enfilade (or flanking) fire: shooting on the line of attackers from the side, significantly increasing firing efficiency of the defender. Flanking fire allows guns placed in the side wall of the bastion (pr...

Imagine that you are defending a fort with old-fashioned round bastions in the Middle Ages. Your walls are high, but once the enemy comes close and starts scaling the walls, very few of your defenders can engage them.

These outcroppings are called Bastions and they became common when muskets and cannons became common in European warfare. The problem with a square or circle forts is that when the enemy has reached the wall, they are in your dead zone.

items.model_answer:
If gunpowder-era fortresses had been built as simple circles or squares instead of star forts, they would generally have been much weaker against artillery and easier for attackers to besiege.

The key reason star forts developed was not aesthetic but geometric. Cannon made medieval high walls and simple towered layouts obsolete, because artillery could batter straight walls from a distance and create breaches. Star forts solved this by using angled bastions and low, thick ramparts. Those angles let defenders fire along the faces of adjacent walls, creating overlapping fields of fire and eliminating “dead ground,” where attackers could approach without being shot at.

A circular fortress would have some advantages over a square: it would distribute stress fairly evenly and present no sharp corners that concentrated damage. But it would still have a major problem: defenders on a smooth circular wall could not easily fire along the base of the wall itself. Attackers who reached the foot of the wall would be relatively sheltered. A square fortress would be worse, because its corners would create especially vulnerable zones and weak spots for artillery concentration, while also leaving blind areas that were hard to defend effectively.

By contrast, the star-shaped layout projected bastions outward so each point could cover the next. If one wall face was attacked, defenders from neighboring bastions could rake the assault from the side. This flanking fire was one of the central principles of early modern fortification. Without it, besiegers could dig trenches, move up artillery, and assault breaches with much less punishment.

So in a counterfactual world of circular or square gunpowder fortresses, a few things likely follow. First, siege warfare becomes shorter and more favorable to attackers, because fortresses fall faster. Second, states may need larger field armies and more mobile defenses, since static strongpoints would be less reliable. Third, military engineers would probably invent some other external works—detached batteries, ravelins, caponiers, or ringed outworks—to compensate for the geometric weakness of pure circles and squares. In other words, even if the central fort started as a circle or square, it would tend to evolve outward into something more like a star anyway.

If rulers stubbornly insisted on true circular or square plans with no angled outworks, these forts would still work to some extent, especially if made low, thick, and surrounded by ditches. They would not be useless. But they would be noticeably inferior in the artillery age because they could not provide the same mutual flanking fire that made star forts so hard to take.

So the short answer is: circles or squares could exist, but against gunpowder siege tactics they would usually be less defensible than stars, and military architecture would either suffer for it or gradually reinvent the star-fort principle in another form.

edus.text: If gunpowder-era fortresses had been built as simple circles or squares instead of star forts,
they would generally have been much weaker against artillery and easier for attackers to besiege.
The key reason star forts developed was not aesthetic but geometric.
Cannon made medieval high walls and simple towered layouts obsolete,
because artillery could batter straight walls from a distance and create breaches.
Star forts solved this by using angled bastions and low, thick ramparts.
Those angles let defenders fire along the faces of adjacent walls,
creating overlapping fields of fire and eliminating “dead ground,”
where attackers could approach without being shot at.
A circular fortress would have some advantages over a square:
it would distribute stress fairly evenly
and present no sharp corners that concentrated damage.
But it would still have a major problem:
defenders on a smooth circular wall could not easily fire along the base of the wall itself.
Attackers who reached the foot of the wall would be relatively sheltered.
A square fortress would be worse,
because its corners would create especially vulnerable zones and weak spots for artillery concentration,
while also leaving blind areas that were hard to defend effectively.
By contrast, the star-shaped layout projected bastions outward
so each point could cover the next.
If one wall face was attacked,
defenders from neighboring bastions could rake the assault from the side.
This flanking fire was one of the central principles of early modern fortification.
Without it, besiegers could dig trenches, move up artillery, and assault breaches with much less punishment.
So in a counterfactual world of circular or square gunpowder fortresses,
a few things likely follow.
First, siege warfare becomes shorter and more favorable to attackers,
because fortresses fall faster.
Second, states may need larger field armies and more mobile defenses,
since static strongpoints would be less reliable.
Third, military engineers would probably invent some other external works
to compensate for the geometric weakness of pure circles and squares.
In other words, even if the central fort started as a circle or square,
it would tend to evolve outward into something more like a star anyway.
If rulers stubbornly insisted on true circular or square plans with no angled outworks,
these forts would still work to some extent,
especially if made low, thick, and surrounded by ditches.
They would not be useless.
But they would be noticeably inferior in the artillery age
because they could not provide the same mutual flanking fire
that made star forts so hard to take.
So the short answer is:
circles or squares could exist,
but against gunpowder siege tactics they would usually be less defensible than stars,
and military architecture would either suffer for it or gradually reinvent the star-fort principle in another form.

items.question: What If Germany Had Blockaded the Strait of Gibraltar in World War II?
human_answers: > ...but if the Strait is guarded such that they can't get them without braving an enfilading strafe of torpedoes, then it wouldn't do much good even if they knew where they are. From this comment by the OP, and others like it, it seems they don't appreciat...

Gibraltar during the war had a quite formidable British naval presence (Force H), an airfield, and significant coastal gun emplacements easily capable of covering the entire strait. > The primary batteries were a set of twin 9.2" naval guns guns at the sout...
While you are at it why not blockade the port of London? Isn't that a better target?

I'm not a historian nor a scholar of sorts, but I was lucky to be at the right place at the right time and found out from one of the most capable people who could answer this question. I lived in Madrid, Spain in the late 60s, early 70s.

Blockade requires local superiority To enforce a blockade at a chokepoint, you need to arrive there and stay there, winning any engagements. To win local engagements, you need to be stronger than an expected blockade-breaking force.
items.original_question: 二战时德国为何不封锁直布罗陀海峡？直布罗陀海峡最窄处宽约14公里。二战时德国为何不封锁？在我看来，只有少数潜艇和驱逐舰可以完成这项工作。难道德国海军（Kriegsmarine）没有能力封锁它吗？海底狼群至少在那个咽喉要道捕猎过吗？封锁将适用于美国/英国/苏联船只，但当然允许西班牙和其他中立国家。想必这对西班牙来说不会是一个政治问题。注意：我不是在谈论英国控制下的直布罗陀要塞。那是另一回事了。

items.model_answer:
If Germany had somehow been able to blockade the Strait of Gibraltar during World War II, the effects would have been very serious for Britain and for the wider Mediterranean war, but the outcome would depend heavily on how complete and how long the blockade lasted.

The Strait of Gibraltar was the narrow entrance between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. If Germany had closed it, Britain’s naval movement between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean would have been badly disrupted. Supplies, warships, and reinforcements going to Malta, Egypt, and the Middle East would have had to rely much more on the long route around the Cape of Good Hope. That would mean more time, more fuel, fewer ships available, and slower support for British forces.

The most immediate consequence would likely have been a much worse position for Malta. Malta depended on British resupply and was already under intense pressure. If the western entrance to the Mediterranean were blocked, keeping Malta supplied would become much harder. A weakened or starving Malta would matter a lot, because Malta was one of the main bases from which the British attacked Axis shipping going to North Africa. If Malta were neutralized, Axis convoys to Libya would suffer fewer losses, and Rommel’s Afrika Korps would probably receive fuel, ammunition, and replacements more reliably.

That, in turn, could have strengthened the Axis campaign in North Africa. Rommel’s biggest recurring problem was logistics, not just battlefield skill. Better supply from Italy to Libya could have allowed stronger offensives toward Egypt. The British position in Egypt and around the Suez Canal would become more dangerous. A successful Axis thrust to the Suez Canal was still not guaranteed, because long desert supply lines, British resistance, and American material support would remain major obstacles, but Germany and Italy would have had a better chance than they did historically.

The blockade would also hurt British naval flexibility. The Royal Navy used Gibraltar as a key base connecting fleets and escort routes. If the strait were closed, British control inside the Mediterranean would weaken, and the central and eastern Mediterranean might become much more contested or even temporarily dominated by Axis air and naval power. British operations in North Africa, Greece, and support for the eastern Mediterranean would all become harder.

Politically and strategically, such a blockade could also strengthen Axis influence in Spain and Vichy France if their cooperation were involved. In reality, Germany could not easily blockade Gibraltar without either capturing Gibraltar itself, gaining Spanish entry into the war, or deploying sustained air and naval power close enough to make passage impossible. So the scenario implies a much stronger Axis strategic position than Germany actually achieved. If Spain joined the Axis and Gibraltar fell, the whole western Mediterranean balance could shift.

Even so, it probably would not win the war for Germany by itself. Britain would still have the Atlantic, American industrial support, and the ability to reroute shipping globally. The Soviet front would still absorb most German strength after 1941. The United States would still be an overwhelming long-term factor once it entered the war. So a Gibraltar blockade could have prolonged the war, made the North African and Middle Eastern theaters much more dangerous for the Allies, and perhaps led to temporary Axis gains such as the fall of Malta or a deeper advance toward Egypt. But by itself it is unlikely to have changed the final global outcome unless it was part of a much larger chain of Axis successes, especially against Britain in the Mediterranean and against the Soviet Union in the east.

So the best short answer is: blocking Gibraltar would probably have made the Mediterranean far more favorable to the Axis, endangered Malta and Egypt, and strengthened Rommel significantly, but it still likely would not have been enough on its own to give Germany overall victory in World War II.

The blockade would also hurt British naval flexibility.
The Royal Navy used Gibraltar as a key base connecting fleets and escort routes.
If the strait were closed, British control inside the Mediterranean would weaken,
and the central and eastern Mediterranean might become much more contested or even temporarily dominated by Axis air and naval power.
British operations in North Africa, Greece, and support for the eastern Mediterranean would all become harder.
Politically and strategically, such a blockade could also strengthen Axis influence in Spain and Vichy France if their cooperation were involved.

In reality, Germany could not easily blockade Gibraltar without either capturing Gibraltar itself, gaining Spanish entry into the war, or deploying sustained air and naval power close enough to make passage impossible.
So the scenario implies a much stronger Axis strategic position than Germany actually achieved.
If Spain joined the Axis and Gibraltar fell, the whole western Mediterranean balance could shift.
Even so, it probably would not win the war for Germany by itself.
Britain would still have the Atlantic, American industrial support, and the ability to reroute shipping globally.
The Soviet front would still absorb most German strength after 1941.
The United States would still be an overwhelming long-term factor once it entered the war.

So a Gibraltar blockade could have prolonged the war, made the North African and Middle Eastern theaters much more dangerous for the Allies, and perhaps led to temporary Axis gains such as the fall of Malta or a deeper advance toward Egypt.
But by itself it is unlikely to have changed the final global outcome
unless it was part of a much larger chain of Axis successes, especially against Britain in the Mediterranean and against the Soviet Union in the east.
So the best short answer is: blocking Gibraltar would probably have made the Mediterranean far more favorable to the Axis, endangered Malta and Egypt, and strengthened Rommel significantly,
but it still likely would not have been enough on its own to give Germany overall victory in World War II.

items.question: What If You Opened a 10-Meter Drain to Space at the Bottom of Challenger Deep?
human_answers: I want to get one thing out of the way first: According to my rough calculations, if an aircraft carrier sank and got stuck against the drain, the pressure would easily be enough to fold it up[1]Extrapolated from the maximum pressure tolerable by icebreaker ship hull plates http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf (http://www.iacs.org.uk/document/public/Publications/Unified_requirements/PDF/UR_I_pdf410.pdf) and suck it through. Cooool. Just how far away is this portal? If we put it near the Earth, the ocean would just fall back down into the atmosphere. As it fell, it would heat up and turn to steam, which would condense and fall right back into the ocean as rain. The energy input into the atmosphere alone would also wreak all kinds of havoc with our climate, to say nothing of the huge clouds of high-altitude steam. So let's put the ocean-dumping portal far away—say, on Mars. (In fact, I vote we put it directly above the Curiosity rover; that way, it will finally have incontrovertible evidence of liquid water on Mars's surface.) What happens to the Earth? Not much. It would actually take hundreds of thousands of years for the ocean to drain. Even though the opening is wider than a basketball court, and the water is forced through at incredible speeds,[2]xkcd.com/969 (http://xkcd.com/969/) the oceans are huge. When you started, the water level would drop by less than a centimeter per day. There wouldn't even be a cool whirlpool at the surface—the opening is too small and the ocean is too deep.[3]An experimental study of critical submergence to avoid free-surface vortices at vertical intakes (http://www.leg.state.mn.us/docs/pre2003/other/840235.pdf) (It's the same reason you don't get a whirlpool in the bathtub until the water is more than halfway drained.) But let's suppose we speed up the draining by opening more drains. (Remember to clean the whale filter every few days), so the water level starts to drop more quickly. Let's take a look at how the map would change. Here's how it looks at the start: [Image: image] And here's the map after the oceans drop 50 meters: [Image: image] It's pretty similar, but there are a few small changes. Sri Lanka, New Guinea, Great Britain, Java, and Borneo are now connected to their neighbors. And after 2000 years of trying to hold back the sea, the Netherlands are finally high and dry. No longer living with the constant threat of a cataclysmic flood, they're free to turn their energies toward outward expansion. They immediately spread out and claim the newly-exposed land. [Image: image] When the sea level reaches (minus) 100 meters, a huge new island off the coast of Nova Scotia is exposed—the former site of the Grand Banks. You may start to notice something odd: Not all the seas are shrinking. The Black Sea, for example, shrinks only a little, then stops. This is because these bodies are no longer connected to the ocean. As the water level falls, some basins cut off from the drain in the Pacific. Depending on the details of the sea floor, the flow of water out of the basin might carve a deeper channel, allowing it to continue to flow out. But most of them will eventually become landlocked and stop draining. [Image: image] At 200 meters, the map is starting to look weird. New islands are appearing. Indonesia is a big blob. The Netherlands now control much of Europe. [Image: image] Japan is now an isthmus connecting the Korean peninsula with Russia. New Zealand gains new islands. The Netherlands expand north. [Image: image] New Zealand grows dramatically. The Arctic Ocean is cut off and its the water level stops falling. The Netherlands cross the new land bridge into North America. [Image: image] The sea has dropped by two kilometers. New islands are popping up left and right. The Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are losing their connections with the Atlantic. I don't even know what New Zealand is doing. [Image: image] At three kilometers, many of the peaks of the mid-ocean ridge—the world's longest mountain range—break the surface. Vast swaths of rugged new land emerge. [Image: image] By this point, most of the major oceans have become disconnected and stopped draining. The exact locations and sizes of the various inland seas are hard to predict; this is only a rough estimate. [Image: image] This is what the map looks like when the drain finally empties. There's a surprising amount of water left, although much of it consists of very shallow seas, with a few trenches where the water is as deep as four or five kilometers. Vacuuming up half the oceans would massively alter the climate and ecosystems in ways that are hard to predict. At the very least, it would almost certainly involve a collapse of the biosphere and mass extinctions at every level. But it's possible—if unlikely—that humans could manage to survive. If we did, we'd have this to look forward to: [Image: image]
