rubrics.question_focus: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?

criteria.name: Endpoint Plausibility for the Steak-Drop Question
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically plausible conclusion about how far a steak must be dropped to become cooked, including the distinction between searing, cooking through, freezing, and destruction.
criteria.1-2: Claims a simple modest height cooks the steak, or gives an arbitrary distance with no plausible physical endpoint.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes very high altitude is needed but incorrectly says the steak cooks through cleanly from a single drop.
criteria.5-6: States that tens to hundreds of kilometers may sear or heat the surface, but is vague about whether the interior cooks.
criteria.7-8: Correctly concludes that no practical drop cooks it through; around space/suborbital heights may singe or sear while the inside remains raw.
criteria.9-10: Accurately frames the best result as Pittsburgh-rare-like: high-altitude/suborbital drops can char or sear the outside, but full cooking fails because higher speeds cause ablation/destruction before heat penetrates.

criteria.name: Aerodynamic Heating Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains the correct cause and conditions of heating during the fall: compressive shock heating at high Mach numbers, not ordinary rubbing friction.
criteria.1-2: Attributes cooking mainly to simple air friction or impact heat with no discussion of compression or Mach effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions fast fall heating but confuses friction, pressure, and atmospheric effects.
criteria.5-6: Identifies compression or shock heating but gives little detail about when it matters.
criteria.7-8: Explains that noticeable heating begins at supersonic/hypersonic speeds and depends on atmospheric density and shock-layer temperature.
criteria.9-10: Clearly links altitude, Mach number, shock/compressive heating, thin air, and rapid deceleration, avoiding the common misconception that friction alone cooks the steak.

criteria.name: Trajectory and Atmospheric Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer tracks the long-range causal chain from release altitude through acceleration, peak speed, deceleration, terminal velocity, and impact.
criteria.1-2: Treats the steak as falling at one constant speed or ignores atmospheric drag and altitude changes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions drag or terminal velocity but does not connect them to the changing atmosphere.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that higher drops produce faster speeds and later slowing, but the sequence is incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Describes acceleration in thin upper air, slowing in denser lower atmosphere, and arrival near terminal velocity rather than orbital reentry speed.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent end-to-end path: little heating at Baumgartner-like heights, supersonic near roughly 50 km, brief heating near 70–100 km, stronger heating from hundreds of km, followed by deceleration and low-altitude cold-air exposure.

criteria.name: Heat Transfer, Cooking, Freezing, and Ablation Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes surface temperature from internal doneness and accounts for heat penetration, cold stratospheric exposure, charring, and material loss.
criteria.1-2: Assumes hot outside air instantly cooks the whole steak or ignores the steak’s interior.
criteria.3-4: Mentions surface heating but misses heat-transfer time or cold-air effects.
criteria.5-6: Notes that short exposure may sear the surface while the center stays raw, with limited explanation.
criteria.7-8: Explains that brief hot blasts are followed by minutes of subfreezing high-speed airflow, preventing thorough cooking.
criteria.9-10: Fully captures the tradeoff: low altitudes do not heat enough, intermediate heights singe/sear briefly, and higher hypersonic drops char and ablate outer layers faster than heat can cook the interior.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles assumptions and uncertainties specific to a falling steak while avoiding internally inconsistent claims.
criteria.1-2: Presents overconfident numerical claims, contradicts itself, or ignores basic assumptions such as steak size, drag, and tumbling.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but still makes unsupported or conflicting claims about speed, cooking, or survival.
criteria.5-6: States reasonable assumptions but leaves key uncertainties underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty about drag coefficient, orientation, tumbling, breakup, and landing while maintaining a consistent conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates robust conclusions from model-dependent details, noting uncertainties in steak shape/tumbling/ablation while preserving a contradiction-free causal story.

items.model_answer:
If you mean “could a steak be cooked just by dropping it from a great height,” the basic answer is: in principle, yes, but only from an absurdly large drop, and in practice it would burn on the outside, stay undercooked inside, and probably be ruined.

The key idea is that falling converts gravitational potential energy into heat, but only if that energy is actually dissipated into the steak, mainly through air resistance or impact. To estimate the minimum height, suppose you want to raise a steak to a cooked temperature.

Take a roughly 0.3 kg steak. Meat is mostly water, so a reasonable specific heat is about 3500 J/kg·K. If it starts at refrigerator temperature, say 5°C, and you want the center around 60°C, that is a temperature rise of about 55 K. The thermal energy needed is roughly

Q ≈ mcΔT ≈ (0.3)(3500)(55) ≈ 58,000 joules.

The gravitational potential energy from a drop height h is

E = mgh.

Setting mgh equal to 58,000 J gives

h ≈ 58,000 / (0.3 × 9.8) ≈ 20,000 meters,

so about 20 km.

Interestingly, the mass cancels if all the gravitational energy heats the steak, so the estimate is of the same order for different steak sizes. More generally,

h ≈ cΔT / g ≈ (3500 × 55) / 9.8 ≈ 20,000 m.

That is already extremely high, but this is an unrealistically optimistic lower bound. In reality, not all the lost gravitational energy goes into heating the steak. Most of it goes into heating the surrounding air, generating turbulence, sound, and possibly heating only the surface. If the steak reaches terminal velocity, then extra height no longer increases impact speed; instead, the energy is dissipated gradually through drag, mostly into the air. That might char the surface somewhat, like atmospheric reentry, but it would not heat the interior evenly the way cooking does.

If you relied on impact instead, the steak’s kinetic energy at ordinary terminal velocity is far too small. For a steak-sized object, terminal speeds might be on the order of 50–100 m/s. The impact energy of a 0.3 kg steak at 100 m/s is only

½mv² ≈ 0.5 × 0.3 × 100² = 1500 J,

which is nowhere near the roughly 58,000 J needed.

So the careful answer is: the absolute best-case energy estimate says on the order of 20 kilometers, but in the real atmosphere there is no practical drop height that would “cook” a steak properly. A very high fall might heat or damage the outside, but it would not reliably cook the steak through.

edus.text: If you mean “could a steak be cooked just by dropping it from a great height,”
the basic answer is: in principle, yes,
but only from an absurdly large drop,
and in practice it would burn on the outside, stay undercooked inside, and probably be ruined.
The key idea is that falling converts gravitational potential energy into heat,
but only if that energy is actually dissipated into the steak, mainly through air resistance or impact.
To estimate the minimum height,
suppose you want to raise a steak to a cooked temperature.
Take a roughly 0.3 kg steak.
Meat is mostly water,
so a reasonable specific heat is about 3500 J/kg·K.
If it starts at refrigerator temperature, say 5°C,
and you want the center around 60°C,
that is a temperature rise of about 55 K.
The thermal energy needed is roughly Q ≈ mcΔT ≈ (0.3)(3500)(55) ≈ 58,000 joules.
The gravitational potential energy from a drop height h is E = mgh.
Setting mgh equal to 58,000 J gives h ≈ 58,000 / (0.3 × 9.8) ≈ 20,000 meters,
so about 20 km.
Interestingly, the mass cancels if all the gravitational energy heats the steak,
so the estimate is of the same order for different steak sizes.
More generally, h ≈ cΔT / g ≈ (3500 × 55) / 9.8 ≈ 20,000 m.
That is already extremely high,
but this is an unrealistically optimistic lower bound.
In reality, not all the lost gravitational energy goes into heating the steak.
Most of it goes into heating the surrounding air, generating turbulence, sound, and possibly heating only the surface.
If the steak reaches terminal velocity,
then extra height no longer increases impact speed;
instead, the energy is dissipated gradually through drag, mostly into the air.
That might char the surface somewhat, like atmospheric reentry,
but it would not heat the interior evenly the way cooking does.
If you relied on impact instead,
the steak’s kinetic energy at ordinary terminal velocity is far too small.
For a steak-sized object, terminal speeds might be on the order of 50–100 m/s.
The impact energy of a 0.3 kg steak at 100 m/s is only ½mv² ≈ 0.5 × 0.3 × 100² = 1500 J,
which is nowhere near the roughly 58,000 J needed.
So the careful answer is:
the absolute best-case energy estimate says on the order of 20 kilometers,
but in the real atmosphere there is no practical drop height that would “cook” a steak properly.
A very high fall might heat or damage the outside,
but it would not reliably cook the steak through.

items.question: What If You Went Swimming in a Spent Fuel Pool?
human_answers: Assuming you’re a reasonably good swimmer, you could probably survive treading water anywhere from 10 to 40 hours. At that point, you would black out from fatigue and drown. This is also true for a pool without nuclear fuel in the bottom. Spent fuel from nuclear reactors is highly radioactive. Water is good for both radiation shielding and cooling, so fuel is stored at the bottom of pools for a couple decades until it’s inert enough to be moved into dry casks. We haven’t really agreed on where to put those dry casks yet. One of these days we should probably figure that out. Here’s the geometry of a typical fuel storage pool: [Image: image] The heat wouldn't be a big problem. The water temperature in a fuel pool can in theory go as high as 50°C, but in practice they're generally between 25°C and 35°C—warmer than most pools but cooler than a hot tub. For the kinds of radiation coming off spent nuclear fuel, every 7 centimeters of water cuts the amount of radiation in half. The most highly radioactive fuel rods are those recently removed from a reactor. Based on the activity levels provided by Ontario Hydro in this report (http://www.osti.gov/energycitations/servlets/purl/7284014-xaMii9/7284014.pdf), this would be the region of danger for fresh fuel rods: [Image: image] Swimming to the bottom, touching your elbows to a fresh fuel canister, and immediately swimming back up would probably be enough to kill you. Yet outside the outer boundary, you could swim around as long as you wanted—the dose from the core would be less than the normal background dose you get walking around. In fact, as long as you were underwater, you would be shielded from most of that normal background dose. You may actually receive a lower dose of radiation treading water in a spent fuel pool than walking around on the street. [Image: image] That’s if everything goes as planned. If there’s corrosion in the spent fuel rod casings, there may be some fission products in the water. They do a pretty good job of keeping the water clean, and it wouldn’t hurt you to swim in it, but it’s radioactive enough that it wouldn’t be legal to sell it as bottled water. (Which is too bad—it’d make a hell of an energy drink). We know spent fuel pools can be safe to swim in because they’re routinely serviced by human divers. However, these divers have to be careful. On August 31st, 2010 (http://www.isoe-network.net/index.php/publications-mainmenu-88/isoe-news/doc_download/1756-ritter2011ppt.html), a diver was servicing the spent fuel pool at the Leibstadt nuclear reactor in Switzerland. He spotted an unidentified length of tubing on the bottom of the pool and radioed his supervisor to ask what to do. He was told to put it in his tool basket, which he did. Due to bubble noise in the pool, he didn’t hear his radiation alarm. When the tool basket was lifted from the water, the room’s radiation alarms went off. The basket was dropped back in the water and the diver left the pool. The diver’s dosimeter badges showed that he’d received a higher-than-normal whole-body dose, and the dose in his right hand was extremely high. The object turned out to be protective tubing from a radiation monitor in the reactor core, made highly radioactive by neutron flux. It had been accidentally sheared off while a capsule was being closed in 2006. It sank to a remote corner of the pool floor, where it sat unnoticed for four years. The tubing was so radioactive that if he’d tucked it into a tool belt or shoulder bag, where it sat close to his body, he could’ve been killed. As it was, the water protected him, and only his hand—a body part more resistant to radiation than the delicate internal organs—received a heavy dose. [Image: image] So, as far as swimming safety goes, the bottom line is that you’d probably be ok, as long as you didn’t dive to the bottom or pick up anything strange. But just to be sure, I got in touch with a friend of mine who works at a research reactor, and asked him what he thought would happen to you if you tried to swim in their radiation containment pool. “In our reactor?” He thought about it for a moment. “You’d die pretty quickly, before reaching the water, from gunshot wounds.”

items.model_answer:
If you went swimming in a spent fuel pool, the outcome would depend almost entirely on where the fuel was, how much water was above it, and whether the pool was operating normally.

In a normally operating spent fuel pool, the water is doing two jobs: cooling the fuel and shielding radiation. Water is actually very effective at blocking much of the dangerous radiation coming from spent fuel, especially if there are several meters of it above the assemblies. That means the surface of the pool can be safe enough for trained workers to be nearby, and in some cases people have even been in the water for maintenance under tightly controlled conditions. So simply touching the water or being near the top of a properly managed pool would not automatically kill you.

But swimming down toward the fuel would become extremely dangerous. As you got closer, the water shielding between you and the radioactive material would decrease, and the radiation dose rate could rise very quickly. Close to recently discharged fuel, the dose could be lethal in a short time—potentially minutes or less, depending on distance and fuel age. You would not feel radiation itself, so there might be no immediate warning before serious injury occurred.

The water itself is usually very clean, but that does not mean harmless. It is carefully treated and monitored, yet it can contain some radioactive contamination. Swallowing it or getting it into wounds would be a bad idea, though the main danger is usually external radiation from the fuel, not the water acting like acid or poison.

There are also non-radiation hazards. Spent fuel pools are industrial facilities, not swimming pools. The water may be warm, visibility may be odd because of the blue Cherenkov glow, and there are racks, equipment, and operational restrictions. You could interfere with safety systems or expose yourself to contamination and physical danger.

So the short answer is: if the pool is functioning normally and you stayed near the surface far above the fuel, you might survive the swim without immediate harm. If you dove down near the spent fuel, you could receive a massive radiation dose and die.

items.question: What If You Flew an Ordinary Airplane over Other Worlds in the Solar System?
human_answers: Here’s our aircraft: [Image: image] The Cessna 172 Skyhawk, probably the most common plane in the world. Here’s our pilot: [Image: image] Here’s what happens when the aircraft is launched above the surface of the 32 largest Solar System bodies: [Image: image] In most cases, there’s no atmosphere, and the plane falls straight to the ground. (If it’s dropped from one kilometer, in a few cases, the crash will be slow enough that the pilot may survive—although the life-support equipment probably won’t.) There are nine Solar System bodies with atmospheres thick enough to matter: Earth—obviously—Mars, Venus, the four gas giants, Saturn’s moon Titan, and the Sun. Let’s take a closer look at what would happen to a plane on each one. The Sun: This works about as well as you'd imagine. If the plane is released close enough to the Sun to feel its atmosphere at all, it's vaporized in less than a second. Mars: To see what happens to aircraft on Mars, we turn to X-Plane (http://www.x-plane.com/desktop/home/?utm_expid=25103718-8). X-Plane is the most advanced flight simulator in the world. The product of 20 years of obsessive labor by a hardcore aeronautics enthusiast who uses capslock a lot when talking about planes, it actually simulates the flow of air over every piece of an aircraft’s body as it flies. This makes it a valuable research tool, since it can accurately simulate entirely new aircraft designs—and new environments. In particular, if you change the X-Plane config file to reduce gravity, thin the atmosphere, and shrink the radius of the planet it can simulate flight on Mars (http://www.x-plane.com/adventures/mars.html). (Note: Thank you to Tom J and the folks in the X-Plane community for their help with aerodynamic calculations in different atmospheres.) X-Plane tells us that flight on Mars is difficult, but not impossible. NASA knows this, and has considered surveying Mars by airplane (http://marsairplane.larc.nasa.gov/). The tricky thing is that with so little atmosphere, to get any lift, you have to go fast. You need to approach Mach 1 just to get off the ground, and once you get moving, you have so much inertia that it’s hard to change course—if you turn, your plane rotates, but keeps moving in the original direction. The X-Plane author compared piloting Martian aircraft to flying a supersonic ocean liner. Our Cessna 172 isn’t up to the challenge. Launched from 1 km, it doesn’t build up enough speed to pull out of a dive, and plows into the Martian terrain at over 60 m/s (135 mph). If dropped from four or five kilometers, it could gain enough speed to pull up into a glide—at over half the speed of sound. The landing would not be survivable. Venus:Unfortunately, X-Plane is not capable of simulating the hellish environment near the surface of Venus. But physics calculations give us an idea of what flight there would be like. The upshot is: Your plane would fly pretty well, except it would be on fire the whole time, and then it would stop flying, and then stop being a plane. The atmosphere on Venus is over 60 times denser than Earth’s, which is thick enough that a Cessna moving at running speed would rise into the air. Unfortunately, the air it’s rising into is hot enough to melt lead. The paint would start melting off in seconds, the plane’s components would fail rapidly, and the plane would glide gently into the ground as it came apart under the heat stress. A much better bet would be to fly above the clouds. While Venus’s surface is awful, its upper atmosphere is surprisingly Earthlike. 55 kilometers up, a human could survive with an oxygen mask and a protective wetsuit; the air is room temperature and the pressure is similar to that on Earth mountains. You need the wetsuit, though, to protect you from the sulfuric acid. (I’m not selling this well, am I?) The acid's no fun, but it turns out the area right above the clouds is a great environment for an airplane (http://ntrs.nasa.gov/archive/nasa/casi.ntrs.nasa.gov/20030003716_2002108457.pdf), as long as it has no exposed metal to be corroded away by the sulfuric acid. And is capable of flight in constant Category-5-hurricane-level winds, which are another thing I forgot to mention earlier. Venus is a terrible place. Jupiter: Our Cessna can’t fly on Jupiter; the gravity is just too strong. The power needed to maintain level flight is three times greater than that on Earth. Starting from a friendly sea-level pressure, we’d accelerate through the tumbling winds into a 275 m/s (600 mph) downward glide deeper and deeper through the layers of ammonia ice and water ice until we and the aircraft were crushed. There's no surface to hit; Jupiter transitions smoothly from gas to solid as you sink deeper and deeper. Saturn: The picture here is a bit friendlier than on Jupiter. The weaker gravity—close to Earth’s, actually—and slightly denser (but still thin) atmosphere mean that we’d be able to struggle along a bit further before we gave in to either the cold or high winds and descended to the same fate as on Jupiter. Uranus: Uranus is a strange, uniform bluish orb. There are high winds and it’s bitterly cold. It’s the friendliest of the gas giants to our Cessna, and you could probably fly for a little while. But given that it seems to be an almost completely featureless planet, why would you want to? Neptune: If you’re going to fly around one of the ice giants, Neptune (Motto: “The Slightly Bluer One”) is probably a better choice than Uranus. It at least has some clouds to look at before you freeze to death or break apart from the turbulence. Titan: We’ve saved the best for last. When it comes to flying, Titan might be better than Earth. Its atmosphere is thick but its gravity is light, giving it a surface pressure only 50% higher than Earth’s with air four times as dense. Its gravity—lower than that of the Moon—means that flying is easy. Our Cessna could get into the air under pedal power. In fact, humans on Titan could fly by muscle power. A human in a hang glider could comfortably take off and cruise around powered by oversized swim-flipper boots—or even take off by flapping artificial wings. The power requirements are minimal—it would probably take no more effort than walking. The downside (there’s always a downside) is the cold. It’s 72 kelvin on Titan, which is about the temperature of liquid nitrogen. Judging from some numbers on heating requirements for light aircraft, I estimate that the cabin of a Cessna on Titan would probably cool by about two degrees per minute. The batteries would help to keep themselves warm for a little while, but eventually the craft would run out of heat and crash. The Huygens probe, which descended with batteries nearly drained (taking fascinating pictures (http://www.beugungsbild.de/huygens/huygens.html) as it fell), succumbed to the cold after only a few hours on the surface. It had enough time to send back a single photo (http://www.esa.int/Our_Activities/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/New_images_from_Titan) after landing—the only one we have from the surface of a body beyond Mars. If humans put on artificial wings to fly, we might become Titan versions of the Icarus story—our wings could freeze, fall apart, and send us tumbling to our deaths. [Image: image] But I've never seen the Icarus story as a lesson about the limitations of humans. I see it as a lesson about the limitations of wax as an adhesive. The cold of Titan is just an engineering problem. With the right refitting, and the right heat sources, a Cessna 172 could fly on Titan—and so could we.

criteria.9-10: Comprehensively classifies the relevant Solar System bodies, including Earth, Mars, Venus, gas giants, Titan, and the Sun, with clear implications for flight.

criteria.1-2: Relies on vague statements or fantasy physics with little connection to lift, drag, speed, or gravity.
criteria.3-4: Uses some aviation terms but often applies them incorrectly, such as assuming low gravity alone guarantees easy flight.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic lift and drag tradeoffs and recognizes that thin air requires high speed while dense air enables slow flight.
criteria.7-8: Correctly links atmospheric density, gravity, speed, control authority, and power requirements to different worlds' outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent aerodynamic account across cases, including Mars needing near-supersonic speeds, Venus/Titan dense-atmosphere lift, and gas-giant gravity/drag complications.

criteria.name: Planet-by-planet outcome plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the plausibility and specificity of predicted outcomes for the main worlds discussed in the prompt: Sun, Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Titan.
criteria.1-2: Provides broad or incorrect conclusions with little distinction between worlds.
criteria.3-4: Covers only a few worlds or gives outcomes that conflict with known environmental conditions.
criteria.5-6: Gives plausible outcomes for several key worlds but misses important details or has some inaccurate predictions.
criteria.7-8: Covers most major atmospheric worlds with generally correct outcomes: crash on Mars, heat failure on Venus, crushing/descent on gas giants, easy-but-cold flight on Titan.
criteria.9-10: Covers all major cases with nuanced outcomes, including solar vaporization, Mars high-speed glide/crash, Venus surface versus upper atmosphere, gas-giant descent, and Titan as the best flight environment.

criteria.name: Long-range causal chain coherence and downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer follows consequences beyond initial flight, including aircraft failure modes, pilot survival, environmental exposure, thermal effects, and eventual crash or destruction.
criteria.1-2: Stops at simple yes/no claims and ignores what happens after launch.
criteria.3-4: Includes some downstream effects but chains are short, disconnected, or physically unsupported.
criteria.5-6: Traces several plausible chains from environment to flight behavior to crash, failure, or survival limits.
criteria.7-8: Maintains coherent multi-step causal chains for most worlds, connecting launch conditions, aircraft performance, structural/thermal stresses, and final fate.
criteria.9-10: Provides robust long-range reasoning throughout, including life-support limits, heat/cold degradation, turbulence, corrosion, crushing pressure, lack of surface on gas giants, and survivability implications.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming, states assumptions such as altitude and ordinary Cessna-like design, and remains internally consistent with the counterfactual setup.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, unsupported certainty, or changes the premise to a specially designed spacecraft or aircraft.
criteria.3-4: Has multiple inconsistencies or makes precise claims without basis while only loosely respecting the ordinary-airplane premise.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves the premise and avoids major contradictions, though uncertainty and assumptions are unevenly handled.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states relevant assumptions, distinguishes ordinary aircraft from engineered alternatives, and keeps claims internally consistent.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates uncertain estimates, notes dependence on altitude/environmental layer, avoids false precision, and consistently reasons from an ordinary airplane under the stated counterfactual.

items.model_answer:
An ordinary airplane would only fly where there is enough atmosphere for wings and engines to work, and where the temperature, pressure, and chemistry do not immediately destroy the aircraft or its occupants. In the Solar System, that means the answer is mostly “no,” but with a few interesting partial exceptions.

On the Moon, Mercury, and Pluto, an ordinary airplane could not fly at all because there is essentially no atmosphere. Wings need air to generate lift, and normal jet or propeller engines also need air. The same basic problem applies to most asteroids.

On Mars, things get more interesting. Mars does have an atmosphere, but it is very thin, less than 1 percent of Earth’s sea-level pressure. An ordinary airplane designed for Earth would not fly there. Its wings would not generate enough lift at normal speeds, and its engines would not perform properly because the air is too thin and has very little oxygen. To fly on Mars, you need something specially designed: very large wings, very low weight, very high speed, or rotorcraft built for the thin air, like NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter.

On Venus, the atmosphere is actually thick enough for aerodynamic flight, especially high in the atmosphere. In principle, wings could work very well there. But an ordinary airplane still would not survive. Near the surface, Venus is hot enough to melt lead and the pressure is crushing, around 90 times Earth’s. The atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide with sulfuric-acid clouds higher up. A normal airplane and its engines would fail quickly. If you had a specially built aircraft operating high in the Venusian atmosphere, flight is actually one of the more plausible possibilities in the Solar System.

On Titan, Saturn’s large moon, flying is surprisingly favorable in aerodynamic terms. Titan has a thick atmosphere and low gravity, which makes it easier for wings or rotors to generate lift. In some ways, Titan is one of the easiest places in the Solar System to fly. But an ordinary airplane still would not work well because the air is mostly nitrogen with almost no oxygen, so normal engines could not burn fuel, and the temperatures are extremely cold. A specially designed aircraft could fly there very effectively.

In the gas giants like Jupiter and Saturn, there is no solid surface to take off from in the usual sense, but there is plenty of atmosphere. If you somehow placed an airplane in the right layer of the atmosphere, wings could generate lift. However, an ordinary airplane would still fail because the atmospheric composition is wrong for normal engines, the winds are extreme, and deeper down the pressure becomes enormous. Uranus and Neptune have similar issues, along with intense cold and violent atmospheric conditions.

So the short version is this: an ordinary Earth airplane would only really fly on Earth. On most other worlds there is either too little atmosphere, the wrong kind of atmosphere, or conditions so extreme that the aircraft would not function. But if you allow specially designed aircraft, Mars, Venus’s upper atmosphere, Titan, and even parts of the giant planets become possible and in some cases very promising places to fly.

items.question: What If Hubble Pointed at Earth Instead of Deep Space?
human_answers: This is a common question. The Hubble operators get it a lot, and their FAQ page answers it (http://hubblesite.org/reference_desk/faq/answer.php.id=78&cat=topten). The problem isn’t—as some people say—that the Earth is too bright. As Phil Plait of Bad Astronomy pointed out (http://www.badastronomy.com/mad/2000/hubbleearth.html), Hubble looks at Earth pretty regularly. The real problem is that Hubble is moving over the surface at over 7 kilometers per second. Even a short exposure would be a blur. That’s no fun. Is there a way we could make it work? I decided to take a closer look. As our picture target, we’ll use this typical desk: [Image: image] The Earth’s atmosphere won’t be a problem. It’s actually much more of a problem for surface-based telescopes looking at space than for space-based telescopes looking at the surface. The reason for this is geometric: [Image: image] Hubble is the best visible-light telescope we have, but its resolution does have limits. Pluto, out in the Kuiper belt, lies right at those limits. The best pictures we have of Pluto (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/solar-system/pluto/2010/06/) come from Hubble, but the ex-planet is still little more than a mysterious blur. At that resolution (about 0.05 arcseconds, give or take) and Hubble’s distance from the desk (about 570 kilometers) the desk would look like this: [Image: image] But that desk is also zooming by, so even a perfect image will be blurred: [Image: image] Combining the two effects gives us an end result that looks like this: [Image: image] That’s no good. Could we rotate Hubble to track the surface, and eliminate the blur? Hubble swivels to follow targets. Usually, they’re far enough away that we can assume they’re at infinite distance. The automatic on-board parallax algorithms can’t handle targets closer than about ten times the distance to the Moon. When astronomers want to use it to take pictures of the Moon, sometimes they send it commands to rotate manually (http://www.stsci.edu/hst/HST_overview/documents/uir/UIR-2007-01.pdf), then turn on the camera mid-maneuver. It doesn’t work very well. Moving Hubble at those speeds is cumbersome with the current guidance package. The resulting photos (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/1999/14) are better than what you can see with the naked eye, but they’re not very good by Hubble standards. Here’s our desk, with the image degraded by a similar amount that the Moon one was: [Image: image] Fortunately, the Moon is bright enough that if you’ll settle for a short exposure, you can avoid the problem. This photo (http://hubblesite.org/newscenter/archive/releases/2012/22/fastfacts/) was taken with a half-second exposure, short enough that it didn’t have to do much in the way of tracking. Unfortunately, our desk is moving across the telescope’s field of view about 600 times faster than the Moon. Tracking is unavoidable. The strange thing is, the desk really isn’t moving all that fast. Hubble is just really slow. To track the surface, it would need to rotate less than a degree per second at maximum. But Hubble wasn’t built for surface tracking. The telescope’s top rotational (“slew”) speed is only a few degrees per minute (about the speed of a minute hand on a clock) and even those speeds are fast enough that its gyroscopes cause it to vibrate (http://www.pha.jhu.edu/groups/hst10x/pdffiles/HST10X_Technical.pdf), which destroys the image quality. Clearly, we’d need to disable Hubble’s guidance system and bolt on our own control system. Hubble’s rotational moment of inertia (http://www.dept.aoe.vt.edu/~cdhall/courses/aoe5984/bs.pdf) is similar to that of a small carousel; too hard for the existing gyroscopes to move, but not hard in the absolute sense. With our custom control system, it could be made to track the surface, and get photos pretty close to optimal quality: [Image: image] But this isn’t just a hypothetical situation. Much of the technology in military spy satellites is believed to be similar to that of Hubble. So in a sense, pointing a Hubble-type telescope at the surface is not only possible—it’s what the US government actually does (http://www.onorbit.com/node/3850).

criteria.name: Core counterfactual conclusion and causal fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches the correct high-level outcome for Hubble imaging Earth: it can point at Earth, but normal Hubble would produce poor Earth-surface images mainly because of rapid apparent ground motion and tracking limits, not because Earth is simply too bright.
criteria.1-2: Gives a fundamentally wrong conclusion, such as claiming Hubble would be destroyed, blinded, or easily take perfect spy photos with no caveats.
criteria.3-4: Identifies that Earth imaging would be difficult but attributes the problem mostly to incorrect causes such as brightness, atmosphere, or focus alone.
criteria.5-6: States that Hubble could look at Earth but images would be poor; mentions motion blur or tracking but with limited causal explanation.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains that orbital speed over the surface causes severe apparent motion and blur, making ordinary exposures and guidance inadequate.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual: Earth is observable, brightness/atmosphere are not the main barriers, and the dominant issue is fast ground-track motion relative to Hubble’s design.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage: optics, resolution, exposure, and tracking
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the physical mechanisms that determine the image quality if Hubble observed Earth: diffraction-limited angular resolution, altitude-to-ground resolution conversion, exposure time, smear from orbital motion, and telescope pointing control.
criteria.1-2: Omits almost all relevant mechanisms or relies on vague statements about telescopes zooming in.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one relevant mechanism, such as resolution or motion, but ignores how it affects actual Earth-surface imaging.
criteria.5-6: Covers several mechanisms but leaves gaps, such as discussing resolution without exposure smear or motion without pointing constraints.
criteria.7-8: Explains how Hubble’s finite angular resolution and rapid apparent ground motion combine to degrade surface images.
criteria.9-10: Integrates optics, altitude, exposure time, smear, target tracking, and attitude-control limits into a coherent account of image quality.

criteria.name: Long-range chain coherence under the premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the downstream consequences of repointing Hubble toward Earth over multiple steps, from initial feasibility to operational limitations and possible engineering workarounds.
criteria.1-2: Provides disconnected claims with no causal chain from the counterfactual premise to consequences.
criteria.3-4: Has a simple chain but skips key transitions, such as going directly from pointing at Earth to image quality without explaining why.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly sensible sequence but leaves some important links underdeveloped or mildly confused.
criteria.7-8: Clearly traces the chain: Hubble can point, Earth passes rapidly through view, exposures blur, normal guidance cannot track well, resulting images are poor.
criteria.9-10: Develops the full long-range chain including manual tracking attempts, slew-rate/vibration constraints, possible custom control systems, and relation to Earth-observation satellites.

criteria.name: Quantitative and comparative grounding
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses appropriate magnitudes or comparisons for Hubble’s Earth-observation scenario, such as orbital speed, altitude, angular resolution, ground resolution, Moon-tracking comparison, and slew-rate requirements.
criteria.1-2: Uses no quantitative grounding or gives wildly implausible numbers that drive the reasoning astray.
criteria.3-4: Includes numbers or comparisons but they are mostly irrelevant, unsupported, or significantly misleading.
criteria.5-6: Uses at least one relevant scale, such as Hubble’s altitude or orbital speed, but does not connect it strongly to the conclusion.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible scales, such as about 570 km altitude, about 7 km/s ground motion, or sub-arcsecond resolution, to support the blur/tracking argument.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects multiple scales, including Hubble-like angular resolution, rapid ground-track motion, short exposure limits, and required tracking rates, to justify the expected image quality.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, contradiction control, and boundary cases
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer avoids overclaiming, distinguishes stock Hubble from a modified Hubble-like system, and handles edge cases such as very short exposures, bright targets, atmosphere, and spy-satellite analogues without contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Contains major internal contradictions or absolute claims that conflict with the scenario, such as saying Hubble cannot point at Earth and also that it routinely can.
criteria.3-4: Shows some awareness of caveats but mixes incompatible claims or overstates uncertain details.
criteria.5-6: Mostly avoids contradictions but treats important boundary cases simplistically, such as assuming any short exposure solves the problem.

items.model_answer:
If Hubble pointed at Earth instead of deep space, the main result is that it would not work the way people might imagine. Hubble was designed to observe extremely faint, distant objects, not a bright, nearby, fast-moving target like Earth.

First, Earth would be overwhelmingly bright compared with the galaxies and nebulae Hubble usually studies. That much reflected sunlight could easily saturate its detectors, washing out images and potentially stressing the instruments if proper precautions were not taken. Hubble’s cameras are built for sensitive astronomy, so looking at a sunlit Earth would be more like shining a flashlight into night-vision goggles than using a normal camera.

Second, tracking would be a serious problem. Hubble orbits Earth at about 7.5 km/s, and the ground below moves rapidly through its field of view. Deep-space targets appear nearly fixed, which is ideal for long exposures. Earth features would sweep by quickly, so Hubble would need very different pointing and exposure strategies. It could in principle image parts of Earth briefly, but it is not optimized for that job.

Third, focus and observing geometry matter. Hubble is focused for astronomical distances, effectively infinity. Earth is still far enough away from Hubble—hundreds to a couple thousand kilometers depending on what it looked at—that this is not the biggest obstacle, but it is another reason the telescope is not ideal for Earth observation compared with satellites specifically designed for that purpose.

There is also an operational issue: Hubble usually avoids pointing too close to Earth’s bright limb because scattered light from the planet degrades observations. Earth is more often something to avoid than something to study.

If engineers deliberately commanded Hubble to observe Earth safely, it could probably take very high-resolution images of clouds, coastlines, and large surface features, potentially with resolution on the order of tens of meters under favorable conditions. But it would still be a poor substitute for reconnaissance or weather satellites, which are built for wide fields, rapid imaging, and repeated passes.

So the short answer is: if Hubble pointed at Earth, it would see a very bright, fast-moving target and would perform awkwardly rather than magically. It could likely capture some detailed images, but it is the wrong tool for the job and could not usefully observe Earth the way it observes deep space.

edus.text: If Hubble pointed at Earth instead of deep space, the main result is that it would not work the way people might imagine.
Hubble was designed to observe extremely faint, distant objects, not a bright, nearby, fast-moving target like Earth.
First, Earth would be overwhelmingly bright compared with the galaxies and nebulae Hubble usually studies.
That much reflected sunlight could easily saturate its detectors, washing out images and potentially stressing the instruments if proper precautions were not taken.
Hubble’s cameras are built for sensitive astronomy, so looking at a sunlit Earth would be more like shining a flashlight into night-vision goggles than using a normal camera.
Second, tracking would be a serious problem.
Hubble orbits Earth at about 7.5 km/s, and the ground below moves rapidly through its field of view.
Deep-space targets appear nearly fixed, which is ideal for long exposures.
Earth features would sweep by quickly, so Hubble would need very different pointing and exposure strategies.
It could in principle image parts of Earth briefly, but it is not optimized for that job.
Third, focus and observing geometry matter.
Hubble is focused for astronomical distances, effectively infinity.

Earth is still far enough away from Hubble that this is not the biggest obstacle, but it is another reason the telescope is not ideal for Earth observation compared with satellites specifically designed for that purpose.
There is also an operational issue: Hubble usually avoids pointing too close to Earth’s bright limb because scattered light from the planet degrades observations.
Earth is more often something to avoid than something to study.

If engineers deliberately commanded Hubble to observe Earth safely, it could probably take very high-resolution images of clouds, coastlines, and large surface features, potentially with resolution on the order of tens of meters under favorable conditions.
But it would still be a poor substitute for reconnaissance or weather satellites, which are built for wide fields, rapid imaging, and repeated passes.
So the short answer is: if Hubble pointed at Earth, it would see a very bright, fast-moving target and would perform awkwardly rather than magically.
It could likely capture some detailed images, but it is the wrong tool for the job and could not usefully observe Earth the way it observes deep space.

Earth is still far enough away from Hubble that this is not the biggest obstacle, but it is another reason the telescope is not ideal for Earth observation compared with satellites specifically designed for that purpose.
There is also an operational issue: Hubble usually avoids pointing too close to Earth’s bright limb because scattered light from the planet degrades observations.
Earth is more often something to avoid than something to study.

If engineers deliberately commanded Hubble to observe Earth safely, it could probably take very high-resolution images of clouds, coastlines, and large surface features, potentially with resolution on the order of tens of meters under favorable conditions.
But it would still be a poor substitute for reconnaissance or weather satellites, which are built for wide fields, rapid imaging, and repeated passes.
So the short answer is: if Hubble pointed at Earth, it would see a very bright, fast-moving target and would perform awkwardly rather than magically.
It could likely capture some detailed images, but it is the wrong tool for the job and could not usefully observe Earth the way it observes deep space.

items.question: What If Every Ship Were Removed from Earth's Waters at Once?
human_answers: About six microns—slightly more than the diameter of a strand of spider silk. [Image: image] Archimedes’ principle tells us that the water displaced by a ship weighs as much as the ship itself. If we can figure out the total weight of all the world’s ships, we can figure out how much water they’re displacing, then divide that volume by the surface area of the ocean to figure out how much the water level would drop. Weighing ships is confusing (http://www.pomorci.com/Zanimljivosti/TONNAGE%20MEASUREMENT%20OF%20SHIPS.pdf). There are a bunch of different measurements of the size of a ship, and many of them, like gross tonnage, are actually measures of the volume of the ship’s rooms and other internal spaces, not its weight. The UN Conference on Trade and Development publishes estimates (http://unctad.org/en/Docs/rmt2011ch2_en.pdf) of the size of the world shipping fleet. What the UNCTD publishes is “deadweight tonnage”, which is the maximum weight of the ship’s fuel, cargo, and crew. What we want is “displacement”. Unfortunately, comprehensive numbers for displacement are harder to find. Fortunately, we can estimate it. Brian Barrass’s book Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates gives a table of ratios of deadweight tonnage to displacement for different types of ships. Extrapolating from the last few years of UNCTD data, and using the coefficients from the book, suggests that the world fleet weighs about 2.15 billion tons when fully loaded. The main component of the fleet by weight is oil tankers and bulk ore-carrying ships, which make up over two-thirds of the total. (The UNCTD data doesn’t include small recreational boats or naval fleets. However, based on some numbers for naval fleets (http://www.csbaonline.org/4Publications/PubLibrary/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti/R.20090217.The_US_Navy_Charti.pdf) and recreational boats (http://nmma.net/assets/cabinets/Cabinet445/2011_abstract_preview.pdf), neither one contributes much to the total.) A ton of water is about a cubic meter. 2.15 billion cubic meters divided by the surface area of the oceans equals about 6 microns (0.006 mm). But you don’t have to worry about that six-micron sea level drop. The oceans are currently rising at about 3.3 millimeters per year due to global warming (through both glacial melting and thermal expansion of seawater). At that rate (normalized for seasonal variation and short-term fluctations), if you removed every ship from the ocean, the water would be back up to its original average level in 16 hours. [Image: image] Sea levels will likely rise a few feet by the year 2100 (https://what-if.xkcd.com/33). Current fish wet biomass is about 2 billion tons (http://phys.org/news151251277.html), so removing them won’t make a dent either. (Marine fish biomass dropped by 80% over the last century (http://news.aaas.org/2011_annual_meeting/0228declining-fisheries.shtml), which—taking into consideration the growth rate of the world’s shipping fleet—leads to an odd conclusion: Sometime in the last few years, we reached a point where there are, by weight, more ships in the ocean than fish.) And what about the old joke about how much deeper the ocean would be without sponges? While estimates of sponge biomass are hard to come by, the answer is probably that if you removed all the sponges, sea level would drop by no more than a few microns ... and much less if you squeezed them out first. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Archimedes-Based Sea-Level Estimate
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response correctly applies buoyancy/displacement reasoning to estimate the immediate global mean sea-level change from removing all ships from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Does not use displacement or buoyancy; predicts a large or directionally wrong sea-level change.
criteria.3-4: Mentions displaced water but confuses ship volume, cargo capacity, or tonnage, leading to an implausible estimate.
criteria.5-6: Uses Archimedes' principle qualitatively and gets the drop direction right, but gives only a rough or poorly supported magnitude.
criteria.7-8: Correctly estimates displaced mass/volume from world fleet weight and ocean area, yielding a micron-scale sea-level drop.
criteria.9-10: Accurately explains displacement versus tonnage, uses plausible fleet mass and ocean-area assumptions, and arrives near about 6 microns.

criteria.name: Scope of Removed Vessels and Mass Accounting
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the response defines 'every ship' and accounts for commercial, naval, recreational, cargo, fuel, and load-state contributions without overcounting.
criteria.1-2: Treats ships as empty geometric objects or ignores fleet composition entirely.
criteria.3-4: Considers only one class of vessels or relies on arbitrary guesses with no distinction among ship types.
criteria.5-6: Includes major commercial vessels but handles cargo/load state, naval fleets, or small boats vaguely.
criteria.7-8: Identifies commercial shipping as dominant and notes that naval and recreational craft are comparatively minor.
criteria.9-10: Carefully distinguishes displacement, deadweight, cargo/fuel load, and vessel categories while explaining why omitted small fleets barely affect the result.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects and Relative Scale
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of physical, environmental, and societal consequences after instantaneous ship removal, while keeping them proportional to the tiny water-level effect.
criteria.1-2: Claims catastrophic ocean drainage, tsunamis, climate shifts, or ecosystem collapse from sea-level change alone.
criteria.3-4: Lists effects but greatly exaggerates the sea-level, tidal, or geological consequences.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the sea-level effect is tiny but gives limited discussion of other consequences such as transport disruption or pollution changes.
criteria.7-8: Separates negligible ocean-level effects from major human impacts like global trade disruption, stranded cargo, fuel loss, and maritime safety issues.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent hierarchy of downstream effects: micron-scale sea-level change, no meaningful tidal/geophysical impact, but severe logistics, economic, rescue, and possible pollution consequences depending on removal details.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Mechanism Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the response maintains a consistent causal chain under the premise that all ships are removed at once from Earth's waters.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the premise or contradicts it repeatedly, such as leaving ships in place while analyzing their removal.
criteria.3-4: Applies the premise inconsistently, mixing removal of ships, water, cargo, or marine life without clear rules.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the premise but leaves ambiguous whether cargo, people, fuel, or displaced water vanish or are relocated.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions about instantaneous removal and consistently traces immediate and later consequences.
criteria.9-10: Explicitly handles alternative interpretations, such as removing vessels only versus ships plus contents, and explains how each changes outcomes without breaking causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether numerical claims and speculative effects are appropriately qualified, internally consistent, and compared to relevant baselines such as modern sea-level rise.
criteria.1-2: Presents unsupported precise claims, contradictions, or physically impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Uses some plausible facts but mixes incompatible numbers or fails to flag major uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty generally but lacks clear bounds or relevant scale comparisons.
criteria.7-8: Uses order-of-magnitude reasoning, avoids false precision, and compares the result to ocean area, fleet mass, or annual sea-level rise.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates all estimates with transparent assumptions, sensible error bars, and comparisons such as millimeters-per-year sea-level rise overwhelming a few-micron drop within hours.

items.model_answer:
If every ship on Earth vanished from the oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes all at once, the immediate physical effect on the water itself would be surprisingly small, but the human consequences would be enormous.

Physically, sea level would fall by a tiny amount because ships displace water. All the world’s ships together have a total mass on the order of a few billion tonnes, which means they displace a similar volume of water, only a few cubic kilometers in total. Spread over the surface of the global ocean, that corresponds to only a few micrometers to perhaps around ten micrometers of sea-level change, far too small for people to notice. You would not get giant waves just from the disappearance itself, except possibly very local disturbances where large vessels had been sitting, especially in harbors or narrow channels. Those disturbances would behave more like localized sloshing than a planet-scale tsunami.

The real effects would be economic and logistical. Modern civilization depends heavily on shipping. Most international trade by mass moves by sea, including oil, liquefied natural gas, coal, iron ore, grain, fertilizers, containers full of manufactured goods, and many industrial chemicals. If all ships were removed instantly, global supply chains would begin failing within days. Ports would become useless, factories would run out of parts, supermarkets in import-dependent regions would see shortages, and energy markets would be hit hard. Island nations and remote coastal communities would be especially vulnerable because they rely on ships for food, fuel, medicine, and construction materials.

Oil and fuel distribution would be one of the first major crises. A large fraction of crude oil and petroleum products is transported by tanker. Countries that depend on imported fuel would face shortages quickly, affecting electricity generation, transportation, agriculture, and emergency services. Natural gas markets would also be disrupted because LNG shipping would stop completely. Some regions could compensate partly with pipelines or local production, but many could not.

Food systems would also be stressed. Bulk carriers move huge amounts of grain, soybeans, and fertilizers. Countries that import staple foods would face rising prices and shortages. Fishing fleets disappearing would also abruptly remove a major food source and livelihood for millions of people. In the longer term, some fish stocks might recover because industrial fishing pressure would suddenly drop, but that ecological benefit would come with severe short-term human cost.

Navies, coast guards, ferries, tugboats, research vessels, dredgers, and rescue craft would all be gone too. That would mean immediate losses in maritime security, search and rescue capability, scientific monitoring, offshore maintenance, and passenger transport. Many bridges and tunnels would see increased pressure as people shifted to land routes where possible, but many routes simply cannot be replaced on short timescales.

Environmental effects would be mixed. There would be an immediate drop in ship emissions, underwater noise, ballast-water transport of invasive species, and oil-spill risk from vessels. Marine mammals in some regions might benefit from quieter oceans and fewer ship strikes. But there could also be negative consequences: offshore platforms and coastal infrastructure often depend on ships for maintenance and supply, so failures there could create new hazards. Also, if maritime trade stopped, countries might turn more heavily to trucks, planes, and rail where possible, often increasing emissions per unit cargo.

Rivers and lakes would also be affected. Inland shipping carries large amounts of bulk goods efficiently. Removing barges and ferries would strain roads and rail systems and isolate some communities.

So the best short answer is this: Earth’s waters would barely change physically, aside from a minuscule drop in sea level and some local water disturbances, but human civilization would experience a massive global trade, energy, food, and transportation crisis almost immediately.

edus.text: If every ship on Earth vanished from the oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes all at once,
the immediate physical effect on the water itself would be surprisingly small,
but the human consequences would be enormous.
Physically, sea level would fall by a tiny amount because ships displace water.
All the world’s ships together have a total mass on the order of a few billion tonnes,
which means they displace a similar volume of water, only a few cubic kilometers in total.
Spread over the surface of the global ocean, that corresponds to only a few micrometers to perhaps around ten micrometers of sea-level change,
far too small for people to notice.
You would not get giant waves just from the disappearance itself,
except possibly very local disturbances where large vessels had been sitting, especially in harbors or narrow channels.
Those disturbances would behave more like localized sloshing than a planet-scale tsunami.
The real effects would be economic and logistical.
Modern civilization depends heavily on shipping.
Most international trade by mass moves by sea,
including oil, liquefied natural gas, coal, iron ore, grain, fertilizers, containers full of manufactured goods, and many industrial chemicals.
If all ships were removed instantly,
global supply chains would begin failing within days.
Ports would become useless, factories would run out of parts, supermarkets in import-dependent regions would see shortages, and energy markets would be hit hard.
Island nations and remote coastal communities would be especially vulnerable
because they rely on ships for food, fuel, medicine, and construction materials.
Oil and fuel distribution would be one of the first major crises.
A large fraction of crude oil and petroleum products is transported by tanker.
Countries that depend on imported fuel would face shortages quickly,
affecting electricity generation, transportation, agriculture, and emergency services.
Natural gas markets would also be disrupted
because LNG shipping would stop completely.
Some regions could compensate partly with pipelines or local production,
but many could not.
Food systems would also be stressed.
Bulk carriers move huge amounts of grain, soybeans, and fertilizers.
Countries that import staple foods would face rising prices and shortages.
Fishing fleets disappearing would also abruptly remove a major food source and livelihood for millions of people.
In the longer term, some fish stocks might recover
because industrial fishing pressure would suddenly drop,
but that ecological benefit would come with severe short-term human cost.
Navies, coast guards, ferries, tugboats, research vessels, dredgers, and rescue craft would all be gone too.
That would mean immediate losses in maritime security, search and rescue capability, scientific monitoring, offshore maintenance, and passenger transport.
Many bridges and tunnels would see increased pressure as people shifted to land routes where possible,
but many routes simply cannot be replaced on short timescales.
Environmental effects would be mixed.
There would be an immediate drop in ship emissions, underwater noise, ballast-water transport of invasive species, and oil-spill risk from vessels.
Marine mammals in some regions might benefit from quieter oceans and fewer ship strikes.
But there could also be negative consequences:
offshore platforms and coastal infrastructure often depend on ships for maintenance and supply,
so failures there could create new hazards.
Also, if maritime trade stopped,
countries might turn more heavily to trucks, planes, and rail where possible,
often increasing emissions per unit cargo.
Rivers and lakes would also be affected.
Inland shipping carries large amounts of bulk goods efficiently.
Removing barges and ferries would strain roads and rail systems
and isolate some communities.
So the best short answer is this:
Earth’s waters would barely change physically, aside from a minuscule drop in sea level and some local water disturbances,
but human civilization would experience a massive global trade, energy, food, and transportation crisis almost immediately.

items.question: What If You Put a Running Hair Dryer in a Sealed 1x1x1 Meter Box?
human_answers: A typical hair dryer draws 1875 watts of power. All 1875 watts have to go somewhere. No matter what happens inside the box, if there’s 1875 watts of power being used, eventually there will be 1875 watts of heat flowing out. This is true of any device that uses power, which is a handy thing to know. For example, people worry about leaving disconnected chargers plugged into the wall for fear that they’re draining power. Are they right? You can use heat flow to come up with simple rule of thumb: If an unused charger isn’t warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny of electricity a day. For a small smartphone charger, if it’s not warm to the touch, it’s using less than a penny a year. This is true of almost any powered device (though not necessarily those plugged into a second device. If a charger is connected to something, like a smartphone or laptop, power can be flowing from the wall through the charger into the device.) But back to the box. Heat will flow from the hair dryer out into the box. If we assume the dryer is indestructible, the interior of the box will keep getting hotter until the outer surface reaches about 60°C (140°F). At that temperature, the box will be losing heat to the outside as fast as the hair dryer is adding it inside, and the system will be in equilibrium. [Image: image] The equilibrium temperature will be a bit cooler if there’s a breeze, or if the box is sitting on a wet or metallic surface that conducts away heat quickly. If the box is made of metal, 60°C is hot enough to burn your hand if you touch it (http://www.mascoat.com/assets/files/Insulative_Coating_Evaluation_NACE.pdf) for more than five seconds. If it’s wood, you can probably touch it for a while, but there’s a danger that parts of the box in contact with the mouth of the hair dryer will catch fire. The inside of a box will be like an oven. The temperature it reaches will depend on the thickness of the box wall; the thicker and more insulating the wall, the higher the temperature. It wouldn’t take a very thick box to create temperatures high enough to burn out the hair dryer. But let’s assume an indestructible hair dryer. And if we have something as cool as an indestructible hair dryer, it seems like a shame to limit it. [Image: image] With 18,750 watts flowing out of the hair dryer, the surface of the box reaches over 200°C (475°F), as hot as a skillet on low-medium. [Image: image] I wonder how high this dial goes. [Image: image] The surface of the box is now 600°C, hot enough to glow a dim red. [Image: image] If it’s made of aluminium, the inside is starting to melt. If it’s made of lead, the outside is starting to melt. If it’s on a wood floor, the house is on fire. But it doesn't matter what's happening around it; the hair dryer is indestructible. [Image: image] Two megawatts pumped into a laser (http://what-if.xkcd.com/13/) is enough to destroy missiles. At 1300°C, the box is now about the temperature of lava. [Image: image] One more notch. [Image: image] 18 megawatts are flowing into the box. [Image: image] The surface of the box reaches 2400°C. If it were steel, it would have melted by now. If it’s made of something like tungsten, it might conceivably last a little longer. Just one more, then we'll stop. [Image: image] 187 megawatts is enough to make the box glow white. Not a lot of box materials can survive these conditions, so we’ll have to assume the box is indestructible. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the floor isn’t. Before it can burn its way through the floor, someone throws a water balloon under it. The burst of steam launches the box out the front door and onto the sidewalk. (Note: If you’re ever trapped with me in a burning building, and I suggest an idea for how we could escape the situation, it’s probably best to ignore me.) [Image: image] 1.875 gigawatts (I lied about stopping). According to Back to the Future, the hair dryer is now drawing enough power to travel back in time. [Image: image] The box is blindingly bright, and you can’t get closer than a few hundred meters due to the intense heat. It sits in the middle of a growing pool of lava. Anything within 50-100 meters bursts into flame. A column of heat and smoke rise high into the air. Periodic explosions of gas beneath the box launch it into the air, and it starts fires and forms a new lava pool where it lands. [Image: image] 18.7 gigawatts. The conditions around the box are similar to those on the pad during a Space Shuttle launch. The box begins to be tossed around by the powerful updrafts it’s creating. In 1914, H.G. Wells imagined devices like this in his book The World Set Free (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_World_Set_Free). He wrote of a type of bomb that, instead of exploding once, exploded continuously, a slow-burn inferno that started inextinguishable fires in the hearts of cities. The story eerily foreshadowed the development, 30 years later, of nuclear weapons. [Image: image] The box is now soaring through the air. Each time it nears the ground, it superheats the surface, and the plume of expanding air hurls it back into the sky. [Image: image] 1.875 terawatts is like a house-sized stack of TNT going off every second. [Image: image] A trail of firestorms—massive conflagrations which sustain themselves by creating their own wind systems—winds its way across the landscape. A new milestone: The hair dryer is now, impossibly, consuming more power than every other electrical device on the planet combined. [Image: image] The box, soaring high above the surface, is putting out energy equivalent to three Trinity tests every second. At this point, the pattern is obvious. This thing is going to skip around the atmosphere until it destroys the planet. Let's try something different. [Image: image] We turn the dial to zero as the box is passing over northern Canada. Rapidly cooling, it plummets to Earth, landing in Great Bear Lake with a plume of steam. And then … [Image: image] This one goes to 11. Petawatts, in this case. A brief story: The official record for fastest manmade object is the Helios 2 probe, which reached about 70 km/s in a close swing around the Sun. But it’s possible the actual holder of that title is a two-ton metal manhole cover. The cover sat atop a shaft at an underground nuclear test site operated by Los Alamos as part of Operation Plumbbob. When the one-kiloton nuke went off below, the facility effectively became a nuclear potato cannon (http://nfttu.blogspot.com/2006/01/nuclear-potato-cannon-part-2.html), giving the cap a gigantic kick. A high-speed camera trained on the lid caught only one frame of it moving upward before it vanished—which means it was moving at a minimum of 66 km/s. The cap was never found. 66 km/s is about six times escape velocity, but contrary to the linked blog’s speculation, it’s unlikely the cap ever reached space. Newton’s impact depth approximation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_depth) suggests that it was either destroyed completely by impact with the air or slowed and fell back to Earth. Our suddenly-activated hair dryer box, bobbing in lake water, undergoes a similar process. The heated steam below it expands outward, and as the box rises into the air, the entire surface of the lake turns to steam. The steam, heated to a plasma by the flood of radiation, accelerates the box faster and faster. [Image: image] Rather than slam into the atmosphere like the manhole cover, the flood of radiation heats the air around it, creating a bubble of expanding plasma which offers little resistance. The box exits the atmosphere and continues away, slowly fading from second sun to dim star. Much of the Northwest Territories is burning, but the Earth has survived. Although we may wish we hadn't. items.model_answer:
If you put a running hair dryer in a sealed 1×1×1 meter box, the box would heat up quickly, the air pressure inside would rise somewhat, and the hair dryer would soon stop working normally or fail from overheating.

Here’s the basic physics.

A 1×1×1 meter box holds 1 cubic meter of air, which is about 1.2 kg of air at room conditions. A typical hair dryer uses around 1000–1800 watts. In a sealed box, essentially all of that electrical power ends up as heat inside the box. So the dryer is not “making wind” in any useful external sense; it is just converting electrical energy into thermal energy and stirring the air around.

Air heats fast in that small volume. The heat capacity of 1.2 kg of air is roughly 1200 J/K, so a 1200 W hair dryer could raise the air temperature by about 1 °C per second at first, if you ignore heat loss to the walls. In reality, the walls also absorb heat, so the temperature rise slows, but the box still gets hot very quickly.

The pressure behavior depends on whether the box is truly rigid. In a rigid sealed box, heating the air raises pressure roughly in proportion to absolute temperature. For example, going from 20 °C to 120 °C means going from about 293 K to 393 K, so pressure would rise by about 34%. That is significant, but usually not enough by itself to make a strong box explode. In a flexible box, it would expand instead.

What happens to the hair dryer itself is more important. A hair dryer relies on room-temperature intake air to cool its heating element and motor. In the sealed box, it keeps sucking in hotter and hotter air. That means the element, motor, plastic housing, and thermal cutoff all run under worse conditions. Most likely outcomes are that its thermal protection trips, it shuts off, or it burns out. If the box is very well insulated, this happens sooner.

The fan does not create a lasting pressure difference inside the box. It only circulates the air. In a sealed box, there is nowhere for air to go overall, so after transient local motion, the net effect is just turbulent recirculation and heating.

If the box is perfectly sealed and airtight, oxygen is not replenished, but a hair dryer does not burn fuel, so oxygen depletion is not the main issue. The main issue is electrical heating and lack of cooling. If there are flammable materials in the box, the rising temperature could become a fire hazard, especially if the dryer malfunctions.

So the short answer is: the inside of the box gets hot fast, the pressure rises moderately, the air churns around, and the hair dryer will probably overheat and shut off or fail before anything more dramatic happens.

items.question: How Much Cornstarch Can You Pour down a Drain before Bad Things Happen?
human_answers: It depends what you consider unpleasant. If you watered down the cornstarch enough, you could likely pour it down the drain for years without any ill effects. If it didn’t clog the sink, the rest of the pipes could probably handle it. It might provoke some confusion among the sewage treatment people, but it wouldn’t break anything. But it’d be terrifically boring (and thus unpleasant) to pour cornstarch down a sink all day, so I guess that’s— [Image: image] … Oh. Huh. Well, let’s thicken the cornstarch. When you mix cornstarch and water in a bit under a 2:1 ratio, you get oobleck, a substance with some odd physical properties. This is a great kitchen science experiment everyone should try at least once. At low speeds, oobleck behaves like a liquid. If you gently swish your fingers in a bowl of it, it feels like milk or heavy cream. However, if you make a fist and punch the surface, your hand bounces off with a thud—it’s like hitting a slab of raw meat. If you vibrate oobleck, even stranger things happen (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3zoTKXXNQIU). It wouldn’t take much of the mixture to clog a drain. It depends on your plumbing, but you could probably stop up your sink with a small bowl of it. Since your drain is clogged, I guess that’s the answer to your question. [Image: image] Well, ok. I guess some people don’t mind clogged drains. If you keep at it, after a few minutes, your sink will overflow, spilling goop onto your floor. [Image: image] Financially, this will be hard to keep up. If you’re mixing as fast as the water will come out of the sink, this project may cost you in the neighborhood of $5,000 per day if you can’t find a good bulk distributor. [Image: image] At this rate, it should build up on the floor at a rate of an inch or two per day. [Image: image] If your doors are sealed well, it will continue to build up. Once it reaches knee height (a week or two after you started), you may be able to hold the rising tide at bay for a little bit—at least in one room—by getting someone to flush the toilet repeatedly. The pipes there are larger and harder to clog; the limiting factor would probably be how fast the tank filled with water. [Image: image] Eventually, after a month or two, the oobleck would reach the living room window. The pressure would quickly rise, and sooner or later the window would burst. As the deadly Boston Molasses Flood (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Molasses_Disaster) proved, even thick, viscous fluids can flow quickly when in large enough quantities. The oobleck would pour rapidly out onto the lawn, carrying you with it. At this point, the local officials would probably notice and, at the very least, shut off your water. [Image: image] But I guess if you really like cornstarch that much, nothing unpleasant has happened.

items.model_answer:
Very little. As a practical rule, you should treat the safe amount as essentially none.

Cornstarch is tricky because when it is mixed with water it does not behave like something that simply dissolves and washes away. It forms a suspension and then can settle, clump, and make a paste, especially in slower-moving parts of plumbing like the trap or in partially blocked pipes. If enough accumulates, it can contribute to a clog. In a wider sewer system, small amounts are unlikely to matter, but inside household plumbing repeated “small” disposals can add up.

So the direct answer is: there is no reliable threshold like “half a cup is fine” or “one tablespoon is dangerous.” The amount before “bad things happen” depends on pipe diameter, water flow, existing grease or debris, and whether the starch is dry, slurried, or mixed with other waste. In a typical home drain, even a few tablespoons dumped repeatedly is unwise; a large dump such as a cup or more could plausibly create a blockage, especially if it thickens in the trap or sticks to residue already in the pipe.

If you only sent a tiny accidental amount down with lots of running water, it will probably be fine. But if you have leftover cornstarch or a cornstarch slurry, the best practice is not to pour it down the drain at all. Let it dry and throw it in the trash, or wipe it out with paper towels first.
