items.question: What If You Lived on a Tiny but Ultra-Massive Asteroid?
human_answers: Last week, we looked at at life on a giant world (http://what-if.xkcd.com/67/). This week, let's look at a small one. [Image: image] The Little Prince, by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, is a story about a traveler from a distant asteroid. It's simple and sad and poignant and memorable.[1]For another take on the Petit Prince, scroll down to the last section of this wonderful piece (http://the-toast.net/2013/08/02/texts-from-peter-pan-et-al/) by Mallory Ortberg. It's ostensibly a children's book, but it's hard to pin down who the intended audience is. In any case, it certainly has found an audience; it's among the best-selling books in history. [Image: image] It was written in 1942. That's an interesting time to write about asteroids, because in 1942 we didn't actually know what asteroids looked like. Even in our best telescopes, the largest asteroids were only visible as points of light. In fact, that's where their name comes from—the word asteroid means "star-like." We got our first confirmation of what asteroids looked like in 1971, when Mariner 9 visited Mars and snapped pictures of Phobos and Deimos.[2]Here's (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/m09_mtvs4109_09.html) a picture of Phobos looking like the archetypical asteroid. The archived images from the mission are at the NASA Space Science Data Center (http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/masterCatalog.do?ds=PSPG-00235), but strangely, the NSSDC refers readers to someone's personal Tripod page (http://petermasek.tripod.com/mariner9.html) to browse the actual images. These moons, believed to be captured asteroids,[3]Ironically, while Phobos and Deimos look like asteroids, new research suggests they're not. See Craddock, Robert A.. "Are Phobos And Deimos The Result Of A Giant Impact? (http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0019103510004100)". Icarus (2010) solidified the modern image of asteroids as cratered potatoes. [Image: image] Before the 1970s, it was common for science fiction to assume small asteroids would be round, like planets.[4]Not always; plenty of people had a good idea of what they would look like. And there were stranger ideas (http://pencilink.blogspot.com/2010/08/uncle-scrooge-29-carl-barks-art-cover.html) ... The Little Prince took this a step further, imagining an asteroid as a tiny planet with gravity, air, and a rose. There's no point in trying to critique the science here, because (1) it's not a story about asteroids, and (2) it opens with a parable about how foolish adults are for looking at everything too literally. So rather than trying to take things away from the story, let's see what strange new pieces science can add. If there really were a superdense asteroid with enough surface gravity to walk around on, it would have some pretty surprising properties. If the asteroid has a radius of 1.75 meters, then in order to have Earth-like gravity at the surface, it would need to have a mass of about 500 million tons. This is roughly equal to the combined mass of every human on Earth. If you stood on the surface, you'd experience tidal forces. Your feet would feel heavier than your head, which you'd feel as a gentle stretching sensation. It would feel like you were stretched out on a curved rubber ball, or were lying on a merry-go-round with your head near the center. [Image: image] The escape velocity at the surface would be about 5 meters per second. That's slower than a sprint, but still pretty fast. As a rule of thumb, if you can't dunk a basketball, you wouldn't be able to escape by jumping straight up. [Image: image] However, the weird thing about escape velocity is that it doesn't matter which direction you're going.[5]... which is why it should really be called "escape speed"—the fact that it has no direction (which is the distinction between "speed" and "velocity") is actually very significant here. If you go faster than the escape speed, as long as you don't actually go toward the planet, you'll escape. That means you might be able to leave our asteroid by running horizontally and jumping off the end of a ramp. [Image: image] If you didn't go fast enough to escape the planet, you'd go into orbit around it. Your orbital speed would be roughly 3 meters per second, which is a typical jogging speed. [Image: image] But this would be a weird orbit. Tidal forces would act on you in several ways. If you reach your arm down toward the planet, it would be pulled much harder than the rest of you. And if you reach down with one arm, the rest of you gets pushed upward, which means other parts of your body feel even less gravity. Effectively, every part of your body would be trying to go in a different orbit. A large orbiting object under these kinds of tidal forces—say, a moon—will generally break apart into rings. This wouldn't happen to you. However, your orbit would become chaotic and unstable. These types of orbits were investigated in an interesting paper by Radu D. Rugescu and Daniele Mortari.[6]Rugescu, Radu D., Mortari, Daniele, "Ultra Long Orbital Tethers Behave Highly Non-Keplerian and Unstable (http://www.academia.edu/3453325/Ultra_Long_Orbital_Tethers_Behave_Highly_Non-Keplerian_and_Unstable)", WSEAS Transactions on Mathematics, Vol. 7, No. 3, March 2008, pp. 87-94. Their simulations showed that large, elongated objects follow strange patterns around their central bodies. Even their centers of mass don't move in the traditional ellipses; some adopt pentagonal orbits, while others spin chaotically and crash into the planet. [Image: image] This type of analysis could actually have practical applications. There have been various proposals over the years to use long, whirling tethers to move cargo in and out of gravity wells—a sort of free-floating space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator). Such tethers could transport cargo to and from the surface of the Moon, or to pick up spacecraft from the edge of the Earth's atmosphere. The inherent instability of many tether orbits poses an interesting challenge for this kind of project. As for the residents of our superdense asteroid, they'd have to be careful; if they ran too fast, they'd be in serious danger of going into a tumble and losing their lunch. Fortunately, vertical jumps would be fine. [Image: image]

criteria.3-4: Recognizes strong gravity on a tiny body but gives little or incorrect quantitative support.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that extreme density/mass is required and includes roughly plausible gravity or size estimates.
criteria.7-8: Uses the core scales well: meter-sized radius, hundreds of millions of tons, Earth-like surface gravity, low escape speed.
criteria.9-10: Accurately anchors the scenario with consistent numbers and explains how small radius plus huge mass produces the unusual effects.

criteria.name: Surface gravity and tidal-force mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates explanation of how gravity would feel on a body only a few meters across, especially head-to-foot gravity gradients.
criteria.1-2: Ignores tidal effects or assumes gravity feels uniform like on Earth.
criteria.3-4: Mentions odd gravity but does not explain the gradient across a human body.
criteria.5-6: Explains that feet would feel heavier than the head and that posture/orientation would matter.
criteria.7-8: Clearly describes stretching, curvature, changing gravity with height, and why daily movement would feel strange.
criteria.9-10: Gives a physically faithful account of local gravity gradients, body forces, balance, and how different body parts experience different accelerations.

criteria.name: Movement, escape, and orbital dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces the consequences of low escape speed and nearby orbital speeds for jumping, running, and falling around the asteroid.
criteria.1-2: Claims you could move normally or fly off for the wrong reasons.
criteria.3-4: Notes that escape is possible but confuses escape speed, direction, or orbital motion.
criteria.5-6: Correctly states that fast running/jumping could launch a person into orbit or escape.
criteria.7-8: Explains that escape speed is only a few m/s, orbital speed is jogging speed, and horizontal motion can matter as much as vertical jumping.
criteria.9-10: Accurately develops the full movement chain: ramps/running, low-speed orbit, failed escape paths, unstable tumbling, and likely collisions or recontacts.

criteria.name: Habitability and downstream environmental consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of longer-range implications for actually living there, beyond the immediate gravity trick.
criteria.1-2: Provides only a superficial fantasy answer with little physical follow-through.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few survival issues but misses major consequences of the tiny surface and extreme density.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant effects such as tiny horizon, lack of atmosphere, anchoring, supplies, and danger of falling/orbiting.
criteria.7-8: Connects gravity, surface area, escape speed, atmosphere retention, construction, safety, and daily logistics into a plausible living scenario.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly traces major downstream effects while separating the artificial premise from realistic survival constraints, including material impossibility or exotic matter if relevant.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control

criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, unsupported claims, or violations of the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct ideas but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates speculative details.

items.model_answer:
If you lived on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, life would be dominated by extreme gravity and by the strange consequences of packing a huge amount of mass into a very small object.

If the asteroid were tiny in size but had only moderately high mass, the main effect would be surface gravity far stronger than you would expect from something “asteroid-sized.” You might be standing on a world only a few kilometers or even meters across, yet feel heavier than on Earth. Walking could become difficult or impossible. Your body would be compressed, your heart would struggle to pump blood, and ordinary structures, air, and loose rocks might not stay arranged the way they do on normal small bodies. Jumping would be dangerous because the gravity could pull you down hard, but if the asteroid were still small enough, the horizon would be very close and the curvature obvious.

If it were truly ultra-massive for its size, then the situation becomes much more extreme. The density would have to be enormous, far beyond ordinary rock or metal. That means the object would resemble something exotic, more like a chunk of degenerate matter than a normal asteroid. Near the surface, gravity could become lethal. The difference in gravity between your feet and your head could be large enough to stretch or crush you. This is called a tidal effect. On a very small but very massive object, those tidal forces can become severe because gravity changes rapidly with distance.

Another issue is escape velocity. Even if the asteroid is small, if it is massive enough, escaping it could require tremendous speed. Throwing an object upward might do nothing useful. Light itself could be bent noticeably if the mass were high enough. Time would also pass slightly more slowly near the surface compared with far away, due to gravitational time dilation.

Push the idea far enough, and the asteroid would stop being something you could live on at all. If enough mass were packed into a small enough radius, it would become a black hole. Then there would be no solid surface to stand on. If it were just above that threshold, the gravity and radiation environment around it would still be fatal.

So the careful answer is: on a tiny but ultra-massive asteroid, you probably could not live normally, and in the most extreme cases you could not live there at all. A small size does not mean weak gravity; gravity depends on mass and distance from the center. If the mass is enormous and the radius is tiny, the surface gravity, tidal forces, and escape velocity could make the object far more hostile than a planet.

items.question: Could You Boil Water by Stirring It?
human_answers: No. The basic idea makes sense. Temperature is just kinetic energy. When you stir tea, you're adding kinetic energy to it, and that energy goes somewhere. Since the tea doesn't do anything dramatic like rise into the air or emit light, the energy must be turning to heat. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the heat is that you're not adding very much of it. It takes a huge amount of energy to heat water; by volume, it has a greater heat capacity than any other common substance.[1]Hydrogen and helium have a higher heat capacity by mass, but they're diffuse gasses. The only other common substance with a higher heat capacity by mass is ammonia. All three of these lose to water when measured by volume. If you want to heat water from room temperature to nearly boiling in two minutes, you'll need a lot of power: \[1\text{ cup}\times\text{Water heat capacity}\times\tfrac{100^\circ\rm{C}-20^\circ\rm{C}}{2\text{ minutes}}=700\text{ watts}\] (Note: Pushing almost-boiling water to boiling takes a large burst of extra energy on top of what's required to heat it to the boiling point—this is called the enthalpy of vaporization (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy_of_vaporization).) Our formula tells us that if we want to make a cup of hot water in two minutes, we'll need a 700-watt power source. A typical microwave uses 700 to 1100 watts, and it takes about two minutes to heat a mug of water to make tea. It's nice when things work out![2]If they didn't, we'd just blame "inefficiency" or "vortices". 700 watts for two minutes is an awful lot of energy. When water falls from the top of Niagara Falls, it gains kinetic energy, which is converted to heat at the bottom. But even after falling that great distance, the water only heats up by a fraction of a degree.[3]\(\text{Height of Niagra Falls}\times\frac{\text{Acceleration of gravity}}{\text{Specific heat of water}}=0.12^\circ\text{C}\) To boil a cup of water, you'd have to drop it from higher than the top of the atmosphere. [Image: image] How does stirring compare to microwaving? Based on figures from industrial mixer engineering reports,[4]Brawn Mixer, Inc., Principles of Fluid Mixing (http://www.craneengineering.net/products/mixers/documents/craneEngineeringPrinciplesOfFluidMixing.pdf) (2003) I estimate that vigorously stirring a cup of tea adds heat at a rate of about a ten-millionth of a watt. That's completely negligible.[5]Tea loses heat a much higher rate than this. See: Ben Harden, Tea temperature vs. Time graph (http://www.whoi.edu/vanishingarctic/page.do?pid=48597&tid=441&cid=120786&ct=61&article=82910) The physical effect of stirring is actually a little complicated.[6]In some situations, mixing liquids can actually help keep them warm. Hot water rises, and when a body of water is large and still enough (like the ocean) a warm layer forms on the surface. This warm layer radiates heat much more quickly than a cold layer would. If you disrupt this hot layer by mixing the water, the rate of heat loss decreases. This is why hurricanes tend to lose strength if they stop moving forward—their waves churn up cold water from the depths, cutting them off from the thin layer of hot surface water that was their main source of energy. Most of the heat is carried away from teacups by the air convecting over them, and so they cool from the top down. Stirring brings fresh hot water from the depths, so it can help this process. But there are other things going on—stirring disturbs the air, and it heats the walls of the mug. It's hard to be sure what's really going on without data. Fortunately, we have the internet. StackExchange user drhodes measured the rate of teacup cooling (http://physics.stackexchange.com/a/5510) from stirring vs. not stirring vs. repeatedly dipping a spoon into the cup vs. lifting it. Helpfully, drhodes posted both high-resolution graphs and the raw data itself, which is more than you can say for a lot of journal articles. The conclusion: It doesn't really matter whether you stir, dip, or do nothing; the tea cools at about the same rate (although dipping the spoon in and out of the tea cooled it slightly faster). Which brings us back to the original question: Could you boil tea if you just stirred it hard enough? No. The first problem is power. 700 watts is about a horsepower, so if you want to boil tea in two minutes, you'll need at least one horse to stir it hard enough. [Image: image] You can reduce the power requirement by heating the tea over a longer period of time, but if you reduce it too far the tea will be cooling as fast as you're heating it. Even if you could churn the spoon hard enough—tens of thousands of stirs per second—fluid dynamics would get in the way. At those high speeds, the tea would cavitate; a vacuum would form along the path of the spoon and stirring would become ineffective. And if you stir hard enough that your tea cavitates, its surface area will increase very rapidly, and it will cool to room temperature in seconds: [Image: image] No matter how hard you stir your tea, it's not going to get any warmer.

items.model_answer:
In principle, yes. In practice, no.

Stirring adds mechanical energy to the water, and that energy eventually turns into heat through viscosity and turbulence. So if you kept stirring, the water would warm up. This is the same basic idea as friction heating.

But to actually boil water by stirring alone, you would need to put in a huge amount of energy. To raise 1 kilogram of water from room temperature, say 20°C, to 100°C takes about

\( 4.2 \,\text{kJ/kg·°C} \times 80\,°C \approx 336 \,\text{kJ} \)

and then to boil it away takes even more because of the latent heat of vaporization, about

\( 2260 \,\text{kJ/kg} \)

So just getting it to the boiling point already requires a lot of work, and keeping it boiling requires still more. Human stirring power is small by comparison, and much of the heat would also leak out to the surroundings while you stir.

There is one subtlety: “boiling” usually means vapor bubbles form because the liquid reaches its boiling point at the local pressure. Vigorous stirring can create bubbles, but those are usually just air bubbles or cavitation, not true thermal boiling. So seeing bubbles while stirring does not mean the water has been boiled by heating.

So the careful answer is: stirring can heat water, but not realistically enough to boil it under ordinary conditions.

items.question: What If a Nearby Supernova Hit Earth with Lethal Neutrino Radiation?
human_answers: The phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" is a weird one. I had to turn it over in my head a few times after I heard it. If you're not a physics person, it might not sound odd to you, so here's a little context for why it's such a surprising idea: Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with the world at all. Look at your hand—there are about a trillion neutrinos from the Sun passing through it every second. [Image: image] The reason you don't notice the neutrino flood is that neutrinos hardly interact with ordinary matter at all. On average, out of that massive flood, only one neutrino will "hit" an atom in your body every few years.[1]Less often if you're a child, since you have fewer atoms to be hit. Statistically, my first neutrino interaction probably happened somewhere around age 10. In fact, neutrinos are so shadowy that the entire Earth is transparent to them; nearly all of the Sun's neutrino flood goes straight through it unaffected. To detect neutrinos, people build giant tanks filled with hundreds of tons of material in the hopes that they'll register the impact of a single solar neutrino. This means that when a particle accelerator (which produces neutrinos) wants to send a neutrino beam to a detector somewhere else in the world, all it has to do is point the beam at the detector—even if it's on the other side of the Earth! [Image: image] That's why the phrase "lethal dose of neutrino radiation" sounds weird—it mixes scales in an incongruous way. It's like the idiom "knock me over with a feather" or the phrase "football stadium filled to the brim with ants".[2]Which would still be less than 1% of the ants in the world. If you have a math background, it's sort of like seeing the expression "ln(x)e"—it's not that, taken literally, it doesn't make sense, but it's hard to imagine a situation where it would apply.[3]If you want to be mean to first-year calculus students, you can ask them to take the derivative of ln(x)e dx. It looks like it should be "1" or something, but it's not. Similarly, it's so hard to get enough neutrinos to compel even a single one of them to interact with matter, making it hard to picture a scenario in which there'd be enough of them to affect you. Supernovae[4]"Supernovas" is also fine. "Supernovii" is discouraged. provide that scenario. The physicist who mentioned this problem to me told me his rule of thumb for estimating supernova-related numbers: However big you think supernovae are, they're bigger than that. Here's a question to give you a sense of scale: Which of the following would be brighter, in terms of the amount of energy delivered to your retina: A supernova, seen from as far away as the Sun is from the Earth, or The detonation of a hydrogen bomb pressed against your eyeball? [Image: image] Applying the physicist rule of thumb suggests that the supernova is brighter. And indeed, it is ... by nine orders of magnitude. That's why this is a neat question; supernovae are unimaginably huge and neutrinos are unimaginably insubstantial. At what point do these two unimaginable things cancel out to produce an effect on a human scale? A paper by radiation expert Andrew Karam provides an answer.[5]Karam, P. Andrew. "Gamma And Neutrino Radiation Dose From Gamma Ray Bursts And Nearby Supernovae. (http://wayback.archive.org/web/20120313045458/http://www.andrewkaram.com/andy/pdf/HPJ.pdf)" Health Physics 82, no. 4 (2002): 491-499. It explains that during certain supernovae, the collapse of a stellar core into a neutron star, 1057 neutrinos can be released (one for every proton in the star that collapses to become a neutron). Karam calculates that the neutrino radiation dose at a distance of one parsec[6]3.262 light-years, or a little less than the distance from here to Alpha Centauri. would be around half a nanosievert, or 1/500th the dose from eating a banana.[7]xkcd.com/radiation (http://xkcd.com/radiation/) A fatal radiation dose is about 4 sieverts. Using the inverse-square law, we can calculate the radiation dose: \[ 0.5\text{ nanosieverts} \times\left ( \frac{1\text{ parsec}}{x}\right )^2 = 5\text{ sieverts} \] \[ x=0.00001118\text{ parsecs}=2.3\text{ AU} \] 2.3 AU is a little more than the distance between the Sun and Mars. Core collapse supernovae happen to giant stars, so if you observed a supernova from that distance, you'd probably be inside the outer layers of the star that created it. [Image: image] The idea of neutrino radiation damage reinforces just how big supernovae are. If you observed a supernova from 1 AU away—and you somehow avoided being being incinerated, vaporized, and converted to some type of exotic plasma—even the flood of ghostly neutrinos would be dense enough to kill you. If it's going fast enough, a feather can absolutely knock you over. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
A supernova “killing Earth with neutrino radiation” is essentially not a realistic scenario.

Neutrinos are produced in enormous numbers in a supernova, but they interact so weakly with matter that almost all of them pass straight through Earth, through your body, and even through entire stars without doing anything. In the 1987 supernova SN 1987A, a huge burst of neutrinos reached Earth from about 168,000 light-years away, and it had no biological effect at all.

Even if a supernova happened much closer, neutrinos still would not be the main danger. To make neutrino radiation itself lethal at Earth’s surface, the explosion would have to be implausibly close—so close that Earth would already be destroyed or sterilized by other effects first. Those other effects include intense gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet radiation, high-energy cosmic rays, and the blast’s impact on the atmosphere, especially ozone depletion. A supernova within perhaps a few tens of light-years could seriously damage the biosphere, but not because neutrinos are suddenly efficient at depositing dose in tissue.

If, counterfactually, neutrinos did interact strongly enough to deliver a lethal dose, the consequences would be bizarre and catastrophic. They would penetrate the whole planet, irradiating everything nearly uniformly, including underground shelters and the deep ocean. There would be little shielding, because the usual reason shielding works is that radiation interacts with matter—and ordinary neutrinos mostly do not. In that imaginary case, humans and most complex life could receive fatal whole-body doses almost simultaneously worldwide. Electronics and infrastructure might be less affected than biology unless the interaction strength were so different that matter in general absorbed large amounts of energy.

But in real physics, that is not how neutrinos behave. So the careful answer is: a nearby supernova could be dangerous to Earth, but not through “lethal neutrino radiation.” If a supernova were close enough for neutrinos to be a direct lethal hazard, the Earth would already be in far worse trouble from the rest of the explosion.

items.question: What If Humans Kept Growing at the Rate of a One-Month-Old Baby?
human_answers: Tall. According to the National Center for Health Statistics, the average newborn's height (length) is approximately 0.5 meters,[1]or 0.56 meters in heels. or a quarter of the diameter of the Death Star thermal exhaust port. [Image: image] From this initial height of 0.5 meters, they grow to about 1.5 or 2.0 meters: [Image: image] Babies grow fastest right after they're born. During their first month, infants grow about 4.4 centimeters, ten times their growth rate during their early teenage years. [Image: image] In Maria's scenario, this growth rate continues until about age 20: [Image: image] Let's follow that child's growth over the years. By its first birthday, the baby would be a meter long: [Image: image] At 2 years and 3 months, the kid would reach 169 centimeters (5'7"), the average adult height in the US. [Image: image] By age 3, we'd have a 2.08 meter (6'10") toddler, taller than Darth Vader ... [Image: image] ... and much taller than Yoda: [Image: image] By age 4, the child would be nearly nine feet tall, able to dunk a basketball without jumping.[2]A 7'8" Harlem Globetrotters player can almost dunk without jumping (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HTnC0RBXwws), so the threshold for a clear no-jump dunk is probably around 8 feet. [Image: image] A few months later, the kid would surpass Robert Wadlow (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wadlow) to become the tallest human in history. At age 5, the child would be π meters tall (10'4"): [Image: image] At age 7, the child would be 4.2 meters tall, able to stare down a T-rex: [Image: image] By age 10, the child would be 5.8 meters tall (19 feet). If we assume these giants are proportioned like adult humans, this kid would weigh over a metric ton. [Image: image] Actual humans wouldn't be able to grow to such heights. Thanks to the square-cube law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-cube_law), our bones would be too thin to support our weight and our hearts would be unable to pump blood around our bodies. Even breathing would be difficult; we might be able to position ourselves to keep our airways opened, but to breathe in a lungful of air would require very high airflow rates; we'd experience tornado winds all the way down our airways. Our giant would reach a final height of between 10 and 12 meters, assuming growth tapered off around age 20. At that height, they'd be able to comfortably dunk a basketball while keeping one hand on the court outside the three-point line.[3]A creative NBA 2K3 mod shows us what that player might look like (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vGt10eu4XB8). [Image: image] In addition to the insurmountable health problems, someone with this rapid growth rate would face another hardship. To ride roller coasters, you have to be above a certain minimum height. However, they generally also have a maximum height. [Image: image] Bizarro, a coaster at Six Flags New England, has a minimum height of 137 cm (4'6") and a maximum height of 193 cm (6'4"). Our child would be tall enough to ride Bizarro at age 2 ... and too tall by age 3. Their coaster-riding window would last only 387 days. It's a sad truth: Roller coasters just aren't for everyone. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
A one-month-old baby grows astonishingly fast compared with an older child or adult. A typical newborn is about 50 cm long, and by one month may be around 54 cm, so the growth rate is roughly 4 cm per month.

If a human kept growing at that same linear rate forever, the consequences would be absurdly dramatic. At 4 cm per month, that is about 48 cm per year. Starting from about 50 cm at birth, a person would be around 1.94 meters tall by age 3, about 5.8 meters by age 11, about 10.6 meters by age 21, and around 39 meters by age 81.

But biology would not allow this to work. The main problem is the square-cube law. As height increases, body volume and mass grow roughly with the cube of size, while the strength of bones and muscles depends more on cross-sectional area, which grows only with the square. So a person scaled up this way would become far too heavy for their skeleton and muscles. Their bones would likely fail, movement would become impossible, and the heart and lungs would struggle to support such a huge body.

Metabolism and food needs would also become enormous. A giant human several times normal height would need vast amounts of energy, oxygen, water, and nutrients. Heat removal would become difficult too, because large bodies trap heat more easily.

So in a purely mathematical sense, humans would become gigantic—tens of meters tall over a lifetime. In a physical and biological sense, they would die long before reaching those sizes, because the human body is not built to keep scaling up at an infant’s growth rate.

items.question: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?
human_answers: About half of an adult, or one ten-year old child: [Image: image] Tyrannosaurus rex weighed about as much as an elephant.[1]This always seemed a little off to me; my mental image of elephants is that they're in the same size range as cars or trucks, whereas T-rex, as Jurassic Park showed, is big enough to stomp on cars. But a Google image search for car+elephant (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=elephant+car) shows elephants looming over cars just like the T-rex in Jurassic Park. So, great, now I'm also afraid of elephants. [Image: image] No one is totally sure what dinosaur metabolism looked like, but the best guesses for how much food T-rex ate seem to cluster around 40,000 calories per day.[2]Food calories (kcal). Sources: This (http://www.pnas.org/content/106/29/12184.full) and this (http://palaeo-electronica.org/1999_2/gigan/issue2_99.htm), and this (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2666002) with some notes from this (http://www.plosone.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0026037) and distraction from this (http://regex.alf.nu/). If we assume dinosaurs had metabolisms similar to today's mammals, they'd eat a lot more than 40,000 calories each day. But the current thinking is that while dinosaurs were more active (loosely speaking, "warm-blooded") than modern snakes and lizards, very large dinosaurs probably had metabolisms that more closely resembled komodo dragons than elephants and tigers.[3]For big sauropods, we know this must be the case, because otherwise they would overheat. However, there's a lot of uncertainty surrounding T-rex-sized dinosaurs. Next, we need to know how many calories are in a human. This number is helpfully provided, by Dinosaur Comics author Ryan North, on this wonderful t-shirt (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Store_Code=TO&Product_Code=QW-PERSON&Category_Code=QW). Ryan's shirt tells us that an 80-kg human contains about 110,000 calories of energy. Therefore, a T-rex would need to consume a human every two days or so.[4]Although a T-rex would likely be willing to eat several days to weeks worth of food in one meal, so if it has the option, it might eat a bunch of people at a time, then go for a while without eating. The city of New York had 239,736 births in 2011, which could support a population of about 1,000 tyrannosaurs. However, this ignores immigration—and, more importantly, emigration, which would probably increase substantially in this scenario. [Image: image] The 33,000 McDonald's restaurants worldwide sell something like 15 billion hamburger patties per year,[5]They stopped reporting the "x billions served" number on their signs, but this website (http://overhowmanybillionserved.blogspot.com/) has some extrapolations. for an average of 1,245 burgers per restaurant per day. 1,245 burgers is about 600,000 calories, which means that each T-rex only needs about 80 hamburgers per day to survive, and one McDonald's could support over a dozen tyrannosaurs on hamburgers alone. [Image: image] Ands if you live in New York, and you see a T-rex, don't worry. You don't have to choose a friend to sacrifice; just order 80 burgers instead. And then if the T-rex goes for your friend anyway, hey, you have 80 burgers. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If a Tyrannosaurus Rex Were Released in New York City?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Biological Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons from the specific premise of a Tyrannosaurus rex suddenly released in modern New York City while maintaining plausible T. rex biology, scale, metabolism, sensory abilities, locomotion, and behavioral constraints.
criteria.1-2: Treats the T. rex as a fantasy monster or ignores the NYC premise; major biological claims are implausible.
criteria.3-4: Uses the premise but relies on cinematic assumptions; includes several inaccurate claims about size, speed, diet, or behavior.
criteria.5-6: Mostly plausible biology and setting; some oversimplifications or unsupported assumptions remain.
criteria.7-8: Grounds the scenario in reasonable estimates of mass, food needs, movement, predation, and stress responses.
criteria.9-10: Carefully applies uncertain but evidence-based T. rex biology to the exact NYC release scenario without sensationalism.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage of Immediate Urban Interactions
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the direct mechanisms by which a T. rex would interact with New York City: streets, crowds, vehicles, buildings, transit systems, noise, barriers, police response, and animal-control logistics.
criteria.1-2: Gives only vague destruction or panic with no concrete urban mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few effects such as traffic or panic but lacks causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Covers several immediate interactions, including people, vehicles, and emergency services, with moderate detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains how NYC infrastructure, congestion, visibility, barriers, and responders would shape the event.
criteria.9-10: Provides a rich, mechanically coherent account of the first minutes to hours across crowds, transport, buildings, and containment.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces coherent downstream effects beyond the initial release, including containment, casualties, public behavior, institutional response, media, legal consequences, scientific interest, and city recovery.
criteria.1-2: Stops at the initial encounter or gives disconnected consequences.
criteria.3-4: Includes some later effects but with weak sequencing or missing causes.
criteria.5-6: Presents a plausible short-to-medium-term chain but omits major downstream domains.
criteria.7-8: Links immediate events to longer-term emergency, political, economic, scientific, and social consequences.
criteria.9-10: Builds a well-sequenced long-range scenario from release through containment and aftermath with minimal causal gaps.

criteria.name: Food, Energy, and Survival Reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly estimates or qualitatively reasons about the T. rex's caloric needs, feeding opportunities, prey availability, scavenging, zoo/livestock/human food sources, and whether it could survive in NYC.
criteria.1-2: Ignores food needs or makes absurd claims about constant mass killing or starvation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions eating people or animals but gives little metabolic or availability reasoning.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes large but finite food requirements and identifies plausible food sources.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable quantitative or comparative estimates and connects them to NYC food systems and human behavior.
criteria.9-10: Carefully analyzes survival using calibrated caloric needs, feeding intervals, available food, and containment timescale.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes knowns from uncertainties, avoids internal contradictions, and resists overconfident claims about extinct-animal behavior, emergency outcomes, or exact casualty counts.
criteria.1-2: Highly overconfident, contradictory, or internally inconsistent.
criteria.3-4: Some uncertainty is acknowledged, but key claims conflict or are asserted without support.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent; notes a few uncertainties but still overstates some outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertain areas such as T. rex behavior, response time, and casualties while keeping the scenario consistent.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight internal consistency and well-calibrated uncertainty across biological, logistical, and social consequences.

items.model_answer:
If a Tyrannosaurus rex were somehow released in modern New York City, the result would be chaotic and dangerous at first, but it would probably not become a long-term unstoppable threat.

A real T. rex was an enormous predator, roughly 12 meters long and weighing around 7 to 9 tons. In a dense city, that size would make it terrifying but also limit it. It could smash cars, break through some storefronts, and cause panic in streets and parks. Crowds would be at greatest risk in the first minutes to hours, especially if people ran unpredictably or traffic trapped them nearby. Its bite force and mass would make individual vehicles, barriers, and small structures poor protection.

But New York City is not a prehistoric ecosystem. The animal would face major disadvantages. Streets are narrow relative to its turning radius, many spaces are cluttered, and tall buildings create bottlenecks. It could not easily move through subways, stairwells, or most building interiors. Bridges, tunnels, and dense traffic could channel its movement. It would also be under constant observation from cameras, helicopters, drones, and police.

Modern response would matter more than the dinosaur itself. Law enforcement would first try to isolate the area and evacuate civilians. Standard small arms might not reliably stop such a large animal quickly, but specialized rifles, armored vehicles, heavy tranquilizers if available, and ultimately military-grade weapons could kill or disable it. Tranquilization would be difficult because dosage for an animal that size is uncertain, onset may be too slow, and stress could make it even more dangerous before sedation took effect. In practice, authorities would likely choose lethal force if civilians were at risk.

Biologically, the animal might also struggle. A T. rex adapted to a Late Cretaceous environment, not modern pathogens, climate, noise, pavement, and artificial lighting. It might overheat, become disoriented, injure its feet on concrete and debris, or suffer stress-related collapse. If it were healthy enough to function, it could still survive for some time, but not indefinitely.

So the most likely outcome is this: there would be severe local destruction, multiple casualties, and a massive emergency response, but the T. rex would probably be tracked, contained, and killed within hours to perhaps a day or two, not allowed to roam the city for long. The real danger would be the initial surprise and panic, not the dinosaur

the result would be chaotic and dangerous at first,
but it would probably not become a long-term unstoppable threat.
A real T. rex was an enormous predator, roughly 12 meters long and weighing around 7 to 9 tons.
In a dense city, that size would make it terrifying
but also limit it.
It could smash cars, break through some storefronts, and cause panic in streets and parks.
Crowds would be at greatest risk in the first minutes to hours,
especially if people ran unpredictably or traffic trapped them nearby.

The animal would face major disadvantages.
Streets are narrow relative to its turning radius, many spaces are cluttered, and tall buildings create bottlenecks.
It could not easily move through subways, stairwells, or most building interiors.
Bridges, tunnels, and dense traffic could channel its movement.
It would also be under constant observation from cameras, helicopters, drones, and police.
Modern response would matter more than the dinosaur itself.
Law enforcement would first try to isolate the area and evacuate civilians.
Standard small arms might not reliably stop such a large animal quickly,
but specialized rifles, armored vehicles, heavy tranquilizers if available, and ultimately military-grade weapons could kill or disable it.

It might overheat, become disoriented, injure its feet on concrete and debris, or suffer stress-related collapse.
If it were healthy enough to function,
it could still survive for some time,
but not indefinitely.
So the most likely outcome is this:
there would be severe local destruction, multiple casualties, and a massive emergency response,
but the T. rex would probably be tracked, contained, and killed within hours to perhaps a day or two,
not allowed to roam the city for long.
The real danger would be the initial surprise and panic,
not the dinosaur.

items.question: What If You Dumped All the World's Tea into the Great Lakes?
human_answers: Weak, bordering on homeopathic. The standard cup of tea, as described by the International Organization for Standardization in ISO 3103 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=8250), contains two grams of tea per 100 mL of water.[1]Further ISO standards concerning tea include ISO 3720 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51541) (black tea), ISO 11287 (http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=51540) (green tea), and ISO 14502-2 (http://www.iso.org/iso/iso_catalogue/catalogue_tc/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=31357) (the difference between black tea and green tea). The Great Lakes have a volume of about 22,600 cubic kilometers, which means we would need about 450 billion tons of tea to reach proper strength. According to the Tea Board of India, one year's global tea harvest totals only about 4.8 million tons,[2]Using figures from this report (http://www.teaboard.gov.in/pdf/Tea%20Statistics%20Global%20Scenario.pdf) extrapolated forward to 2014. only 1/100,000th of what we'd require to make Great Lake Tea. If we dumped those 4.8 million tons into the lakes, the resulting tea would be about as strong as if we'd dripped two drops of tea in a bathtub.[3]Technically, calling this kind of tea "homeopathic" is an exaggeration, since substances in homeopathy are diluted way more than this. Proper bathtub tea, of course, requires one 3-kg bag. [Image: image] For better lake tea, we should find a lake with a volume of 240 million cubic meters (0.24 cubic kilometers). Wular Lake in Kashmir is one candidate. Its volume varies with the seasons, but during the winter it's just about exactly the right size.[4]Unfortunately, it's shrinking (http://www.ramsar.org/pdf/wurc/wurc_mgtplan_india_wular.pdf). (For winter volume, see the chart on page 18 of that report.) India is the world's second-largest tea producer, so it's also conveniently located. Ullswater, in the UK's Lake District, is another great candidate. With a relatively stable year-round volume of about 0.23 cubic kilometers, it would be an excellent site for brewing a global cup of tea. Of course, while neither Wular Lake or Ullswater has ever been used as a giant teakettle, something like this was—famously—attempted in my own backyard in Boston. In 1773, a group of colonists disguised as American Indians[5]They dressed up as American Indians to align themselves politically with the Americas—against Britain—invoking the popular European stereotype of the free and noble savage. The Mohawk people, the actual Indians who the protesters were mimicking, mistrusted the settlers encroaching on their land, sided with the British during the subsequent war, and afterward were driven from their homes by the Americans and fled to Canada. boarded three British ships and threw the cargo of tea—around 44 tons of it—into Boston Harbor to protest British-run tax policy. Boston Harbor has a volume of about 0.44 cubic kilometers, which means that the "tea" brewed in 1773 would have been even more dilute than our Great Lakes tea. The harbor is also somewhat larger[6]The tidal range in Boston is so large (over three meters) that the harbor's volume at high tide is nearly double what it is at low. than Wular Lake or Ullswater, so all the tea in the world would still make Boston Harbor slightly too weak. [Image: image] There's another problem: Heat. If you wanted to make tea from a lake, such as Ullswater or Wular Lake, you'd have to heat the water up. Is that even possible? There's clearly enough stored energy in the world to do it. After all, we presumably heat that amount of water for tea every year already; we just do it in small batches around the world. To heat up Ullswater to 80°C[7]Lots of people have very strong opinions on what this temperature should be. Please direct any corrections on this matter to What-If Tea-Related Complaints Dep't, c/o Her Majesty The Queen, Buckingham Palace, London SW1A 1AA. would take \(6.6 \times 10^{16}\) joules of energy—about 20 days worth of British electricity consumption. which is roughly what would be released if you dropped a water bottle full of antimatter in the lake. [Image: image] Asking Britain to go without electricity for 20 days just to fill one of their lakes with tea seems like it might be a hard sell. Fortunately, there's an easier solution. Boiling Lake in Dominica is a volcanic lake about 60 meters across. Its temperature varies, but it's often near boiling at the edges and vigorously boiling in the center. Measuring the depth of the lake is difficult, so it's hard to get an estimate of the total volume. [Image: image] Frying Pan Lake in New Zealand, on the other hand, is the largest hot lake in the world. It has a volume of about 200,000 m3, and an average temperature of around 50°C—not quite hot enough for tea, but much closer than Ullswater or Wular Lake. New Zealanders consume about 600 grams of tea per person,[8]Kerryn Pollock. 'Tea, coffee and soft drinks (http://www.teara.govt.nz/en/tea-coffee-and-soft-drinks)', Te Ara - the Encyclopedia of New Zealand, updated 15-Jul-13 for a total of 2,700 tons of tea. If they waited until Frying Pan Lake got particularly hot, then dunked it all in at once ... [Image: image] ... they could brew a year's worth of tea in minutes.

items.model_answer:
If you dumped all the world’s tea into the Great Lakes, the result would be dramatic visually and locally, but it would not literally turn the lakes into “tea” in the everyday sense.

The key issue is scale. The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or roughly 2.3 × 10^16 liters. Global annual tea production is on the order of a few million metric tons, say around 6 million tons as a rough figure. Even if every bit of that were dumped in at once, it would still be tiny compared with the lakes’ total mass of water.

If we imagine 6 million metric tons of dry tea leaves spread through the whole Great Lakes system, that is about 6 × 10^12 grams of tea in about 2.3 × 10^16 liters of water, giving an average of roughly 0.00026 grams per liter, or about 0.26 milligrams per liter. That is an extremely weak concentration. A normal cup of tea might use around 2 grams of tea in 250 milliliters, equivalent to about 8 grams per liter before brewing losses. So the lakes-wide average would be tens of thousands of times weaker than a drinkable cup.

In practice, though, the tea would not instantly dissolve. Most of it would be floating or sinking plant matter. Near the dumping sites, the water would become brown, murky, and full of organic debris. There would be a strong local ecological effect: decomposition would consume oxygen, microbes would bloom, and fish and invertebrates could be harmed in affected regions. Nutrients and tannins released from the leaves could alter water chemistry somewhat, especially near shorelines or in enclosed bays.

Over time, currents and mixing would spread the material out. The visual staining would fade as the tea compounds diluted, settled, decomposed, or were flushed downstream through the St. Lawrence system. The lakes would not become a giant potable tea beverage; they are simply far too large. What you would really get is a massive pulse of organic pollution, with local water-quality damage and ecological stress, but only a vanishingly weak “tea concentration” on the scale of the entire Great Lakes.

but it would not literally turn the lakes into “tea” in the everyday sense.

The Great Lakes contain about 22,700 cubic kilometers of water, or roughly 2.3 × 10^16 liters.
Global annual tea production is on the order of a few million metric tons, say around 6 million tons as a rough figure.
Even if every bit of that were dumped in at once, it would still be tiny compared with the lakes’ total mass of water.
If we imagine 6 million metric tons of dry tea leaves spread through the whole Great Lakes system,
that is about 6 × 10^12 grams of tea in about 2.3 × 10^16 liters of water,
giving an average of roughly 0.00026 grams per liter, or about 0.26 milligrams per liter.
That is an extremely weak concentration.
A normal cup of tea might use around 2 grams of tea in 250 milliliters, equivalent to about 8 grams per liter before brewing losses.

Most of it would be floating or sinking plant matter.
Near the dumping sites, the water would become brown, murky, and full of organic debris.

microbes would bloom,

Nutrients and tannins released from the leaves could alter water chemistry somewhat, especially near shorelines or in enclosed bays.
Over time, currents and mixing would spread the material out.
The visual staining would fade as the tea compounds diluted, settled, decomposed, or were flushed downstream through the St. Lawrence system.
The lakes would not become a giant potable tea beverage; they are simply far too large.
What you would really get is a massive pulse of organic pollution, with local water-quality damage and ecological stress,

items.question: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?
human_answers: It would be a huge pile, but human viruses would make up only a tiny fraction of it. HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, has killed tens of millions of people worldwide, and over 30 million people are currently living with HIV. The number of copies of the virus carried in someone's blood can vary dramatically,[1]Data on viral load—the number of copies of the virus per mL of blood—can be found in this paper (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23196933). but across all the people in the world, there probably exists about a spoonful worth of HIV. [Image: image] The typical healthy human body contains about \(3 \times 10^{12}\) viruses. This is actually not as many as you might expect; by volume, humans are apparently a less friendly environment for viruses than, say, soil.[2]An area of wetlands in Delaware (http://www.rcn.montana.edu/pubs/pdf/2008/Srinivasiah%20Res%20%20Micro%202008.pdf) contains something like four billion viruses per mL of soil, in case you were looking for a fun vacation destination. If you gathered together all the viruses in all the humans in the world, they would fill about ten oil drums: [Image: image] These 10 barrels only represent a tiny portion of the global virus community. Most of the world's viruses aren't found in humans. They're found in the sea. Seawater is full of microorganisms, and we've recently learned that those microorganisms are preyed on by viruses in a big way. Every day, about one in five living cells in the ocean is killed by a virus.[3]Marine viruses—major players in the global ecosystem (https://www.uni-due.de/imperia/md/content/water-science/ws0910/2031b_02z_ws0910_suttle_marine_viruses.pdf) These viruses are found from the surface of the ocean down to the depths.[4]Oddly, as you go further offshore and further down, the concentration of viruses doesn't decrease as much as the concentration of bacteria, so the virus-to-bacteria ratio is higher in the deep oceans than near the shore. Because the sea is so big,[5]Citation: Go and look at the sea. It's big. it contains a staggering number of viruses. If you piled up all these viruses—more than 1030 of them—in one place, they would be the size of a small mountain. [Image: image] It's hard to say exactly what the virus mountain would look like, but it would probably resemble something in between pus and meat slurry.[6]Blame Dave—he's the one who asked. Regardless of its exact appearance, it would almost certainly be disgusting. [Image: image] The pile wouldn't stay mountain-shaped for long, any more than a mountain of any organic secretion would.[7]If you don't believe me, try building a mountain of earwax or snot. You'll find you can't make it higher than a few inches before your friends and family show up and sit you down for a talk. To avoid a gigantic flood, it might be better to collect them into some kind of container. MetLife Stadium, host of Super Bowl XLVIII, has a volume of about 1.5 million cubic meters. Earth's viruses could fill the stadium about 150 times over. So if you watch the Super Bowl, take a moment to picture all the players floating, suspended, in a sea of yellowish-white secretions. [Image: image] Enjoy the game!

rubrics.question_focus: What If All the World's Viruses Were Gathered in One Place?

criteria.name: Scale and Source Attribution of the Virus Pile
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons about the quantity, volume, and dominant sources of all viruses on Earth under the gathering premise.
criteria.1-2: Gives wildly incorrect scale claims, such as saying the pile is microscopic, planet-sized, or mostly human viruses.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes viruses are numerous but gives vague or materially wrong estimates and misses that humans contribute only a tiny fraction.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that most viruses are environmental, especially marine, and gives a broadly large but imprecise pile size.
criteria.7-8: Uses reasonable order-of-magnitude reasoning, noting around 10^30 viruses and a pile comparable to a small mountain or many stadium volumes.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes human, soil, and ocean contributions, keeps estimates order-of-magnitude plausible, and avoids false precision.

criteria.name: Physical Consequences of Gathering Viruses in One Place
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer plausibly models what the gathered viruses would physically be like and how the mass would behave.
criteria.1-2: Treats viruses as magical, gaseous, glowing, or self-organizing matter with no physical constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a pile but gives implausible physical behavior, such as a stable sharp mountain or a solid block without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes the gathered material would be a large biological slurry and would not retain a tall pile shape for long.
criteria.7-8: Explains that water, organic material, capsids, and host-associated residues would form a disgusting fluid or paste needing containment.
criteria.9-10: Connects volume, density, fluid collapse, containment needs, decomposition, and environmental exposure in a physically coherent way.

criteria.name: Virology and Infectious-Risk Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accurately reasons about infectivity, host specificity, and disease risk from concentrating all viruses.
criteria.1-2: Claims all viruses would instantly merge, become one supervirus, or infect every organism indiscriminately.
criteria.3-4: Overstates pandemic risk while ignoring host specificity, viability limits, and the need for susceptible hosts.
criteria.5-6: Notes that many viruses would not infect humans, though some concentrated pathogens would pose local hazards.
criteria.7-8: Explains host range, environmental decay, dose, exposure routes, and the difference between virions being present and causing infection.
criteria.9-10: Balances severe local biosafety danger with rejection of universal-contagion claims, including bacteriophages, plant viruses, animal viruses, and human pathogens.

criteria.name: Long-Range Ecological and Biological Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences of removing and relocating Earth's viruses.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or gives unrelated apocalyptic claims with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions ecosystem disruption but only in generic terms and without linking to viral ecological roles.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that removing viruses would affect oceans, microbes, and disease dynamics, but with limited causal detail.
criteria.7-8: Connects viral removal to microbial population changes, nutrient cycling, marine food webs, phage control of bacteria, and microbiome disruption.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent multi-step chain from viral disappearance to microbial blooms/crashes, altered carbon and nutrient fluxes, ecosystem instability, and possible recovery or replacement dynamics.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Consistency, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a clear interpretation of the counterfactual and calibrates uncertainty without contradicting itself.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise, shifts scenarios repeatedly, or presents impossible outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Uses an unclear version of the premise and mixes incompatible assumptions, such as viruses both remaining everywhere and being fully gathered.
criteria.5-6: Mostly follows the gathering premise but leaves key assumptions ambiguous and makes some overconfident claims.
criteria.7-8: States reasonable assumptions, distinguishes immediate from long-term effects, and flags uncertain estimates or biological responses.
criteria.9-10: Maintains one consistent counterfactual, separates physical aggregation from ecological removal effects, and uses uncertainty ranges without undermining causal reasoning.

items.model_answer:
If you gathered all the viruses on Earth into one place, the total amount would be astonishingly large in number but surprisingly small in physical size.

A common estimate is that there are about 10^31 viruses on Earth. That is ten nonillion—far more than the number of stars in the observable universe. But viruses are extremely tiny, typically on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers across.

If you lined up all the viruses end to end, they would stretch an enormous distance—often estimated at around 100 million light-years or more, depending on the assumed average size. That comparison is often used to show just how many there are.

But if instead you physically packed them together into one volume, they would not make something planet-sized. Their total volume would likely be on the order of a few hundred million cubic meters, depending on the average virus size and how tightly they were packed. That corresponds roughly to a large mountain, a small asteroid, or a cube a few hundred meters on a side. If the average virus were larger, the estimate could rise to around a cubic kilometer or more, but still nowhere near the size of a city or planet.

The more important issue is biological, not geometric. Putting all the world’s viruses in one place would create an unimaginably dangerous reservoir of infectious material. Many viruses infect only bacteria, plants, or specific animals, so not all would threaten humans. In fact, most viruses on Earth are probably bacteriophages in the oceans and soils. Still, concentrating all viruses together would massively disrupt ecosystems and create extreme risks of cross-species exposure, recombination, and environmental contamination.

So the short answer is: all the world’s viruses gathered in one place would form a physically modest but biologically extraordinary mass—probably something like a large hill or small mountain of viral particles, containing an incomprehensibly large number of entities and posing immense ecological danger.

nodes.text: If you gathered all the viruses on Earth into one place, the total amount would be astonishingly large in number but surprisingly small in physical size.
A common estimate is that there are about 10^31 viruses on Earth.
That is ten nonillion—far more than the number of stars in the observable universe.
But viruses are extremely tiny, typically on the order of tens to hundreds of nanometers across.
If you lined up all the viruses end to end, they would stretch an enormous distance—often estimated at around 100 million light-years or more, depending on the assumed average size.
That comparison is often used to show just how many there are.
But if instead you physically packed them together into one volume, they would not make something planet-sized.
Their total volume would likely be on the order of a few hundred million cubic meters, depending on the average virus size and how tightly they were packed.
That corresponds roughly to a large mountain, a small asteroid, or a cube a few hundred meters on a side.
If the average virus were larger, the estimate could rise to around a cubic kilometer or more, but still nowhere near the size of a city or planet.
The more important issue is biological, not geometric.
Putting all the world’s viruses in one place would create an unimaginably dangerous reservoir of infectious material.
Many viruses infect only bacteria, plants, or specific animals, so not all would threaten humans.
In fact, most viruses on Earth are probably bacteriophages in the oceans and soils.
Still, concentrating all viruses together would massively disrupt ecosystems and create extreme risks of cross-species exposure, recombination, and environmental contamination.

So the short answer is: all the world’s viruses gathered in one place would form a physically modest but biologically extraordinary mass—probably something like a large hill or small mountain of viral particles, containing an incomprehensibly large number of entities and posing immense ecological danger.

items.question: What If You Tried to Catch a Bullet after It Slowed Down?
human_answers: Yes. The "bullet catch" is a common magic trick in which a magician appears to catch a fired bullet in mid-flight—often between their teeth. This an illusion, of course; it's not possible to catch a bullet like that.[1]This was confirmed (http://www.discovery.com/tv-shows/mythbusters/mythbusters-database/catch-bullet-teeth.htm) by Mythbusters in episode 4 of Season 4. But under the right conditions, you could catch a bullet. It would just take a lot of patience.[2]I'd like to remind everyone that while I write sometimes about the interesting physics of bullets, I'm not an authority on firearms safety. I was raised Quaker (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers); I've never held a gun, much less fired one. A bullet fired straight up would eventually reach a maximum height.[3]Don't do this. In neighborhoods where people fire guns upward in celebration, bystanders are routinely killed (http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/PDF/wk/mm5350.pdf) by falling bullets. It probably wouldn't stop completely; more likely, it would be drifting sideways at a couple meters per second. At that speed, as long as you were in the right place at the right time, you could snatch it out of the air. If someone fired a bullet upward ... [Image: image] ... and you were hanging out in a hot-air balloon directly above the firing range ... [Image: image] ... it's possible that you could reach out and snag the bullet at the apex of its flight. If you succeeded, you might notice something odd: In addition to being hot, the bullet would be spinning. It would have lost its upward momentum, but not its rotational momentum; it would still have the spin given to it by the barrel of the gun. [Image: image] This effect can be seen, dramatically, when a bullet is fired at ice.[4]Floor water. As confirmed by dozens of YouTube videos (https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=bullet%20spinning%20ice) (and Mythbusters), bullets fired into ice are often found still spinning rapidly. You'd have to grab the bullet firmly; otherwise, it might jump out of your hand. If you don't have a balloon, you could potentially make this work from a mountain peak. Mount Thor, which you may remember from question #51 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/51/), features a vertical drop of 1,250 meters. According to ballistics lab Close Focus Research, this is almost exactly how high a .22 Long Rifle bullet will fly if fired directly upward.[5]Close Focus Research, Maximum Altitude For Bullets Fired Vertically (http://www.closefocusresearch.com/maximum-altitude-bullets-fired-vertically) [Image: image] If you want to use larger bullets, you'll need a much larger drop; an AK-47's bullet can go over two kilometers upward. There are no purely vertical cliffs that are that tall, so you'd need to fire the bullet at an angle, and it would have significant sideways speed at the top of its arc. However, a suitably tough baseball glove might be able to snag it.[6]In fact, according to Rifle Magazine, a gun writer once claimed (https://www.riflemagazine.com/magazine/article.cfm?magid=78&tocid=1094) that at a thousand yards, he could catch ordinary rifle bullets with a baseball glove. Of course, he was being figurative—you wouldn't see the bullet coming, so you'd be just as likely to catch it with your face as with your glove. In any of these scenarios, you'd have to get extraordinarily lucky. Given the uncertainty in the bullet's exact arc, you'd probably have to fire thousands of shots before catching one at exactly the right spot. And by that point, you may find you've attracted some attention. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a bullet had really slowed down enough, then yes, in principle you could catch it safely. The key issue is not that it is “a bullet” but how fast it is moving when it reaches your hand.

A normal fired bullet is far too fast to catch. Handgun bullets are often a few hundred meters per second, and rifle bullets can be much faster. At those speeds, the bullet carries enough kinetic energy to tear through skin, bone, and tissue. Your hand would not “grab” it; the bullet would punch into or through it.

But if the bullet were slowed dramatically, the situation changes. Kinetic energy scales with the square of speed, so cutting the speed a lot cuts the danger a lot. If the bullet had slowed to something like the speed of a tossed pebble, then catching it would be more like catching any small metal object. It might still hurt because bullets are dense and often irregularly shaped, but it would not necessarily penetrate your hand.

There is a real-world example behind this idea: bullets fired straight up can lose most of their initial speed on the way up, then fall back down. Even then, they can still be dangerous or deadly, because a falling bullet can still reach speeds high enough to injure. So “slowed down” does not automatically mean “safe.”

Also, trying to catch even a slow bullet is risky because bullets can tumble, be hot, or have sharp deformed edges. And if the bullet is only “somewhat” slowed, your reaction time is another problem: you are not likely to track and grab a small fast object reliably.

So the direct answer is: if the bullet slowed enough, you could catch it, but only once it had become slow enough that it was basically no different from catching any other small thrown object. At ordinary bullet speeds, catching it is impossible and would badly injure you.

nodes.text: If a bullet had really slowed down enough, then yes, in principle you could catch it safely.
The key issue is not that it is “a bullet” but how fast it is moving when it reaches your hand.
A normal fired bullet is far too fast to catch.
Handgun bullets are often a few hundred meters per second, and rifle bullets can be much faster.
At those speeds, the bullet carries enough kinetic energy to tear through skin, bone, and tissue.
Your hand would not “grab” it; the bullet would punch into or through it.
But if the bullet were slowed dramatically, the situation changes.
Kinetic energy scales with the square of speed, so cutting the speed a lot cuts the danger a lot.
If the bullet had slowed to something like the speed of a tossed pebble, then catching it would be more like catching any small metal object.
It might still hurt because bullets are dense and often irregularly shaped,
but it would not necessarily penetrate your hand.
There is a real-world example behind this idea: bullets fired straight up can lose most of their initial speed on the way up, then fall back down.
Even then, they can still be dangerous or deadly,
because a falling bullet can still reach speeds high enough to injure.
So “slowed down” does not automatically mean “safe.”
Also, trying to catch even a slow bullet is risky because bullets can tumble, be hot, or have sharp deformed edges.
And if the bullet is only “somewhat” slowed, your reaction time is another problem:
you are not likely to track and grab a small fast object reliably.
So the direct answer is: if the bullet slowed enough, you could catch it,
but only once it had become slow enough that it was basically no different from catching any other small thrown object.
At ordinary bullet speeds, catching it is impossible and would badly injure you.

items.question: What If Astronauts Tried to Reach the Moon by Hitting Golf Balls in Orbit?
human_answers: It depends how good your swing is. That sounds glib, but it's sort of true. The answer to this question hinges on exactly how fast you can hit a golf ball. Sometimes, exact numbers don't matter that much. If my baseball, car, dog, or Zamboni goes a little faster than yours,[1]$20 says they will! it will go a little farther. But that's not how it works in rocket golf. The design of our spaceship turns out to involve an equation where the speed of the golf ball is in the exponent. That means a small change in speed can make a big difference. The equation in question—which might be my favorite in all of physics—the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \[ \Delta v = v_\text{exhaust} \ln \frac{m_\text{initial}}{m_\text{final}} \] This equation comes up a lot in What If calculations. I like it both because it says something fundamental about our ability to explore the universe, and because you can use it to get really good at Kerbal Space Program. With some rearranging, the equation can help us figure out how much of our ship's weight has to be golf balls: \[ \frac{\text{Mass of ship plus golf balls}}{\text{Mass of ship alone}} = e ^ \left ( \frac{\text{Ship's change in speed}}{\text{Speed of golf ball}} \right ) \] Someone who, like me, has never been golfing before, might—after swinging and missing a few times—manage to hit the ball at 120 mph (50 m/s).[2]See Trackman's page on ball speed (http://mytrackman.com/explore/trackman-data/trackman-ball-data/ball-speed) To get to the Moon from low Earth orbit, you would need enough fuel to add 5,300 m/s to your ship's speed. By putting those numbers into the rocket equation, we can find out how large a sack of golf balls would have to be for the average golfer to reach the Moon. If we plug it in to Wolfram|Alpha (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=please+calculate+2*%28%283%2F%284*pi%29%29*%28%28e%5E%285300+m%2Fs+%2F+120mph%29%29*200+kg%29+%2F+%2865%25*1.15+kg%2FL%29%29%5E%281%2F3%29+thank+you) ... [Image: image] ... we find that the bag of golf balls will have to be just about exactly 100 billion miles in diameter. That's much, much bigger than our Solar System.[3]As a Fermi rule of thumb, planets in the inner Solar System are 100 million kilometers away and planets in the outer Solar System are a billion kilometers away. Or miles; either one works. [Image: image] It would also promptly and violently collapse into a black hole. Fortunately, we should be able to avert that disaster by making relatively small changes to the "120" in that equation. If we increase the golf ball's speed from 120 mph to 150, it shrinks the answer dramatically, and the required number of golf balls would fit snugly between the Sun and Mars. Still too big to avoid a catastrophic collapse, but we're getting somewhere. [Image: image] Tiger Woods can hit a golf ball at about 180 mph, which means that if he were powering our spaceship, the bag of golf balls would be only twice the diameter of the Sun! [Image: image] According (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/records-10000/fastest-golf-drive/) to the Guinness Book of World Records, the record for fastest golf drive is 211 mph, set by Maurice Allen in 2012. This corresponds to a bag of golf balls only 100,000 kilometers across—smaller than Jupiter, but still (obviously) not practical. However, golfer Ryan Winther claims (http://www.ryanwinther.com/about_records.htm) to have beaten this record, though without Guinness observers there.[4]And, obviously, it doesn't count unless it's overseen by people from a beer company. If you want to set a world record, hit a golf ball at a radar gun and get it certified by the Mike's Hard Lemonade people. His ball speed was measured by something called the "Titleist Performance Institute" to be 226.7 mph, and he claims a personal best of 237 mph. If he could consistently hit 237 mph, we could shrink our fuel container down to the size of Earth[5]Although it would still be large enough to partially collapse under its own gravity, similar to what happened to the mole of moles (http://what-if.xkcd.com/4/). [Image: image] This still wouldn't work; even in a high orbit, the massive tides from your ship—which is much more massive than the Moon—would be highly disruptive. We could probably shrink the fuel tank further by using "illegal" equipment. There are Superball-style balls and "trampoline face" clubs which can hit much farther, and which would not be permitted in tournament play.[6]On the other hand, we're talking about a sport that brought whites-only clubs with it into the 21st century (http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/06/01/AR2010060103918.html), and Agusta, host of the Masters, admitted its first woman in 2012 (http://www.reuters.com/article/2012/08/20/us-golf-augusta-idUSBRE87J0IE20120820). So maybe we shouldn't worry too much about their traditional rules. A hypothetical 270 mph drive would allow a fuel tank the size of the Moon. At this point, why are we even using a club? According (http://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0966) to research from the US Air Force Academy and BTG Research,[7]Oddly, both researchers have the name "Courtney". There are probably about 200,000 people in the US named Courtney (first or last); maybe we should recruit them to all build potato cannons. a potato cannon fueled by acetylene can launch a potato at 140 m/s (310 mph). If it were capable of launching golf balls at that speed,[8]We're not factoring in the weight of the acetylene—but then again, we also weren't factoring in the weight of the hamburgers the golfer would need to eat to keep hitting those drives. our ship would have a diameter of only 150 miles! [Image: image] There's the small problem that manufacturing that many golf balls would cost quintillions of dollars. You could bring the size down further by making the potato cannon more and more powerful and efficient, but at that point you're simply building a rocket. And the potato cannon scenario has an extra perk. If you somehow made the balls durable enough to survive atmospheric entry, and you set up your maneuver so the ejected golf balls covered the middle latitudes evenly, then over the course of this maneuver you would be statistically likely to hit a hole-in-one ... at every golf course in the world. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If astronauts in orbit tried to reach the Moon by hitting golf balls, the balls would not make it there in any practical or controlled way.

In low Earth orbit, everything is already moving sideways around Earth at about 7.8 km/s. A golf club can only add maybe tens of meters per second to that speed, which is tiny compared with orbital speed. So hitting the ball would not send it straight toward the Moon the way a golf shot works on Earth. It would just slightly change the ball’s orbit around Earth.

To get from low Earth orbit to the Moon, an object needs a major change in velocity, on the order of several kilometers per second, not a few dozen meters per second. A golf swing is short by roughly two orders of magnitude at least. The ball would most likely end up in a slightly higher orbit, slightly lower orbit, or a different elliptical path, depending on the direction of the hit.

There are also practical problems. A golf ball has very little mass and no guidance or propulsion. Tiny errors in direction matter enormously. Even if an astronaut somehow hit it in exactly the “right” direction, the Moon is moving, the transfer path is precise, and the ball would be affected by Earth’s gravity, the Moon’s gravity, and small perturbations like sunlight pressure. A normal golf shot is nowhere near accurate enough.

If the astronauts were already far from Earth and on a trajectory set up for a lunar transfer, then hitting a golf ball could slightly alter its path. But even then, it would still be an unguided object, so the chance of actually striking the Moon would be extremely small.

So the careful answer is: hitting golf balls in orbit would not be a realistic way to reach the Moon. The balls would just become space debris in altered Earth orbits unless they were already given most of the needed velocity by a spacecraft.

A normal golf shot is nowhere near accurate enough.

The balls would just become space debris in altered Earth orbits unless they were already given most of the needed velocity by a spacecraft.
