items.question: What If Every River in America Froze in Midsummer?
human_answers: This is another question that turns out even worse than I expected. [Image: image] For starters, pretty much every animal in the water would die. This would wipe out several fish species completely (this site (http://wwf.panda.org/about_our_earth/ecoregions/lower_mississippi_river.cfm) lists a number of species found only in the Mississippi and its tributaries) and seriously damage many others. Then all the ice would start to melt. Melting ice takes a lot of heat energy, but the ice in this scenario would be spread out in thin strands across the country, so it would all melt pretty fast.[1]Strangely, solid ice usually melts faster than snow—not only in terms of weight, but in terms of inches melted per day.[2] Or[3]Whoa, I can nest footnotes! centimeters. This seems a little counterintuitive, since ice is a lot denser than snow, so it requires a lot more energy to melt a given volume. But snow reflects a lot more light than solid ice, keeping it from absorbing energy, and its air pockets help insulate it. As ice melts, if it stays in contact with water, the water speeds up the melting, since water can transfer heat more efficiently than air. This can be demonstrated by a simple household experiment (http://www.cockeyed.com/science/moment/colander.shtml). Snow is partly protected from this effect because it can't conduct heat in from the edges as easily. This would cause some localized cooling of the air, but we're talking about a relatively small amount of heat energy compared to the environment's overall energy budget.[4]To estimating the river volume, I found a book (http://www.amazon.com/Water-Crisis-Guide-Worlds-Resources/dp/0195076281) that collected estimates of the total world surface water volume in rivers (Chapter 2). It didn't have a breakdown of that number by continent, but it had total discharge rates by continent, so I just used that as a proxy to figure out how to apportion the water between the continents and came up with 16.5% for North America. To get a rough idea, we can apportion that water by surface area (I found a page saying Canada has 9% of the world's freshwater discharge, which seems consistent, although using two numbers from different sources like this creates large potential for error. That leaves 7.5% for the rest of the continent. Dividing up that 7.5% by land area between the US and Central America, the US has about 5%, which works out to 77 km3 of water. [Image: image] We can use data on iceberg melt rates (http://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/1520-0485%281980%29010%3C1681%3AOTEOAI%3E2.0.CO%3B2) to estimate how quickly individual rivers would melt. Small streams would melt in days in all but the coldest areas, while ice in larger rivers would take longer. But before that could happen, things would get weird. To help me out with this question, I talked to Charlie Hohn (http://coyot.es/slowwatermovement), a Vermont field naturalist with an interest in river behavior. I brought Zoe's question to him, and he made a lot of interesting observations. He pointed out that the water feeding into the rivers—from tiny rivulets and raindrops and melting snow all over the watershed—would suddenly find its path blocked by a wall of ice. [Image: image] But all that water still has to go somewhere. And if the riverbed is full, it will go somewhere else. "Any place with rain or snowmelt would have horrific flooding because the water would have nowhere to go," Charlie told me. "Water would shoot down narrow canyons, and once it hit the floodplain it would probably jump into old river channels where they exist, but in many areas that would mean towns and farms." The problems would get worse as the ice melted and broke up, starting upstream and progressing down the river. The floating ice would pile up, damming the water and creating huge lakes. Charlie notes that even a small ice dam can cause terrible flooding. When the Winooski river in Vermont was clogged by an ice dam in 1992, the water spilled over the banks and flooded Montpelier in a matter of minutes (http://www.montpelier-vt.org/community/351/Flood-of-1992.html). And that's just a tiny river, he says. "The Winooski here is narrow enough to throw a rock across, and usually only a few feet deep. In a dry year you could wade across in summer in shorts without getting them wet. So scale that up to the Mississippi and 12-foot-thick ice." As part of its normal meandering, the Mississippi has been trying for 150 years to jump its banks and flow down the Atchafalaya river's route. The Atchafalaya offers a steeper path to the Gulf of Mexico, but if it captured the Mississippi's flow, it would leave the major ports of New Orleans and Baton Rouge high and dry. The Army Corps of Engineers has been trying to stop it (http://www.americaswetlandresources.com/background_facts/detailedstory/LouisianaRiverControl.html). [Image: image] Charlie says that if the Mississippi froze solid, "you'd have the Atchafalaya disaster, without a doubt." And the problems wouldn't be limited to the Mississippi. "The California delta system would also flood, causing a collapse of most of California's water system—though if the aqueducts and reservoirs froze, it wouldn't matter that you couldn't get water from the delta." If man-made reservoirs do freeze in this scenario (which I guess depends whether they count as "rivers") the ice could damage the dams by expanding in the turbines. Whether or not the reservoir froze,[5]We spent a while debating whether, if Lake Meade froze (and expanded), the Hoover Dam would burst due to the expansion. My gut feeling is that it wouldn't, but I'm really not sure. I think we should just try it. the dams could collapse, causing cataclysmic flooding. And where there aren't dams to collapse, the ice would create them ... and when ice dams break up, the result can be pretty spectacular (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ezcgPAptbIk). According to Charlie, the vegetation around the rivers would handle the sudden freeze pretty well, but the effect on the broader ecosystem would be huge and complex. "If there were salmon in the rivers, the bears would feast on them when they thawed. But later, if the fishery crashed, there would be a bunch of desperate hungry bears unleashed on the environment." He mentions that salmon spend part of their life cycle in the ocean, so some of them would survive the rivers freezing. "But if their food were gone, the fishery would still fail. Then again, with all the dams destroyed, maybe it would be a net benefit for salmon ... which is kind of sad." Although agriculture would take a serious hit, humans would probably make it through ok. We wouldn't run out of drinking water; we get a lot of it from underground aquifers, and there would be plenty of quickly-melting ice lying around in most areas. In the worst case scenario, people could just use hair dryers to melt ice to make drinking water for only pennies (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%28334+J%2Fg%29+*+%28water+density%29+*+%282+liters%2Fday%29+*+%28price+of+electricity%29+to+USD%2Fday) per person per day. We'd probably limp through the scenario tattered but alive, buying food overseas. At least, most of us would. I think the most horrifying part of this summer freeze wouldn't be the large-scale, long-term devastation. It would be the immediate consequences. As a kid, I spent summers swimming in the James River (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=james+river+richmond) in Virginia. Now, thanks to Zoe, every time I set foot in a river ... [Image: image] ... I'm going to feel a faint chill.

rubrics.question_focus: What If Every River in America Froze in Midsummer?

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Handling and Physical Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly interprets the premise that American rivers suddenly freeze in midsummer and reasons plausibly about ice volume, melting, heat exchange, and the limited but real atmospheric cooling effects.
criteria.1-2: Misreads the premise or treats the event as ordinary winter freezing, with major physical impossibilities or no causal reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes rivers freeze but gives vague or flawed physics, such as permanent continental cooling or instant harmless melting.
criteria.5-6: Explains basic melting and summer heat effects plausibly, but lacks scale estimates or misses important distinctions between rivers, lakes, snow, and ice.
criteria.7-8: Gives a mostly sound physical account including rapid melting, latent heat, river-size variation, and localized cooling without exaggeration.
criteria.9-10: Precisely handles the sudden-freeze premise with credible scaling, melt-rate reasoning, heat-budget calibration, and careful treatment of what counts as a river.

criteria.name: Hydrologic Cascade and Flooding Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of how frozen river channels would block inflow, redirect runoff, form ice dams, cause flooding, alter channels, and create catastrophic break-up events.
criteria.1-2: Ignores hydrology after freezing or claims rivers simply stop with no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Mentions flooding only generically, with little explanation of why blocked channels, runoff, or meltwater matter.
criteria.5-6: Covers some flooding and melting consequences but misses key mechanisms such as ice dams, upstream-to-downstream breakup, or channel avulsion.
criteria.7-8: Explains blocked drainage, overbank flow, ice jams, dam-like behavior, and severe regional floods in a coherent sequence.
criteria.9-10: Provides a detailed causal cascade including watershed inflows, floodplains, old channels, ice-dam failures, major river rerouting risks such as the Mississippi-Atchafalaya system, and reservoir/dam complications.

criteria.name: Ecological and Biological Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures immediate aquatic mortality and longer-term ecosystem effects on fish, endemic species, food webs, riparian habitats, and wildlife.
criteria.1-2: Claims ecosystems are unaffected or gives biologically implausible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions fish deaths or animal disruption but only superficially and without mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies major aquatic mortality and some food-web impacts, but misses endemic species, life-cycle differences, or delayed ecosystem effects.
criteria.7-8: Explains widespread aquatic die-offs, habitat disruption, scavenger/predator effects, and longer-term fishery collapse or partial recovery.
criteria.9-10: Offers nuanced ecological reasoning including river-specific endemism, oxygen/thermal shock, salmon/ocean life-stage survival, riparian resilience, food-web cascades, and complex recovery tradeoffs.

criteria.name: Human Infrastructure, Water, Agriculture, and Economic Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the answer's treatment of consequences for cities, dams, navigation, ports, aqueducts, drinking water, farms, power systems, emergency response, and national economic resilience.
criteria.1-2: Overlooks human impacts or makes unsupported claims such as total extinction or no disruption.
criteria.3-4: Lists human problems vaguely, such as 'transportation stops' or 'people lack water,' without scale or mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Covers some infrastructure and economic impacts but misses major systems such as dams, ports, irrigation, aqueducts, or drinking-water alternatives.
criteria.7-8: Reasonably explains severe floods, damaged dams and turbines, disrupted shipping, agricultural losses, water-system failures, and survivability through alternate water/food sources.
criteria.9-10: Integrates regional and national impacts, including Mississippi and California water-system vulnerabilities, reservoir and dam risks, port disruption, farm losses, emergency drinking-water options, imports, and uneven mortality.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a coherent timeline from instant freeze to melting, flooding, ecological collapse, infrastructure damage, and recovery while clearly distinguishing robust conclusions from uncertain ones.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, severe contradictions, or outcomes that violate the premise or basic conservation/causal logic.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose timeline but frequent overclaims, unsupported certainty, or inconsistent assumptions about what freezes and for how long.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent short-term reasoning, but long-term effects are incomplete, weakly linked, or only vaguely qualified.
criteria.7-8: Builds a clear causal chain across immediate, medium-term, and long-term effects with few contradictions and appropriate caveats.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous long-range coherence, explicitly tracks assumptions, handles regional variability, flags uncertainties such as reservoirs/dams inclusion, avoids sensationalism, and preserves causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If every river in America suddenly froze in midsummer, the result would be a continent-scale environmental and infrastructure crisis.

First, this would imply an extraordinary and physically unrealistic cold event or some unknown mechanism removing heat from flowing water. Rivers in summer carry large amounts of thermal energy, so freezing all of them at once would require a massive energy extraction. That alone would likely mean the surrounding air and land were also experiencing severe temperature disruption. So the river ice would not be an isolated curiosity; it would signal a major breakdown of normal climate conditions.

The immediate effects would hit water supply systems. Many cities draw drinking water from rivers directly or indirectly, and intake structures, pumps, and treatment facilities could fail if blocked by ice. Power plants that rely on river water for cooling could be forced to reduce output or shut down. Barges and inland shipping on the Mississippi, Ohio, Missouri, Columbia, and other major rivers would stop abruptly, disrupting fuel, grain, fertilizer, coal, and industrial transport.

Ecologically, the shock would be devastating. Fish and aquatic invertebrates adapted to warm-season conditions could die in large numbers from rapid freezing, oxygen disruption, and habitat loss. River plants and wetlands would be stressed or destroyed. Migratory and breeding cycles for birds, amphibians, and insects would be thrown off. In many places, river-connected agriculture would also suffer because irrigation access could be interrupted at the peak of the growing season.

Flooding would become a serious risk, especially if the freeze happened unevenly. Ice jams can block channels and force water over banks, damaging towns, bridges, levees, and farmland. If the rivers later thawed quickly, a second crisis could follow: sudden high flows, erosion, infrastructure damage, and contamination from overwhelmed sewage and industrial systems.

Weather and regional climate would also shift. Rivers exchange heat and moisture with the atmosphere; widespread summer ice would alter local temperatures, humidity, and fog patterns. Areas near large river systems could become cooler at first, but if this event reflected a broader atmospheric anomaly, crop-killing cold could extend far beyond riverbanks. Agriculture across the Midwest, South, and West could face severe losses.

Economically, the effects would be enormous. Transportation delays, crop losses, power disruptions, water shortages, ecological damage, and emergency response costs would likely total hundreds of billions of dollars or more, depending on duration. If the freeze lasted only a day or two, the damage would still be severe; if it persisted for weeks, it could trigger a national emergency with long-term food and energy consequences.

So, if every river in America froze in midsummer, the country would face simultaneous failures in water access, transport, power generation, ecosystems, and agriculture. The frozen rivers themselves would be dangerous, but the deeper implication would be even more alarming: something extreme enough to freeze them would mean the broader environment was undergoing a profound and possibly catastrophic disturbance.

items.question: What If You Made a Lava Lamp with Real Lava?
human_answers: This is a surprisingly reasonable idea, by What If standards. I mean, it's not that reasonable. At the very least, I'm guessing you would lose your teaching license, and possibly some of the students in the front row. But you could do it. [Image: image] Just a warning: I'm going to be linking to a lot of videos (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K2x7FGzjbqQ) of lava flowing and people poking it with sticks (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SbcM7lh6DSQ), so you may have a hard time getting to the end of the article without getting sidetracked into watching a bunch of them (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6M-YX-r0Ll4) like I did while writing it. You have a few choices for transparent materials that could hold the lava without rupturing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a6pXf05Ph9Q) and splattering half the classroom with red-hot droplets. Fused quartz glass would be a great choice. It's the same stuff they use in high-intensity lamp bulbs, the surface of which can easily get up to mid-range lava (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kHO389dvj6Y) temperatures.[1]This bulb (http://www.amazon.ca/Philips-400w-GY9-5-Short-Light/dp/B0062ATTRW), for example, can supposedly handle bulb temperatures of up to 1000°C, which is hotter than many types of lava. Another possibility is sapphire, which stays solid up to 2,000°C, and is commonly used as a window (http://www.newport.com/Sapphire-Optical-Windows/378626/1033/info.aspx) into high-temperature chambers.[2]That link wasn't a lava video, but this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v_VyKplXtOM) is. [Image: image] The question of what to use for the clear medium (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=scGvM_VoPwk#t=31) is trickier. Let's say we find a transparent glass that melts[3]Some people say glass is a liquid that flows very slowly. Other people smugly point out that this is actually wrong. Then another group of people dissects how we know it's wrong, and where this incorrect idea got started. And then at the end of the chain, a Metafilter user steps back and asks some supremely insightful questions about what's really going on here (http://www.metafilter.com/141772/MetaFolkloreFilter#5676767) as we variously repeat and debunk these kinds of factoids. at low temperatures. Even if we ignore the impurities from the hot lava that would probably cloud the glass, we're going to have a problem.[4]And later, when the school board finds out, we'll have another. Molten glass is transparent (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1WmJOhbpyKY). So why doesn't it look transparent?[5]Which sounds sorta contradictory. "This music is loud, but it doesn't sound loud." The answer is simple: It glows. Hot objects give off blackbody radiation (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-QhU8eMR4IQ); molten glass glows just like molten lava does, and for the same reason. So the problem (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bWswq8PmRII) with a lava lamp is that both halves of it will be equally bright (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xsJn8izcKtg), and it will be hard to see the lava. We could try having nothing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xiYzYaLM-hQ) in the top half of the lamp—after all, when it's hot enough, lava bubbles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EFVQhcuT2U0) pretty well on its own. Unfortunately, the lamp itself would also be in contact with the lava. Sapphire might not melt (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2dww24LeoEk) easily, but it will glow, making it hard to see whatever the lava was doing inside. [Image: image] Unless you hooked it up to a really bright bulb, this lava lamp would cool down quickly. Just like individual blobs of lava, the lamp would solidify and stop glowing within the first minute, and by the end of the class period (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zf4wKY8PJtg) you'd probably be able to touch it without being burned. A solidified lava lamp is just about the most boring thing (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TszHiC6fjDg) in the world. But the scenario made me wonder: If making a lamp out of molten lava wouldn't be very exciting, then what about a volcano made of lamps (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7V2_aMG3YsI)? [Image: image] This is probably the most useless calculation I've ever done,[6]Ok, there's no way that's true. but ... what if Mount Saint Helens (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jxvisqt-U-8) erupted again today, but instead of tephra,[7]The technical term for "whatever crap comes out of a volcano." it spewed compact fluorescent bulbs? Well, if it did, the mercury (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cFvijBpzD_Y) released into the atmosphere would be several orders of magnitude larger than all manmade emissions combined.[8]45% of which (http://www.chem.unep.ch/mercury/Atmospheric_Emissions/UNEP%20SUMMARY%20REPORT%20-%20CORRECTED%20May09%20%20final%20for%20WEB%202008.pdf) come from gold mining. [Image: image] All in all, I think making a lava lamp out of lava would be kind of anticlimactic, and would much rather go find some actual lava and poke it with a stick. I also think that it's probably good that Mount Saint Helens didn't erupt compact fluorescent bulbs. And I think that if I were in Ms. Johnstone's class, I'd try to sit toward the back of the room. Lastly, for old time's sake, I'd like to share one final link with you: The music video for Rick Astley's "Never Gonna Give You Up." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q8NXO6YxBmU#t=3)

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, distinguishes possible designs from likely outcomes, and remains internally consistent under the real-lava premise.
criteria.1-2: Makes absolute, contradictory, or fantastical claims with no caveats.

items.model_answer:
If you tried to make a lava lamp with real lava, it would not work as a normal lava lamp, and it would be extremely dangerous.

Real lava is molten rock, typically around 700 to 1,200 °C or more. A regular lava lamp works because two liquids with different densities expand and contract gently as they are heated by a small bulb. Real lava is nothing like that. It is far too hot to be contained in ordinary glass, metal, or household materials. Most glass would soften, crack, or shatter, and many containers would fail from the heat.

Even if you used a very high-temperature container, real lava would not flow in the smooth blobs seen in a lava lamp. Molten rock is much denser and often much more viscous than the wax in a lava lamp. As it cools, it would quickly begin to solidify into rock, especially near the container walls. Instead of rising and falling in neat globules, you would likely get a partly molten mass, crust formation, trapped gases, and possibly violent cracking or splattering.

There is also the issue of heating. Keeping lava molten would require an enormous and continuous heat source, more like an industrial furnace than a lamp bulb. Without that, it would just cool into solid rock. With such a heat source, the outside of the device would also become dangerously hot.

So the realistic result is not a decorative lamp but a high-temperature rock furnace, with major risks of burns, fire, toxic gases, pressure buildup, and container failure. In short: a real-lava lava lamp would be more like a miniature volcano experiment than a lamp, and it would almost certainly be impractical and hazardous.

items.question: What If Every Child's First Laugh Created an Immortal Fairy?
human_answers: "There are always a lot of young ones," explained Wendy, who was now quite an authority, "because you see when a new baby laughs for the first time a new fairy is born, and as there are always new babies there are always new fairies. They live in nests on the tops of trees; and the mauve ones are boys and the white ones are girls, and the blue ones are just little sillies who are not sure what they are." —Peter Pan Interestingly, fairies in the Peter Pan mythology definitely don't live forever. At the end of the book, Peter comes to visit Wendy a year after their adventures. Wendy asks about Tinker Bell, and Peter says he can't remember her and assumes she's died, and Wendy observes that fairies don't live very long.[1]When she expressed a doubtful hope that Tinker Bell would be glad to see her he said, "Who is Tinker Bell?" "O Peter," she said, shocked; but even when she explained he could not remember. "There are such a lot of them," he said. "I expect she is no more." I expect he was right, for fairies don't live long, but they are so little that a short time seems a good while to them. This suggests that at any given time, there are probably be far fewer fairies than humans in the Peter Pan universe, since they have the same birth rate and shorter lifespans. [Image: image] But Mira's scenario assumes immortal fairies, so let's talk about immortal fairy demographics. A fairy is created by every[2]Approximately, anyway, but we'll round up by assuming that all babies laugh. newborn baby. The total number of humans who have ever lived is somewhere around 100-120 billion,[3]There are various groups who have estimated this, and they all tend to come up with a number around in this range. If you take a set of estimates for ancient human population (Wikipedia has a table of them (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population_estimates)) and assume a birth rate near the biological maximum before the 20th century (35 to 45 births per 1,000, according to this paper (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/231918377_The_Use_of_Historical_Demography_in_Ancient_History)), you can derive a similar number yourself. meaning 100-120 billion fairies have been created. How much do all those fairies weigh? Tinker Bell, the main fairy from the Peter Pan universe, seems to be a little under six inches tall. In a scene in Hook, Tinker Bell (played by the 5 foot 9 inch Julia Roberts) fits comfortably in a 1/12 scale dollhouse, suggesting a height of 5.75 inches. As another data point, the statue of Tinker Bell (http://www.madametussauds.com/london/newsandevents/tinkerbell/) at Madam Tussaud's wax museum is 5.5 inches. This suggests that fairies in Peter Pan are pretty close to 1/12th scale. If fairies are 1/12th the size of humans, then they weigh \( \left( \tfrac{1}{12\text{th}}\right) ^3=\tfrac{1}{1728\text{th}} \) as much as us, which means Julia Roberts's Tinker Bell is probably around 35 grams.[4](two mice) As of 2015, total fairy biomass would be about 4 million tons. That's less than humans or horses (http://xkcd.com/1338/), and probably comparable to the total mass of all humpback whales (http://iwc.int/estimate).[5]Fairies also probably outweigh wild birds. At these numbers, fairies would be a minor piece of the ecosystem, although possibly a pretty annoying one. [Image: image] But it wasn't always the case. In the early days of our species, our high birth rates (and death rates) plus our low population mean that we would have accumulated fairies quickly. The exact numbers depend on when the modern human (fairy-generating) species developed, but by the time the last ice age was over, the accumulated fairies could have outweighed our tiny living human population 10 to 1. [Image: image] Once our population started growing following the agricultural revolution (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution), we would have quickly outstripped fairies in terms of weight. In 2015, fairy biomass would be down to about 1.2% of human biomass, and by the mid-21st-century, they'd bottom out at less than 1%. But as long as humans keep reproducing, the fairy population would keep growing. If we assume the human population will level off (http://www.un.org/esa/population/publications/longrange2/WorldPop2300final.pdf) at around 9 billion partway through this century, then the share of mass occupied by fairies would continue rising steadily. If our population stays at a stable 9 billion indefinitely, by 2100, they'll be back above 1% of human biomass, and they'll reach 2% by the year 3000. In the year 100,000, if our species is somehow still around, they'll outweigh us. This makes things interesting. Let's assume fairies need to eat. If fairies weigh about as much as us, they'd presumably be consuming a similar share of food and water. So even if the Earth can support 400 million tons of human, it may not be able to support 400 million tons of human and another 400 million tons of fairy. This suggests that, sometime in the next hundred millennia, the growing fairy population would start to crowd out the human population. But if fairies crowd out humans, that would in turn reduce the growth rate of the fairies, slowing down the replacement process. The end result (in this idealized model) would be that the fairy population growth would taper off as the human population declined. The situation would never quite reach a stable equilibrium, because every 1,728 human births would create one human's weight in fairies, reducing the Earth's total human carrying capacity by 1. But since the rate of fairy creation would slow down as the human population shrank, the process would stretch out for a very long time. This odd situation would only exist because fairies—in Mira's scenario—are immortal. The scenario would change dramatically if we introduced a fairy death rate. Perhaps fairies don't age or experience natural deaths, but can still die from other causes. What would kill the fairies? Who knows.[6]J. M. Barrie introduces a fairy-killing mechanism in Peter Pan; any time anyone says "I don't believe in fairies", a random fairy dies. In a world of immortal fairies, this could serve as an effective feedback. If no one has heard of fairies, no one will say they don't believe in them, and their population will grow. As fairies start to be common enough to be noticed, people will have a reason to say they don't believe in them, and their population will drop. Eventually, civilization would start documenting (http://xkcd.com/1235/) the existence of fairies, and then no one would have any reason to disbelieve their existence, and the feedback loop would break down. But ecosystems aren't static. If you mess with one part, the other parts change in response. Fairies could become the dominant species, but the system they learned to dominate wouldn't be there forever. If fairies represent most of the biomass in the ecosystem, eventually, given enough time ... [Image: image] ... something will learn to eat them.

items.model_answer:
If every child’s first laugh created an immortal fairy, the world would be transformed socially, biologically, economically, and philosophically almost immediately.

First, there would be an enormous fairy population. Human births number in the hundreds of thousands per day worldwide, so very quickly millions, then billions, of immortal fairies would exist. Since they cannot die of old age, their numbers would only increase unless they could also be destroyed by injury or magic-like constraints. Even if they were tiny and low-impact individually, their cumulative effect would become one of the major features of Earth’s ecology.

That leads to the next question: are these fairies physical? If they are tangible, they would become a new biological or quasi-biological class of being. They would need space, energy, and perhaps food. If they consume ordinary resources, then humanity has acquired a permanently growing dependent population tied directly to reproduction. Governments would study them, regulate them, and eventually plan around them. If they are magical and need little or nothing, then the material burden is lower, but their informational and social influence could still be immense.

Because each fairy is linked to a child’s first laugh, people would probably treat them as personal counterparts or life-twins. Parents might see the fairy as a sacred sign that the child is healthy and truly “arrived” in the world emotionally. In many cultures, the first laugh could become a ceremonial event, carefully anticipated and perhaps even recorded, because it is no longer just a milestone but the moment a new conscious being comes into existence. Hospitals or families might try to witness and authenticate it. There would likely be disputes when the “first laugh” is ambiguous.

Religion and philosophy would change dramatically. The existence of immortal beings born from joy would be taken as evidence that emotion has world-creating power. Some faiths would interpret fairies as souls, guardians, blessings, or divine witnesses. Others would build moral systems around the idea that innocence literally generates eternal life. Philosophers would debate whether these fairies are persons with rights, whether they are extensions of the child, and whether creating children now also means creating immortal moral patients.

Law would have to expand fast. An immortal fairy raises immediate questions: can it own property, testify in court, vote, enter contracts, inherit wealth, or be imprisoned? Since fairies would outlive humans indefinitely, they could accumulate knowledge and assets over centuries. Even if physically weak, an immortal population with endless memory would become a formidable political force. History itself would change because fairies could provide direct eyewitness testimony across generations, making the distant past much less uncertain.

That permanence would deeply affect family life. A person might die, but the fairy born from their first laugh would remain, perhaps carrying memories of them from infancy onward. Fairies might become treasured links between generations, almost like living archives of a family line. But that also means grief changes: no one is fully gone if an immortal companion tied to their earliest joy still exists. People might seek comfort, or feel haunted, by that continuing presence.

Science would focus intensely on the mechanism. Researchers would ask why laughter, why only the first one, and whether the fairy contains genetic, mental, or spiritual information from the child. If the fairy resembles the child’s temperament, then it might be studied as an externalized emotional structure. If it behaves independently, then the universe appears to turn a specific human event into a new autonomous person. Either answer would force a revision of physics and biology.

There would also be incentives and abuses. If a first laugh creates an immortal being, some people would try to control the circumstances of that laugh for status, prophecy, or engineering purposes. Perhaps people would believe the tone or context of the first laugh shapes the fairy’s nature, leading to elaborate rituals to produce “better” fairies. Black markets, cults, and pseudosciences would emerge around infant laughter. States might try to register every fairy at birth-equivalent.

Over very long timescales, immortal fairies would become one of the dominant intelligences on Earth. Unlike humans, they persist through all eras. They could become humanity’s long memory, cultural stabilizers, manipulators, or guardians. Their society would likely diverge sharply from ours because immortality changes incentives: they may think in centuries, care more about continuity than urgency, and become either exceptionally wise or dangerously detached.

So the core answer is this: a world where every child’s first laugh creates an immortal fairy would stop being an ordinary human world. It would become a dual-civilization planet, where transient humans and ever-accumulating beings born from joy must learn to coexist. The biggest consequences would not just be magical charm, but population growth, legal upheaval, religious reinvention, and the arrival of immortal witnesses to every generation.

edus.text: If every child’s first laugh created an immortal fairy, the world would be transformed socially, biologically, economically, and philosophically almost immediately.
First, there would be an enormous fairy population.
Human births number in the hundreds of thousands per day worldwide,
so very quickly millions, then billions, of immortal fairies would exist.
Since they cannot die of old age, their numbers would only increase
unless they could also be destroyed by injury or magic-like constraints.
Even if they were tiny and low-impact individually, their cumulative effect would become one of the major features of Earth’s ecology.
That leads to the next question: are these fairies physical?
If they are tangible, they would become a new biological or quasi-biological class of being.
They would need space, energy, and perhaps food.
If they consume ordinary resources, then humanity has acquired a permanently growing dependent population tied directly to reproduction.
Governments would study them, regulate them, and eventually plan around them.
If they are magical and need little or nothing, then the material burden is lower,
but their informational and social influence could still be immense.
Because each fairy is linked to a child’s first laugh, people would probably treat them as personal counterparts or life-twins.
Parents might see the fairy as a sacred sign that the child is healthy and truly “arrived” in the world emotionally.
In many cultures, the first laugh could become a ceremonial event, carefully anticipated and perhaps even recorded,
because it is no longer just a milestone but the moment a new conscious being comes into existence.
Hospitals or families might try to witness and authenticate it.
There would likely be disputes when the “first laugh” is ambiguous.
Religion and philosophy would change dramatically.
The existence of immortal beings born from joy would be taken as evidence that emotion has world-creating power.
Some faiths would interpret fairies as souls, guardians, blessings, or divine witnesses.
Others would build moral systems around the idea that innocence literally generates eternal life.
Philosophers would debate whether these fairies are persons with rights, whether they are extensions of the child, and whether creating children now also means creating immortal moral patients.
Law would have to expand fast.
An immortal fairy raises immediate questions: can it own property, testify in court, vote, enter contracts, inherit wealth, or be imprisoned?
Since fairies would outlive humans indefinitely, they could accumulate knowledge and assets over centuries.
Even if physically weak, an immortal population with endless memory would become a formidable political force.
History itself would change because fairies could provide direct eyewitness testimony across generations, making the distant past much less uncertain.
That permanence would deeply affect family life.
A person might die, but the fairy born from their first laugh would remain, perhaps carrying memories of them from infancy onward.
Fairies might become treasured links between generations, almost like living archives of a family line.
But that also means grief changes: no one is fully gone if an immortal companion tied to their earliest joy still exists.
People might seek comfort, or feel haunted, by that continuing presence.
Science would focus intensely on the mechanism.
Researchers would ask why laughter, why only the first one, and whether the fairy contains genetic, mental, or spiritual information from the child.
If the fairy resembles the child’s temperament, then it might be studied as an externalized emotional structure.
If it behaves independently, then the universe appears to turn a specific human event into a new autonomous person.
Either answer would force a revision of physics and biology.
There would also be incentives and abuses.
If a first laugh creates an immortal being, some people would try to control the circumstances of that laugh for status, prophecy, or engineering purposes.
Perhaps people would believe the tone or context of the first laugh shapes the fairy’s nature, leading to elaborate rituals to produce “better” fairies.
Black markets, cults, and pseudosciences would emerge around infant laughter.
States might try to register every fairy at birth-equivalent.
Over very long timescales, immortal fairies would become one of the dominant intelligences on Earth.
Unlike humans, they persist through all eras.
They could become humanity’s long memory, cultural stabilizers, manipulators, or guardians.
Their society would likely diverge sharply from ours because immortality changes incentives:
they may think in centuries, care more about continuity than urgency, and become either exceptionally wise or dangerously detached.
So the core answer is this: a world where every child’s first laugh creates an immortal fairy would stop being an ordinary human world.
It would become a dual-civilization planet, where transient humans and ever-accumulating beings born from joy must learn to coexist.
The biggest consequences would not just be magical charm, but population growth, legal upheaval, religious reinvention, and the arrival of immortal witnesses to every generation.

items.question: What If There Were a Lake on the Moon?
human_answers: This would be so cool. In fact, I honestly think it's cool enough that it gives us a pretty good reason to go to the Moon in the first place. At the very least, it's better than the one Kennedy gave. [Image: image] Floating would feel about the same on the Moon as on Earth, since how high in the water you float depends only on your body's density compared to the water's, not the strength of gravity. Swimming underwater would also feel pretty similar. The inertia of the water is the main source of drag when swimming, and inertia is a property of matter[1]♬ BILL NYE THE SCIENCE GUY ♬ independent of gravity. The top speed of a submerged swimmer would be about the same on the Moon as here—about 2 meters/second. Everything else would be different and way cooler. The waves would be bigger, the splash fights more intense, and swimmers would be able to jump out of the water like dolphins. This[2]Not this one. The other one.​[3]The simplest approach, which gives us an approximate answer, is to treat the swimmer as a simple projectile. The formula for the height of a projectile is: \( \frac{\text{speed}^2}{2\times\text{gravity}} \) ... which tells us that a champion swimmer moving at 2 meters per second (4.5 mph) would only have enough kinetic energy to lift their body about 20 centimeters (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=%282+m%2Fs%29%5E2+%2F+%282+*+earth+gravity%29) against gravity. That's not totally accurate, although it's enough to tell us that dolphin jumps on Earth probably aren't in the cards for us. But to get a more accurate answer (and an equation we can apply to the Moon), we need to account for a few other things. When a swimmer first breaks the surface, they don't have to lift their full weight; they're partially supported by buoyancy. As more of their body leaves the water, the force of buoyancy decreases, since their body is displacing less water. Since the force of gravity isn't changing, their net weight increases. You can calculate how much potential energy is required to lift a body vertically through the surface to a certain height, but it's a complicated integral (you integrate the displacement of the submerged portion of their body over the vertical distance they travel) and depends on their body shape. For a human body moving fast enough to jump most of the way out of the water, this effect probably adds about half a torso-length to their final height—and less if they're not able to make it all the way out. The other effect we have to account for is the fact that a swimmer can continue kicking as they start to leave the water. When a swimmer is submerged and moving at top speed, the drag from the water is equal to the thrust they generate by kicking and ... whatever the gerund form of the verb is for the things your arms do while swimming. My first thought was "stroking," but it's definitely not that. Anyway, once the jumping swimmer breaks the surface, the drag almost vanishes, but they can keep kicking for a few moments. To figure out how much energy this adds, you can multiply the thrust from kicking by the distance over which they're kicking after breaking the surface, since energy equals force times distance. The distance is most of a body length, or 1 to 1.5 meters. As for the force from kicking, random Google results for a search for lifeguard qualifications suggest that good swimmers might be able to carry 10 lbs over their heads for a short distance, which means they're generating a little more than 10 pounds-force (50+ N) of kicking thrust. We can combine all these together into a big ol' equation: \[ \text{Jump height}=\left(\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\times\text{body mass}\times\left(\text{top speed}\right)^2+\text{kick force}\times\text{torso length}}{\text{Earth gravity}\times\text{body mass}}\right)+\left(\text{buoyancy correction} \right) \] footnote contains some detail on the math behind a dolphin jump. Calculating the height a swimmer can jump out of the water requires taking several different things into account, but the bottom line is that a normal swimmer on the Moon could probably launch themselves a full meter out of the water, and Michael Phelps may well be able to manage 2 or 3. [Image: image] The numbers get even more exciting when we introduce fins. Swimmers wearing fins (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finswimming) can go substantially faster than regular swimmers (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Schwimmer) without them (although the fastest swimmer wearing flippers will still lose to a runner, even if the runner is also wearing flippers and jumping over hurdles (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sRDnajV1A3w)). Champion finswimmers can go almost 3.2 m/s wearing a monofin, which is fast enough for some pretty impressive jumps—even on Earth (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z09RmuaPyVU). Data on swimfin top speeds (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_finswimming) and thrusts[4]This paper (http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/xmlui/bitstream/handle/123456789/3936/12841609.pdf) provides some sample data. suggest that on the Moon, a champion finswimmer (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanna-Maria_Sepp%C3%A4l%C3%A4) could probably launch themselves as high as 4 or 5 meters into the air. In other words, on the Moon, you could conceivably do a high dive in reverse. [Image: image] But it gets even better. A 2012 paper (http://www.plosone.org/article/fetchObject.action?uri=info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0037300&representation=PDF) in PLoS ONE, titled Humans Running in Place on Water at Simulated Reduced Gravity, concluded that while humans can't run on the surface of water on Earth,[5]They actually provide a citation for this statement, which is delightful. they might just barely be able to do so on the Moon. (I highly recommend reading their paper, if only for the hilarious experimental setup illustration on page 2.) Because of the reduced gravity on the Moon, the water would be launched upward more easily, just like the swimmers. The result would be larger waves and more flying droplets. In technical terms, a pool on the Moon would be more "splashy".[6]The SI unit of splashiness is the splashypant. To avoid splashing all the water out, you'd want to design the deck so water drains quickly back into the pool. You could just make the rim higher, but then you'd spoil one of the key joys of a pool on the Moon—exiting via Slip 'N Slide: [Image: image] I 100% support this idea. If we ever build a Moon base, I think we should absolutely build a big swimming pool there. Sure, sending a swimming pool's worth of water (135 horses (http://xkcd.com/1461/)) to the Moon's surface would be expensive.[7]If you decided to bundle a backyard pool into individual two-liter bottles, and sent them in 3,000 batches of 10 each via the startup Astrobotic (https://www.astrobotic.com/), it would cost you $72 billion (according to their website's calculator (https://www.astrobotic.com/configure-mission)). But on the other hand, this lunar base is going to have people on it, so you need to send some water anyway.[8]Sending a supply of water and a filter system is probably cheaper than sending a replacement astronaut every 3 or 4 days, although I encourage NASA to run the numbers on that to be sure. And it's really not impossible. A large backyard swimming pool weighs about as much as four Apollo lunar landers. A next-generation[9](or, heck, previous-generation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn_V)) heavy-lift rocket, like Boeing's NASA SLS or Elon Musk's SpaceX Falcon Heavy, would be able to deliver a good-sized pool to the Moon in not too many trips. So maybe the next step, if you really want a swimming pool on the Moon, is to call Elon Musk and ask for a quote. [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Setup and Physical Boundary Conditions
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines a plausible version of 'a lake on the Moon' and respects lunar constraints such as vacuum, low gravity, temperature swings, regolith, radiation, and the need for containment or pressurization.
criteria.1-2: Treats the lake as an ordinary Earth lake with little or no mention of lunar vacuum, pressure, temperature, or containment.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two lunar constraints but leaves the lake's survival mechanism vague or internally inconsistent.
criteria.5-6: Explains that exposed liquid water would rapidly boil, freeze, or sublimate, and offers a basic containment or artificial-environment assumption.
criteria.7-8: Clearly distinguishes exposed versus enclosed/pressurized scenarios and reasons from lunar gravity, pressure, thermal, and environmental conditions.
criteria.9-10: Establishes a precise, coherent counterfactual setup and tracks how enclosure, atmosphere, heat control, and lunar surface conditions determine all later effects.

criteria.name: Fluid Mechanics and Human Interaction in Lunar Gravity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates causal reasoning about how water, waves, splashes, swimming, buoyancy, drag, jumping, and surface motion would change under one-sixth Earth gravity.
criteria.1-2: Makes unsupported claims such as people would float much higher or swimming would be effortless without explaining buoyancy or drag.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes lower gravity but confuses buoyancy, weight, inertia, or swimming speed in major ways.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that buoyancy depends on density while waves, splashes, jumps, and falling water would differ because of lower gravity.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple mechanisms: similar submerged swimming drag, larger/slower waves, higher jumps from the water, longer splash trajectories, and altered surface activity.
criteria.9-10: Provides quantitatively plausible or well-scaled reasoning for lunar swimming, wave behavior, splashiness, jumping height, fins/running-on-water possibilities, and related limits.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequences for Lunar Environment and Infrastructure
criteria.criteria_description: Measures coverage of downstream effects beyond the immediate lake, including engineering, habitat design, resource logistics, contamination, safety, and mission implications.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on novelty or recreation with almost no downstream consequences.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few consequences, such as tourism or cost, but without causal links to the lake's lunar setting.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant impacts, including water delivery or sourcing, containment, maintenance, safety, and possible use by a lunar base.
criteria.7-8: Connects the lake to broader systems: life support, thermal regulation, shielding, dust control, leakage risk, habitat layout, transport cost, and emergency hazards.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent long-range scenario showing how the lake would reshape lunar engineering, settlement planning, resource economics, recreation, science, and risk management over time.

criteria.name: Scientific Plausibility and Quantitative Calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether claims are physically plausible, appropriately scaled, and calibrated with estimates where useful rather than relying on spectacle.
criteria.1-2: Uses fantasy-like outcomes or severe numerical errors, such as Earthlike weather around an exposed lake or gravity changing water density.
criteria.3-4: Includes some correct science but exaggerates effects or omits scale, making the scenario hard to judge.
criteria.5-6: Uses broadly plausible orders of magnitude for lunar gravity, swimmer motion, water mass, and engineering scale, with limited quantification.
criteria.7-8: Employs reasonable comparisons or simple calculations to support claims about gravity, waves, evaporation/freezing, transport mass, and human motion.
criteria.9-10: Consistently grounds the counterfactual in sound physics with clear assumptions, order-of-magnitude estimates, and explicit limits on what can and cannot happen.

criteria.name: Coherence, Uncertainty Handling, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a consistent scenario, avoids contradictions, and signals uncertainty where the counterfactual depends on assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts itself frequently, shifts between exposed and enclosed lake assumptions without notice, or presents impossible outcomes as certain.
criteria.3-4: Has a partially coherent narrative but contains unresolved conflicts about atmosphere, temperature, gravity, or whether humans can safely use the lake.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent and acknowledges some uncertainty, though a few assumptions or causal transitions remain unclear.
criteria.7-8: Maintains clear causal chains, separates speculative from well-established effects, and flags dependencies such as lake size, enclosure, heat input, and habitat pressure.
criteria.9-10: Delivers an internally consistent long-range analysis with explicit assumptions, no major physical contradictions, and well-calibrated uncertainty across competing scenarios.

items.model_answer:
If there were a lake on the Moon, it would change the Moon’s environment a lot, but the exact effects would depend on what the lake was made of and how it could exist.

A normal liquid-water lake could not last on the Moon under present conditions. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, so the pressure is far too low for liquid water to remain stable at the surface. Water exposed there would either freeze or boil away and then slowly be lost to space or trapped as ice in permanently shadowed craters. So if you imagine a lake on the Moon today, it would need some special condition to survive, such as being covered by ice, enclosed under a dome, or existing in a pressurized basin.

If such a lake did exist and remained liquid, it would create a local source of water vapor around it. Because the Moon’s gravity is weak and its atmosphere is essentially absent, that vapor would not form weather like on Earth. There would be no rain clouds, no wind-driven waves in the usual sense, and no real water cycle. Some vapor and ice might migrate across the surface and collect in colder regions, especially near the poles.

The lake itself would behave strangely compared with lakes on Earth. With one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, splashes and ripples would move differently, and sediment would settle more slowly. The surface would also face huge temperature swings between lunar day and night, unless the lake were somehow protected. During the long lunar day it could heat strongly in sunlight, and during the equally long night it could freeze deeply.

A lunar lake would also matter enormously for exploration. Water could support astronauts directly for drinking and hygiene, and it could be split into hydrogen and oxygen for rocket fuel and breathing air. That would make the Moon much more useful as a base for science and future missions deeper into space.

If instead the lake were made of something other than water, like liquid methane or another volatile substance, it would still face the same basic problem: the Moon’s lack of atmospheric pressure and extreme temperatures make stable surface liquids very difficult. So the biggest conclusion is that a lake on the Moon would be scientifically dramatic, but under current lunar conditions, an exposed surface lake is not really possible without special protection or a major change in the Moon’s environment, such as a much thicker atmosphere.

edus.text: If there were a lake on the Moon, it would change the Moon’s environment a lot,
but the exact effects would depend on what the lake was made of and how it could exist.
A normal liquid-water lake could not last on the Moon under present conditions.
The Moon has almost no atmosphere,
so the pressure is far too low for liquid water to remain stable at the surface.
Water exposed there would either freeze or boil away
and then slowly be lost to space or trapped as ice in permanently shadowed craters.
So if you imagine a lake on the Moon today, it would need some special condition to survive,
such as being covered by ice, enclosed under a dome, or existing in a pressurized basin.
If such a lake did exist and remained liquid, it would create a local source of water vapor around it.
Because the Moon’s gravity is weak and its atmosphere is essentially absent, that vapor would not form weather like on Earth.
There would be no rain clouds, no wind-driven waves in the usual sense, and no real water cycle.
Some vapor and ice might migrate across the surface and collect in colder regions, especially near the poles.
The lake itself would behave strangely compared with lakes on Earth.
With one-sixth of Earth’s gravity, splashes and ripples would move differently,
and sediment would settle more slowly.
The surface would also face huge temperature swings between lunar day and night,
unless the lake were somehow protected.
During the long lunar day it could heat strongly in sunlight,
and during the equally long night it could freeze deeply.
A lunar lake would also matter enormously for exploration.
Water could support astronauts directly for drinking and hygiene,
and it could be split into hydrogen and oxygen for rocket fuel and breathing air.
That would make the Moon much more useful as a base for science and future missions deeper into space.
If instead the lake were made of something other than water, like liquid methane or another volatile substance, it would still face the same basic problem:
the Moon’s lack of atmospheric pressure and extreme temperatures make stable surface liquids very difficult.
So the biggest conclusion is that a lake on the Moon would be scientifically dramatic,
but under current lunar conditions, an exposed surface lake is not really possible without special protection or a major change in the Moon’s environment,
such as a much thicker atmosphere.

items.question: What If You Dropped a 7-Kilogram Bowling Ball into the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: It is a good thing you mentioned the weight, because of a very surprising fact: Most bowling balls float. It's true. Bowling balls all have about the same volume, so they all displace the same weight in seawater—12.13 lbs, or about 5.5 kg. But their weights vary substantially, from as little as 6 lbs to a max of 16. Only the balls that weigh more than 12.13 lbs will sink. [Image: image] "Hang on a moment," the serious bowlers reading this are saying, "most bowling balls are at the heavy end of that range. The usual range is more like 14-16 lbs for men and 10-14 lbs for women. Maybe the average women's ball floats, but the overall average ball surely sinks." This is definitely true for serious bowlers, but for casual bowlers, it might be better to define the "average" ball using the distribution on the rack of balls at the local bowling alley. These house balls often list the weight on them, so rather than go to a bowling alley, I just sifted through all the Flickr photos of bowling balls and tallied up all the visible weights. The average was 10½ lbs. [Image: image] So at the very least, for most people, the average bowling ball they've picked up in their lives probably floats. If nothing else, this makes the popular simile "sank like a bowling ball"—which appears in a number of books (https://www.google.com/search?q=%22sank+like+a+bowling+ball%22&btnG=Search+Books&tbm=bks&tbo=1)—seem a little poorly chosen.[1]In defense of the authors of Volume 53 of North Dakota Quarterly, the simile they used is, "sank like a bowling ball in whipped cream," which is perfectly reasonable. On the other hand, How To Hook a Man (And a Baby) and The Year's Work in Lebowski Studies are on their own. But Doug's bowling ball is 7 kg (15.5 lbs), making it plenty heavy enough to sink in the ocean. How fast will it fall? Small falling spheres in viscous (goopy) liquids (like hair gel (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1108.3427.pdf)) exhibit weird behaviors and sometimes complex oscillation, but bowling balls falling through water are pretty straightforward. Their falling speed is determined by the drag equation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_equation) and their weight (accounting for buoyancy). For Doug's bowling ball, that terminal velocity will be roughly 1.3 meters per second, which means it will take two hours and 20 minutes to reach the bottom. That's plenty of time to enjoy a two-hour movie (http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0118715/). A 13-pound bowling ball, which is much closer to neutrally buoyant in seawater, would take four and a half hours to reach the bottom. On the other hand, a bowling ball made of solid iron would reach the bottom in half an hour. A bowling ball made of lead would reach the bottom in 23 minutes, and a bowling ball made of solid gold would make it in 17. However, a bowling ball made of solid gold would also weigh more than the average bowler.[2]At least, I think it would, but I can't think of a way to sample the weight of the average bowler without getting punched. A bowling ball made of solid osmium, the heaviest naturally-occurring element, would weigh 120 kilograms, and could sink to the bottom of the Mariana Trench in just 16 minutes. But what if you got the weight wrong? What if the bowling ball you were using turned out to be 7 pounds, not 7 kilograms? Or maybe it's 10.5 pounds—the "average" bowling ball, at least according to a dubious Flickr sample. In that case, the ball would never reach the bottom. Instead, it would drift sideways with the currents. We can track what course it would take using the Adrift.org.au ocean plastic tracking tool (http://www.adrift.org.au/map?lat=11.3&lng=142.6&center=-180&startmon=Jan). The bowling ball would first drift west, past Luzon in the Philippines, then probably north along the coast of China, turning right at Japan and heading out over the Pacific. Sometime in the summer of 2018, it would approach the coast of California. Most likely, it would follow the coast for a little while, then become swept up in the great Pacific garbage patch (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pacific_garbage_patch). However, it's possible that it would be swept up on shore instead. If, during those three years, Doug took his boat from the Mariana islands to Los Angeles, found a nice, sheltered cove, and set up ten carefully weighted bowling pins just below the surface, then there is a tiny, tiny chance ... [Image: image] ... that he could succeed in bowling the single most improbable strike of all time.

items.model_answer:
If you dropped a 7-kilogram bowling ball into the Mariana Trench, it would sink all the way to the bottom, but not especially fast, and it would not get crushed.

A bowling ball is much denser than seawater, so gravity would pull it downward. A typical bowling ball has a density around 1.7 to 2 times that of water, which means it has plenty of negative buoyancy. But as it falls, water resistance would oppose the motion, so after a short time it would reach a terminal velocity rather than keep accelerating. For an object about the size of a bowling ball, that speed would likely be only a few meters per second, depending on the exact ball, its surface, and whether the finger holes trap or release water.

The Mariana Trench is about 11 kilometers deep at its deepest point, so at a fall speed of roughly a few meters per second, the descent would probably take on the order of an hour or so, maybe somewhat less or more.

The pressure at the bottom is enormous, roughly 1,100 atmospheres, or about 110 megapascals. That is enough to crush hollow or compressible objects, but a bowling ball is a solid, rigid object, usually made from dense plastic or resin around a weight block. Since it is not full of air, it would not implode dramatically. It would experience only a tiny compression. If it had small flaws, coatings, or trapped air pockets, those might crack or collapse, but the ball itself would mostly remain intact.

As it sank, it would also become colder, eventually reaching near-freezing deep-ocean temperatures, but that would not matter much structurally. Once it hit bottom, it would just land on the seafloor and stay there unless it rolled on a slope or settled slowly into soft sediment.

So the basic outcome is simple: it sinks, takes roughly tens of minutes to perhaps around an hour to reach the bottom, survives the pressure, and ends up resting on the floor of the trench.

edus.text: If you dropped a 7-kilogram bowling ball into the Mariana Trench, it would sink all the way to the bottom, but not especially fast, and it would not get crushed.
A bowling ball is much denser than seawater, so gravity would pull it downward.
A typical bowling ball has a density around 1.7 to 2 times that of water, which means it has plenty of negative buoyancy.
But as it falls, water resistance would oppose the motion,
so after a short time it would reach a terminal velocity rather than keep accelerating.
For an object about the size of a bowling ball, that speed would likely be only a few meters per second, depending on the exact ball, its surface, and whether the finger holes trap or release water.
The Mariana Trench is about 11 kilometers deep at its deepest point,
so at a fall speed of roughly a few meters per second, the descent would probably take on the order of an hour or so, maybe somewhat less or more.
The pressure at the bottom is enormous, roughly 1,100 atmospheres, or about 110 megapascals.
That is enough to crush hollow or compressible objects,
but a bowling ball is a solid, rigid object, usually made from dense plastic or resin around a weight block.
Since it is not full of air, it would not implode dramatically.
It would experience only a tiny compression.
If it had small flaws, coatings, or trapped air pockets, those might crack or collapse,
but the ball itself would mostly remain intact.
As it sank, it would also become colder, eventually reaching near-freezing deep-ocean temperatures,
but that would not matter much structurally.
Once it hit bottom, it would just land on the seafloor and stay there
unless it rolled on a slope or settled slowly into soft sediment.
So the basic outcome is simple:
it sinks,
takes roughly tens of minutes to perhaps around an hour to reach the bottom,
survives the pressure,
and ends up resting on the floor of the trench.

items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]

criteria.3-4: Mentions one issue such as oxygen or fatigue but leaves most survival and logistics mechanisms unexplained.

criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, tangential velocity, geostationary radius, tether rotation, and launch/reentry options, showing how the elevator and stairway would complement or fail to complement each other.

items.model_answer:
If there were both a space elevator and a literal “stairway to space,” the elevator would be the practical megastructure and the stairway would mostly be a physical absurdity unless we reinterpret it very generously.

A space elevator is at least physically discussable: a tether stretching from Earth’s equator past geostationary orbit, kept taut by rotation. If materials and engineering were good enough, it could make access to orbit far cheaper and safer than rockets for many payloads. You could send cargo and people up electrically powered climbers instead of launching everything on chemical rockets. That would transform satellite deployment, space industry, and perhaps settlement in orbit.

A true stairway to space is much harder. Ordinary “space” begins around 100 km up. A staircase that rises 100 km through the atmosphere would have impossible structural demands under Earth gravity. The lower steps would need to support the entire weight above them, and the structure would face wind, thermal expansion, weather, earthquakes, and buckling. Also, humans cannot just walk into space: above a few kilometers oxygen becomes scarce, and by near-space altitudes the pressure is too low to survive without a suit. So even if the stairs existed, you would still need life support, insulation, and probably pressurized waystations. Walking all the way up would take days to weeks and enormous energy from the climber’s body.

If both somehow existed anyway, then the “stairway” would probably not be used as an actual staircase for routine access. It might instead function as a rigid tower, a symbolic structure, a tourist route with habitats along the way, or a support/access framework attached to the elevator system. In that combined world, the elevator carries freight and most passengers efficiently, while the stairway serves ceremonial, recreational, or emergency purposes.

The biggest combined effect would be proof that materials science and structural engineering had advanced far beyond what we have now. A civilization capable of building either one, especially the stairway, would likely also have orbital habitats, massive power systems, advanced weather management around the structure, and very cheap access to near-Earth space. So the real implication is not “people climbing stairs to orbit,” but that Earth would have entered a mature space-infrastructure era.

In short: with both a space elevator and a stairway to space, the elevator would revolutionize transportation to orbit, while the stairway would only make sense as a fantastical or highly specialized megastructure, not as a normal way to reach space on foot.
