items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.

items.model_answer:
If a tug-of-war team pulled on a rigid iron rod instead of a rope, the basic physics of who can win would be almost the same, but the experience and some details would change a lot.

In ordinary tug-of-war, the rope is flexible and can only transmit tension. Each team pulls on it, and the rope carries that pulling force from one side to the other. With an iron rod, the connection would be rigid, so forces could be transmitted through compression as well as tension depending on how people push or pull and how the rod is aligned. But if both teams simply lean back and pull, the rod would still mainly act to transmit force between them.

The key point is that winning tug-of-war is not really about the rope itself. It is about friction with the ground. Each team pushes backward on the ground with their feet, and the ground pushes them forward through static friction. That forward friction force is what lets them pull the other side. So whether the teams are connected by a rope or a rod, the side that can generate the greater horizontal force against the ground without slipping is the side that wins.

The biggest difference is in stability and safety. A rope can sag, stretch a bit, and accommodate small mismatches in height or timing. A rigid iron rod cannot. If one side jerks, stumbles, or changes height, the rod would transmit that motion abruptly. It could twist, jam, or shove people off balance. If the rod is long and thin, it could also buckle under compression if the teams end up pushing toward each other rather than maintaining pure tension. If it is thick enough not to buckle, it would still be awkward and dangerous because any sideways motion would create torques and sudden impacts.

Another difference is that with a rope, people can arrange themselves naturally in a line and each contribute tension along the rope. With a rigid rod, unless everyone had some carefully designed handles, it would be hard for many people to pull effectively at once. The rod does not distribute grip positions as conveniently as a rope does. In practice, a long rigid rod would make teamwork much harder.

So in idealized physics, replacing the rope with an iron rod would not change the fundamental condition for winning: the team with better traction can exert the larger horizontal force and pull the other team. But in real life, an iron rod would be far less practical, less stable, and much more dangerous.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Gravitational Equivalence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise that the Moon is replaced by a black hole of the same mass, preserving the Moon's external gravitational field while changing its size, luminosity, and surface properties.
criteria.1-2: Treats the black hole as vastly more massive or as immediately swallowing Earth; ignores the same-mass premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions same mass but still predicts major orbital or tidal changes without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Earth's orbit and tides would be mostly unchanged, but gives limited explanation.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that external gravity depends on mass and distance, so tides, lunar orbit, and Earth-Moon dynamics remain broadly similar.
criteria.9-10: Accurately applies shell/external-field reasoning throughout, distinguishing unchanged gravitational effects from changed optical, accretion, and surface-related effects.

criteria.name: Black Hole Physical Scale, Stability, and Hawking Radiation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response correctly describes the physical properties of a lunar-mass black hole, including its tiny event horizon and negligible evaporation risk.
criteria.1-2: Claims the black hole would be planet-sized, explode, rapidly evaporate, or otherwise misstates basic black hole scale.
criteria.3-4: Identifies it as small but gives no reliable sense of scale or wrongly emphasizes Hawking radiation as dangerous.
criteria.5-6: States that the event horizon would be tiny and that evaporation is not an immediate threat, with minimal detail.
criteria.7-8: Gives an appropriate scale, such as sand-grain-sized, and explains that a lunar-mass black hole is stable over astronomical timescales.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively or semi-quantitatively captures the Schwarzschild-radius scale and correctly notes that Hawking emission is negligible compared with environmental absorption.

criteria.name: Accretion, Radiation, and Hazard Assessment
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of whether the black-hole Moon would consume matter, emit radiation, or become dangerous through accretion rather than gravity alone.
criteria.1-2: Assumes it rapidly sucks in Earth, the atmosphere, or the Solar System without considering distance or accretion limits.
criteria.3-4: Mentions accretion but greatly exaggerates its rate or ignores that space near the Moon is mostly empty.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that little matter is available to eat, so immediate radiation hazards are probably small.
criteria.7-8: Explains that accretion could produce intense radiation if supplied with matter, but normal lunar-orbit conditions provide little fuel.
criteria.9-10: Balances low geometric capture rates, orbital perturbations of dust/debris, possible bright accretion episodes, and Eddington-limit-style self-regulation without sensationalism.

criteria.name: Downstream Earth Effects: Darkness, Climate, Biology, and Observation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the main non-gravitational consequences on Earth, including loss of moonlight, lunar infrared emission, night ecology, human observation, and small temperature effects.
criteria.1-2: Claims no effects at all or invents dominant catastrophic climate consequences unrelated to the premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions darkness but misses most downstream effects or overstates climate impacts.
criteria.5-6: Covers loss of visible moonlight and some ecological or cultural consequences, with rough plausibility.
criteria.7-8: Adds that thermal/climate effects would be tiny, while nocturnal ecosystems, sky brightness, tides' appearance, and lunar exploration would change.
criteria.9-10: Integrates visible light, reflected sunlight, lunar infrared, small 28-day energy-balance effects, ecological impacts, and observational consequences with correct relative magnitudes.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the full answer maintains a coherent causal chain over short-, medium-, and long-term consequences without contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected or mutually contradictory claims, such as unchanged gravity plus immediate tidal destruction.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes them with major contradictions or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly coherent sequence but lacks nuance about timescales, magnitudes, or conditional hazards.
criteria.7-8: Separates immediate effects from long-term effects and calibrates uncertainty about accretion, climate, and biological impacts.
criteria.9-10: Maintains consistent physics across all mechanisms, ranks effects by magnitude, flags speculative branches, and avoids both catastrophic exaggeration and false 'nothing changes' oversimplification.

items.model_answer:
If the Moon were instantly replaced by a black hole with exactly the Moon’s mass, the Earth’s orbit and the Moon’s orbital motion would, at large distances, stay almost exactly the same. Gravity outside a spherical body depends only on its total mass, not on whether that mass is rock or a black hole. So the Earth would still orbit the Sun as before, and this “black-hole Moon” would still orbit Earth at roughly the current lunar distance.

The biggest immediate difference would be that there would no longer be a visible Moon. The night sky would lose moonlight, lunar eclipses as we know them would disappear, and tides would change little at first because the tidal force depends mainly on mass and distance, both assumed unchanged. So ocean tides would remain nearly the same.

The black hole itself would be tiny. A black hole with the Moon’s mass would have a Schwarzschild radius of only about 0.1 millimeters. So all the Moon’s mass would be compressed into something about the size of a grain of dust, or smaller.

Would it swallow Earth? Not quickly. Despite the dramatic idea, a black hole of lunar mass at the Moon’s distance would not act like a cosmic vacuum cleaner. Objects do not get “sucked in” unless they come extremely close. Earth would not spiral into it just because it is a black hole. Its gravitational pull on Earth would be the same as the Moon’s is now.

There would be some important secondary effects. Since the Moon would no longer reflect sunlight, we would lose bright moonlit nights. Also, depending on how the replacement happened, the black hole might begin accreting interplanetary dust, solar wind particles, and perhaps some stray gas, but at the Moon’s distance and with so little available matter, this would be a very weak effect. It would probably emit little radiation.

Long-term, the black hole could in principle pass through matter if something perturbed its orbit enough, but under the stated condition—same mass, replacing the Moon in the same orbit—the Earth-Moon system would remain largely dynamically similar. The biggest practical consequence for life on Earth would be the disappearance of visible moonlight, while the most surprising scientific point is that the system would not become catastrophically unstable just because the Moon had become a black hole.

nodes.text: If the Moon were instantly replaced by a black hole with exactly the Moon’s mass,
the Earth’s orbit and the Moon’s orbital motion would, at large distances, stay almost exactly the same.
Gravity outside a spherical body depends only on its total mass, not on whether that mass is rock or a black hole.
So the Earth would still orbit the Sun as before,
and this “black-hole Moon” would still orbit Earth at roughly the current lunar distance.
The biggest immediate difference would be that there would no longer be a visible Moon.
The night sky would lose moonlight,
lunar eclipses as we know them would disappear,
and tides would change little at first
because the tidal force depends mainly on mass and distance,
both assumed unchanged.
So ocean tides would remain nearly the same.
The black hole itself would be tiny.
A black hole with the Moon’s mass would have a Schwarzschild radius of only about 0.1 millimeters.
So all the Moon’s mass would be compressed into something about the size of a grain of dust, or smaller.
Would it swallow Earth?
Not quickly.
Despite the dramatic idea,
a black hole of lunar mass at the Moon’s distance would not act like a cosmic vacuum cleaner.
Objects do not get “sucked in” unless they come extremely close.
Earth would not spiral into it just because it is a black hole.
Its gravitational pull on Earth would be the same as the Moon’s is now.
There would be some important secondary effects.
Since the Moon would no longer reflect sunlight,
we would lose bright moonlit nights.
Also, depending on how the replacement happened,
the black hole might begin accreting interplanetary dust, solar wind particles, and perhaps some stray gas,
but at the Moon’s distance and with so little available matter, this would be a very weak effect.
It would probably emit little radiation.
Long-term, the black hole could in principle pass through matter if something perturbed its orbit enough,
but under the stated condition—same mass, replacing the Moon in the same orbit—
the Earth-Moon system would remain largely dynamically similar.
The biggest practical consequence for life on Earth would be the disappearance of visible moonlight,
while the most surprising scientific point is that the system would not become catastrophically unstable just because the Moon had become a black hole.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Mounting a high-power microwave on a car to “melt ice” sounds plausible at first, because microwaves can heat water, but in practice it would be a very poor, inefficient, and potentially dangerous way to de-ice roads or vehicles.

The basic issue is that microwaves heat materials by coupling to their molecules, especially polar molecules like water. Liquid water absorbs microwave energy well, which is why a kitchen microwave works. Ice, however, absorbs microwaves much less effectively than liquid water, especially when it is cold. So if you beam microwaves at a sheet of ice, much of the energy may not be absorbed efficiently until some melting has already begun. That means it is not a very effective way to start de-icing.

There is also a huge power problem. Melting ice takes a lot of energy. To melt 1 kilogram of ice at 0°C, you need about 334 kilojoules just for the phase change, not counting the energy required to warm colder ice up to 0°C first. A car can only supply limited electrical power. Even a powerful vehicle alternator or EV battery system would struggle to deliver microwave power at the scale needed to clear substantial ice continuously while driving. You would likely need industrial-scale power, not something practical for an ordinary car.

Another problem is targeting and losses. A microwave beam emitted from a moving car would spread, reflect, and interact unpredictably with the road, nearby vehicles, metal objects, and people. Roads are not uniform microwave absorbers. Some energy would be wasted heating wet patches, slush, the car itself, or the air very little, while some could reflect in hazardous ways. You would have difficulty delivering heat only where needed.

Safety is a major concern. High-power microwaves can interfere with electronics, damage sensors, and create serious exposure hazards for people nearby. Modern cars, traffic infrastructure, medical devices, and communications systems could all be affected. Shielding and beam control would be complicated. In public settings, this would be much harder to make safe than simply using mechanical scraping, chemical de-icers, or resistive heating systems embedded in specific surfaces.

If the goal is to melt a thin layer of frost on your own windshield, directed heating methods already work better: resistive defrosters, warm air, heated glass, or fluid de-icers. If the goal is to clear roads, plows and salt are far more practical. If the goal is to de-ice a fixed surface like a runway or bridge, then stationary systems with controlled power and shielding are much more realistic than putting a microwave source on a moving car.

So the short answer is: you probably could melt some ice with a sufficiently powerful microwave mounted on a car, but it would be inefficient, power-hungry, hard to control, and unsafe enough that it is not a practical solution.

edus.text: Mounting a high-power microwave on a car to “melt ice” sounds plausible at first,
because microwaves can heat water,
but in practice it would be a very poor, inefficient, and potentially dangerous way to de-ice roads or vehicles.
The basic issue is that microwaves heat materials by coupling to their molecules, especially polar molecules like water.
Liquid water absorbs microwave energy well,
which is why a kitchen microwave works.
Ice, however, absorbs microwaves much less effectively than liquid water, especially when it is cold.
So if you beam microwaves at a sheet of ice,
much of the energy may not be absorbed efficiently until some melting has already begun.
That means it is not a very effective way to start de-icing.
There is also a huge power problem.
Melting ice takes a lot of energy.
To melt 1 kilogram of ice at 0°C, you need about 334 kilojoules just for the phase change,
not counting the energy required to warm colder ice up to 0°C first.
A car can only supply limited electrical power.
Even a powerful vehicle alternator or EV battery system would struggle to deliver microwave power at the scale needed to clear substantial ice continuously while driving.
You would likely need industrial-scale power,
not something practical for an ordinary car.
Another problem is targeting and losses.
A microwave beam emitted from a moving car would spread, reflect, and interact unpredictably with the road, nearby vehicles, metal objects, and people.
Roads are not uniform microwave absorbers.
Some energy would be wasted heating wet patches, slush, the car itself, or the air very little,
while some could reflect in hazardous ways.
You would have difficulty delivering heat only where needed.
Safety is a major concern.
High-power microwaves can interfere with electronics, damage sensors, and create serious exposure hazards for people nearby.
Modern cars, traffic infrastructure, medical devices, and communications systems could all be affected.
Shielding and beam control would be complicated.
In public settings, this would be much harder to make safe than simply using mechanical scraping, chemical de-icers, or resistive heating systems embedded in specific surfaces.
If the goal is to melt a thin layer of frost on your own windshield,
directed heating methods already work better: resistive defrosters, warm air, heated glass, or fluid de-icers.
If the goal is to clear roads,
plows and salt are far more practical.
If the goal is to de-ice a fixed surface like a runway or bridge,
then stationary systems with controlled power and shielding are much more realistic than putting a microwave source on a moving car.
So the short answer is:
you probably could melt some ice with a sufficiently powerful microwave mounted on a car,
but it would be inefficient, power-hungry, hard to control, and unsafe enough that it is not a practical solution.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a person fell off a roof, caught a flagpole on the way down, and tried to “swing” back onto the roof, the basic physics says it would almost certainly not work unless they grabbed the pole almost immediately after stepping off.

Here’s the key idea: once the person has fallen some distance, gravity has already given them a large downward speed. Grabbing the pole does not erase that energy. Instead, the pole and the person’s body have to redirect that motion into a swing. To get back to roof height, they would need enough mechanical energy to rise back up to that same height. But in reality, grabbing the pole is a very violent, highly dissipative event: the hands, arms, shoulders, and pole absorb energy, and the sudden force is enormous.

If we imagine an idealized case with no energy loss and a perfectly rigid pole, then yes: in principle, if the person could latch on instantly and survive the force, they could swing like a pendulum and rise back up to approximately their starting height, but not higher. So in pure textbook mechanics, “back to the roof” is barely possible only in that ideal limit.

In real life, several things make it fail. First, the force required to stop the person’s downward motion over the short distance of their arm span is huge, likely enough to tear their grip loose or badly injure them. Second, a real flagpole bends, rotates, or breaks, which wastes energy. Third, their grab would not be perfectly timed or centered, so the motion would not neatly convert into a roofward swing. And finally, even if they did swing upward, they would still need to release at exactly the right moment and have enough horizontal reach to land safely on the roof edge.

So the realistic answer is no: grabbing a flagpole while falling would not let someone neatly swing back to the roof. The Hollywood version only works if the fall was tiny, the grab happened almost instantly, and we ignore the extreme forces involved.

edus.text: If a person fell off a roof, caught a flagpole on the way down, and tried to “swing” back onto the roof, the basic physics says it would almost certainly not work unless they grabbed the pole almost immediately after stepping off.
Here’s the key idea:
once the person has fallen some distance, gravity has already given them a large downward speed.
Grabbing the pole does not erase that energy.
Instead, the pole and the person’s body have to redirect that motion into a swing.
To get back to roof height, they would need enough mechanical energy to rise back up to that same height.
But in reality, grabbing the pole is a very violent, highly dissipative event:
the hands, arms, shoulders, and pole absorb energy, and the sudden force is enormous.
If we imagine an idealized case with no energy loss and a perfectly rigid pole, then yes:
in principle, if the person could latch on instantly and survive the force, they could swing like a pendulum and rise back up to approximately their starting height, but not higher.

Second, a real flagpole bends, rotates, or breaks, which wastes energy.
Third, their grab would not be perfectly timed or centered, so the motion would not neatly convert into a roofward swing.
And finally, even if they did swing upward, they would still need to release at exactly the right moment and have enough horizontal reach to land safely on the roof edge.
So the realistic answer is no:
grabbing a flagpole while falling would not let someone neatly swing back to the roof.
The Hollywood version only works if the fall was tiny, the grab happened almost instantly, and we ignore the extreme forces involved.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]
items.original_question: 我经常开玩笑说我希望将我的遗体送入轨道。不是“撒我的骨灰”的意思，而是“把我赤裸的尸体扔出气闸”的意思。老实说，我的主要动机是让遥远的未来的某人感到困惑，但这是一个有趣的科学问题：在几年、几十年或几个世纪的过程中，我在轨道上的身体会发生什么？

rubrics.question_focus: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?

criteria.name: Immediate vacuum exposure and preservation mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately explains the body's early physical and biological changes in orbit, especially dehydration, freezing/thermal cycling, oxygen loss, radiation, and suppression of normal decomposition.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary Earth-like rotting, instant explosion, or other false dramatic effects with little mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions some vacuum or freezing effects but misses dehydration/mummification or misstates decomposition substantially.
criteria.5-6: Describes drying/freezing and reduced decay, with some correct causes but limited detail or minor misconceptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains rapid desiccation/freeze-drying, microbial shutdown, oxygen absence, temperature extremes, and radiation effects.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced, mechanistic account of mummification-like preservation, water loss, tissue changes, and why normal decomposition largely stops.

criteria.name: Orbit-dependent long-term fate
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes different orbital regimes and traces how altitude and environment affect the corpse over time.
criteria.1-2: Gives one fixed outcome for all orbits, ignoring altitude, drag, and orbital stability.
criteria.3-4: Vaguely says it may fall or drift forever but does not connect outcomes to orbital conditions.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes low orbit decay versus higher orbit persistence, but with weak timing or incomplete distinctions.
criteria.7-8: Explains low-Earth reentry, longer survival in higher orbits, debris-rich regions, and more stable high/geosynchronous orbits.
criteria.9-10: Accurately compares LEO, higher Earth orbit, GEO-like regions, and escape/interplanetary trajectories with plausible timescales and causal drivers.

criteria.name: External space environment impacts over decades to millennia
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of downstream effects from debris, micrometeorites, solar radiation, thermal stress, and possible atmospheric reentry.
criteria.1-2: Omits long-term environmental interactions or invents implausible effects unrelated to orbit.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one long-term hazard, such as burning up or radiation, without explaining cumulative effects.

items.model_answer:
A human body left in orbit would not instantly “explode” or freeze solid, but it would undergo a series of severe physical changes depending on whether it was exposed directly to space, inside a dead spacecraft, or eventually reentered the atmosphere.

If the body were directly exposed to space with no spacesuit, the immediate problem would be lack of pressure and oxygen. The person would lose consciousness within about 10–15 seconds because the brain would no longer get oxygen. Death would follow within a couple of minutes. The body would swell because fluids and gases in tissues expand in vacuum, but the skin and connective tissue are strong enough to prevent literal bursting. Water on moist surfaces, such as in the eyes, mouth, and lungs, would begin to boil at body temperature because of the low pressure. The body would also cool, but not instantly, because in space heat is lost mainly by radiation, which is slower than many people imagine.

After death, decomposition would be very different from decomposition on Earth. Normal decay depends heavily on bacteria, oxygen, moisture, and moderate temperatures. In orbit, those conditions are limited or absent. If the body were in direct sunlight, it could become very hot; in shadow, it could become extremely cold. Repeated heating and cooling cycles would gradually damage tissues. Vacuum would dry the body out, potentially causing a kind of desiccation or natural mummification rather than ordinary rotting. Radiation from the Sun and cosmic rays would slowly break down skin and other exposed tissues over time.

What happened next would depend on the orbit. In low Earth orbit, the body would not stay up forever. Even very thin traces of atmosphere create drag, so over time it would lose altitude and eventually reenter the atmosphere. On reentry, most or all of the body would likely burn up or be torn apart by aerodynamic heating and stress, much as space debris does. In a higher orbit, where drag is negligible, it could remain for a very long time, slowly drying, irradiating, and physically degrading.

If the body were inside a sealed spacecraft, the process would be different. There would be no vacuum exposure, so swelling and boiling of surface fluids would not occur. Instead, the body would decay more like it does in an enclosed environment, though still affected by cabin temperature, humidity, available oxygen, and microbes. In a cold, dry spacecraft, decomposition could be slowed substantially.

So the short answer is: a body left unprotected in orbit would die quickly from vacuum and lack of oxygen, then gradually dry out, suffer radiation and temperature damage, and in low orbit would eventually reenter and mostly burn up.

edus.text: A human body left in orbit would not instantly “explode” or freeze solid,
but it would undergo a series of severe physical changes
depending on whether it was exposed directly to space, inside a dead spacecraft, or eventually reentered the atmosphere.
If the body were directly exposed to space with no spacesuit,
the immediate problem would be lack of pressure and oxygen.
The person would lose consciousness within about 10–15 seconds
because the brain would no longer get oxygen.
Death would follow within a couple of minutes.
The body would swell
because fluids and gases in tissues expand in vacuum,
but the skin and connective tissue are strong enough to prevent literal bursting.
Water on moist surfaces, such as in the eyes, mouth, and lungs, would begin to boil at body temperature
because of the low pressure.
The body would also cool, but not instantly,
because in space heat is lost mainly by radiation,
which is slower than many people imagine.
After death, decomposition would be very different from decomposition on Earth.
Normal decay depends heavily on bacteria, oxygen, moisture, and moderate temperatures.
In orbit, those conditions are limited or absent.
If the body were in direct sunlight, it could become very hot;
in shadow, it could become extremely cold.
Repeated heating and cooling cycles would gradually damage tissues.
Vacuum would dry the body out,
potentially causing a kind of desiccation or natural mummification rather than ordinary rotting.
Radiation from the Sun and cosmic rays would slowly break down skin and other exposed tissues over time.
What happened next would depend on the orbit.
In low Earth orbit, the body would not stay up forever.
Even very thin traces of atmosphere create drag,
so over time it would lose altitude and eventually reenter the atmosphere.
On reentry, most or all of the body would likely burn up or be torn apart by aerodynamic heating and stress,
much as space debris does.
In a higher orbit, where drag is negligible, it could remain for a very long time,
slowly drying, irradiating, and physically degrading.
If the body were inside a sealed spacecraft, the process would be different.
There would be no vacuum exposure,
so swelling and boiling of surface fluids would not occur.
Instead, the body would decay more like it does in an enclosed environment,
though still affected by cabin temperature, humidity, available oxygen, and microbes.
In a cold, dry spacecraft, decomposition could be slowed substantially.
So the short answer is:

then gradually dry out, suffer radiation and temperature damage,
and in low orbit would eventually reenter and mostly burn up.

items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]

criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly reasoned counterfactual chain, calibrates uncertainty and local variation, explains when the scenario leaves ordinary physics for fantasy, and maintains internal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If you could somehow dig straight down continuously at one foot per second, the short answer is: you would not make it very far before heat, pressure, and rock mechanics stopped you. And if we imagine all engineering problems are magically solved so the hole stays open and you can keep removing material, then after about 42 minutes you would reach the crust–mantle boundary under continents, after many days you would enter the core, and after about 218 days you would reach Earth’s center.

At one foot per second, your speed is about 0.305 meters per second, or 86,400 feet per day. Earth’s radius is about 20.9 million feet, so going from the surface to the center would take about 20.9 million seconds, which is roughly 242 days if you started at sea level and went all the way through a radius. If instead you mean “straight down until the center,” that is the relevant number. If you mean “through the whole Earth and out the other side,” it would take about 484 days at that constant digging rate.

But real physics makes this impossible long before that. The deepest hole humans have ever drilled, the Kola Superdeep Borehole, reached only about 12.3 kilometers, less than 0.2% of the way to the center. At those depths, temperatures were already around 180 °C, much higher than expected, and the rock became plastic and difficult to drill. As you go deeper, temperature rises into the hundreds and then thousands of degrees, pressure becomes enormous, and rock stops behaving like brittle solid material you can just excavate. In the mantle, the rock is solid overall but flows slowly under pressure, so any shaft would tend to deform and close. Deeper still, the outer core is liquid iron alloy, so there would be no stable “hole” in any ordinary sense.

There is also the gravity issue. As you go down, gravity does not keep increasing. Inside Earth, the pull from the material above you cancels out, and only the mass beneath your depth contributes to the net force. So gravity gradually decreases as you approach the center, reaching zero at the exact center. That means if you somehow dropped material or yourself into a perfectly frictionless tunnel, you would not just keep accelerating forever; you would speed up at first, then slow down approaching the center. But since your question is about digging at a fixed one foot per second, gravity mainly changes the work environment rather than the travel time.

Another complication is what “straight down” means. If you always dig in the local direction of gravity, your path is radial, aiming toward Earth’s center. If instead you tried to maintain a fixed geometric direction relative to your starting orientation, Earth’s curvature would matter and you would not follow a radius.

So the careful answer is this: in a purely mathematical sense, digging straight down at one foot per second would get you to Earth’s center in about 242 days and through the whole Earth in about 484 days. In the real world, you would be stopped after only a tiny fraction of that distance by extreme temperature, pressure, collapsing rock, and eventually molten metal.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them. [Image: image] In the sea, on the other hand, the density of the fluid stays relatively constant. That means the submarine can find its appropriate pressure range and float there. In other words, submarines only work because water doesn't follow the ideal gas law. But there's one more twist: Water sort of does obey the ideal gas law. The equations governing water under normal pressure are similar to (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0534.pdf) the equation for a gas under about twenty thousand atmospheres of pressure. In a sense, this is why water seems incompressible to us—it behaves as if it's already compressed so much that an extra atmosphere or two hardly makes a difference. So, in some ways, water and air are more similar than they seem, but in the ways that matter for a submarine, they really are different. Which, of course, brings us back to why it's called a submarine—it operates under a "mare". A vehicle designed to operate beneath a sea of air would be called a subaerine.[5]The "gas" in "gas giant" is from the Greek word for void (χάος, kháos), so maybe a vessel (σκάφη, skáphē) that travels through a gas giant's atmosphere would be a khaoskaphe. Which, come to think of it, is a perfectly good description of a car. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you somehow “dropped a submarine into Jupiter,” it would not float around like it would in Earth’s ocean. It would be destroyed very quickly as it fell deeper into an atmosphere-ocean-like planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

At first, the submarine would enter Jupiter’s upper atmosphere, where it would face extreme heating from falling at enormous speed through dense gas. It would need heat shielding far beyond what any real submarine has. Even if it survived the entry, the pressure would rise fast as it descended.

Unlike Earth, Jupiter has no solid ocean surface and probably no ordinary solid ground you could reach in a conventional sense. The deeper you go, the atmosphere just gets denser and denser, gradually turning into exotic forms of matter. Hydrogen gas becomes compressed into a liquid-like state, and much farther down it may become metallic hydrogen, a form that conducts electricity.

A normal submarine is built to withstand water pressure in Earth’s oceans, not the crushing pressures inside Jupiter. It would be crushed long before reaching the deep interior. As it went deeper, it would also be heated to thousands of degrees, so even before total mechanical collapse, its materials would weaken, melt, or vaporize.

There is also the problem of buoyancy. A submarine works by adjusting its density relative to liquid water. In Jupiter, there is no simple water ocean for it to operate in. It would just sink through increasingly dense hydrogen-rich fluid unless it were designed in some extraordinary way to match the local density and survive the pressure and heat. No known submarine could do this.

So the short answer is: if you dropped a submarine into Jupiter, it would plunge into the planet, be heated, crushed, and ultimately destroyed, probably long before reaching the deeper layers. It would not reach a normal “bottom,” because Jupiter does not have one like Earth’s oceans do.

It would be destroyed very quickly as it fell deeper into an atmosphere-ocean-like planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
At first, the submarine would enter Jupiter’s upper atmosphere, where it would face extreme heating from falling at enormous speed through dense gas.
It would need heat shielding far beyond what any real submarine has.
Even if it survived the entry, the pressure would rise fast as it descended.

items.question: What Would It Be Like to Ride a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: We don't know! We've only flown spacecraft into a gas planet's atmosphere twice (both Jupiter). One had no cameras, and one went in at night (and was being disposed of, so wasn't taking pictures anyway). If you took a submarine to Jupiter, it would burn up. Jupiter has a deep gravity well; after falling down toward it from space, you're going very fast. There's no easy way to shed that speed other than slamming into the atmosphere and letting it slow you down, but the entry is about four times faster than the Space Shuttle or Apollo Earth reentries. Only the Galileo probe has survived a Jupiter atmospheric entry. [Image: image] The Galileo probe survived by being a bullet with a big heat shield, and several inches of the shield were burned away before it finished slowing down and started falling vertically by parachute. The probe only sent back about half a megabyte of data to the Galileo orbiter, and had no camera, so we don't know what it saw. We could, I guess, try to do the same thing with a submarine—by mounting a giant heat shield on the front—but it would probably qualify as the most Kerbal (https://youtu.be/vwrLR2kv5KA?t=1119) vehicle ever built. [Image: image] If our submarine survived, what would we see?[1]I mean, submarines don't usually have a lot of windows, but we at least have a periscope, right? The best pictures we have of Jupiter's atmosphere are probably these carefully processed mosaics (http://www.planetary.org/blogs/emily-lakdawalla/2010/2644.html) of the Great Red Spot, but they're still taken from very far away. At those resolutions, a huge Earth thunderstorm would appear as roughly one pixel. Trying to figure out what Jupiter's clouds would look like from those pictures is like using this (http://visibleearth.nasa.gov/view.php?id=78314) to reconstruct these (http://stormandsky.smugmug.com/Thumbnail-Galleries). By combining the pictures with other science data, we've been able to put together a pretty good idea of what Jupiter's atmosphere is like, but there are some pretty big questions still unanswered which make it hard to be too confident about what it would actually look like. For example, you know the Great Red Spot? We don't know what all that red stuff is. [Image: image] Author Michael Carroll has done a lot of thinking about planetary atmospheres, and his book Drifting on Alien Winds (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160) vividly describes of what it would be like to descend through Jupiter's clouds. He was also kind enough to answer some of my questions about Jupiter. Here's a rough sketch of what you'd see as you descended through the clouds; for more, definitely check out his book (http://www.amazon.com/Drifting-Alien-Winds-Exploring-Weather/dp/1441969160). [Image: image] Jupiter's upper atmosphere (the part we would see before we died (http://what-if.xkcd.com/138/)) has three main layers—an upper layer of haze and ammonia clouds, similar to cirrostratus (https://www.google.com/search?q=cirrostratus&tbm=isch) clouds on Earth. Below that is a thick, reddish-brown ammonium hydrosulfide cloud layer. The lowest layer consists of white water clouds, which occasionally rise into towering thunderstorms that occasionally push through the middle layer. Between these cloud layers, the air is probably pretty clear. At those levels, it would be less dense than the air on Earth, so you could see a long way. Thanks to Rayleigh scattering (https://xkcd.com/1145/), the sky would be blue, and objects far off in the distance would fade to blue just like they do on Earth (http://thehelpfulartteacher.blogspot.com/2010/11/landscapes-continuedatmospheric.html). But since Jupiter is so huge, we might not see the clouds disappear over the horizon; the towers might just fade off into the distance. We don't really know how accurate these pictures are, though, until we send a camera to fly down into Jupiter's atmosphere and send pictures back. Juno, scheduled to reach Jupiter next year, carries a pretty nice camera (http://www.msss.com/all_projects/junocam.php),[2]Thank you to Emily Lakdawalla for her helpful background about various spacecraft cameras, including her many thorough spreadsheets. which should give us slightly better-resolution pictures, but it still won't really give us a sense of what the cloud decks look like from within them. For that, we need to send in a probe with a camera—and there's nothing like that on the horizon. There's certainly more science value in visiting Europa than in satisfying our curiosity about the Jovian sky. But with interplanetary cubesats (http://www.nasa.gov/directorates/spacetech/niac/staehle_interplanetary_cubesats.html) soon to make their debut, who knows—maybe someone out there will put together a camera, heat shield, and parachute, and hitch a ride on the next outer planets mission. And then, finally, we'll get to look at Jupiter's clouds from both sides (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v9j_j-cUwKc). [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be nothing like diving into an ocean. Jupiter has no solid surface and no ordinary sea to float on, so a “submarine” there would really be a pressure vessel sinking through an atmosphere that gets denser and hotter with depth.

At first, descending into Jupiter would feel more like entering an immense storm system than entering water. You would pass through thick clouds of ammonia and other chemicals, with violent winds, lightning, turbulence, and darkness increasing below the sunlit upper layers. The pressure would rise very quickly. On Earth, submarines deal with water pressure increasing in a predictable way, but in Jupiter the gas becomes so compressed that it gradually behaves more like a fluid ocean of dense hydrogen.

As you went deeper, the ride would become deadly fast. The pressure would climb from Earth-like levels to thousands, then millions of times Earth’s atmospheric pressure. Temperatures would also soar from very cold cloud tops to hundreds, then thousands of degrees. Any realistic submarine made of ordinary materials would be crushed, cooked, or both long before reaching the deep interior.

If somehow your craft were fantastically strong and perfectly cooled, the environment would still become stranger. The hydrogen would become a dense liquid, and deeper still it would likely turn into liquid metallic hydrogen, a state of matter in which hydrogen conducts electricity like a metal. This region is thought to help generate Jupiter’s enormous magnetic field. At that point the submarine would no longer be moving through anything resembling air or seawater, but through an exotic, superhot, ultra-compressed planetary fluid.

There would also be no clear “bottom” in the familiar sense. Jupiter may have a diluted, fuzzy core of heavier elements mixed into the surrounding material rather than a neat rocky floor you could land on. So the trip would not end with surfacing on an undersea plain. It would end either with the submarine being destroyed, or, in a science-fiction version, with it entering ever denser and hotter layers until approaching the deep central region where conditions are extreme beyond ordinary engineering.

So, riding a submarine into Jupiter would be like plunging through a global hurricane into a deepening ocean made first of gas, then liquid hydrogen, then metallic hydrogen, while pressure, heat, darkness, and violence rapidly become overwhelming. In practice, you would not survive very far.

edus.text: Riding a submarine into Jupiter would be nothing like diving into an ocean.
Jupiter has no solid surface and no ordinary sea to float on,
so a “submarine” there would really be a pressure vessel sinking through an atmosphere that gets denser and hotter with depth.
At first, descending into Jupiter would feel more like entering an immense storm system than entering water.
You would pass through thick clouds of ammonia and other chemicals,
with violent winds, lightning, turbulence, and darkness increasing below the sunlit upper layers.
The pressure would rise very quickly.
On Earth, submarines deal with water pressure increasing in a predictable way,
but in Jupiter the gas becomes so compressed that it gradually behaves more like a fluid ocean of dense hydrogen.
As you went deeper, the ride would become deadly fast.
The pressure would climb from Earth-like levels to thousands, then millions of times Earth’s atmospheric pressure.
Temperatures would also soar from very cold cloud tops to hundreds, then thousands of degrees.
Any realistic submarine made of ordinary materials would be crushed, cooked, or both long before reaching the deep interior.
If somehow your craft were fantastically strong and perfectly cooled, the environment would still become stranger.
The hydrogen would become a dense liquid,
and deeper still it would likely turn into liquid metallic hydrogen,
a state of matter in which hydrogen conducts electricity like a metal.
This region is thought to help generate Jupiter’s enormous magnetic field.
At that point the submarine would no longer be moving through anything resembling air or seawater,
but through an exotic, superhot, ultra-compressed planetary fluid.
There would also be no clear “bottom” in the familiar sense.
Jupiter may have a diluted, fuzzy core of heavier elements mixed into the surrounding material rather than a neat rocky floor you could land on.
So the trip would not end with surfacing on an undersea plain.
It would end either with the submarine being destroyed,
or, in a science-fiction version, with it entering ever denser and hotter layers until approaching the deep central region where conditions are extreme beyond ordinary engineering.
So, riding a submarine into Jupiter would be like plunging through a global hurricane into a deepening ocean made first of gas, then liquid hydrogen, then metallic hydrogen,
while pressure, heat, darkness, and violence rapidly become overwhelming.
In practice, you would not survive very far.
